The *Śivadṛṣṭi*,
composed by the venerable Somānanda,
accompanied by the commentary (*vṛtti*) composed by the venerable Mahāmāheśvara Ācārya Utpaladeva.
Homage to the one with the unequal eye, who creates the painting of the universe within his own limb consisting of the space of consciousness, and who is the source of the arising of all wonders. [1]

1. Regarding the phrase "to the one with uneven eyes" (*viṣamacakṣuṣe*): for that universe, characterized by means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and objects of knowledge (*prameya*), is shown by the Blessed One through his two eyes to be truly false due to the appearance of duality;
yet, even while possessing that [dual] nature, it consists solely of the radiance of his own self (*svātmasphurattāmātra*).

There is no conceptualization of the defect of the stain of duality; thus it is illuminated by the third eye. And that [third eye] belongs to the Blessed One alone, for no other possesses the status of being the presiding subject of duality. Consequently, it is only toward Him that homage is appropriate;
as for others, what fruit could there be? This has been determined in the *Vākyārthasamanvayadīpikā*.

He supports that very point with the words "to the one who produces the painting of the universe within his own limb" (*svāṅge viśvālekhyavidhāyine*). "Within his own limb" (*svāṅge*) means not anywhere separate from himself. As was stated by the former teacher:
"They manifest [the world] upon no wall at all, without any collection of material causes."
"Salutations to that Śūlin, who is praised for his artistic skill and by whom the world is variegated. (Stavacintāmaṇi 5.5).
Thus it was also said by the venerable Vīra Vyāsa:
"My source is the Great Brahman; in that I place the seed."
"From that arises the origin of all beings, O Bhārata" (Bhagavad Gītā 14.3).
Even through the world-picture appearing in various forms at different times, there is no alteration in its essential nature;
thus, there is a comparison to space and an implied contrast [to other elements]. For the creation of a picture occurs precisely upon a groundless surface.
What a great marvel! (p.
2) I have been urged by my own son, who is known as Vibhramākara.
And likewise by his fellow student named Padmānanda. || 2 ||
In this section on the *Śivadṛṣṭi*, composed by the Guru as an extensive commentary on the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, I provide a word-by-word concordance.
In accordance with the established tradition of this treatise, the author performs a salutation to his chosen deity:
"May Śiva—who has entered into our very form—perform the warding off of obstacles for himself by means of his own power, through obeisance to that [reality] which is the Self of all. (1)
He whom I revere is Śiva, who has attained identity with my own form;

for in reality, Śiva is the embodiment of all principles (*tattva*) according to the principle to be explained hereafter. He [Śiva], for the sake of the world (*saṃsāra*), through the non-apprehension of identity produced by the power of *māyā*—
The *Īśvarapratyabhijñā* demonstrates, through its elaborated reasoning, that entities do not abide in a self-nature.

Therefore, it will again establish certain things such as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within worldly transactions by means of the distinction of subjects in our own form, even though those objects of cognition (*prameya*) have been rendered differentiated.
1. *Ghaṭapaṭa*:
"Those who follow the vow and conduct of the one Brahman are *sabrahmacārin*s (fellow-students) toward one another"—this is the lexicon (*kośa*).
2. The present treatise follows the non-dual Śaiva system (*śaivādvayanaya*). This is the subtle meaning here:

At the beginning of a treatise, according to the principle that "all auspicious undertakings encounter many obstacles," a salutation must necessarily be performed for the purpose of dispelling them; by means of which [salutation], possessing its intensely radiant majesty, obstacles are rendered powerless and unable to prevail. In this regard:
With the intention that, since everything is unmanifest, nothing would be established, and thus what could be refuted by whom and of what?
he says "prakṛta" and so forth. And thus, the Viśvātman, whose form is pervasive and whose power is infinite, is worthy of salutation.

The agency of the bound soul (*paśu*), who consists of the non-recognition of freedom (*svātantryābodha*) and the loss of autonomy as manifested within the abode of *paśyantī*— which is the nature of the contracted power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) of Sadāśiva and others—
is due to his resting in a state that takes the form of subordinating that very [freedom], even though it is contracted.
Even though its true nature is vibration (*spanda*) and its greatness is that of *śakti*, it functions as an instrument (*karaṇatva*).

3. "He" (*saḥ*) refers to [the Lord] who has entered into the plane of the subject (*pramātṛ*) whose form is "us"—that is, those who have become vessels for the non-apprehension of identity (*aikyākhyāti*) produced by the power of *māyā*.
4. "Then" (*tataḥ*) means [the state of] not being established in the self (*anātmasthatva*).

5. With the words "in worldly affairs" (*lokayātrāsu*) and so forth, he indicates the underlying intention that the distinction between subjects (*pramātṛbhedah*) arises precisely through the distinction between objects of knowledge (*prameyabhedenaiṣa*). "Wherein" (*yatra*) refers to practical activity (*vyavahāraḥ*).

3) It is said that one enters [the state] by perceiving [the object] as non-different from oneself through its distinctness from the divine. To whatever extent there is entry, to that same extent there is the possibility of attaining accomplishments (*siddhi*). First, then:
The union of knowledge and action follows from the state of being an agent. As it is said in the Spandaśāstra:
"This [union] does not function as an impeller by means of the impulse of desire;
rather, through contact with the power of the Self, the person becomes equal to That. (1.8)

Thus it is said; likewise, it is stated elsewhere that "this is the sovereign activity. By this very perspective, it is also indicated that for the sake of each respective supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), an even greater immersion (*samāveśa*) must be practiced through one's own effort as well. And one who is thus immersed is called even "Śiva."

And Devadatta and others as well, because there is no distinction in their attaining oneness with both [the individual and the universal]; such a Śiva is for the sake of the infinite expansion of the Self through the manifestation of the Lord Sadāśiva and others, who possess both transcendent and immanent forms.

Let one offer salutation to that which is one’s own essential nature, known as Paramaśiva. This is in the imperative mood (*loṭ*), used for invitation and so forth, as in the expression "salutation be unto you.
The meaning is: "We, whose very self is Śiva, offer salutation to the Supreme Lord. By virtue of its supremacy...

The use of the third person (prathamapuruṣa) is intended to show that the artificial sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva), being devoid of any real nature, possesses only the status of an agent; and since everything consists of Śiva, even the instruments such as speech and mind are Śiva alone in the act of salutation. Thus he says: "by one's own self."

Even obstacles are to be warded off as being of that very same nature; thus he says, "in the warding off of the self. And regarding the act of salutation, he says, "by one's own power," meaning that the power of our will and so forth belongs solely to Śiva.
Just as one perceives even the objects of cognition—such as the vital breaths (prāṇa) and others—which have been differentiated, as non-different from the Self.
The meaning is that everything is likewise pervaded.

2. *Niyogakaraṇa* means an invitation; in the case of what is necessary, it means an instigation. Consequently, the resulting meaning is "an instigation toward one who has not yet engaged [in action]," which implies that there is no room for a formal command (*preṣaṇā*).
This has been stated by Hari:

"For when there is an injunction for one who has not yet acted, the *loṭ* suffix is prescribed [after roots such as] *praśna*; but when there is an injunction for one who is already acting, that is the domain of the causative (*ṇic*)."
Thus, one should not be deluded into thinking that in the expression "let him do," there is the instigation of another.
By this [it is shown that] all actions whatsoever— such as going, eating, and so forth— are accompanied by factors of action (*kāraka*) and possess results.
It has been shown that they are to be understood in exactly this same way. || 1 ||
Now, he declares the entire meaning of the treatise in brief, together with its reasoning:

"The Self alone, manifesting within all existents, is the pervasive Lord whose consciousness is blissful; He is Śiva, whose flow of will is unobstructed and whose powers of vision and action are ever-expanding. (2)

1. Regarding the phrase "by this [it is said]": one should understand that this verse, although its ultimate purpose is solely to offer salutation, has been employed here as an illustrative example. Thus he says, "walking, eating, and so forth.
By this, [he means] that activities such as consuming food, walking, speaking, and lying down are made to appear as a manifestation of differentiation by means of their causal factors (*kāraka*).

The sense is that all that manifests as the causal relationship between an effect and its cause should be understood as nothing but the mere radiance (sphuraṇamātra) of that very reality which is the Self (tatātman).
Reasoning (yukti) is logic that conforms to direct experience (anubhava).
3. It is indeed self-luminous.
4. Because of its sovereignty as the nature of the "I" (ahaṃprathā).
5. That which is the ultimate, supreme reality of objects such as jars, that alone [is it].
This is the meaning: that which is the self (*ātman*) of all entities, known as "knowability" (*vedyatā*), is Śiva himself.
According to the principle that "without him, an object would be non-manifest, just as it was before," there would follow the undesirable consequence of universal blindness.
For this very reason, nothing external exists from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*). And thus, regarding the object...
In the state of luminosity, the light is the object and the object is also the light; thus, with this internalization of their essential nature, Vyāsa Muni stated in the *Gītā*:
"He who sees Me everywhere and sees everything in Me" (6.30).
Thus [it is said]. Likewise:
"The Self abiding in all beings, and all beings in the Self" (6.29).
And elsewhere, the author of the commentary has stated that because objects have the nature of being manifest, they are the Supreme Self.

Because it possesses a universal form (*viśvarūpa*). It has been stated elsewhere that within each individual principle (*tattva*), the nature of all thirty-six principles exists. Likewise, the Vedāntins also say:
"Even a single part of Brahman does not transcend its omniformity and is beyond conceptualization."
Thus it is said. For this very reason, there is no dispute here regarding those who perceive and worship the body itself—which consists of the thirty-six principles—as being the form of Śiva;
they too attain perfection. Or, even if one perceives an object such as a jar by becoming absorbed in it in that same manner, [perfection follows];
thus, there is no disagreement on this point.
(1) The thesis (*pratijñā*) is that Śiva alone is to be designated as one's own self within all existing things.

(2) The collection of qualifiers such as "the consciousness of cessation" (*nirvṛtacit*) constitutes the reason (*hetu*). (3) "Manifesting" (*sphuran*) refers to the subject (*dharmin*), and (4) it also refers to the reason (*hetu*).
Self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For this very reason, "shining forth" (*sphuran*) is a separate word.
Furthermore, by the phrase "because the mind is fulfilled," etc., the definition of Śiva is also implicitly shown.
Once that object is established, one merely establishes the conventional designation of "Śiva-ness" with respect to it.

According to the sequence set forth in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, just as consciousness (*cit*), fulfillment (*nirvṛtti*), will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*) flash forth within all existing things— from a jar to a cloth— as they manifest, so it will be explained further on. Because there is no difference between power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimat*), and because the possessor of power is one, [there is] the pentad of powers.

The state of being "higher," "lower," and so forth, is dependent upon the cognizing subject who employs conventional discourse; this will be explained later according to the principle stated in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*. [The term] "nirvṛtā" [is used].
To bring about the cognition of others, he provides an example of a five-membered statement, beginning with the "proposition" (*pratijñā*).
The statement of the position (pakṣa) together with the object to be proven (sādhya) is the proposition (pratijñā).
2. The indicator (liṅga) which expresses [the reason] is the logical ground (hetu).
3. [This refers to the realization] that one's own self is indeed Śiva.
Regarding this term "nirvṛtacit" (consciousness at rest):
inference indeed has perception as its root.
Rest (*nirvṛti*) is repose in one's own self-luminous nature, characterized by bliss; therein—

The suffix *ac* is applied in the sense of possession (*matvartha*) to denote a constant connection (*nityayoga*). By means of this, the formation of the compound *citaḥ* (of consciousness) demonstrates, through the single-semantic integration (*ekārthībhāva*) of the words in the compound, their absolute inseparability and their state of having become a single semantic unit;
thus, it reveals the Lord’s status as the substratum (*dharmin*), whose nature consists of both consciousness and bliss (*vijñānānanda*).
He says: And it is stated in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*:
"But because of delusion, although this [Lord] is seen, He is not perceived;
therefore, this recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is demonstrated by means of the manifestation of His powers" (1.1.3).
Thus [it is said].
7. Regarding the phrase "the perception of a jar and so forth" (ghaṭādigraha), etc., 8. here, having raised the objection concerning differentiation by means of the fivefold power alone, he says:
9. Anticipating the doubt that there might be even a division within his own self, he says:
10. "The state of Sadāśiva [arises] from the predominance," and so forth.
11. Once unity is established, fullness is obtained by its very force; thus, there is no desire for anything external.
Indeed, the repose of the light within itself due to its lack of differentiation is proclaimed as the sense of "I" (ahambhāva);
and that very repose is said to arise from the cessation of all dependence.
"Autonomy, as well as agency and primary lordship," (Aparokṣānubhūtiprakaraṇasiddhi 23k)—this means that its essential nature is supreme bliss. (p.

He is Śiva, characterized as follows: he whose consciousness (*cit*) is full and has no further desire for objects of knowledge (*vedya*); likewise, he who is all-pervasive (*vibhu*), having assimilated all knowable objects into his own self; he whose flow of will (*icchā*) is unobstructed (*aniruddha*); and he in whom vision (*dṛk*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*) are ever-expanding.
In all [beings], it is the Self alone. || 2 ||

Thus, since it is established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) that "everything is of the nature of Śiva," and the point to be proven is merely a conventional designation (*vyavahāramātra*), the author— seeking to dispel the disagreements of other disputants— proceeds to demonstrate the persistence of this state of Śiva-nature, from the supreme level (*paradaśā*) down to the existence of jars, cloths, and so forth.
When He remains absorbed in the experience of mere bliss of consciousness,
His will is of that extent, His knowledge is of that extent, and indeed, His action is of that extent.
Then it exists in the state of equilibrium of the three extremely subtle powers; it is of the nature of consciousness, supreme bliss, undivided, and transcendent.

As long as the state of saṃsāra—which consists of the delusion characterized by the non-recognition (akhyāti) of identity with Śiva—has not yet dawned, even then there exists that very same Śiva-nature described above. Likewise, at that time, the five powers also exist indeed; though they are of one single form, they exist in view of conventional usage because of the possibility of [their] effects.

For indeed, that very light which, in its successive states, consists of the innate reflective awareness "I am," remains as such—autonomous, independent of anything else, blissful by virtue of its fullness, and composed of liberated consciousness. That alone is the primary, sovereign state of Śiva-hood. Thus it is said: "the joy of consciousness" (cidāhlāda).
Experience is the manifestation within the pure plenitude of consciousness and bliss, and not in the external;
therefore, he whose dissolution (*laya*) occurs in that very [plenitude] is so described.
By this—because the Self (*ātman*) is independent as "I" within all states of being, for that very reason.
2. Illumination and reflective awareness;
3. [The view] of the Vedāntins and those who maintain that the objects of knowledge are distinct;
4. That which possesses the stated pervasion.
5. The inference of the cause from the effect.
6. Therein, first of all, he establishes the nature of consciousness and bliss (*cidānanda*) as being both supreme and non-supreme.
7. Because there is no existence of anything distinct from pure consciousness and bliss, like a separate cognition, for that very reason...
Therein alone is manifestation and dissolution.
7) Consciousness is said to be quiescent; however, will, knowledge, and action appear distinct in dependence upon objects and other such factors.

They become manifest. Furthermore, in the supreme state (*parāvasthā*), one's own essential nature shines forth as "I am full" alone; because it is luminous to that extent, that itself is knowledge (*jñāna*); because it is of the nature of intense impulse (*saṃrambha*), that itself is action (*kriyā*); and since it is accepted as having that very nature, will (*icchā*) is also present—thus he says, "that [is] will."

"Of that extent" (*tāvatī*): it should be construed as "the essential nature (*svarūpa*) is of that extent, and the action (*kriyā*) is of that extent. Alternatively, in the phrase "knowledge of that extent" (*tāvaj-jñāna*), the word *tāvat*—which is feminine in gender when applied to the action—must be transformed [to agree with the noun].

However, the second occurrence of the word *tāvat* at the end has the sense of sequence (*krama*), referring to the states of the supreme (*parā*), the non-supreme (*aparā*), and so forth. Precisely for this reason:

Even in the absence of distinct objects, because the acts of acceptance (*abhyupagama*), manifestation (*prakāśa*), and exertion (*saṃrambha*) are always inseparable from the light [of consciousness] and thus remain undisturbed, they possess the very fitness for the conventional usage of "will" (*icchā*) and so forth;

this is what is meant by the term "extremely subtle" (*susūkṣma*). This extreme subtlety arises because, in the absence of things to be desired and the like, no conceptual differentiation (*vibhāga*) is imagined.

For this very reason, it is said that there is a state of equilibrium with power (*śakti-sāmarasya*), because its nature consists in the manifestation of pure, full consciousness alone, and that its ultimate aim is the bliss of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa-āhlāda*). This very state of indivisibility is the supreme condition (*parāvasthā*);
when it abides in this way, it is called "the Beyond" (*para*). (3–4)
He says that even in other states, that state of the pure Supreme Śiva— which is empty of such objects of knowledge as previously described— exists:
"Furthermore, this established order is fixed within that state."
Even in states where one touches the entirety of knowledge and the supreme state of the Knower. || 5 ||
"And she (consciousness) is perceived as remaining [constant] through that repose in the fruit.
By this, the sense is that there is no deviation in the state of non-differentiation, where the objects are not distinct;
for consciousness, whose nature is bliss, is of a single form everywhere and is therefore unfailing.

It is thus illuminated that the status of being powers (śaktitva) belongs to will and the other [faculties] as they are about to manifest through the force of the intensification of the Lord’s sovereignty, while He Himself abides in the form of the possessor of attributes (dharmī) as the essence of the possessor of power (śaktimat).
2. The surging forth of one's own self.
3. The meaning is that the extent [of this] is the action (*kriyā*).
4. Because there is an absence of succession in the supreme state (*parāvasthā*), [this] acceptance is the will (*icchā*); [it is] the manifestation (*prakāśa*).
Knowledge; exertion is action.
(5) Because of its non-deviation.
(6) "Extremely subtle"—it is precisely because of its subtlety that it is [unperceivable] by those who perceive only the gross.

The meaning is that for those who profess a self whose nature is pure awakening (*viśuddhabodha*), yet whose reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) has been made the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), this is an error.
[This occurs] within the manifestation of distinctions such as jars, cloths, and so forth.

8. But surely, by the previous statement, "The Self alone [resides] in all entities," it was established that Śiva exists as the very form of the Self, which constitutes the knowability of all categories; therefore, that alone should have been supported. What is the use of this statement beginning with "When He remains... and so forth? For...

Fearing the fault known as *prakṛtavidhāta* (the abandonment of the subject at hand), which consists in speaking of something else when one has left the topic under discussion—thereby rendering it like the talk of a madman—he says, "Not merely [that]," and so on. In that regard, first the very nature of the Possessor of Power (*śaktimat*) was established;
and once that fundamental cause is proven, whatever else is described...
The sense is that it will be established otherwise, according to the maxim of a painting on a wall-less surface.
8) This rule does not apply solely to the non-manifestation of the supreme, the non-supreme, and so forth; [it applies elsewhere as well].
This applies even to other states; for at the stage when all cognitions such as conceptual constructions are about to arise,
contact with the nature of the knower— which is unstained by [the duality of] cognition and the cognizable— is necessarily present.

Even in those states, there is the state of the Supreme (para). Although at that time it is not the state of the Supreme—because the state of the knower characterized by the *puryaṣṭaka* persists, as in deep sleep (*sauṣupta*)—nevertheless, when it comes to rest in certain portions of the summit of knowledge (*jñānāgra*), then it is the state of the Supreme. And yet...

Resting occurs even in the stage of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇabhūmi*), yet even there, one is distracted by the object of knowledge consisting of the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇaspanda*).

Therefore, there is a resting even beyond the knowledge of the objects of knowledge such as the vital breath. In reality, the supreme state that belongs to the initial phase of deep sleep remains ever-present, and it is indeed perceived.

Because illumination cannot be perceived as an object, so too it is with respect to the fruit: when another cognition arises which consists of the fruit of the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) in the form "this has been known by me," at that time there is a resting in repose within mere cognition itself. Or else, just as at the commencement of all cognitions, so too it is with respect to the fruit.

Upon completion, there is rest in that very state; without rest in that, the object cannot be known at all. Wholeness consists in the necessary presence of the possessor of power whose nature is the equilibrium of all powers, in its manifold forms.
2. *Utpitsā* is the desire to arise.

3. Now, one might object: even if there exists in that state a contact with the nature of the knower who is unstained by [the distinction between] knowledge and the object of knowledge, how can there be an establishment of "otherness" (*paravyavasthā*)? For a thing cannot exist by means of itself alone; yet such a self-nature (*svarūpa*) does indeed exist.

It is the state of deep sleep (*sauṣupta*), because one is suppressed by impurity (*mala*); however, since one is as if awakened here by *kalā*, and because of that suppression [of *mala*], one is "well asleep" (*suṣupta*).
With the intention that it is called "deep sleep" even while in that state of being a knower (*jñātṛ-avasthāna*), he says: "even though" (*yadyapi*).
As stated by the author of the *Vṛtti* itself:
"What, then, is the other state? He says:
Because cognitions exist as the inner self (*pratyagātman*) only in their intermediate state,
whereas at the prior and posterior limits, all of them are simply the one pure Śiva.
This should be examined in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*.
Concluding that the nature of the five powers is present everywhere, he says:
"Thus, there is never a separation of the mind from the triadic self. (6)
For one whose consciousness is liberated, there is never any separation from power— whether in its state of non-manifestation or its manifestation—

consisting of that triad in the manner described, namely the nature of will, knowledge, and action; for it is beyond dispute that his consciousness is eternally liberated, being of the very nature of consciousness (*cidrūpatva*).
Likewise, because [the presence] of consciousness (*cit*) and bliss (*ānanda*) is established even in the states of *parā*, *aparā*, and so forth;

it was merely concluded that, although there is no object of desire (*eṣitavya*) and so on in the state of *parā*, the possibility of will (*icchā*) and the rest exists there, by way of restating [their presence as] consciousness and bliss. Of these...
In the states of non-distinction and distinction among powers, in the differences of conditions such as priority and posteriority,
and in the existence of objects of knowledge and so forth, because there is the conventional usage of the "distinction" of powers, that cognizer is never devoid of powers such as will. 6.
Just as the state of the five powers exists within the division [of the principles], so it must be explained; he states this according to that sequence:
"But when, through the unfolding of the joy of the majesty of his conscious nature... (verse 7).
1. "Thus" (*evam*) refers to the fact that the matter has been established through a previously unmentioned method.
2. By the phrase beginning with "for instance" (*tathāhi*), etc., 3.
it is ascertained by means of a portion of the conclusion (*nigama*).
4. Furthermore, by the words "in the supreme state" and so forth;

5. thus, within the Śiva-tattva, which is the self whose nature is pure consciousness, the fivefold power has been established for the purpose of bringing about unification; and in connection with that—

Furthermore, even in the state of the other [the individual soul], it has been established once again for the sake of strengthening the realization of its such nature; thus it is proven that in the state of the supreme Śiva, which is not different from the individual soul,
there exists only the full, blissful essence consisting of the equilibrium of the five powers.

"It exists as the very nature of consciousness. Regarding that, he establishes the occurrence of the pentad beginning with will (*icchā*) even within that state characterized by the power (*śakti*) whose essence is vibration (*spanda*), which is both supreme and non-supreme (*parāpara*),
by means of the passage beginning with "But when," and so forth.
When the mind becomes intent upon setting in motion the creation of various effects through diverse arrangements, that is the first *tuṭi* of Will (*icchā*). (8)

The *jṛmbhā* (expansion) of the *āmoda* (delight) or *camatkāra* (wonder)— which consists of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of His own nature— is the *dharma* (attribute) or *svabhāva* (essential nature) of the Lord Śiva, who is of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), namely, that manifestation (*vibhava*) which possesses the fitness for the accomplishment of the fivefold acts.
It is the blossoming as the self of all. As I have stated in my hymn:
"Shining forth by your own nature, you expand everything; perceiving the universe, you perceive your own form."
"That which you yourself reel with through your own innate flavor—that is the radiant circle of aesthetic emotion (*bhāva-maṇḍala*). (Utpaladeva’s *Stotrāvalī*, Stotra 13, verse 15).
Here, "reeling" (*ghūrṇana*) refers to yawning; by means of that yawning, which serves as the cause, the state—

The creation of various effects is that which has as its very nature the manifestation of the diversity of the non-apprehension of difference within its own form through *māyā*. When it is oriented toward the initiation of that [creation], it acts as if oriented;
yet, because there is in reality no second entity, it is consciousness (*caitanya*) itself, being inward-turned due to its independence.
Then, that *tuṭi* is the first portion of Will, delimited by a subtle measure of time;
and herein lies this very distinction of [this system] from other proponents.
I bow to the God who is compassionate toward his devotees, the creator of creation and dissolution, the cause of preservation and destruction, and the bestower of grace.
Thus:
"For sequentiality belongs to worldly action due to the power of time, but it does not belong to the eternal activity of the Lord, which is like that of the Sovereign. (Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā)

According to this principle, just as sequential succession (*sakramatva*) is impossible for the Lord, so too is it impossible for His power, which consists of absolute freedom (*svātantrya*) and will (*icchā*). Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And here... and so forth. The meaning is that, due to connection with time (*kālayoga*), even that [power] would become non-eternal. Alternatively, he accepts that [position] through reasoning by means of another perspective.

Regarding the phrase "above Māyā": the sense is that because of the state of being both transcendent and immanent (parāparatā), within that supreme unfolding (antyonmeṣa), the subtle power of time necessarily exists.

The collection of powers (*śaktikalāpa*) is thus described as being conceivable for those practitioners who desire to ascend to the state of ultimate reality (*paramārthapada*); however, there is no contact with the divisions of time above the level of the *māyā*-principle. Alternatively, even above *māyā*, [it may be so].

Because the specific state possesses both prior and posterior forms, there must also be a division of time; for this very reason, it is called a *tuṭi*. All of this has been stated in the *Pratyabhijñā*. (8)
And she was visible in the region of the heart from the time of recollecting the task, at the moment of feeling intense joy, and at the instant of her faint glimpse. (9)
Due to lack of observation when there is a visible occasion for emission, as well as in the context of speaking of emission, and likewise in reading or running; (10)
In these very instances, there is a state of agitation through all powers;

and that [agitation], which consists of the power of subtle orientation, is to be perceived in the region of the heart during the recollection of a task previously intended but forgotten, as well as in other such cases.

At the time of announcing the birth of a son or other causes for great joy; at the very moment of perceiving or beginning to experience fear; when suddenly seeing a desired object without prior reflection;
at the point of emitting the final element; and likewise, in the context of uttering the sound *visarjanīya*.
In the rapid recitation of the text,
the word "api" (also/even) indicates that its duration is like a flash of lightning;
it is clearly visible and should be distinctly characterized.
3. At the time of hearing news of the death and subsequent resurrection of one's most beloved son;
4. At the first moment of the onset of fear;
5. Upon the sudden sight of a marvelous object never before heard of.

6. Thus, that very subjectivity which consists of the nature of the creator and is characterized by acceptance is itself *icchā* (will). And because it is established through the self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) of those who possess aesthetic sensitivity (*sahṛdaya*), it remains with an essence that cannot be denied—just as:

In expressions such as "I am going," that which is to be grasped as the object of movement and so forth— namely, the body, senses, vital breath, intellect, and so on— is of a general nature; and that which is the grasper, by not specifying particularities,
is characterized as the commonality of their mutual manifestations.
Having analyzed the expansion characterized by will, which is denoted by the term *paśyantī*,

he states [the following] beginning with "And that," etc., for the sake of those who are awakened, as a means for the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of that [will], preceded by the manifestation of objects. And this...
"And in the rite of running" (p. 12): at these very occasions, there is a state of agitation and mutual blending of all the powers according to the previously mentioned sequence. || 10 ||

"Whether extremely angry or intensely joyful, or reflecting 'What shall I do?', or while running—whatever state one enters, therein vibration (spanda) is established. This and other such passages summarize [the doctrine] in the *Spanda*. Likewise:

Having rendered the intellect steady amidst the sphere of desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy, that very reality remains. (Viṣṇu Bhakti Kalpa-latā 101) When great bliss is attained, or when a long-lost kinsman is seen, [the mind becomes steady].

Having meditated upon the one arisen as bliss, one should become absorbed in that and have the mind fixed on it. (Viśvasārottara-tantra-bhaṭṭāraka 71) In hunger and other such states, in fear, in grief, in warding off [danger], in flight, in battle, in curiosity, and at the end of hunger and so forth, the reality of Brahman is near. (Viśvasārottara-tantra-bhaṭṭāraka 110)

Thus. The underlying meaning here is as follows: when consciousness, by its own freedom, reflects upon that nature of the Intellect which consists of the plenitude of all powers, then, within that state of being turned toward itself, the nature of consciousness [is fully realized].
Abiding in the bud of will (*icchākalikā*), which is characterized by the first unfolding of that expansion,

he remains undifferentiated from all things while contemplating the future categories of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge— the forms that are destined to be utilized— which are yet to undergo differentiation.
Having condensed the powers (*śakti*) by means of the very process of non-differentiation,
he brings them forth through various conceptualizations such as the "golaka" (the seed-vessel) or the "śimbikā" (the pod); and from that alone,
the effect arises with its future sequence predetermined— just as one thinks, "I shall remember this verse."
By means of a single desire to remember (*susmūrṣā*), even among the letters, words, and so forth situated in the middle [of a sequence],
there arises a succession of memories with a fixed order, without the need for a search that would otherwise serve as the cause for awakening each individual stream of memory.

For if, in running and such activities, there were no actual manifestation of the undivided reality consisting of the subject and object— even though their distinction is not pointed out— then [there would be no] rapid reading of scripts, swift movement, quick speech, or the transition from one line to another.

For one who moves from one place to another place, or from one articulatory organ (*sthāna*) and effort (*karaṇa*) to another, having abandoned each respective [place or organ], how could there be those various acts of abandonment and acquisition, given that there is no reflective awareness (*aparāmarśa*) of either the agent of that abandonment or the agent of that acquisition?

They would [be considered cognitions] because they are seen to be preceded by a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). Therefore, these [cognitions] lead one to infer their own causes; yet, this reflective awareness of theirs is not necessarily distinct [from the cognition itself].
For if the reflective awareness were indeed distinct—
If there were a continuous presence of the recollection of linguistic conventions through a succession of vocal and mental movements, then rapidity itself would not be possible.

Anticipating the objection—"How can there be an inclination toward this effect (the body), which is to be abandoned because it is impure by its very nature of being composed of pleasure and pain?"—he says:
"If it be asked: 'How could there be an inclination toward the loathsome [body] on the part of that which is not loathsome? (11)
The state of being censured due to the desire for the expansion of form is illogical,
because [the Lord] is Śiva by virtue of performing his own fivefold activities.
Where is there any search for other causes in that which has already come forth?

For this Lord, whose nature consists of the non-manifestation (*akhyāti*) of His own full form produced by the power of *māyā*, there is the outpouring of His own essence in the form of various effects, proceeding from the delight of such an expansion.
The state of being contemptible is untenable; for thus, even in the supreme and subordinate states, when one possesses the nature of Sadāśiva and Īśvara,
[one thinks] "I am the universe," and rests in the bliss of one's own essential nature which is the form of the universe.
2. Because the very expansion of its own nature is the tasting of bliss (ānanda), therefore— 3. [The term] *ayukti* means "illogical" or "inappropriate. 4.
It is called *māyā* because it binds (*mīnāti*) the individual subjects (*paśu-pramātṛ*); and that is the power (*śakti*). By that—

The very sovereignty of the Supreme Lord, characterized by His desire to act (*cikīrṣā*), is that which constitutes the power of *māyā* toward the subjects of *māyā*; for even while His own undivided nature shines as "I," it is that very manifestation of His nature as an expansion [of consciousness] appearing there as "this" that constitutes the power of *māyā*.
5. By that [Lord] who possesses power, through His own sovereign power of *māyā*, there is produced this non-recognition (*akhyāti*) of the Full One as "this" and "I.
6. [This refers to the non-recognition] of that which consists in the expansion of one's own essential nature.

7. Regarding the state of being both supreme and non-supreme (parāparāvasthā), which consists of the forms of Sadāśiva and Īśvara: even if the unfolding of the essential nature of Śuddhavidyā has not been effected therein, its absence should not be considered a state of non-supremacy (aparāvasthātva) for it; for, just as in the case of the Śivatattva...

When there is an outward orientation, that is called "Power" (śakti), yet in the supreme state (parāvasthā) it does not attain a status separate from the principle of Śiva (śivatattva); likewise, the outward orientation of Sadāśiva and Īśvara is called "Knowledge" (vidyā), and therefore it is not mentioned here separately.

(14) You alone shine forth within consciousness; even in the state of duality, when one perceives "I know this jar" or "this is a jar," there is no [manifestation] apart from the nature of consciousness.

The very state of being manifest would not be possible [if it were otherwise]; therefore, its nature is precisely that, yet due to the power of *māyā-śakti*, there is a non-reflection (*aparāmarśa*) of non-duality. Since this is always simply the expansion of one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*), how could it be censurable? It is precisely the non-reflection of non-duality that constitutes the form of delusion (*bhrānti*) and is thus contemptible.
And that [consciousness] is nothing whatsoever, because it consists merely of non-manifestation (akhyāti); it is not the manifestation of anything previously non-existent.

Furthermore, the state of being the self of the universe belongs to that which consists of consciousness, because all entities abide as having a true nature of pure, transparent consciousness, just as reflections exist within the ultimate reality of a mirror. And this—
All of this has been skillfully examined in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā-ṭīkā*. 1. Therefore, there is no suspicion whatsoever of anything being objectionable here.
2. In this regard, if the nature of light (prakāśasvarūpa) were not resting in the subject (pramātṛviśrānta), such that [one could say] "this jar here," [it would not be possible].
In that case, how could that which is embraced by "I-ness" (ahantā) appear within the [notion] "I"? [Objection:

Let it be granted that the subtle reflective awareness (vimarśa), because it rests in "I-ness," is indeed an immersion into the nature of light in such cases as "I know this jar"; however, where there is an absence of rest in "I-ness," [it would not be so].

The nature of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is seen in such expressions as "the jar" (in its gross form) and "this" (as a specific object); therein, even the word appears as something distinct from the blue [quality] itself. To the question, "In that case, how can it have the nature of light (*prakāśātmatā*)?", he says "without the nature of consciousness" (*cidātmakatām vinā*), etc., while internalizing this underlying intention. It has been said:
And in recognition,
the determination "this is a jar" appears as the supreme power of the Lord, like the Self itself, transcending name and form, and not as a mere "this-ness. (1.5.20)
Thus [it is said]. 4. "That nature" means the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpatā*).
5. If this is so, then with the intention of asking, "What then is this other miserable thing called?", he says: "But rather... (*kiṃtu*).
6. Reflection occurs precisely through differentiation as "this-ness. 7. "At all times" refers to the intermediate (parāpara) state and so forth.
8. That is its state of being contemptible; and thus, it would be contemptible because it is distinct from its own essential nature.
9. *Prathā* means expansion.
10. Regarding the term *pratibimba* (reflection), as it is stated in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*: "The manifestation of the multitude of objects residing within the Self belongs to the Lord."
"Therefore, desire and reflective awareness proceed only when that [object] exists, and not otherwise.

The expression "one whose fivefold function consists of creation, maintenance, dissolution, grace, and concealment" refers to that which is called Śiva-nature. Therefore, for Him who is engaged in His own activity—
consisting of the manifestation of the categories (tattvas) and so forth— where is there any need for external causes such as compassion and the like?

Since there is no possibility of an attachment to the pursuit of signs (*nimitta*), the objection as to how [the mind] could thus proliferate does not arise; thus, it has been established that the orientation toward the object is indeed non-reprehensible. || 12 ||
To clarify this now by means of an illustration, he says: "The extreme turbulence of water that was flowing without waves... (13).
For by directing one's gaze toward the beginning, one indeed attains an orientation toward that [end];
just as the initial trembling of the hand is observed before it becomes a clenched fist while moving. || 14 ||
The satisfaction of consciousness, which is established in its own self, regarding its creative manifestation—that expansion of its interest is what they call its "orientation" (unmukhatva). (15)

1. That illusory worldly transaction which appears in the case of the seed, the sprout, and so forth, from the perspective of ordinary perception, is concealed by ignorance (*satirodhikṛta*). However, that which exists even therein as the ultimate reality is produced by the power of grace (*anugraha-śakti*). For this alone is its distinction from other proponents [of doctrines], namely, that it is eternal.

Regarding the "performance of the fivefold act," it is said: "He who, though incessantly fashioning the three worlds through hundreds of mental constructions, remains ever-unwearied—victorious is that certain, unborn, and non-conceptual One. (Stavacintāmaṇi 112)
Thus:

the expansion of the principles (tattva) and so forth occurs in the form of emanation (sṛṣṭi) and the rest; therein lie the powers of concealment (tirodhāna) and grace (anugraha) regarding the ultimately real and conceptual relations of cause and effect, and so on.

3. Regarding "of the causes" (*nimittānām*): as some say, "The Lord has attained all desires within his own self; what purpose, then, would he have in creation and so forth? For everyone who engages in activity does so only by aiming at a specific purpose, and since He has attained all desires, that [purpose] does not exist for Him.
If it is argued that the Blessed One acts solely for the sake of favoring the world,

then why does he create a creation consisting of suffering? Since his compassion and other qualities would be the cause [of such action], what need is there to search for further motives in this system?
"It has been established" means that even what is impossible to prove has been proven.
16) That very slight swelling is what is called "greatness" by certain people.
His will becomes an effect through which he is born as one who possesses that will.
The expansion of that orientation which is gross is established as will (icchā);
however, due to the occurrence of non-orientation, Śiva never partakes in grossness anywhere.

Just as when water, previously still and waveless, begins to become highly agitated, a subtle initial tremor in the form of an inclination is perceived; and just as when a hand is being formed into a fist,
a very subtle initial trembling is seen— so it is with consciousness.

The first unfolding of the capacity for creation through mere desire, belonging to the Full One who abides in His own nature with regard to the manifestation of the universe— that orientation they call the commencement of activity (*pravṛttyārambha*). And this commencement of activity—
Because even in the state of liberation (*nirvṛti*), that [consciousness] manifests as having non-differentiation and non-apprehension (*akhyāti*) as its nature;

this very orientation (*aunmukhya*) is described by Bhaṭṭa Pradyumna in the *Tattvagarbha* as "slight swelling" (*kiṃcid-ucchūnatā*). Others also describe it using terms such as "wave," "ripple," and so forth. The will (*icchā*) is the [active] aspect of that orientation.

It must be made so; for that which is its expansion—the upper portion, extensive and composed of firmness, capable of producing effects such as knowledge—is precisely because of the stability and firmness of its structural arrangement, it is gross, and therein His will is established. Nor does Śiva [become subject] to the contingency of being designated by terms such as "swelling" (ucchūnatā) and the like.

It possesses grossness like a seed; or rather, even when desire and the like are present, there is in reality no grossness in the conscious self (cidātman), because it does not increase by means of entities that are like reflections. Nor is the manifestation of its identity with those [entities] an illusion—this has all been stated in the *Ṭīkā*. 17.
Even in empirical usage, there is no such distinction at the outset because the lack of such reflective awareness persists; thus he says:
"For the transformation of milk occurs from the falling [of the drop] from the cow's udder, and for that very reason."
And at that very moment, the designation "milk" does not yet exist.
1. Of that cessation (*nirvṛti*). 2. At the stage of being free from longing (*nirākāṅkṣatā*).
3. Because it appears as such.
From the falling of the cow’s udder, a transformation occurs in the milk immediately thereafter; yet,
at that very moment, there is no lack of awareness of the milk, as long as that awareness remains unified.
In that case, there is indeed always absolute identity.
Thus, the orientation toward desire has been stated; now, establishing it through reasoning, he says: "Because one desires to know or to do something, action arises from that desire.
Its prior and posterior parts must be conceptualized, for that [desire] existed previously. (19)
The inclination toward the attainment of the manifestation of that action is its blossoming.
As for what is said—that the Lord desires to know or to act—that verbal form expresses the action characterized by desire through the word "desires. Of that desire...
The prior and posterior portions must be conceptualized because [the action] consists of parts arranged in a temporal sequence;

this is due to the designation of desire as "action. Furthermore, the mutual identity of desire and the other [mental states] would be all the more evident in the state of their potentiality (*śakti*). Consequently, in the ultimate sense, there is only one power (*śakti*).
It has been established that [the will] is indeed capable. However, in the account of its arising, that which precedes the desire— namely,

the attainment of fulfillment (*nirvṛti*) consisting in being established in that action, its orientation toward it— that is, fulfillment delimited by the action or fulfillment not so delimited, is "orientation" (*aunmukhya*).

The power of bliss (*ānanda-śakti*) is simply cessation (*nirvṛti*); its orientation toward that [cessation] is its blossoming, which is described as the expansion of the abiding consciousness (*cid-āsthā-pravikāsa*). || 19 ||
For immediately thereafter follows the capacity for the knowledge and vision of that effect.
For that purpose, the power of knowledge exists; indeed, that gross exertion is called the power of action (kriyā-śakti), and from it the entire world is established.
As it has been said:
"A collection of parts produced in succession,
whose non-difference is mentally constructed by the intellect through its subordinate constituent parts, is designated as 'action' (kriyā)."
Thus [it is said].
(2) The meaning is: the non-apprehension of the distinction from the nature of full bliss.
In that effect characterized as the universe, the knowledge which exists extrinsically is the nature of the power of manifestation;
though it is unknowable by all perceivers within their own conscious selves, that effect manifests like the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).

For this reason—that [power] is the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*). Immediately thereafter, the exertion which results in the attainment of the form of gross effects cognizable by all subjects is precisely the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) directed toward the object of will. From that alone comes completion.
It has been stated that [the world exists] because of the attainment of the objects of worldly activity; therefore, the entire universe is established. || 21 ||
This is not only the case during the creation of the universe; even at the time of making a single jar, such a state of being consists of the three powers.
Thus he says: "In this way, at the time of the arising of everything, it consists of the nature of the three powers."
It has not ceased, nor has its orientation ceased, nor even is there cessation [of it]. || 22 ||
The nature of will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*) is established as such at the time of producing an object like a jar.
Furthermore, there exists an orientation (*aunmukhya*) which is the prior stage of will, consisting of a specific fulfillment delimited by an object of action.
Moreover, another fulfillment, which is the nature of undelimited bliss, remains unceasing; for in its absence, [the aforementioned would not exist].

Because there is no manifestation of distinction—just as in the absence of awakening, there is no specific cognition of jars and the like—it is for this very reason that the term "attainment" (*prāpti*) was mentioned first, [indicating] that manifestation results in the acquisition of a specific form. Alternatively, by the word "manifestation" (*nirvṛti*), the full power of consciousness (*pūrṇacicchakti*) is intended, consisting of the five powers. || 22 ||

He says that even if there were only a single power, the production of an effect would not occur: "Since an effect is never produced when either one [of the two] is absent, therefore the state of equilibrium (sāmarasya) of all things is established. (23)
1. There is no deviation here. 2. Of that which consists in the form of orientation. 3. Non-existence.
4. Regarding the phrase "the attainment of the completion of that action":
5. "Departure" means going away. 6. In the arising of all entities, that which possesses power remains established.
19) Since it has been stated that if one particular capacity were to depart or cease, the effect would never arise, therefore, at the time of the production of all things—
Since the application of the Śiva-principle consists of all principles, there is never any lack of contact with the form of Śiva; for just as at the beginning of the great creation,
so too even in the liberation of each individual entity, the flavor of the touch of the Supreme Lord remains entirely unbroken.

"Equilibrium" (sāmarasya): even for a potter, in the act of making a jar, there is the nature of Śiva who possesses all powers; however, due to ignorance of that [nature], he is merely a "potter"—this is the meaning. Regarding the reading *ekatarā*, the suffix *-tarap* is used in view of the duality between "orientation" (*aunmukhya*) and "fulfillment" (*nirvṛti*). 23.
It is not only at the time of producing a jar or the like that all powers are present; rather, they are present even at the time of apprehension. Thus he says:
"Even at the time of apprehending a jar, that action [of cognition] knows the jar."
In this very state, one knows knowledge; for the desireless, there is no injury to experience. || 24 ||
Without the absence of such orientation, there is no cessation;
and without bliss, one does not engage with what is loathsome, nor can one know anything without consciousness.

At the time of the cognition of a jar or similar object, that which is called the manifestation of the cognized (the jar) and the cognizer (Devadatta)— distinguished by the variety of the non-manifestation of their difference from Consciousness—
is a sequential and unprecedented form; this is what is termed the action characterized as cognition (*jñānalakṣaṇā kriyā*).
It consists of sequential parts, yet it does not exist at the very moment the verbal expression "I know" occurs.
Because its nature is that of knowing, cognition remains right here within the self of the action.
There can be no perception for one who is devoid of desire and lacks attentiveness, because of the absence of the mind's presiding influence.

Desire is simply perception accompanied by attention. In that context, the prior stage of desire and action is "orientation" (*aunmukhya*), which is the fulfillment of that action. From the absence of such orientation, there is the cessation of that perceiver or of the cognition; for [without it], there is no fulfillment of that action in the form of orientation.

It proceeds even toward that which is hateful. Furthermore, without the power of the reflective awareness of non-duality (*abhedapratyavamarśa*), the agent—who is essentially perfect and pure consciousness—does not perceive objects such as jars.
"I know" is an uninterrupted manifestation (*avicchinnābhāsa*), whereas "he knows" is an interrupted manifestation (*vicchinnābhāsa*).
(20) Since the determination of objects is grounded in consciousness, that very power of consciousness is the universal power of fulfillment,
whose nature is bliss. (25)
Anticipating the objection that there would be an absence of Śiva-nature at the time of cognition, he says:
"How can there be consciousness without the intellect? That intellect is born from Prakṛti.
And if it is argued that there is no connection between Him (the Self) and that [intellect] when another state [of liberation] exists... (26)
Furthermore, that intellect which is subtle, established in all directions, and consists of pure consciousness—that is the innate, eternal knowledge of Śiva. (27)
Now, is it not said that this is too little,

namely, that when one knows— during the time of subsequent cognition— even when there is the manifestation of non-difference, the Śiva-principle, which rests in bliss and is complete with all powers, remains operative throughout the agitation of the object and the subject? For, to such an extent...

It has been stated that the cognition "at the time of grasping a jar and so forth" occurs in this very [cognition]; and such being the case, what indeed is this so-called "time of grasping a jar and so forth"? Furthermore, if even there it is merely pure consciousness (*jñāna*), then enough with the intellect (*buddhi*) and other factors imagined for the sake of establishing objects. And if even there it truly exists...
If that is the application of those respective principles, then how is its manifestation through purity possible?

To shatter the delusions of others, he says "Buddhim" and so forth. Regarding this, some of very limited vision have disagreed, [asking]: "Even in that pure consciousness which is self-luminous, if..."
The knowledge consisting of the surging forth of one's own self is accepted and experienced;

however, because it consists of the activity of the intellect (*buddhi*), and because the complete subsiding of the play of the intellect alone constitutes the attainment of one's true nature (*svarūpa*), it is indeed conceptualization (*vikalpana*). That which is the absolute absence of that [intellectual activity] is...

Thinking, "Lest they be deluded by the misconception that ultimate liberation consists in the attainment of the true nature of reality," the illustrious Teacher, intent on bestowing grace, spoke the words beginning with "without the intellect" (buddhiṃ vinā), preceded by this objection.
2. To the question "Why?", he states the reason: "Because that [is so]. 3.
To the question "Even so, what of it?", he says: "And not [so]. 4. It is precisely the apprehension of difference.
5. "Subtle" means not being an object of intellectual cognition (*buddhi*) or knowledge (*jñāna*), because therein the distinction between intellect, knowledge, and the self (*ātman*) has dissolved.
6. By the term "established," it is implied that the qualified cognizer (*pramātṛ*) is occasional.

7. Regarding the [levels] of the inferior-inferior, the intermediate-inferior, and the superior-inferior: there is no equality with those [lower systems] such as Nyāya, for by them [is produced] only that which is ordinary cognition.
It is accepted that this [validity] belongs to that very [cognition] as its own nature, and not to that which makes another aware.

This indeed is clearly the logical principle regarding desire: [it must belong to the Self]. Now, one might object: "Cognition (*jñāna*) is that which knows; it is awareness, a modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*).

How could there be [cognition] without the intellect, which possesses that modification? Furthermore, the intellect is born from *prakṛti* and is insentient (*jaḍa*). And by means of that [insentient intellect], [the Self]..."

If it is argued that this is simply the connection with the stainless Śiva-tattva, which possesses all powers, that is not so. That cognition belongs to the subjects of the *puryaṣṭaka* during the non-supreme state (*aparāvasthā*), which is characterized by non-duality and consists of a single flavor. However, as for [the cognition] in the state of fullness, it belongs to the supreme state (*parāvasthā*), and for that very reason—
Subtle, undivided, not having entered the state of being an object of knowledge, and for that very reason all-pervasive,

[this] cognition— unbroken by space and time, consisting of pure awareness alone, and whose nature is beyond being known— is that [reality] of his. Having found an opportunity, he speaks to the opponent who argues through cavil (vitaṇḍāvādin).
"By means of logic and so forth" (nyāyādibhiḥ).
[This refers to verse 2. Anticipating the Vaiśeṣika position that desire is a quality of the mind, he says "this" (eṣa) [in verse 3].
[This refers to] a thing whose true nature and essence have not been lost.

The function (*vṛtti*) is said to be the assumption of the shadow of another form belonging to the category of phenomena (*dharma-kalpa*), just as a jar has the function of carrying water or Caitra has the function of walking. Thus, despite the differences in those functions, there is no difference in the function itself, because it remains the object of uncontradicted recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) in that very same form.

4. Because there is no distinction in reality (tattva). 5. Now, let it be that she is insentient; just as the object projects its reflection there, so too does the light of the subject (puṃsprakāśa) project it, otherwise even the determination of the object would not occur in that manner.
And consciousness would likewise [be established]; however, he refutes this with the word "and" (ca), as follows:

[consciousness] exists in all directions but is not delimited by them; otherwise, its omnipresence would be undermined. This is an illustration, and by it, one should also understand that it is eternal.
Regarding this, he says "space and time.
Here, the suffix *mayaṭ* in the sense of the base [word] signifies that which consists of consciousness; the meaning is "having the nature of consciousness.
He expresses this by saying "mere consciousness" (*bodhamātra*). That very state of being mere consciousness is the state of not having anything else as its object.
Regarding this, it is said: "It is of the nature of non-enlightenment" (p.
This is because Śiva's innate [nature] is always present, even when there is the manifestation of ordinary cognition.

Because without that [Prakṛti], that [knowledge] would not exist. Now, one might object: even so, an equivalence with the Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, and other schools arises if knowledge is accepted as being dependent on Śiva; for they maintain that knowledge is inherent in the self (*ātman*), and it has been stated by the Nyāyikas and others that Śiva is of the nature of the self. Therefore, there is no equality with Prakṛti.

This is because such a designation applies to knowledge—which consists of the intellect and its connection—in the state of differentiation; it does not, however, apply to the Lord, who is the supreme form and the Knower.
As it has been said: "This same logic should clearly be understood with respect to Will (icchā).
Will, which rests upon the inner self of consciousness, is indeed said to consist of differentiation."
These are of the nature of mental constructs, and not the supreme and non-supreme states that constitute the very essence of the Supreme Lord. || 28 ||

Because it consists of all principles (tattvas), he describes the abiding state of the principle of Śiva: "Thus, when the Lord has thus expanded forth, He sometimes [abides] in mere power (śakti) alone. (29)
1. It is innate (*sahaja*), having the nature of the reflective awareness of one's own true form (*svarūpa-pratyavamarśa-svabhāva*), and nothing else.

2. That very state is "naturalness" (*svābhāvikatva*): even when there is the appearance of difference due to its [the innate nature's] apparent departure, there is no loss of it; thus he says, "always" (*sadā*).

3. Because a particular, which has the form of agitation, cannot exist without the universal. 4. Of those proponents of logic (nyāyavādins). 5. Nor are all his activities accomplished by means of external organs.
For the eyes and other sense organs are not the means for memory, pleasure, desire, and so forth.
Therefore, neither the mind nor the sense faculties are indeed the support for desire, memory, pleasure, pain, and sensation;
even the body does not attain the status of being their locus.
Therefore, we postulate a Person other than those.
And the author of the Sūtras [states]: "Desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain, and cognition are the marks of the self"— thus by the proponents of Nyāya.

"Consisting of all reality" means, as it has been stated: whatever collection of worlds has been described— which, though consisting of manifestations, contains within itself the infinite and diverse enjoyers and objects of enjoyment— therein,
that which is the pervasive form of great light is like a great universal generality (*mahāsāmānya*).
Regarding the *śivatattva*, it is stated in the *Tantrāloka* (p.
"It assumes a form sometimes through the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) and sometimes through the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*)."
From the sealing of the state of Sadāśiva, one occasionally attains the state of Īśvara.
Through the full manifestation of the power of action (kriyā-śakti) and, at times, through gross perception,
[the soul attains] the state of being a Vidyā, an Āvidyeśa, a Mantra, or a Mantreśvara.

Or, for one who somehow performs the play of concealing the self, [the text speaks of] the nature of the thirty-six principles, beginning with the phrase "the form of illusion" (māyārūpa), and so forth. 32.
Bearing [all] forms, it sustains them through conventional usage to the extent that they are gross, appearing as insentient, composite, earthly, and solid. Therefore,
by the sequence thus described, [it proceeds].

The Supreme Lord Śiva, who is full and consists of light and bliss, possessing the two powers whose nature is the bliss of consciousness inherent within His own essence, has at times first become manifest.
That which was previously described as these various Purāṇas— in whatever is pervaded by them...
Form shines as densely packed with the light of another; that is the one Lord Śiva.

Yet, when a division from that state of Śiva arises through the savor of His sovereignty, that supreme form which follows along in manifold ways—this is the "tattva" (reality-principle) within the teaching of the All-pervasive One. (9.2)
Thus [it is said].
(1) Due to the intensification of the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti).
(2) Because the manifestation of "this-ness" (idantābhāsa), from Śiva down to the Great Lords of Mantra (mantramaheśa), exists only within the Self as "I" (ahamātman).
To illuminate that there is no alteration of one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*) due to this repose, it is stated that "the form of *māyā* consists in the concealment of the Self" and so forth;
[this means] by some form that is beyond all calculation.
By the statement "bearing, it bears," it is shown that even when appearing in such a form, they possess no autonomy whatsoever within their own self; or rather,
it is precisely indicated in the Āgamas that these [powers] possess both natures, being both the possessor of power (*śaktimat*) and the nature of power (*śakti*).
5. Even here, the sequence is in relation to the subsequent principles (*tattva*).
When there is mere potency (*śaktimātraka*) in a state of orientation (*aunmukhya*) that is not yet attached to objects and consists of bliss (*nirvṛtimaya*), [the first principle arises].

In the eastern part of Icchā, during the stage of the commencement of the states of Parā and Aparā, it assumes a form corresponding to that, serving as the object of meditation for those who meditate. This occurs sometimes by "will," meaning due to the cause of its being the nature of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*); or else, having attained the form of will, it assumes a form corresponding to that.

As before, it bears the form of *rūpa*. At other times, however, because its nature is the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), it bears the form of Sadāśiva; for, according to the method previously stated, there is a preeminence of knowledge over action (*kriyā*).
And at times, it bears the state of Īśvara due to the full manifestation of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*).

It sustains [the universe] because its expansion has reached its ultimate limit. At times, it assumes the form of the Mantras and so forth through the state of the subject—the self consisting of consciousness—which is the knower and the known of all things, differentiated by various internal states of higher and lower levels. Indeed, the entire universe of the knowable is characterized by absolute differentiation.
Coarseness (*sthūlatva*). And although cognizers are essentially consciousness, they attain coarseness due to the will of Śiva. Therefore, even sensation (*vedana*) possesses coarseness;
this is the nature of the presiding subject.
2. "From desire" (*icchātaḥ*) is the ablative case used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta*).
3. In the phrase "having the form of desire" (*icchārūpam*), the ablative case is used with the elision of a verbal suffix (*lyablope*).
4. The meaning is: "the object of meditation for those who meditate."
5. According to the principle that "the object of knowledge is like the internal organ" (antaḥkaraṇa).

6. In the state of the supreme and the non-supreme (parāparāvasthā), which consists of the forms of Sadāśiva and Īśvara, the very essence of consciousness itself—distinguished solely by internal differentiation—is characterized by specific qualities corresponding to will and the rest, taking the form of both the object of knowledge and the knower.
It shines forth; within that very totality, through the unfolding of the subject (*pramātṛ*), there arises the nature of mantra and so forth.
Even therein, a distinction exists according to the principle of the "unfolded" and the "not yet unfolded. Now, one might ask: what is this so-called "gross perception" here?
To that he replies: "absolute difference. And it should be understood that this [difference] occurs through the subject's attachment (*abhiniveśa*).

But one might object: since there is no distinction in this state of the subject (pramātṛ), which consists of the cognition of the object and the knower, how can there be multiple subjects therein? To this he says: "by the will of Śiva" (śivecchātaḥ). Therefore—because it is dependent upon the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) and the objects of knowledge (prameya).
9. [The state of] being Vidyā consists of the nature of Vidyā, Vidyeśāna, Mantra, and Mantreśvara.
Furthermore, others consider this to be Vidyā due to the manifestation of differentiation (*bhedollāsa*).

They maintain that [the Lord] desires the Great Illusion (mahāmāyā). For, because his nature is such, he somehow performs as a mere sport the delusion consisting of the non-apprehension of difference (abhedākhyāti), which has the form of saṃsāra and consists of the concealment of the Self (ātmapracchādana).

The power of *māyā* is the state called *aparā*, which is said to be the seed-form (*bījarūpa*). It bears in a general sense the nature of those thirty-six principles (*tattvas*) of which it is the primordial source; it also bears their specific forms, for by that much, the accomplishment of established worldly discourse (*vyavahāra*) is achieved.
Let there be another, unestablished conventional usage [regarding the Lord], since His effects are not restricted;
however, their identity with Him is logically consistent and cannot be refuted. This much we maintain, until the number thirty-six is completed, as far as the earth[-element] is concerned.
For while differentiation manifests within *māyā*, here it is the manifestation of that [differentiation] itself. As it is stated in the *Āgama*:
"Above *māyā* is *mahāmāyā*.
Therefore, there is only a difference of synonyms here, not a difference in ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
2. The intense concealment of the Self, who is the density of absolute freedom, is defined as its loss.
3. The non-manifestation of non-duality is also the concealment of the Self.
4. *Bhānti* means appearing again and again through restless longing, having the nature of birth and death, and not as something separate because it does not appear as distinct [from consciousness].
5. *Aparaiva* refers to the form itself, which is the expansion of forms.

6. A *tattva* (reality) is a form that follows through various specific divisions. Now, one might ask: "Are these alone the *tattvas*, or are there others as well? To this he says: "They are of the nature of its specific forms. 7.
Now, if there are indeed others, why have they not been taught? To this he says: "To that extent."
"Unestablished" means not being an object for ordinary worldly consciousness.
Indeed, the defining characteristic of the insentient is that its manifestation is delimited;
for consciousness, which is distinct from the insentient, is not so measured.

Thus, by this principle, there is indeed an absence of limitation; as for what was further stated—that [the Lord] "bears the nature of the thirty-six principles"—that is said so that there might be no lack of regulation.
According to the principle: "Who could impose a limitation upon the power of one whose power is unlimited? (8).
9. Of the things to be accomplished.
10. We make a formal proposition (pratijñā).
11. The meaning is that the word "yāvat" expresses both limitation and a boundary.

The earth-element (*pārthiva-tattva*), being gross, exists at the end [of the series]; it is a specific state produced by the convergence of many auxiliary causes. It is not perceived here in that manner immediately after that [preceding element].
The effect is grosser than the cause because it is more manifest, but not subtle.

Even though the primary cause, such as *pradhāna*, possesses magnitude, it is indeed subtle. Likewise, because everything consists of consciousness (*cinmaya*), there is a persistence of luminosity from the quality of *sattva* down to the water-element (*jalatattva*).

In the case of the white light-colored [element], its causality may indeed be postulated; however, even in the case of the earthly [element], as long as that [causality] exists, it is due solely to the non-recognition (*akhyāti*) of its identity with the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*), despite its having the nature of light distinct from that [consciousness]. As it has been said:
"That which has an insentient appearance is 'insentient-appearing' (*jaḍābhāsa*); because of its blackness (*kārṣṇya*), it is insentient; 'appearance' (*ābhāsa*) means its form."

It is composed of the five subtle elements (tanmātras) consisting of the great elements beginning with space, and is thus a composite. Immediately following this, because no other contact is possible, it is the final effect; for this very reason, due to the aggregation of many parts, it is dense and obstructive to its own location.
It is incapable of being completely mixed with anything else and is situated at the limit of fully developed dualistic perception.

(33) For the earthly element (*pārthiva-tattva*) is indeed the cause of the thirty-five principles (*tattvas*); and thus, because it is refined by its respective auxiliary causes, the effect is more manifest than even the cause, and therefore possesses grossness (*sthūlatva*).
Because the effect is included within the cause;
because it is all-pervading;
and because it is more unmanifest.

4. That earthly element (*pārthivaṃ tattvaṃ*), although its nature is luminosity according to the principle that "that which is not luminous does not shine," exists as something distinct from consciousness solely due to the non-recognition (*akhyāti*) of its identity with the light of consciousness. 5. [This refers to] the earthly element.

6. Even in water, there is indeed a connection with luminosity (*prakāśa*) because of the appearance of a white color; whereas in earth, it does not exist because of the appearance of blackness—this is the meaning.
7. Since particulars are rooted in the universal, they possess the form of the universal.
The five subtle elements (tanmātra-pañcaka).
8. Vyūhana is the arrangement of specific forms.
9. Saṃhata means dense and conjoined.
From the expanded subtle elements (tanmātras) of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, the earthly principle (pārthiva-tattva) arises.
For in water and the other [elements], all of these [qualities] are impossible. These...

For they are incapable of enduring contact with anything else; they are non-material, unimpeded by other regions, yet utterly unable to merge with another; and for this very reason, they do not nourish the perception of duality.

Therefore, he says that from this point upward, whatever effects such as the worlds exist, those— which are the manifestations of these very elements and are innumerable— he himself creates; thus, "likewise, various bodies and likewise various worlds."
Having cast off one form, it assumes another that is superior, inferior, or middling.

Thus, just as the thirty-six-fold nature of reality (*tattva*), which is capable of manifesting the entire cosmic expansion, sustains itself in the form of the *kārya* (the effect), so too must these same principles be brought forth in the form of the generative, transmigrating *puruṣas*, and not directly [as the ultimate cause].

The bodies of the gods and others are the effects of the Creator; however, because the Supreme [Lord] is incapable of acting [independently], according to the principle stated in the *Pratyabhijñā*, He alone [acts] through His own father and mother.
Now, why is it said that He "bears the nature of the thirty-six principles"?
Anticipating the objection that there exists yet another world-born collection consisting of material manifestations, he says "ataḥ" and so forth.
Bodies are the instruments of enjoyment; worlds are the objects of enjoyment.
3. The enjoyer, in the form of gods, animals, and humans.

4. Herein, the intended meaning is this: first, there is a vibration in the form of the sense of incompleteness (*apūrṇamanyatā*), which is a mere desire devoid of action, the fitness for limitation by what is yet to come. Even after that...
Attachment (*rāga*) is a longing delimited by action (*karman*). As for that action, it is merely action;

furthermore, attachment is a quality of the intellect (*buddhi-dharma*) variegated by various types of action. Thus, this action, reinforced by impurity (*mala*), is the instrumental cause for the experience of the diversity of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*); therefore, there is a dwelling in that experience.
It has been stated that for the sake of providing experience (*bhoga*) to atoms (*aṇu*) that are not yet permeated [by karma], He Himself brings forth bodies;
