likewise, [it is said] "in various ways," and so forth. For the sake of providing experience to the body, there are those various and manifold worlds (*bhuvana*) according to one's latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and in accordance with those, [the bodies].
It has been stated that "the assumption of that very form [occurs] until the end of the enjoyment of experience," which is expressed by the word "supreme" (protkṛṣṭa).
5. [This belongs to] the Supreme Lord, the creator of all.
6. The Supreme Lord alone is the essential nature of the sovereignty of consciousness.

In the ultimate sense, he whose body is the universal being is the progenitor of all. If it is asked, "How then can there be the conceit of [having] a mother, father, and so forth? this must be addressed: does the capacity for that [procreation] belong to the body and the senses, or to something else distinct from them? For as for the body and the senses...

Since they are insentient by nature, they are merely cast into the midst of the mass of objective entities; how, then, can they have the conceit of "arising"? As for that which is distinct from them, namely consciousness (*saṃvit*), we shall establish that it is not different from the consciousness of the Supreme Lord. Therefore, as for what some [here] say...
He too accepted the doctrine of the totality (*sāmagrīvāda*) as a refuge, for that [doctrine] also serves to reinforce the agency of the Supreme Lord alone,
as well as that of each respective cognizer and agent.
Having emitted the gods and other beings, as well as the worlds that serve as their abodes, in the form of the elements and so forth,
he assumes the forms of superior and other classes of gods, humans, and the animal realm. || 34 ||
The latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the body and the world assume one another's forms; thus it is said:
"In accordance with the [particular] place, the mental dispositions (*bhāvanā*) take on the form of bodies;
by assuming that very form, they are manifested. (35)

The accomplishment of the distinct activities of these beings, such as the gods and others, occurs precisely through their mutual conformity. And he, assuming a body and so forth, is known as the "Illusory One" (māyī) because he is characterized by that very form of illusion. || 35 ||
He states that because his own true nature is never obscured, he exists even in hell and other such realms:
"By way of play, he performs actions that result in the experience of suffering; thus, while being tormented by their fruits within the deep abyss of the ocean of hell," (36).
The Supreme Lord assumes bodies as His abodes through His inherent nature of playing at the creation of the universe— bodies that will experience suffering in hell,
or [bodies] in which suffering will be experienced in hell.

By the power of the necessity (niyati-śakti) inherent in the nature of illusion (māyā), he assumes here bodies that perform sinful deeds; likewise, hell itself is an ocean. Therein, the divine [creation] is of eight varieties, and the animal realm is fivefold.
And the human realm is of one kind; in brief, this is the elemental creation.
Thus, it should be understood that despite those various intermediate distinctions, there are only three types.

2. It has been stated that whatever appears here, all of that consists solely of the supreme non-dual nature through the instruction of the Paramādvaya system. In this regard, let no one think thus: [text fragment]
Because an ignorant person would sink their own self into hell by practicing what is forbidden, [the text says] "by way of play.

For the ignorant person has their experience dependent solely upon conduct; therefore, by transgressing that [conduct], they inevitably deserve a fall into hell. Likewise, how could even one who is a mass of supreme bliss remain in hell and the like?
Thus, for the sake of strengthening the realization of non-duality for those who are deluded by such [views], he says: "By play" (krīḍayā).
Within its womb dwell beings who are submerged in profound terror, [reaping] the fruits of their own karma.
They will come to understand the connection: that the Supreme Lord resides even in hell, and there is no one else apart from Him; thus, His absolute oneness is firmly established. || 36 ||
He expresses this very point by means of a worldly analogy: "Just as a sovereign emperor is permeated by the fragrance of his majesty... (37).
Playing, he performs the functions of foot-soldiers according to their respective natures;
likewise, the Lord, whose nature is joy, sports in such and such a manner.

Just as a sovereign emperor, permeated by the wonder of his sovereignty, might through unrestrained play adopt the very nature and characteristics of a common foot-soldier and perform the activities associated with one,
so too does the Supreme Lord, by virtue of His fullness, act spontaneously.
In these various ways, through those diverse manifestations whose very nature is that of the elements, He thus sports in a manner consistent with this;
for sport is a vibration that follows upon joy. 38.
In order to conclude the previously mentioned principles beginning with Śakti, he says: "In this way, Śiva consists of pure consciousness; he alone is supreme bliss.
That very [bliss] assumes the state of being oriented toward objects, taking on the nature of will, knowledge, and action. (39)
That very [power], indeed, as the state of being (bhūtatā) consisting of the body of Śakti and so forth down to the hellish realm,
gives birth to everything beginning with her own nature as consciousness and ending with the earthly element.
By virtue of being the ultimate reality (*padārthatva*), the Lord is the very self of everything everywhere.

According to this aforementioned manner, the Lord Śiva is of the nature of pure consciousness, ever full, independent, and the essence of bliss. Likewise, through the power of *māyā*, he appears as the individual self (*ātman*).
1. According to the principle that "the self alone exists within all phenomena";
2. by means of [the passage] beginning with "the consciousness of one who has attained cessation" (nirvṛtacit);
3. and by means of [the passage] beginning with "when, however, of that... (yadā tu tasya).
4. By the passage beginning with "tasyecchā" (his will).
5. By the passage beginning with "kadācit sthūlavedanāt vidyātva" (sometimes, due to gross perception, it is knowledge).
6. By the passage beginning with "krīḍayā" (by way of play).

As if transcending bliss, it attains the state of reality (*tattvatā*) in order to abide in the form of the desire to create the universe. Because that [desire] is an action (*kriyā*), it moves toward an orientation consisting of its own prior portion; and that [orientation], in turn, proceeds gradually.

It attains the nature of will, knowledge, and action. To this extent, by virtue of being the creator, it brings forth forms ranging from the body of power (*śākta-śarīra*) down to the hellish body (*nāraka-śarīra*); that very [consciousness] is born, and that state of being born is the creation of the elements (*bhūta-sarga*).

The Lord brings forth as objects of experience all forms, from the principle of Śiva, which is one's own nature of pure consciousness, down to the earthly principle; therefore, that [consciousness] is the very self of everything.
The reasoning for this will be stated later. 40.
Demonstrating the five types of subjects within the creation of beings, he says: "Not knowing his own Śiva-nature, as if [he were] designated by the term 'bound soul' (paśu-ātman). (41)
Or, perceiving it as having that very form, he remains as if tranquil in some respects;
in others, through the firmness of the Lord alone, there is the state of Kevala-Śambhu alone.
Unawakened and partless, he is in some places the *pralayakevalin*;
possessing self-awareness yet appearing as if possessed of conceptual thought, he is in some places the *vijñānakevalin*.

As if not knowing its own state of Śiva-hood, it remains having assumed the designation of the limited soul (paśu). For it is precisely the non-manifestation of the non-difference from one's own nature that, produced by the power of Māyā,
constitutes the nature of saṃsāra in the form of the grasped and the grasper.
1. Of that will;
2. he himself is born as such;
3. by virtue of being pure Śiva.
Free from the agitation of the grasped and the grasper;

skillful in various emanations, having taken up the respective material causes and instrumental causes, he is the independent creator of the fourteenfold world of beings, yet remains untainted by afflictions, karma, its maturation, or latent dispositions.
The Lord is a specific Person who, being untouched by [karma] himself, bestows fruits upon others according to their own actions while engaging them therein;
for it is through the awakening of one's true nature that the state of being a bound soul (paśutva) withers, and in its absence, [bondage persists].
Even in the case of the emptiness of the perceived object (*bhinnagrāhyaśūnyatā*), there is no severing of the fetters.
The *pralayākala* is the locus of the two impurities, the *kārmamala* and the *āṇavamala*; the *vijñānākala* is the locus of the *āṇavamala* characterized by the loss of autonomy (*svātantryahāni*).
[The subject] remains [in that state] due to the loss of its sovereignty. In that context, the perceiver is the bound soul (*paśu*), which is consciousness delimited by the *puryaṣṭaka*.
That very [Self], because it is limited, is atomic (aṇu); yet, by virtue of being the nature of consciousness, it is eternal and formless.
By abandoning its identity with the universe, it is ignorant; due to a lack of autonomy, it is devoid of the qualities of action and is non-sovereign (anīśvara).
Within the self of the "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka) of the knowable, it is as if divided, and through attachment, it becomes a thinker of the means for enjoyment.
Because it is produced by *māyā*, he resides within the womb of *māyā*. Ignorance regarding one's own Śiva-nature is improper for the venerable Lord Śiva, because his nature is eternally pure;

for, in the absence of that [ignorance], impurities (*mala*) themselves could not arise, since they depend upon that [state of non-recognition]. Therefore, the individual soul (*aṇu*) is the locus of that portion of ignorance.

At that very moment, by the power of *māyā-śakti*, he arises; thus there is the emergence of the two impurities (*mala*) of *āṇava* and *māyā*. And the *kārmamala* (impurity of action) originates from that. Regarding the phrase "as if his own Śiva-nature," the inclusion of "as if" (*iva*) and the use of the term "designation" (*vyapadeśa*) indicate that this is of the nature of ignorance; in reality, no such thing exists.

This is said in order to express the distinction between the grasped (grāhya) and the grasper (grāhaka). This has been analyzed in detail in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*. In some cases, by the power of *vidyā-śakti*, which is synonymous with *mahāmāyā*, one perceives oneself as having that very nature (*tadrūpatvena*) in every respect.

1. It is said that what is called the "bound soul" (paśu) is indeed the manifestation of both the conscious and the unconscious; moreover, its state of being unconscious is characterized by impurity (mala), and he describes that nature as well with the words "ignorant," and so forth.
2. By this, its dual nature is established. For instance, while he is creating...

It consists of the will of the Supreme Lord; for that very reason, it is eternal; and because it is to manifest as insentient due to the insentience inherent in the form of the objects to be created, it is insentient; and because it takes the form of the activity of all effects and so forth, it is pervasive—this is what is called *māyā*.

The masters, the venerable Abhinavaguptapādas, maintain that reality (*tattva*) is the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*), and that the power of Māyā belonging to the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), which causes that [reality] to appear, is indeed other than it.
Nor [is the manifestation] through connection with impurity (*mala*); thus he says, "without that."
4. Because it consists of the will of the Supreme Lord.
5. As it has been said in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*:
"The loss of freedom for consciousness, and the lack of consciousness for freedom."
This impurity consists of two kinds of atoms, because it conceals one's own true nature.

Right here, the manifestation of differentiated objects of cognition is called *māyā*, which bestows birth and experience; however, when there is non-awareness in the agent, it is *kārma* (karmic). Thus, this triad [of impurities] exists solely through the power of *māyā*.
Thus [ends section] 6. [Section] 7: Arising from Māyā, by way of being Śiva.
p.

32) "He has entered into the state of being the self of the universe and is, as it were, tranquil. Here too, the word "as it were" (iva) is used to indicate that his tranquility results from a particular state of knowledge, and not because there is an actual absence of his universal nature.

The word "iva" (as if) should also be applied for that purpose in the subsequent passage as well. Furthermore, due to the distinction arising from the varying degrees of the power of knowledge (*vidyā-śakti*), [the practitioner] may, in some cases, remain with a firm conviction solely in the Lord (*īśvara*) according to the systems of the Vaiśeṣikas and others;
in other cases, [he remains] through a specific division of Śiva known as Kevala-Śambhu.

In one state, being composed of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*) while abiding in a particular condition, yet possessing an unfaded state of a bound soul (*paśubhāva*), he becomes a *pralayakevalin*, devoid of the separate objects of perception presented by the impurity called *māyā*.
In another case, he possesses self-awareness but does not reside within the *puryaṣṭaka* (the subtle body), and like a *pralayākala*, he is devoid of objects of perception.
Untouched by the impurity of karma, he is of the nature of consciousness alone. || 43 ||
He provides an example supported by many authorities to show that such a state exists solely by the power of will:
"Just as yogins manifest various forms through their own will, there is no means whatsoever for the Lord [to do so] apart from his will, such as clay and other materials. (44)
In the same way, the very will of the Blessed One arises as suchness;
the remainder [of the meaning] is that by the mere will of yogins, the state of being composed of action— the manifestation in the form of various houses and so forth— is attained.
The proponent of the "many-voiced" [theory] is not seen, because of your attachment to appearances; in a dream, there is no other cause for the variety of objects.
Because its power has been observed [in this way], it is always the sole cause for the manifestation of the manifold universe.
Thus, although according to the principle stated by Bhaṭṭa Divākara Vatsa,

the capacity of consciousness alone to construct the appearance of objects— whether existent or non-existent— as perceived in dreams, volitions, desire, grief, and so forth, is experienced, nevertheless, [this is not the case] for a jar or similar external objects.

Having refuted the succession of well-known causes such as clay and so forth, [the author] establishes the creation by will through the example of a yogi for those who are in disagreement, asserting that "here, the jar and other things are unreal.
For it is established that a yogi indeed creates cities, armies, and the like solely by the power of his will. In that regard:
For if it is asserted that the atoms, suddenly assembled by His will, are the material cause, then [the potter] who is well-known as the producer of the jar must be included,
along with all the auxiliary causes such as the training in crafts, merit (dharma), demerit (adharma), the stick, and so forth.

If one accepts that the collection of causes, such as potsherds and so forth, is appropriate for its own material cause, then it follows that this yogi is merely a particular kind of potter. "Oh, then what of that yogi’s status as a yogi?"—to which he replies:
"By mere will, the state of being action itself is attained. Thus, in that case, there is indeed a transgression [of the rule].

And for them, there exists no means such as clay, wood, and so forth—distinct from the will of the Supreme Lord—as there is for carpenters and the like. For they fashion [their objects] by attaining the very form of that [will]. Thus...
The state of possessing a universal form is accomplished through the mere will of the Blessed One alone. || 44 ||
He states the observed example:
"In this world, entities are seen to arise through his will, by way of fear and so forth. (45)

In that regard, if the false nature [of things] is established before one as a reality, then various states— such as those arising from desire, grief, fear, and so forth— are seen appearing vividly before the eyes. In this case,
the will of the Blessed One alone is the cause for that portion.

This occurs through the power of meditative cultivation (bhāvanā) and the immersion into lordship (īśvaratā). Nor do thieves and the like appear there as false forms—for the truth of such things must necessarily be established hereafter. || 45 ||
"This will also be explained further ahead," he says:
"In this way, that nature of Śiva exists within all entities. (46)
Formlessness, or liberation, or the possession of the three powers—this state of being endowed with consciousness must be explained as eternally established before [the disciple]. (47)
Thus it has been stated that the Blessed One is the ultimate referent of the word;
and for yogis, consciousness, even when colored by the body, vital breaths, and so forth—

To that extent, because of its purity, the Creator—relative to other subjects who possess their own bodies, vital breaths, and so forth—is established by direct perception as being external; thus, the *cittattva* (the essence of consciousness) alone is the creator everywhere.
2. [This is] established by direct perception.
3. Precisely because it performs purposeful action through direct perception.

4. Regarding "the will of the Lord" (bhagadicchā): since consciousness (*cittatva*) consists of the nature of one's own self as "I," which is a luminosity and reflective awareness (*prakāśavimarśa*) independent of anything else, therefore [it belongs] to that [Lord].

The meaning is that whatever appears is, first of all, established as not being something to be achieved through effort; and since the entire mass of entities, which is non-different from that [consciousness], possesses the nature of light (*prakāśa*), its manifestation is likewise established.

By such statements as these, the nature of Śiva is established for everything by way of its being the ultimate reality (*tattva*). Now, [it is shown] how even in entities such as jars and cloths there exists the state of Śiva; and because they possess that very nature, despite their limited forms, they are in fact formless, characterized by bliss, endowed with will and the other powers, and possessed of consciousness and non-inertness.
That which is correctly established and logical must necessarily be stated first. || 47 ||
This being the case, he says what follows:
"In this way, the state of Śiva is established as entirely equal for all categories of things;
the distinction between the supreme (para), the non-supreme (apara), and so forth, is merely propounded here by those who possess faith. (48)

The meaning is that from Supreme Śiva down to objects such as a jar, the state of being Śiva (śivatā) is equal—neither deficient nor excessive—for all things, because it does not exceed the nature of perfect consciousness; since all things attain such a state of homogeneity (sāmarasya), there is no particular fixed condition [of difference]. And thus:

Because everything is in a state of aesthetic identity (*sāmarasya*) with the form of Śiva, the distinctions among entities—such as superior and inferior, or pure and impure—which consist of their non-manifestation, have been described.
In this regard, for living beings, there is an attainment based on mere faith, devoid of logical proof; however, this does not apply to objective things (*vastu*).
There is no such thing as purity or impurity whatsoever.
Thus he declares the reality of all things:
in that regard, all entities possess suchness as Śiva-nature provided there is also a connection with those attributes; otherwise it is not so—therefore, everything supports that [reality].
He supports [this] by stating "because it has that nature.
2. It is delimited by action and consists of the form of directedness (aunmukhya).
3. It is experienced through reasoning.

4. Since all things are established in their state as Śiva, which is complete with all powers; 5. [An objection: "If indeed Śiva-nature is complete even in those [limited beings], then why is the distinction between the higher (para), the lower (apara), and so forth, taught as a rule in the Āgamas? Anticipating this doubt, he says "the higher, the lower," and so on.
6. [This] is necessarily present for the entire collection of categories.

7. Now, one might object: "Granted that the application of the state of being the perfect Śiva exists everywhere, nevertheless, since it resides within one's own self, what kind of extraordinary wonder (*camatkārātiśaya*) is there? To this, he says: "The state" (*sthiti*). For if such [a state] belongs to the yogin...
The meaning is that at that time, stability is indeed the wonder of all.
Thus, the Śiva-principle is eternal, infinite, and characterized by differentiation.
Likewise, because it is established in that manner, there is truth even in its manifold forms. (49)

According to the stated sequence, it consists of differentiation (*bheda*), yet it is not separate from the differentiation of entities (*bhāvabheda*). Differentiations, too, have that as their essence; for this very reason, it is infinite. If there were the existence of distinct objects, there would be an end [to it], because its nature would not pervade those forms. Thus, it has such a nature of being established.
Thus, even though the universe consists of manifold forms, it is indeed real for the Supreme Lord. || 49 ||
Thus ends the first chapter in the commentary on the *Śivadṛṣṭi* composed by the venerable master Utpaladeva. || 1 ||
1. By the phrase "through the essence of the expansion of form" (*rūpaprasārarasataḥ*) and so forth;
2. by this, it is indicated that they do not possess any form of their own whatsoever;
3. [Objection: But even difference appears; what is the recourse here? To this he says: "they consist of that" (*tadātmakāḥ*).
(p. 36) Now, in the Śrīśivadṛṣṭi:
The Second Daily Lesson.
In order to state that the doctrine of the non-duality of Īśvara alone is consistent with reason, and not the doctrine of the non-duality of Śabda-Parabrahman,
[the author], beginning by refuting the monism of Śabda as maintained by the Grammarians (Vaiyākaraṇas), proceeds as follows:
He said:
"Now, that power of our knowledge which is the nature of Sadāśiva—that is the *paśyantī* [vision] of the grammarians; it is the supreme state (*parā sthiti*). (1)

1. Thus, by means of this first chapter (āhnika), which serves as an introduction (upodghāta) in the form of a prologue (pīṭhikābandha) indicating the summary meaning of the entire teaching, it has been shown that the Supreme Lord is indeed one alone, yet He manifests through the expansion of His own nature in forms such as the Supreme (parā) and the Intermediate (parāpara); and even while being so, [He remains one].
He is not one whose designation or worldly transaction is subject to fragmentation. For instance:

in the supreme state (*parā*), he is indeed of the nature of full bliss; in the intermediate state (*parāparā*) as well, because of the very essence of the expansion of form, there is no conceptualization whatsoever that could serve as a stain of dualistic thought; and furthermore, in the lower state (*aparā*).
It has also been established that even among those of ordinary intellect, there exists an innate awakening of light.
Thus, although this threefold nature has been supported by demonstrating its impossibility within the systems of other doctrines, it appears as if weakened;
for once that [opposing view] is refuted, all of this [is clarified] like the clearing away of a veil of clouds.

The mass of rays of the self-luminous sun shines with extreme clarity and not otherwise; for indeed, the high value of a gem does not depart even when dust falls upon it, though it appears soiled. In this context, the doctrine of the non-duality of the Supreme Brahman is primarily what must be refuted, as well as that which arises incidentally.

The refutation of the doctrine of the non-duality of the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahmādvayavāda*) is like the removal of the husks during the purification of rice; therefore, for the sake of its refutation, he says "not the Word-Brahman," and so forth.
Reasoning (*yukti*) is a method of sound logic that conforms to experience.
3. Now, the word "atha" (now/then) indicates the commencement of the system of another [school] immediately after the exposition of one's own established doctrine.
37) Although Paśyantī perceives the universe in the form of sound (*nāda*),...
Although she is endowed with the nature of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), nevertheless, because vision is predominant in the state called *paśyantī*,

even when its nature as the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) is accepted in a figurative sense, it remains extremely remote from the nature of Supreme Śiva; for this final stage is not the power of knowledge itself, since that [power] has the nature of Sadāśiva.
This is the determination of the higher and lower states. Furthermore, among those, that state is considered the "supreme" (parā).
And even in the state of Sadāśiva, the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) is not abandoned, as it has been said: "Knowledge and action constitute the state called Sādākhya."

Thus, because of the non-difference between power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimat*), Sadāśiva is the one possessed of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), while Īśvara is the one whose power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) is predominant. For this very reason, Śiva consists of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*), and as he extends up to the one possessed of the power of the autonomy of consciousness (*citsvātantrya-śakti*) at the ultimate limit, he is Paramaśiva. Within this interval—
The emergence of additional principles occurs in view of the cessation of the fourfold orientation.
(1) Since that which existed as the seed within the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*)— namely, within the will (*icchā*)— is itself what has blossomed,
how can it be said here that this [power] is the power of knowledge, given that self-awareness (*amarśa*) is impossible therein?

Regarding the phrase "the fitness for knowledge and vision," the word "fitness" (yogyatā) is used; therefore, having considered how it was stated that "the power of knowledge is Paśyantī," he says "even though" (yadyapi).
Here, the particle *api* indicates that its status as the power of knowledge is merely figurative due to proximity, and not in reality.

Now, if you have accepted that the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) itself is the power of vision (*paśyantī*) by virtue of being the nature of the power of resonance (*nāda-śakti*), as expressed in the passage beginning with "even though," then how can it be that the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) is the form of Sadāśiva according to the author of the Sūtras? This has resulted in a great internal contradiction within your own system.

Anticipating this objection, he says, "And in the state of Sadāśiva-nature"; the meaning is that Sadāśiva-hood is the fitness for the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) and the commencement of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*).
Now, as to the question, "What is this designation 'the power of knowledge is Sadāśiva'?", he says, "The power... and so forth.
5. He states what follows from the context with the words "for this very reason" (*ata eva*).
38) Whether that [objection] be granted or not, this is not what is to be established here in its primary sense; therefore—

Even though such an excess of power has been demonstrated, it is stated that [the universe] "bears the nature of the thirty-six principles. However, the rule remains that the essential intent of non-difference from Śiva is never undermined; for even on the path transcending Māyā, and even when the light of consciousness (*vidyā*) unfolds, the impurity of action (*kārmamala*) does not manifest.

Even in the absence of contact with the cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*), because the manifestation of difference from the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) is never interrupted in any way, there occurs an acceptance of the stated principles— designated as the higher and lower states— which arise by the power of the will of the Lord known through scripture.
This refers to "the grammarians' [view of] the correct words."

The inclusion of the term "sage" (sādhu) regarding these [beings] is for the purpose of manifesting their dullness; for even if they were to see another form, it is said that they have attained meditative composure (samādhāna).
Thus,
and it is pure.
Thus.
1. Now, what exactly is to be established here? For if everything were stated in its entirety, the intended goal would be accomplished; therefore, he says, "non-difference from Śiva.
The rule is that the intended goal to be established here is, in every respect, non-difference from Śiva. And as for that, let there be more [than that], or let there not be.
Or rather, the meaning is that it is not fragmented.

Now, one might object: "In all cases, indeed, the destruction of *māyā* alone is accepted, and that [destruction] exists even in the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*); therefore, enough with this [distinction], for us the supreme [power] is the power of knowledge."
Anticipating the doubt that this might be a state of abiding [in reality], he says, "transcending illusion" (māyottīrṇa).
Therefore, the meaning is that there is no abiding in the supreme reality (paratattva) here;
just as in common worldly usage, one might say of someone who is extremely foolish, "this person is virtuous."
5. It is the state of meditative absorption (*samāhiti*) whose own nature is devoid of the objects and words of conceptualization.
6. It is free from the surging waves of the grasped object and the grasping subject.
And it is characterized by a perfectly tranquil manifestation.
Thus, even if there were something else superior or more excellent than this for her, nevertheless,
she is the cause of the sequence that unfolds within the *madhyamā* as "sara-ū-rasa."

The power of succession certainly exists therein; for it has been said that even when succession has been withdrawn within, although there is non-duality, *paśyantī* is that which possesses the power of succession fully immanent. Therefore, since she is not the final state of fullness, how can she be of the nature of the "beyond"?
The nature of the Supreme Brahman, and the nature of the Word-Brahman. || 1 ||
And so, they speak thus; regarding this, he says:
"They call that the Supreme Brahman which is beginningless and likewise imperishable;
that is the syllable (akṣara) whose form is sound, for that is indeed the supreme speech known as Paśyantī. (2)

That which is beginningless and endless, the supreme Brahman, whose nature is consciousness—that is the imperishable (*akṣara*), changeless, and consists of the form of sound. That alone is the supreme speech (*parā vāk*) known as *paśyantī*.
Without this nature of speech, even the luminosity of consciousness called the supreme Brahman [would not exist].
1. The manifestation of external conceptual constructions has dissolved.

2. "Nevertheless"—because that [consciousness] is the fundamental ground—if there were no subtle process of succession within it, then in the case of *saro rasa*, since there would be no cause for the recollection of sequence, [the words] would appear in a disordered order.

Recollection is to be considered [the cause], for it has been stated that letters mounted upon a single recollection (smṛti) possess the capacity to convey meaning; and that occurs when there is such an appearance provided the cause exists,
and not otherwise— this is the meaning.
3. Because the sequence is internalized within [her].
4. Now, one might object: "If Paśyantī is indeed such [as you describe], how can there be any dispute regarding her?
For there exists yet another [level] which is devoid of sequence. To this, he says "evam" (thus), referring precisely to Paśyantī.
The meaning is that it has the nature of both the Supreme Brahman and the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman).
5. It is imperishable (akṣaya), meaning it is without end.
6. It is the Imperishable (akṣara), meaning it is free from conceptual construction (kalpanā).

7. It is subtle because it is full in every respect. 8. Now, since speech consists of the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa), how can the supreme Brahman be of the nature of sound alone? To this he says: "the state of being speech" (vāgrūpatām).
If the eternal nature of speech were to depart from consciousness, its manifestation would not be manifest; for that [manifestation] is characterized by reflective awareness.
Thus says Bhartṛhari (p.
it would not manifest; for that [consciousness] is reflective in nature, and reflection itself is...
They say that "manifestation" (prakāśana) is what is meant [by this]. || 2 ||
And he says that this very thing is the Self;
that same Self exists as pervading all bodies. The internal state of seeing itself is the formless nature of consciousness. (3)

That state which perceives internally, characterized by the nature of being an enjoyer, which is empty of the form of the knowable and consists of pure consciousness alone—that is called the Self (ātman).
Pervading all bodies and situated within the locus of its enjoyment, it experiences the objects of enjoyment. || 3 ||
He is indeed that Supreme Self, the omniscient one; so much so that he sees the infinite until the ultimate limit is reached.
(1) Even though the Supreme Brahman is admitted to be nothing but the light of consciousness, how then [is this so] in this case?

If it were of the nature of sound (*śabdarūpatā*), its manifestation as such could not be established in any way; thus, what need is there to mention that it cannot exist "without being of the nature of speech" (*vāgrūpatā*)? No, for that which is the very nature of consciousness (*cidrūpatva*) in that which consists of consciousness is itself the nature of speech—since this is their doctrine, he says: "it is precisely reflective awareness" (*pratyavamarśanameva*).
2. Now, let it be granted that the Śabdabrahman possesses such characteristics—being without beginning or end and complete;
nevertheless, for whose sake is there bondage and for whose sake is there liberation? It is precisely for that purpose that worldly activity proceeds.
Thus, [one must first establish] the enjoyer, who is the subject entitled to bondage and liberation, as being inherently pure despite the adventitious taint of ignorance (avidyā).
He alone provides the support;
he engages with that which is to be enjoyed;
it has as its object the limit of what is to be known.
5. Its existence as the nature of an enjoyer means that its very state (*avasthā*) is established as "living. 6. Of that enjoyer. 7.
Since the state is not distinct from the one who possesses the state, when the state in the form of the object of enjoyment ceases, [the living state likewise ceases].
Furthermore, he says that only the state itself remains:

"8. Here, the phrase 'the supreme limit' (parā kāṣṭhā) should be construed with the sense of repetition. Thus, as long as the supreme limit has been attained, for that long one perceives this entire universe as nothing but the infinite Paśyantī."

He sees. The word "as far as" (*yāvat*) functions here as a restrictive particle; thus, the meaning is that beyond that point, there is only the highest limit (*parā kāṣṭhā*), which is indeed *paśyantī*.
Through the excellence of practice, that [speech] reaches its ultimate limit and becomes *paśyantī* itself;
it perceives the entire infinite universe such that the purpose of its act of seeing is fulfilled.
At that very moment, because ignorance has ceased, he says that this is the ultimate reality (paramārtha):
"Devoid of the functions of the senses and so forth, and empty of space, time, and the like. (4)
The reality of Brahman, which is the mere process of emanation and reabsorption from all sides and is devoid of form, is the supreme limit; that alone is the ultimate truth.

At that time, there is no operation of manifesting objects nor any employment of means such as the senses or sensory perception; furthermore, there is no limitation by space, time, or genus. For this very reason, that which is the sequence from all places and times is merely the instruction of the reality of Brahman, since sequence itself is the nature of saṃsāra.
And for this reason, it is devoid of all forms of the grasped and the grasper; since there is nothing further beyond that, it is the ultimate limit.
That which is attained is itself the supreme reality (*paramārtha*), whose nature is *paśyantī*. || 5 ||
And he says that this very [speech] becomes thus once again:
"That sound, by virtue of the desire to express a meaning, abides in the form of consciousness;
it is called *madhyamā* (the intermediate), and through the sequence of *bindu*, *nāda*, and *marut*, it is that very same [speech]. (6)

1. And it is devoid of the activity of being an object of enjoyment. 2. Having established the transmigrating individual soul (jīva), whose characteristic is that of an enjoyer and whose form is the state characterized by ignorance, and following from that connection, even that which is pure—

Having established that the omniscient one possesses the characteristics of the supreme self (paramātman) and is thus the ultimate goal (upeya), he says "This is the ultimate reality" (paramārtha) and so forth,
because [the omniscient one] is devoid of all limitations (avaccheda).

4. Because [the object] has already been grasped by means of its determined nature through the forms of the apprehended and the apprehender. 5. The particle *eva* (only/itself) is displaced; it should be joined immediately after the word *saḥ* (that). 6. "Devoid of space, time, and so forth" means that space, time, and the rest are empty (*śūnya*) therein; this applies to them as well.
Precisely because its occurrence does not exceed that [of the sequence], it is stated in the *Vṛtti* that there is a delimitation by space, time, and genus.
7. Sequence itself is transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*); therefore, even though it has that as its essence, because of the absence of sequence, it is devoid of that [transmigratory existence].
8. [This refers to] something else that is additional.
That very same word, in the form of *paśyantī*,
abides in the state of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as characterized by the intention (*vivakṣā*) to communicate a meaning; and that indeed is *madhyamā* speech.
It is said in sequence: "By the arousal of the winds of prāṇa and apāna, known as bindu and nāda, there exists eternally that which is one within prāṇa and apāna for everyone. (6)
Furthermore, he says that it remains thus:

"That very [speech] is called *vaikharī* when it has reached the cavity of the mouth through its successive stages in the locations beginning with the throat, by means of external mental impressions. (7)
Excluded from the forms of jars and other objects, she is perceived by the eye and other senses;
here too, it should be understood that she has reached the cavity of the mouth through the sequence of *bindu*, *nāda*, and *marut*, thus becoming *paśyantī*. As it has been said:
"The vital breath (prāṇa), having manifested the phonemes, dissolves back into the phonemes themselves. (Vākyapadīya 1.116) Now,

having first described the ultimate nature of Paśyantī, and subsequently concluded the discussion on the states of the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme Self (paramātman), [the author] proceeds once more according to the sequence of their manifestation.

"By means of this [treatise], he has stated the conventional state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), by which this manifold display of the grasped and the grasper remains in flux"— this is the doubt [that arises] preceded by such a thought.
(2) By the phrase "in the form of mental consciousness," [he refers to] the word in its *paśyantī* form.
That very desire to convey meaning, which takes the form of the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*), is itself the nature of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*);

it is that same manifestation of succession even while the state of non-differentiation exists in the *paśyantī* level; and it is indicated that this very [consciousness], consisting of internal discourse, is the *madhyamā*.
3. It abides in stillness. 4. By that, the very emergence of the prāṇa and apāna breaths is the manifestation of the sequence; this is the meaning. 5. Suṣumṇā is of the nature of Paśyantī.
6. There are eight places for the articulation of phonemes: the chest, the throat, and likewise the head;
the root of the tongue, the teeth, the nose, the lips, and the palate.
Thus,

having reached the interior of the mouth from there, it is described as *vaikharī*, taking the form of articulated phonemes such as the letter *ka* and others in the various locations beginning with the throat.
When the wind is manifested in its locations, speech—assuming the form of articulated phonemes—is called *vaikharī*; it belongs to speakers and is bound to the activity of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

Thus, even from an external perspective, that very speech— manifesting gradually through the impressions (*vāsanā*) of external objects, which are of the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*)— assumes the state of being the perceived object for the eyes and other sense organs in the forms of jars, cloths, and so forth. || 7 ||
He says that they spoke thus because it was said by those very virtuous ones for the sake of engaging with the reality of things.
Brahman, which is without beginning or end, is the reality of sound (*śabdatattva*), that which is imperishable.

It is the reality of sound both by virtue of being apprehended through sound and by virtue of causing sound to be apprehended; for indeed, every cognition as it arises does not arise without delineating sound.
Because that which lacks such delineation has not attained the nature of manifestation and is therefore devoid of an object,
the reflective awareness (parāmarśa) that "this is such-and-such" would not even possess the essence of cognition (*vedanā*) within a consciousness whose form has been stolen away;
hence, [cognition] possesses the nature of manifestation through the power of the emergence of words (*śabdonmeṣa*).

The certainty is that all cognitions have the capacity to convey meaning as permeated by sound (*śabda*); therefore, the reality of sound itself manifests as the form of objects. For indeed, one does not experience any particular cognition that is devoid of the permeation by the specific [form] called sound; thus, everything—
Whether indeterminate (*nirvikalpaka*) or determinate (*savikalpaka*), cognition manifests an object as qualified by a word.

In a cognition that reveals an object delimited by a genus, a quality, or an action—such as "the white cow goes"—the object appears precisely as qualified by the word. This is because it is permeated by that specific [word] known as *śabda*.
When questioned about the specific nature of the qualified object (*viśeṣya*), one points to the word itself.
For one experiences it through an experience whose very nature is luminosity, obtained without abandoning the word;
thus, that qualified object is also of the very nature of the word. Therefore, in this way, the word itself is mounted upon the object.

It is established that "it appears" (*pratibhāti*). Thus, since that upon which a word is mounted shines forth cannot be shown or experienced separately from it, the word itself appears in such and such a manner;
therefore, this object is merely a transformation (*vivarta*) of the word and nothing else whatsoever. And for this reason:

It is established that this single Śabdabrahman, which displays various distinctions through the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of ignorance, manifests in its true nature as it actually exists once ignorance has ceased.
From which proceeds the process of the world, evolving in the form of objective entities.
There is no cognition in the world that is devoid of the accompaniment of words;
one who is proficient in the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman) attains the Supreme Brahman. (10)
"But *paśyantī* is undivided, with its sequential order completely withdrawn from all sides"—thus has it been established by those very compositions of sentences beginning in this manner. (11)
For by those grammarians who are virtuous and excellent, yet deluded, it has been propounded in this manner:

that the reality of speech in the form of *paśyantī*, the imperishable Brahman without beginning or end, manifests as the world of objects (*viśvārthabhāvena*); thus, that [Brahman] assumes within itself an unreal form.

*Vivarta* is the assumption of forms that are unreal, distinct, and other; it is from this *vivarta* that the process (*prakriyā*) arises—the wonderful variety of the arrangement of entities, beings, worlds, and so forth. Likewise, in worldly transaction, there exists no cognition of jars, cloths, and the like, which is devoid of the accompaniment of expressive words.

Without the nature of speech (*vāgrūpatā*), even the manifestation of the reality of Brahman would not manifest, for that [speech] is indeed reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśinī*). Thus, by one who is proficient in this very Brahman— known as *śabda*— in its form as *paśyantī*, the supreme Brahman is attained.

This entire world is indeed *śabdabrahman* (the Word-Brahman), which, through the influence of beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*) and its latent impressions (*vāsanā*), undergoes a phenomenal transformation (*vivarta*) into the appearance of diverse objects; for there is no such thing as an object of denotation that is separate from the denotative word.
This distinction between the denoted and the denotative is merely conceptual; this very ignorance is resorted to as the means to knowledge (*vidyopāya*).
The nature of speech, however, is the reality (tattva) because it never departs from every cognition.
But Paśyantī is undivided, with all succession withdrawn;
she is the light of her own form within, the subtle speech that never departs.
Taking up the intellect alone and following the form of sequential succession,
the intermediate speech (madhyamā-vāk) proceeds by transcending the activity of the vital breath (prāṇa).
Thus [he says]. 3. He accepts [it]. 4. In Brahman, which is designated as "Word" and whose nature is sound.

Because one remains situated in that ignorance, it is argued that it is not logical for hands, feet, and so forth to possess the nature of the ultimate reality through their exclusion; thus he says:

If it is argued that, because there exists a subtle state of speech in the form of *paśyantī*— which is the foremost of all forms of mental construction (*kalana*)— therefore this [reality] is called Brahman, then that nature of truth will be perceived everywhere, both in the hands and other limbs, as well as in jars and other objects, as we shall demonstrate further on.

"How is it not so in other cases by way of predominance? If [it is argued that it is so] because of its exclusion from those others by virtue of having a specific form, he says "no" to that as well: "Being the ultimate reality (paramārthatva) is not tenable.
Consequently, there is either selfhood (ātmatā) or Brahmanhood (brahmatā).

And from this, the following is meant: why is it that Brahman-hood resides only there [in the Self] and not in the hand or other limbs, nor even in a jar or other objects? Alternatively, even though it is designated by the term "speech," its excellence arises from its progression through various locations such as the heart, throat, palate, and the space between the eyebrows during the state of meditative absorption; however, such excellence does not belong to the hands and other limbs in this way. Thus he says:
If the internal sequence [of manifestation] belongs to the heart and so forth, why is there no such reality for the vital breath and so forth? (14)
In every activity, there exists a fullness of internal reflective awareness (*antaḥparāmarśa*).

Even for the vital breaths such as *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *samāna*, and *udāna*, their reality arises from their movement through the heart and other centers. Furthermore, at the time of the manifestation of any object, there is an internal reflective awareness; for indeed, [without it], nothing would exist.
In the state of direct perception, just as there is no reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of a word, so too there is none of the word’s referent;
it is merely [apprehended] without differentiation. If this were the case, everything would be so. (14)
Alternatively, he states that the excellence [of speech] lies in its capacity to bestow success and so forth:
"If it is argued that here, through worship, success consists in union with the deity," (15).
In all the Yoga treatises, the attainment of the deity and the state of a yogi are taught for everyone;

it is said that success belongs to those who worship Speech and who possess knowledge of it, and that Vāgīśvarī is the presiding deity therein— this too is not [the case] in the Yoga treatises and so forth.
There are also supernatural powers (*siddhis*) resulting from the mastery of retention (*dhāraṇā*) over presiding deities, the sense organs, and the gross elements;
therefore, the same [undesirable] consequence applies there as well. || 15 ||
1. Although this [power] is similar to the organs of action (*karmendriya*), it possesses such a nature because it is a power (*śakti*);
whereas the hand and other organs lack such a nature due to the absence of that [power]. With this intention, he says:
2. Just as in that case there certainly exists a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of sound, and it is not the case that it does not exist, so too...

like the hand and other sense organs, this organ of speech cannot be Brahman. (17)

rather, they are fashioned in accordance with those [scriptures]. The same applies to speech. 17.

There is contact with the contemplation of ultimate consciousness (*paramārthasaṃvit*). Furthermore, no methodological procedure attains relevance in investigations of the ultimate reality. For the very commencement of the existence of objects consists of consciousness, and consciousness—

If it is argued that consciousness, whose essence is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), is first permeated by speech alone and not by the hands, feet, and so forth—even so, consciousness whose essence is reflective awareness consists solely of speech. The meaning is that it is indeed endowed with the nature of seeing. || 19 ||

1. Although there is a threefold rule—namely, from scripture, from the teacher, and from oneself—even so, because "from oneself" is the means for those two [other] ways, and because it alone is the primary factor here, by that [means alone...]

Reflecting upon that very point, he says: "If [the mind perceives] appearances as being external, whether they are real or unreal... (21)

In this regard, that she who is real creates unreal forms—this is indeed a marvel due to its impossibility, because it contradicts the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), since it would entail the unreality of the cause apart from the effect; furthermore, even in the case of an unreal creation, there would be the consequence of defilement due to her acting in an inconsistent manner. || 24 ||

If this [impurity] belongs to its own nature, then whose would it be even in the case of another’s nature?

This would be a property of another; for it is not accepted in the scripture that, in the doctrine of non-duality (*advayavāda*), there exists any object other than Brahman. By what would it be prevented, or by what would it be set in motion? For in that case, it would not be independent. To illustrate: just as there is an inference of rain even when it is unperceived by means of the specific rise in a river's flood, so too—

He establishes that [the means of knowledge] is not unestablished by inference, demonstrating that even here— in the case of the non-sequential light whose nature consists of indivisible sound— there must necessarily be an inference, because otherwise the sequence of the differentiation of entities could not be accounted for.
For how could the cognition of difference arise without ignorance? Thus, ignorance certainly exists.

(56) Since it is otherwise impossible to establish the distinction between states of being (*bhāvabheda*), if ignorance (*avidyā*) is characterized as such, the meaning is that it is inferred. If this is so, then it is indeed characterized; why, then, is its lack of characterization asserted?
Or [the consequence would be] its ineffability.
Even so, it is not established; for he says: "Nor is inference accepted by you, because of the refutation beginning with 'it is a state' and so forth. (33)
Furthermore, inference is not accepted by you as a valid means of correct knowledge;
for since the potencies of things vary according to differences in state, place, and time, the establishment of entities through inference is exceedingly difficult to achieve. (Vākyapadīya 1.32)
Thus,
for one who relies primarily on inference, like a blind man running on a treacherous path by means of the touch of his hands, a fall is not difficult to incur. (1.42)

Thus he speaks and more; for if it were capable of establishing the nature of things, perception would not be inferior to [inference]; but if it were incapable, it would simply lack the status of a valid means of knowledge. || 33 ||
1. Because it is the cause of that [effect].

2. Likewise, even in the conceptualization of inference (*anumāna*). Now, let it be granted that it is characterized during its state as an effect, since that [inference] is postulated precisely because the differentiation of entities would otherwise be untenable.

And since it is established that in that causal state there is indeed non-perceptibility, even if that non-perceptibility were granted, the same refutation previously stated applies: if it were perceptible, its ineffability would be lost.
As for this so-called "perceptibility of the imperceptible" which is merely imagined through inference, in that case—
If the primary purposes of a word have not produced its meaningfulness,
then to hope for it in secondary applications is like clutching at kusha and kāśa grass.

By this reasoning, inference itself would be untenable according to your own position, whereby the status of being both characterized and uncharacterized could be established through the "half-old-woman" logic (*ardhajaratīya-nyāya*). Thus he says: "Even so...
[The object], though repeatedly ascertained as being such-and-such in its essential nature, remains so.

Likewise,
for those like you who perceive the universe through direct perception,
what need have they for inference, since they possess divine vision?
Whether it be true or false, there is no middle state [between them]. Knowledge does not exist; thus, some corresponding [consequence] would follow. (34)
If the non-existence of all cognitions were indeed real, then that would be emptiness (śūnyatā).

The meaning is: if it exists, ignorance would be either real (satī) or unreal (asatī); if it does not exist, it would be the opposite of that. There is no possibility of something intermediate, because existence and non-existence are mutually exclusive;
for there is no possibility of a third category. To explain:

This ignorance is not knowledge; thus, by way of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of knowledge, it manifests as the self-nature of the entire universe and is not merely of the nature of a negation. Consequently, there would be some form of ignorance similar to knowledge that is universal and truly existent; and therefore—
It is neither indescribable, nor is it non-dual. [The absence of] "vidyās" means the absence of correct cognitions.
Regarding the phrase "of the middle"—that which consists of being, non-being, or both;
and since its non-existence has been refuted, its existence necessarily follows by force of logic.
For a category distinct from both the existent and the non-existent is utterly difficult to find.
Thus [it is said].

Having raised the two alternatives— whether it be real or unreal— he refutes the position of its reality with the words beginning "knowledge is not," and the position of its unreality with the words beginning "if."

Relying on the position of negation (pratiṣedha), he says: "In that case" (tahi). However, where affirmation is primary and negation is secondary, and where the negative particle (nañ) is connected with a verb, that should be understood as an exclusion (paryudāsa).

Such is the definition of *paryudāsa* (exclusion). Likewise, that which is joined with the negative particle (*nañ*) elsewhere applies to something other than that, namely to what is similar to it; for example, in the sentence "Bring a non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇam ānaya*), one brings someone similar to a Brahmin—one who possesses the same belly, hands, feet, and eyes—but not a horse, nor [something else entirely].
Regarding the term "donkey" (p.

"Something" means whatever it may be. And thus, it is a marvel that the position consisting of right knowledge—namely, the *paśyantī* which is empty and formless—is sublated. For it is precisely through the sublation of right vision that the delusion of duality [arises]; since that which is of the nature of "nothing at all" lacks the power to sublate, [it cannot be the cause of such delusion].

The meaning is that this is possible. Furthermore, you do not accept *paśyantī* as being of the nature of sound (*śabdanātmikā*), the power of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara-śakti*) according to the logic stated in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, because that would entail the undesirable consequence of accepting [the existence of] an independent God; rather, it is held to be subtle, abiding in non-difference from the signified object (*vācya*).
The word is the signifier; thus, it consists of the nature of sound.

He says that even though it lacks the status of being a sense faculty (*indriya*), just as hands and so forth are not ultimately real because they are composed of earth (*pārthiva*), so too is speech composed of air (*vāyavī*): "If hands and the like are of the nature of earth and so forth, why is speech not of the nature of air? (3–4).
1. *Prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation) is that in which mere negation is predominant. Thus it has been said:

Thus: "A Brāhmaṇa who does not eat at a *śrāddha* does not eat at a *śrāddha*"—this is the meaning.
And it has been said by the elders:

Thus [it is said].
For you do not accept the existence of a Lord (īśvara), because of your conceptualization of the doctrine of ignorance (avidyā).
In this manner, having accepted that speech is a sense-faculty (indriya), the position of the opponent has been refuted.

The principle of earth (dharātattva) and so forth is not accepted as the self or the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of the hand and other [limbs] by virtue of being Brahman; likewise, speech is also [not so accepted].
Like the word *sindhu* and others, a word does not arise from the *paśyantī* stage and so forth. || 36 ||
Mere sound is not capable of abiding in the Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and other levels,
just like the roar of the ocean and so forth, because it is not observed to be so there.
There is no sublation by ignorance for one who does not perceive that which has become real; rather, it is for the intermediate [perceiver] that this occurs. Thus he says:
"Now, external entities are indeed grasped by the intermediate ignorance."
For its very conjunction with the intellect, which consists of volition, [is the cause]. (37)

Entities manifested as external and distinct by means of speech called "intermediate" (madhyamā) are perceived as objects of grasping due to the power of ignorance (avidyā). Through the very connection with that [speech]— which, being of the nature of conceptualization (saṃkalpa), consists in the determination of objects— their relation occurs within the internal organ on the path of the prāṇa and apāna breaths.
This is because it remains in that very state, and not in the state of *paśyantī*. [37]
1. "Paśyantī is the beginning" means that *paśyantī* is the *ādiḥ*, i.e., the primary [level] of which;

[this is expressed by] the suffix *tasil* used in the sense of all case-endings (*sārvavibhaktika*). 2. The meaning is that sublation caused by ignorance does not have *paśyantī* as its object; and therefore, [it does not apply].
There is no defect whatsoever in [the view that] Paśyantī [is consciousness]. Thus, it has been established that there is no connection with ignorance (avidyā) in Paśyantī in any way;
and as for the manifestation of duality, how is it established? It is established by the force of the object itself.

Since the manifestation of non-duality appears only in the middle state (madhyamā), there is no inconsistency whatsoever in its connection with that [non-duality], because while the former consists of the light of its own essential nature (*svarūpa-jyotis*), the latter is clearly of the nature of discursive speech (*saṃjalpa*). Thus he says:
The phrase "Now, etc. (*athetyādi*) is used because it anticipates the prima facie objection (*pūrvapakṣa*).

(4) [Objects] are appearing as external. (5) For in the *paśyantī* [speech], which consists of the light of one's own essential nature (*svarūpajyotī*), even the object is entirely composed of that [light].

Therefore, because the middle [state] consists of the determination of the nature of objects, it necessarily involves a connection with ignorance in the form of internal discursive thought; this is the meaning.
But "not" refers to that whose essential nature transcends those [states].
(60) He says that this too is not so:
even there, by what state of the *paśyantī* would the *madhyamā* be seen as its effect?
By what cause would that mother produce such a variegated [offspring]? (38)

In that case as well, if one accepts that ignorance (avidyā) is associated with the middle state of consciousness— which abides at the level of cognition where the duality of the object and subject appears— then the middle speech would only exist occasionally,
because its effect would be absent [at other times].

By the maxim that "the effect of the preceding speech itself should be produced," since there is an absence of any other cause, it follows that she (Speech) must be produced by the state of *paśyantī* alone.
This being the case, for what reason would one [produce] that *madhyamā*, which is variegated (*śabalā*)?
Being of a pure nature, she produces that which is permeated by the distinct object of perception. || 38 ||
He says that it is not at all reasonable to produce such a [view]:

"Seeing it thus, the opponent, through his inability to provide a justification, has grasped this doctrine of ignorance (*avidyāvāda*) as being established solely by the Madhyamaka; unable to tolerate that, he says the following."
No;
because there is no cause distinct [from it].
Herein, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is as follows: the intermediate speech (*madhyamā vāk*) consists of occasional appearances.
It must indeed be an effect (*kārya*). That which consists of some occasional manifestation does not exist, and for that, there is no effect either.
This Paśyantī, however, exists as the absence of occasional manifestation; therefore, she is not of the nature of an effect.
Madhyamā, on the other hand, is of occasional manifestation, and thus it means she is of the nature of an effect.
For even you do not accept the admission of dualistic doctrine;
nor [is it established] by means of ignorance,
for that [dualism] has come upon you by force, even though it is not desired by you.
7. [The world] is colored by [the influence of] the other.

8. Here, the very possession of a pure intrinsic nature (*śuddhasvabhāva*) is the reason for their non-difference. 9. Thus, it is in no way logical that wine and *māyā* are its effects; for if they were its effects, [they would possess that purity].

According to the principle that "the effect is similar to its cause," it is untenable for there to be a difference in essential nature; if it were not its effect, another cause would have to be posited, yet that is not accepted because of the very absence of such a cause, for in that case, duality would ensue.

For that [non-existence], there is neither a causal condition (*nimitta*), nor a cause (*kāraṇa*), nor an inherent cause (*samavāyin*). If it were a causal condition, there would be separateness; if it were an inherent cause, there would be identity with it. (39)

The word "asau" (that) is understood [from the previous context]. That Paśyantī is merely the efficient cause (*nimittamātra*) of that [Speech], not its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), because it exists either as something heterogeneous or as undivided through homogeneity.
If it were merely an efficient cause, there would be the consequence of duality; however, if it were an inherent cause, it would be like milk [transforming into curd].

Given that curd is the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*), it follows that the material cause and its effect possess an identical state of acquisition and preservation (*abhinna-yogakṣematā*) by virtue of being a single continuous stream;
otherwise, even with a difference in time, there would be no such identity. This is just as threads [are related] to a cloth.
If they were inherent [in the same substrate], then Paśyantī and Madhyamā would be non-different in nature, like a thread and a cloth, because they do not manifest as distinct entities. (39)
Then, having stated the fault [in the two positions], he says that even the state of being *paśyantī* is untenable for it—namely, for the *madhyamā*. 2. *Paśyantī*.

3. He states its sublation [by another means of knowledge] with the words "nimitta" (the instrumental cause), etc. 4. "Of that"—referring to the [non-existence] previously introduced as being an effect.
5. That which is of great assistance in the establishment of an effect, yet is itself unconnected [to it], is called the "instrumental cause" (*nimitta*).
6. A cause is dissimilar to its effect, as for example the shuttle and other tools are to the production of a cloth;
[this is so] because the effect and the cause exist separately from one another.
8. That which is eternally connected to the production of an effect is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*)—for example, clay in the production of a jar, or milk in [the production of] curd.
9. Abiding by way of its own nature is *yoga*; abiding by way of possessing purpose is *kṣema*.

By the grammatical rule that "a word heard at the end of a dvandva compound is connected with each member," there would be neither *anyathātva* (alteration) nor *tathātva* (identity); the meaning is that there is neither alteration nor identity between milk and curd. Likewise, there is neither alteration nor identity between the *paśyantī* and the *madhyamā*.
Nor is there suchness; this is the meaning.
In the case of both the threads and the cloth, even when the effect arises, there is no alteration of their essential nature (*svarūpa-anyathābhāva*);
whereas in the former case [the seed], upon the arising of the effect, there is an alteration of the essential nature.
The distinction between these two lies in the fact that [the former] exists by way of transformation, whereas [the latter] does not;
this applies to both—the two positions mentioned previously.
Nevertheless, if the Self were to perceive itself through its union with ignorance, then the entire external world would become as blind and mute as a deaf-mute. (40)

The destroyer of every mental activity, beginning with the sense organs, [is the *paśyantī*]. Because it shares the same security and destiny (*ekayogakṣema*)—that is, through identity—with the *madhyamā*, it would incur the defect of association with ignorance (*avidyā-yoga*), just like the *madhyamā*, due to the loss of its purity. Or, [if one argues that] it is indeed pure...

Since the *paśyantī* does not perceive objects as distinct from itself, but rather perceives them as its own nature (*ātmarūpa*), it is therefore free from the defect of association with ignorance (*avidyā*). This being the case, because the *madhyamā* is also non-different from that [state], it would likewise be so;
and consequently, regarding the external world of diverse objects, one would be blind and ignorant, as well as deaf.
Because of the lack of proficiency in speech and other such faculties, the entire world would become as if mute;

yet, if it were to rely upon your doctrine, [it would not be so]. However, since this is not the case now, he states its contradiction with direct perception: "the sense-faculties, beginning with the eye," and so forth.
Of that mental activity (*manovṛtti*) which is the initiator of everything—whether accompanied by the eyes and other senses or directed toward distinct objects—[the Self is the cause].
"Even so" (*tathāpi*) means: even in the state of being an inherent cause (*samavāyitva*). And thus, for the Seer...
There would be a loss of purity. And if the Seer were indeed pure, then he points out the fault by that very same reasoning as well.
2. [This applies] in the case of relying upon your own doctrine.
3. He states the contradiction with direct perception regarding this matter: "of the sense organs, etc. (indriyādeḥ). 4.

Thus, in this way, the relationship should be applied through the primary and secondary status of both Paśyantī and Madhyamā; and if there were identity, it would be precisely the majesty of Paśyantī that would manifest.

In that case, even though there is the manifestation of duality due to the impurity of ignorance (*avidyā*), how is worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) possible, given that that light exists everywhere? Or rather, because of the power of ignorance, she does not perceive her own nature and remains in the state of *paśyantī*; instead, she is *madhyamā*, while [the state] of *paśyantī* is [otherwise].
Because there is no falling away from its own nature, it is not so; thus, in both cases, the accumulation of faults remains.
5. In the case of a perceptual appearance, [the mind would be like] one who is blind, mute, or deaf.
6. For it is only that which has been seen by the eye and other senses that the mind takes as the object of its conceptualization.
Just as in the case of the expression "the consonants beginning with ka" (kādīni vyañjanāni), the eye is also included by resorting to a *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna-bahuvrīhi* compound.
And being both sublated and useless, it will also be contradicted by direct perception. || 40 ||
Furthermore, reflecting on another point, he said:
"Is she seen situated within the body, outside it, or everywhere? (41)
Since she pervades the interior, what need is there for the intermediate [speech] (madhyamā) and so forth in the exterior?

Is Paśyantī within the body on the plane of the "I-maker" (ahaṃtā), or is she outside as well? She is present everywhere. In the former case, there would be limitation; in the second, it would belong to Madhyamā.

Since [the Word] exists in a state of pervasion even within the "girdle" (kakṣyā) consisting of this very object of knowledge, what is the use of the distinctions of speech in the forms of Madhyamā and Vaikharī? 41.
If she were dependent upon the expansion of nāda, bindu, and so forth, she would not be the Sovereign.

1. Thus, having first refuted the discourse of those who propound ignorance (avidyā) and having thereby precluded that the Madhyamā is its effect, [the author now states: "The Paśyantī, however, is undivided, with all succession withdrawn from it."
The light of one's own true nature is indeed the subtle, inseparable speech within.

Thus, regarding this definition which consists of two parts— namely, that "this very light of one's own nature" is the end— he introduces [an objection] for the purpose of pointing out a flaw with the words "furthermore, another," and so forth;
for even that [objection] does not deviate from being of that same nature.
3. *Kalpa* means "mode" or "manner.
4. Pervasion (*vyāpti*) is the following along [of one thing] by another even in other cases.
5. Now, this is indeed true: pervasion by the *paśyantī* level exists even in the *madhyamā* and other levels.

Because even the *paśyantī* depends upon mental discourse (*saṃjalpa*) and other factors, it receives designations such as *madhyamā* and so forth; for this very reason—that it is dependent—it is designated as *madhyamā*, but not by its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
He refutes the doubt that [this designation] might exist clearly by way of its own nature in the case of *paśyantī*.
By the words "anīśvarī" and so forth:
if the *paśyantī* [speech], while persisting, is dependent upon the *bindu* and *nāda* whose forms are *prāṇa* and *apāna*.
If it were to expand during creation and dissolution, even then it would not be all-pervasive nor non-dual;
this constitutes the state of being a non-Lord (anīśvaratva). || 42 ||
Is she distinct in each body, or does she abide as one everywhere?
If she is manifold, it is due to her distinctness; if she is one, there is equality of designation. (43)

If you maintain that the distinction [of the seer] is due to the bodies, then those bodies are unreal according to your position. Furthermore, that seeing [consciousness], being present in each body, must be either distinct in every body or one and the same in all bodies.
If it were distinct, there would be many seers, and consequently, there would be no non-duality (advaita); whereas if it were one, [non-duality would follow].

Because all embodied beings perceive [the sound] through a single [auditory] faculty, that specific sound— which arises from a particular location struck by the vital breath impelled by an effort preceded by that [perception]— would be produced even when the speaker is alone;
otherwise, it would not be uttered even when everyone else is silent.
In some cases, because it does not perform such an action, its unity would be lost due to the occurrence of a difference in its nature (*svabhāva*).

If it is argued that even though there is unity, the distinction is based on the body, like that of a crystal, that is not so; for in your own system, it is established that those [distinctions] are unreal (*asatya*). And that which is unreal is of no functional form whatsoever.
That is to say, it becomes useful in some cases. || 43 ||
She is well-characterized by the defining mark beginning with "undivided" (avibhāga) and so forth. 44.

1. This is indeed true: from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha), there is only oneness, and the absence of the state of being expressed by the same word occurs due to the difference in bodies; this is the intended meaning.
2. "Stability" (sthiti) refers to the rule of the scripture.
3. Just as a crystal gem, though unitary in its own nature, appears as distinct through the coloring of various dyes, so too does the Paśyantī [appear]; this is the meaning.
4. From which the process of the world evolves in the form of objects.
According to this principle:

[5] Now, who says that there are many [forms] in the state of difference, or that there is equality of words in the state of unity, since *paśyantī* is indeed indivisible? And likewise, what is this so-called "difference," and what is "unity"?
He states "avibhāga" and so forth, preceded by a counter-objection to the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), asserting that there is not even a grain of fault in [the view] that it is indeed so.
If Paśyantī were described by means of defining characteristics (lakṣaṇa), those would be inconsistent with her nature;
for Paśyantī is indeed without division, and in Paśyantī, all sequential order is withdrawn from every side.

If it is said that [the definition] is well-defined by such characteristics as being free from the faults of under-extension (*avyāpti*) and over-extension (*ativyāpti*), then this is a mockery, for it is "distinctly beautiful" (*vilakṣaṇa-mati-śobhana*) because it lacks that very characteristic which constitutes a proper definition.
Regarding this, he says:
"How could she be undivided, since she is traditionally said to be 'seeing'? (45)

Since this [Paśyantī] is traditionally defined as being oriented toward the objects of perception which are differentiated, how could it be undivided? For there is a mutual separation between the state of being the object of definition (lakṣya) and the state of being the defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa). || 45 ||
For instance, when one perceives [an object], does one perceive it as a whole, or by way of its own parts, such as form, direction, and time?

If the definition falls upon only a portion of the object to be defined (*lakṣya*), that is under-extension (*avyāpti*); if the definition falls upon what is not the object to be defined (*alakṣya*), that is over-extension (*ativyāpti*).

Pervasion (vyāpti). 2. "Distinct" (*vilakṣaṇa*) means having a specific characteristic (*viśiṣṭalakṣaṇa*) by way of irony; likewise, it is "contradictory in its true nature" (*paramārthato viruddhalakṣaṇa*), and thus "distinct" (*vilakṣaṇa*) in the sense of being shameful (*lajjāvaha*).

3. Regarding what was stated—that there is a separation between the word denoting the defined (*lakṣya*) and the word denoting the definition (*lakṣaṇa*), where the word for the defined is *paśyantī* and the word for the definition is "undivided" (*avibhāga*) and so forth—it is indeed the case that a definition is employed for the sake of establishing the defined; therefore, such a separation would, on the contrary, bring about contradiction. To this he says: "those which she sees," namely *paśyantī*.
For, being transitive, it necessarily implies some object; and if that object,
which is of the nature of the visible, relies upon the essential nature, location, and temporal portion of that visible entity, then—
since that visible [object] consists of right knowledge— the *paśyantī* you have accepted is indeed logical.

However, the meaning is that since there is an absence of defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇavigama*) therein— because it possesses divisions by way of the nature of those various perceived places and times— how can partlessness (*nirvibhāgatā*) be possible?
To establish the definition [of partlessness], he says again "not thus" (*atathā*), meaning "no."
