If it is argued that one perceives objects together with their own intrinsic natures, locations, and times— thereby avoiding the denial of non-differentiation— but that [the object] is actually devoid of those respective locations and times, then,
since the defined object (*lakṣya*) itself would be impossible even when its defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are absent, enough of that argument! For instance:
The meaning is that false cognition is indeed devoid of its own form, location, and time; because it is based upon that [false cognition], this [world] is also false.
If they perceive it as not being thus, they are said to perceive falsely.
If it perceives [objects] in such a manner, how could it be partless?
What does it perceive among the objects of sight—which it has set out to see—by means of its own respective portions of form, direction, and time? For this is logical; otherwise, it would not be so.

When she perceives through inversion, that perception is false (*tanmithyā*), being of the nature of ignorance; or rather, it is called "false perception" (*mithyā-paśyantī*) in the sense that it is a perception [based on error]. However, at that time, she would be undivided (*avibhaktā*) due to the absence of distinct objects of perception. Nevertheless, in accordance with the state of being *paśyantī*, she exists in her true, established form.

Or rather, it has been stated that if [the speech] perceives while not deviating from its own nature (*svarūpa*), how could it be undivided (*nirvibhāga*) when joined with distinct perceptible objects? Its own nature is indeed its own word (*svākya*).
1. Because of the designation "they see"; 2. [This refers] to each respective object of vision;
3. Because it is logical that this is indeed right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
4. Not by its own form, location, or time.
5. In the first rule, "false" (*mithyā*) is a separate word; in the second, it applies to the whole compound. In that case, the word *paśyantī* must be supplied for the second [rule].
5. "At that time" means at the time of perceiving the respective forms and other qualities of those various objects of perception.
7. For the *paśyantī* [level of speech], because its nature is light (*jyotis*), does not consist of the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) of false cognition.
8. In the word *svākya*, the suffix *ṣyañ* is used in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*).
How can they see that which is future and present as being in the future? (47)

The non-perception [of an object] in one direction or location when it is actually present in another direction or location is due to the fact that all cognizers experience within their own selves only those objects that are currently present in a suitable location. In that regard, an object yet to come—

The meaning is: how could that which is future and not yet reached be seen as being present in its state of presentness, such that it would be a vision in its true form? Likewise, the meaning is: how could there be a vision in the form of right vision when one situated in a location suitable for another perceives what is situated in a location suitable for someone else?

Likewise, when an object exists in a different direction, location, or time, there is no perception of it by means of a cognition directed toward a different direction, location, or time. Therefore, how could [perception], while seeing only that which is present and situated in a suitable location,
see that which is future, not yet arrived, and situated in another location?
And that [cognition] is held to be all-seeing; here, place and time serve as mutual indicators for one another.
Now, as for what was stated previously:
"Action mounted upon the present is declared to be *paśyantī*."

Thus, he supports that [point]. Likewise, as for what was said—how it can be "undivided" when grasping its own form and so on—it is because it grasps an object that is yet to be as if it were present;
and therefore, since the perceived object appears precisely as transcending its own form and so on, and because it is attached to that [perceiver], it is not [divided].

He refutes the argument that "the nature of Paśyantī will be established as free from the two defects of being divisible and possessing false cognition; therefore, enough with this talk of 'false-falsity'," by stating "it will be [refuted] by the words beginning with 'bhaviṣyantīm'" and so forth.
2. The meaning is that the perception of something not yet attained as being present is an error. 3. The word "no" (na) should also be applied here.
4. Therefore, even in this case where there is a designation of time—namely, that the future is present—it is exactly the same.
The location (*deśa*) is also to be understood. The meaning is that in the mention of "going to another direction and location," there is also a mention of time (*kāla*).
Then he perceives some such common knowledge as that. || 48 ||

Nevertheless, through the differentiation of that [reality], there is the state of being differentiated; yet, due to its non-differentiation, nothing at all would be grasped. Likewise, it is otherwise when the sequence has been withdrawn. (49)

She perceives cognitions as being indeed distinct, each grasping an object differentiated by place and time; yet, subsequent to these determinate cognitions of blue, yellow, and so forth that are currently perceived, there exists some indeterminate [entity] common to them all, which is capable of the activity of manifesting the entire proliferation of those various cognitions.
The meaning is that it perceives all; that is, it sees everything.

Nevertheless, because specific cognitions of blue and so forth—which are restricted to particular objects—are distinct, that [universal] would also possess distinction, that is, the state of being divided, rather than universality, since it is non-different from them. And this being the case, it is not...
"Is it something like 'the future' and so forth?

To this he replies: "This is indeed a specific cognition, insofar as there is here a designation of time such as 'will be' and so on; however, the *paśyantī* is of a general nature, and [such designations] do not apply to it."

Anticipating the objection that even designations such as "will be" are possible, and therefore the vision of reality— being untouched by time— is not the ravings of one who does not know the supreme intention [of the Lord], he says: "Now,
that which is common."
2. Here, there is an ellipsis of the words *yat* and *tat*; that is, "that which is such knowledge, that very thing one perceives.
3. [It is] devoid of specific qualities such as blue or yellow, unrestricted, and all-pervasive.
Even regarding this position that it is "knowledge," he raises an objection with the words "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*) and so forth.
While it is indeed true that there exists a common knowledge, he says "nevertheless" to show that what is perceived here is specifically qualified.
4. Among those with different cognitions;
5. because it lacks distinction, it is unfit for designation;
6. nevertheless, let this be something common to all, capable of enduring everything.
And it is pervasive; here, the definition of the nature of Paśyantī must be accomplished in every respect.

Since that [definition] is dependent upon an object (*karman*), it necessarily implies an object in the form of the visible for its own establishment, because perception of them is possible only as specific forms (*viśeṣarūpatvena*) within her—this is the meaning.
7. From those particulars, [there arises the cognition] of that universal.
8. He explains the portion of the meaning regarding "due to its non-difference" with the words "and thus. This is the point:
even when a qualified cognition arises, if that [universal] is common [to all], then, due to its non-difference from that...

Even when a distinguished cognition arises, because there is an absence of specific qualities such as the past or the future, there can be no perception of the future; therefore, what indeed could be called "the visible" in this context?

It might be argued that *paśyantī*, being inseparable from the knowledge of future objects, will grasp them at that very moment. Alternatively, this *paśyantī* possesses differentiation (*bhedatā*), just like the cognitions of blue, yellow, and so forth,
because it too is variegated by future and present objects such as blue and the like.

Now, if there were no variegation consisting of the future and so forth for that [Paśyantī], but rather an absolute non-differentiation due to its being of the nature of pure consciousness alone, then, because of that non-differentiation, nothing such as "blue" or the like would be apprehended by it;
consequently, how could it be Paśyantī? Alternatively, they hold that Paśyantī is differentiated from others by a different characteristic.
"With the sequence withdrawn" (saṃhṛtakrama). || 49 ||
In this [state] called "the process of withdrawal" (saṃhṛtakrama), the Supreme Withdrawer arises.
By what means is this process withdrawn—whether within oneself or elsewhere? || 50 ||

If the self were to possess sequential movement, it would involve conjunction with another [self] elsewhere. Was it previously possessed of sequence? If so, the consequence follows that there would be a duality of forms. (51)
Nevertheless, by means of that distinction,
nothing at all— beginning with "ityādi"— would be apprehended.
He connects [the passage] ending with "thus" to the second sense by means of the words "or rather," etc.
[The phrase] "due to the absence of action" is the meaning.
[This refers to] those who maintain the doctrine of Śabdabrahman.

But surely, it has been said that "the Visionary [speech] (paśyantī) is that in which sequence is withdrawn," and thus the very withdrawal of sequence is the cause of its partless nature (*nirvibhāgatva*). Consequently, what is this notion [of yours]:
that because there is a difference among the specific, determinate, and unique cognitions of blue and so forth, there must also be a difference in that [Visionary speech]?
To crush that [notion], he says:

"For withdrawal depends on a triad—namely, the agent, the instrument, and the locus. He states that very point in sequence with the word "the withdrawer" (*saṃhartā*). Since there is the expectation of "by what?", it must necessarily be by the Supreme (*para*).
In response to the expectation “in what?”, [it is said]:
“the sequence is withdrawn into this. The word “thus” (evam) should be applied as having a displaced position [in the verse]. Thus...

If the *bahuvrīhi* compound is taken in the sense of the locative (*saptamī*), then another meaning as the agent of withdrawal (*saṃhartṛ*) must be sought here; thus, it is contradictory. Alternatively, if it is taken in the sense of the instrumental (*tṛtīyā*), [it means] "by which [power], namely Paśyantī, the sequence was withdrawn. And so, when there is a requirement for a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), [it follows that...]

Is it withdrawn into the Self, or elsewhere? This is the dilemma. If it were withdrawn into the Self through the application of a sequence, that [Self] would possess succession. If it were elsewhere, there would be a connection with a second entity, and from that, the consequence of duality would follow. Or, if it were indeed within the Self, having first existed as possessing succession, and subsequently...

Sequence is withdrawn and set aside, and not otherwise, for that would entail the fallacy of duality; nevertheless, there remains the consequence of a duality consisting of the forms of sequence and non-sequence. || 51 ||
"How could she be without division, since she is traditionally said to 'see'?"—

regarding this, the opponent raises an objection, challenging the claim of her being without division by pointing out that, precisely because she is *paśyantī* (the "seeing" state), she must depend upon the act of seeing as its instrument (*karaṇa*). [4]
Then, perceiving herself as her own self without differentiation, she [realizes that] in the case of a partial aspect, due to its nature as an instrument, there is dependence and insentience. (52)
Beholding herself by herself alone, she remains undifferentiated;
that is to say, she exists as having emerged from any distinct or entirely separate part, remaining merely as the power of action, instrumentality, and so forth. Even there, in that second part—
Because it possesses the nature of instruments and so forth within the self that is the power of the agent, that very [power] would result in dependence and insentience;
for it is precisely due to its autonomy that it has the nature of consciousness. This should be examined in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*. 52.
1. The word "in this" (*asyām*) should be supplied immediately after [the preceding term].
2. Contradiction with one's own statement (*svavacanavirodha*) is *vyāghāta* (self-contradiction). 3. This occurs when resorting to a *bahuvrīhi* compound in the sense of the third case.

4. He raises an objection regarding the very nature of Paśyantī— which was refuted by the passage beginning with "the state of being undivided" (nirvibhāgatva)— as it is now being supported by the opponent through the argument that it itself possesses the form of object, instrument, and so forth.
The opponent says: Just as Devadatta kills himself by means of himself, so [is it here].
In this and that [instance], there will be for him a division by means of his own limbs alone.
For the hand and so forth possess the status of instrument (karaṇatva), while the head and so forth possess the status of object (karmatā);
the mind is the agent (kartā) as its own constituent part. But this [is not the case] for that which is formless. (54)
It might be argued that just as there is a distinction of action and so forth within Devadatta himself, so too would it be here; but this is not so.
For Devadatta, being corporeal and having an extended form, possesses a division [of parts] consisting of his own many limbs which are themselves designated by the word "self. To explain:

The hand or another limb equipped with a weapon and so forth possesses the status of an instrument (*karaṇatā*); the head, heart, or other parts being struck possess the status of the object (*karmatā*); and the agent (*kartā*) is one's own self (*ātman*) conjoined with the mind, who is said to be the whole (*avayavī*) connected with the hand and other limbs, precisely because the nature of the self extends only that far.

Furthermore, for the Seer (paśyantī), who is formless by virtue of being pure consciousness (cinmātra) and thus lacks extension, this conventional usage based on parts does not apply; consequently, if one were to assign portions of her as the instruments (karaṇa) and so forth, she would necessarily fall into insentience (jaḍatā). || 54 ||
"Seeing the unseen self, or seeing [it], how can there be the state of being seen?
Thus, having established the insentience of the portion "by the self" (ātmanā) due to its dependence on another, she now analyzes the objective portion "the self" (ātmānam).

Seeing her own very nature as the Self, which exists merely as the power in the form of action (*karma-rūpa-śakti*), she perceives it while abiding in the power in the form of the agent (*kartṛ-rūpa-śakti*), by means of which the purpose of her act of seeing is accomplished. Here, the term "by the Seer" (*paśyantyā*) is to be applied to both [the preceding and following clauses] according to the maxim of the lamp on the threshold (*dehalī-dīpinyāya*). Therein, by the Seer...

The meaning is that "vision" (darśana) is the state of having seen, which has that [seeing] as its function; whereas in the second case, "vision by the Seer" (paśyantyā darśanam) means vision whose agent is the Seer (paśyantī).
Since the power of action (karma-śakti) is nothing other than one's own essential nature (nijarūpa), there is the state of not having been seen (adṛṣṭatā).
The meaning is: how can there be a lack of luminosity, which is the absence of the act of seeing?
72) For the seeing by the *paśyantī* [speech] is not logically possible through that which has been seen. || 55 ||
When she perceives herself, does she perceive what was never before seen, or what has already been seen?

Neither of these two is tenable; for since she who perceives is of the nature of light, there can be no "unseen-ness" in her—that is, no lack of luminosity—and once the Self has been seen, it cannot be seen again.

The engagement in the act of seeing is logical; however, the self of the seer is not different at every moment, such that it would exist as present through the application of the act of seeing at each successive instant, nor is there any spatial or temporal limitation of that self. || 55 ||
When it sees, does that [consciousness] see itself or something insentient?
If it sees something insentient, its own insentience follows; for if it sees [itself], there is an infinite regress. (56)

And since that [consciousness] is of the nature of light and is essentially the seer, does it see the self as a seer, or as something non-luminous and insentient? If it were insentient, then she too would be insentient; yet, because the self is of the nature of light, it sees her, and she does not see it as something separate.
1. And the word *vā* (or) here has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned. 2.
For it is logical that there should be seeing of that which is unseen; moreover, being unseen is inconsistent with the state of being *paśyantī*, because she is *paśyantī*.

3. Now, suspecting that [the opponent] might argue that perception itself perceives [the object] due to constraint, he says: "perceived" (dṛṣṭa). 4. For in that case, there would be an infinite regress (anavasthā). 5. He states that the word "and" (ca) implies an unexpressed collection of meanings, and he explains that which was said: [The opponent argues: "If it is argued that the cognition of the cognition is established by the very fact that the object is perceived, then we reply: no, because that [cognition] is not perceived. For if the cognition were perceived, then its cognition too would have to be perceived, and so on; thus, an infinite regress would result. Furthermore, the word 'and' indicates an unexpressed collection of reasons, such as the impossibility of simultaneous cognitions and the lack of a means of knowing that [infinite series]."
"Mounted upon the present" means that one conceptualizes even that present portion, or does not;
he states what is conjoined by the word "or" with "nor.
In the preceding verse, "visibility" is the fitness for the act of seeing, and that—

While [the capacity for action] is possible even in the absence of consciousness itself, here, however, he shows that consciousness alone is being considered as the basis for its support, by means of the phrase "She [sees] him who sees"; this is what he expresses with the words:
"because it is of the nature of light and because it consists of the state of Paśyantī."
But even if it were to rest upon itself, then because that too would involve the aforementioned conceptualization, there would be an infinite regress,
since there would be no cessation of the process of abiding through the repose of perception. || 56 ||
If one perceives even the slightest thing, that would follow from our own philosophical position;
for if it were an object, there would be dependence upon another within its very own self. (57)

Or, if you do not see any other gross, differentiated entity such as blue or yellow as an object of sight, but rather see only the seer— who has not entered the state of being an object— as something subtle, non-conceptual, and non-distinct in form, yet you do not truly see him.
Being of the very nature of the seer whose object is the visible, she shines forth as "Paśyantī" (the Visionary).
Consequently, there would be conformity with our own [logical] view; the meaning of Paśyantī would be abandoned as consisting of the divisions of action, agent, object, and time. But in reality...
If it were admitted that [the self] is an object, then, since there exists a substratum in the form of the self which is its subtle observer, there would result a contradiction:
dependence as being an object of perception would exist in that very same single self which is independent as the perceiver. || 57 ||
For either the *paśyantī* is indeed the *sphoṭa*, or it is something other than that; there must be one of these two possibilities.
Whether it is distinct from it or identical to it, [it would be perceived] by means of the form of the tip of a finger. (58)
1. According to the principle that "there is no seeing of what has already been seen";

2. and it has already been stated that this [seeing] would cause the destruction of the very root; 3. But surely, one who sees the self is subtle, yet remains unsullied by the stains of conceptual construction?
If one asks, "Since it sees that [object], what is the problem?"—for there would indeed be an infinite regress;
and since seeing is of the nature of an action belonging precisely to one who has not abandoned the state of being a seer, there is nothing at all that is untenable even from that perspective.
So why point out this fault? To this he says: "something."

"Something" (kiñcit) is indeterminate precisely because it is the very nature [of consciousness] and is therefore incapable of being designated as "this-ness" (idantā). 4. It is devoid of the distinction between the grasped and the grasper.
5. *Anvaya* means acceptance or admission.

But surely, since it is said that "they see," and because this [seeing] possesses an object, it clearly follows—as before—that it must have something visible; so why is there no fault in that case? To this, he says: "And not," and so forth.
7. And thus, this being the case, there is no contradiction whatsoever; such is the meaning. 8. He says, "They perceive," because this is not accepted by you [the opponents].
9. Sound (*śabda*) whose very essence is *sphoṭa* is what conveys the meaning. And so it has been said:
By the force of the sentence here, truthfulness is obtained, not particularity;
[it is] one, eternal, devoid of succession, and that which is imagined as the unreal portion.
The sentence-sphoṭa produces a cognition regarding its own denotation of that nature;
these phonemes, however, being naturally fleeting and established solely in conceptual construction,
do not produce a cognition regarding that object— so enough with such talk.

For they say "tathā hi" (for instance): from what [source] do letters derive their capacity to convey meaning? For those letters, such as *ga* and so forth, when conveying an object, are they either collective (*samasta*) or individual (*vyasta*)? First, they are not individual, because when each letter is heard one by one, the cognition of the object does not arise. As for collectivity...
Furthermore, it is simply not possible for that [word] to exist in the phonemes themselves, for it would have to exist as a reality, and that is untenable. To explain:
because the speakers of the phonemes do not abandon the sequence of effort, place, and articulatory organ, a sequence necessarily occurs. And in that sequence...

For if it were so, the comprehension of meaning would result from each individual phoneme as a cause, and yet that is not observed; thus, because the alternatives of [the phonemes being causes] either individually or collectively are untenable, the phonemes are not the expressers [of meaning]. The cognitions whose objects are the phonemes should be conceived in the same way; they too cannot occur simultaneously. And in the case of succession—
Otherwise, it would follow that there is a comprehension of the meaning from the cognition of each individual phoneme; therefore, the phonemes are not the expressers [of meaning].
Moreover, if they were so, even those employed in a reversed order would convey that meaning. Yet, this comprehension of the meaning occurs from the sound as it is uttered. It does not.
This [cognition] must indeed be without a cause; therefore, its cause is the *sphoṭa*.

Since it is postulated in every way on the basis of the effect characterized by the comprehension of meaning, that cause is called the *sphoṭa*. And it is partless, eternal, unitary, and devoid of parts. Therefore, it is manifested by the phonemes (*varṇas*).

The *sphoṭa* brings about the comprehension of the meaning. People are deluded, thinking that this comprehension of meaning is produced by the phonemes (*varṇa*). Nor should it be said that even in the manifestation of the *sphoṭa*, those alternatives of being [perceived] individually or collectively exist; for there are no such alternatives regarding the manifestation of the *sphoṭa*. To explain: some...

Regarding this, they explain as follows: at the moment of hearing the first phoneme, the *sphoṭa* is manifested. Nor is there any deficiency in the second and subsequent phonemes, because it is precisely through their successive apprehension that an intensification of its manifestation occurs; just as in the examination of a gem, the first sight of it reveals the gem as already shining with purity.
Just as the true nature of a gem shines forth as faultless through repeated examination,
so too, although the *sphoṭa* is manifested by the hearing of the first phoneme, subsequent phonemes are employed for the sake of a clearer perception.
Others, however, say that the sounds (*dhvani*) themselves are the manifestors of the *sphoṭa*, and by them...

This partless *sphoṭa*, being manifested by the vital airs (*marut*), appears as if it were associated with various parts such as the letter *ga* and others, due to the superimposition caused by the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) of the conjunctions between the places of articulation and the organs, such as the palate. Of the vital airs—
Because they perish as soon as they are uttered due to their flickering nature, these conceptual parts appear [as such].
75) Or rather, the investigation into whether [a speaker] is authoritative or non-authoritative ceases altogether. 59.

You have accepted both the *sphoṭa* and the *paśyantī* as being eternal; therefore, either the *sphoṭa* itself must be the *paśyantī*, since there is no difference in their nature as sound (*śabda*), or it must be something other than it, in which case duality would result.
If the position of their difference is abandoned and their identity is accepted, then that [identity] belongs to the *paśyantī*.

The state of perceiving the true meaning would be attained. However, through this perception of a sentence-sphoṭa— such as "a herd of hundreds of elephants stands on the tip of a finger"— one does not attain in this world a distinction for every sphoṭa from a sentence regarded as true, by virtue of its being of the nature of the perception of truth known as *paśyantī*.
But in the view that they are distinct, there is no fault in the fact that even though the *sphoṭa* is real, its object is unreal;
for it is observed that sound consists of *nāda*, while the nature of the *paśyantī* is pure consciousness (*saṃvit*).
It attains diversity through the distinctions of manifesting agents, such as the lute, flute, drum, kettle-drum, and so forth.

Therefore, since words do not exist within the sentence and word-meanings do not exist within the sentence-meaning, both the sentence and the sentence-meaning are partless (*niravayava*). Furthermore, there is a subverting argument against the postulation of parts here, as follows:

Sentences have parts which are words, and words have parts which are phonemes; likewise, phonemes must also have parts, and those parts must have further parts, and so on. Due to this infinite regress, what final determination could there be?

If, however, one must desist from the conceptualization of parts after reaching the phonemes (*varṇas*), then let one desist at the sentence itself. Thus, like a beverage (*pānaka*) and the like, the meaning of the sentence is the *sphoṭa*, which is indeed something other than the word-meanings. For just as a beverage is a distinct entity from the molasses, coconut, black pepper, and so forth [that compose it].
And just as it is established that a painting is indeed something other than the vermilion, lac, yellow orpiment, and so forth [that compose it], so too is this [the sphoṭa] established.
In that regard, if there were a difference between those two—the sphoṭa and the Brahman of sound—there would be the consequence of duality.
They state their non-difference as follows: "Just as phonemes do not exist within a word, nor do words exist within sentences."
Likewise, there would be no intermediate sentences within the great sentences;

for that reason, even the great sentences would not exist in relation to their respective contexts; and for that reason, even the contexts would not exist in relation to the scripture. Consequently, this [scripture] would be nothing but a single whole.
When it is objected that the reality of the treatise (*śāstratattva*) results in a non-dual, undifferentiated state, they reply as follows: "This is true;

this very *śabdabrahman* (the Word-Brahman), which is non-dual, undergoes a transformation (*vivarta*) into the appearance of various objects due to the influence of beginningless impressions of ignorance (*avidyāvāsanā*), thereby appearing with distinctions. However, there is no such thing as a denoted object (*vācya*) that exists as something separate from the denoting word (*vācaka*)."

Therefore, this distinction between the signified and the signifier is purely conceptual; such is the doctrine of *sphoṭa*. He demonstrates its untenability with the words "or, if there were identity" (*tadaikye vā*).
[This is] because of the acceptance of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Seeing that falsity is indeed a defect because the *sphoṭa* is the true meaning through its unity,
the investigation into whether [the words] were composed by a reliable person (*āpta*) or not composed by a reliable person ceases altogether at that time.
Because all [of them] are equally of the nature of the Perfect (samyak), just as there was previously mentioned a plurality of Paśyantī, there would likewise be a plurality of eternal sphoṭas;
consequently, this too is indicated here: that it would result in the loss of non-duality (advaya). || 59 ||
For how could the sphoṭa be manifested by words and the like, which are unreal in nature?
Nor can that which is real in form, such as the Paśyantī level, be manifested by what is unreal. (60)

That [sphoṭa], which is dependent on such phonemes (*vyañjana*), does not arise at all; for the sphoṭa is immutable, eternal, and real, whereas the words, letters, and sounds are adventitious, devoid of its own nature, incapable, and of an entirely different class.
How could there be suggestiveness (*vyaṅgyatā*) [of the sphoṭa], since its capacity to manifest truth would entail that it itself is true?
Furthermore, even if the sphoṭa is of the nature of the *paśyantī* level, it is likewise not logical for it to have unreal manifestors;
for it would be like form manifested by light that is itself unreal and of the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*).

By virtue of its power of manifestation, nothing at all exists; it would be merely ignorance (avidyā) itself, for it is on the basis of taking that which has the form of phenomenal proliferation (prapañca) to be ignorance that this is so.
Or, by what means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is this [self] established when it is being perceived? || 61 ||
Because it is not within the scope of perception, inference has been thoroughly refuted.

For the authority of a word lies in its being composed by a reliable person (āpta), and the Sphoṭa possesses this quality of being composed by a reliable person due to its eternity; whereas the word consisting of phonemes (varṇa) is non-eternal.

This [phoneme] is not the cause for the cognition of meaning, and therefore it is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, that word which is the cause for the cognition of meaning—the *sphoṭa*—is neither impermanent nor produced by a reliable person (*āpta*). Thus, if one accepts the *sphoṭa*, the entire distinction between the speech of reliable and unreliable persons would surely collapse.
2. By this investigation:

3. An entity must indeed be established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); it need not [be established] by its own nature or its definition, because it is firmly established by that very means of valid cognition. Thus, it is the means of valid cognition itself [that establishes it].
This is further reinforced by the passage beginning with "whether one conceptualizes or perceives," and so forth.
It is precisely by you that it is not established that an authoritative person speaks of things never before experienced.

By what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which you perceive established by you? First of all, perception (*pratyakṣa*) does not exist here, because it transcends the range of the eyes and other [senses] as well as the mind. Furthermore, since you yourself have refuted it through [the argument beginning with] "the state" (*avasthā*) and so forth, inference (*anumāna*) is not a correct means of comprehension.
Even for a trustworthy person, there is no speaking of an object not previously experienced; therefore, that too is not a means of valid cognition.
Now, observe her who perceives by means of her own experience alone through reasoning:
in that case, she [the perceiver] becomes the object for another [perceiver]. (63)

For he who sees that which sees is considered the supreme deity. Now, you say to me: "See her by means of your own internal experience as the authority, seeing her through reasoning, through yoga, through meditative absorption, and through attentiveness. If that is so, then for another...
The Paśyantī [speech] becomes the object of the means of valid cognition known as self-experience (*svānubhava*);

consequently, it would not be accepted as the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), because at that time, it is precisely that [self-experience] which has reached its highest limit and is considered by you all to be the deity, existing with supreme excellence.
It might be that one perceives even that all-seeing [nature], and from that follows the abandonment of seeing.
1. The meaning is that even a trustworthy person speaks only of an object that has been experienced.
2. This is stated in the *Paśyantīviveka*.
3. That includes the speech of a trustworthy person as well.
But surely, when a reality is protected by the most firm means of valid cognition known as direct experience, there is no need for any other means of valid cognition— such as perception—
which is directed toward external objects and is ignorant of even a trace of the internal nature of things.
He supports [this] with the words "Now, by one's own experience," and so forth. (5) [The opponent says:
"The proponent of the previous position has accepted me, the proponent of the subsequent position, as having attained suchness, which is the ultimate reality. (6)
7. That very thing is one's own direct experience.
8. He demonstrates its preeminence over all else with the words "He who [attains] that...
Whatever [cognition] is called "intuition" (pratibhā), that too is not inference for you. 64.
Nor can there be any occasional waiting for that which is to be established.

Furthermore, if intuition (*pratibhā*) were the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) when it perceives [an object], then the manifestation of that intuition would be without a cause; like the thought "there is water in the well," it would not be a valid cognition. Alternatively, it is simply the persistence of the self.
[This is] distinct from other types of perception.

1. Regarding this, some say that intuitive perception (*pratibhā-pratyakṣa*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And thus, there exists even for people like us some knowledge of the future in certain cases.
For my intuitive perception was the means of valid cognition [that proved] yesterday that "my brother will come."
Let this be accepted as a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa), provided it is not produced by something useless, not doubtful, not sublated, and does not have a perceptible cause [for its falsity].
If there is sublation in some cases, let that [cognition] be invalid;
but where one encounters [the same object] on the following day, what can be said of that?
To loosen this [objection], he says: "Or that which is called intuition (*pratibhā*).

Here, the word "or" (*vā*) clearly indicates that this is not graspable through direct sensory perception (*pratyakṣa-anubhava*). Thus, this cognition is not born from an object, because its cause—the brother—was non-existent at that time. Now, it might be argued that one perceives him by means of his being imagined (*bhāvitayā*).

It apprehends. In that case, apprehension by means of what has been cultivated is indeed untenable, for "being cultivated" (bhāvitva) means prior non-existence; and what connection can there be between non-existence and existence? If you think that there is the intuition "there is water in the well," and thus there is no suspicion of it being produced from a future object, then—

He also refutes the claim that it is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by stating "without a cause" (*nirnimittam*). And since this [cognition] consists of doubt, if it were said that [the object] is not experienced at that time, then—just as one might wonder, "Is this silver or is it not silver?"—there would be no such perception;
rather, there is the cognition "this is silver. For ordinary people do not act while in a state of doubt, but rather [they act] because...
Since they are indeed determining the object, why would doubt be superimposed upon what is being experienced?

Furthermore, even though this cognition grasps one side [of the alternatives], it falls into the category of doubt precisely because of the absence of a means for certain determination; thus, it is entirely without cause [for being called a certainty].

2. For if this [scripture] were apprehended as being a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), how could it ever be contradicted? But if it were apprehended as not being a valid means of knowledge, it would cause a person to act.
3. Having stated the sublation [of scripture] in the case of its being perception (*pratyakṣa*), he now supports the position of the proponent of inference (*anumāna*) with the word "now" (*atha*).

(79) When there is the intuition (*pratibhā*) that "he speaks thus to me," since that [intuition] consists in a specific state of one's own being, its apprehension of another object through the ascertainment of non-deviation from what is to be proven is nothing other than inference (*anumāna*); and that...
This is undesirable for you; furthermore, if there is no certainty regarding non-deviation, there is a lack of informative power (*anavagamakatva*).

By the force of reasoning, experience might occasionally occur, or there might be an intuition (*pratibhā*), as in the case of one being instructed by a reliable person (an *āpta*) to "see the seeing" (*paśyantīm paśya*); however, this does not happen at all times. Consequently, that [intuition] is interrupted.
There would be a mere perception [of it], not its constant manifestation; nor is this considered to be a waiting for that specific time.
If she perceives herself by means of her own self, then she will exist. || 65 ||
In that case, what has come of the object to be established by its own perception?
One must say that it too perceives that which perceives itself. (66)

This is the meaning: Just as, for instance, upon seeing smoke on a mountain or similar place, there is a certain determination of fire as a distinct object because smoke is non-deviant [from fire], whereas no such comprehension of the object occurs in the case of a lake and so forth due to the observation of deviation; likewise, by means of a distinct state of self-abiding (*ātmasthiti*), [the same result follows].
Some have placed [the intuition] within the category of inference based on intuition (*pratibhānumāna*), thinking that it perceives the non-deviation from the object to be accomplished;
others hold that intuition is an occasional experience. For you, however, the *paśyantī* is accepted as having the nature of being eternally manifest.
There is a contradiction.
4. Of that Paśyantī.
5. Now, we do not maintain that Paśyantī is to be established by means of an occasional experience.

It is accepted that [the object] appears as the very object of experience by means of the subject's own self-luminous nature as the experiencer; otherwise, because it would be occasional, there would follow the defect of impermanence and so forth in the vision of the Paśyantī level, which is characterized by interrupted perception. Rather, it appears precisely as the object of experience through its being manifested by the self-manifesting experiencer.

Seeing, she sees. And by the words "at that time" and so forth, he also refutes the notion that there is merely a constant state of being manifest. Likewise, she reflects upon herself by means of her own self; however, the designation "Paśyantī" (the Visionary) is used only with respect to those who are to be instructed, and not from its own side.
And here he establishes that there is a designation of action;
(6) because it manifests itself;
(7) for an instruction, being something that must necessarily be stated, is characterized as a mandate (*vidhi*). It...

And it has the characteristic of making known what was previously unknown; for when something is already known by oneself, there is no need for further description or discourse on instruction from another.
Even though it knows itself, it nevertheless possesses the status of an object.

If it is thought that the seeing [of perception] does not perceive by means of an experience (*anubhava*) or the like, but rather sees its own self through itself— not through a distinct experience— then:

This being the case, what unprecedented task is there for you, the teachers, to perform for the one to be instructed (*pratipādya*), since she manifests that [reality] by herself? However, you, who are true teachers, must necessarily state this for the one to be instructed: "You have not previously seen *paśyantī*."
Behold: although she perceives herself by herself, nevertheless, with respect to the experience of the one to whom she communicates, she remains an object (*karman*) just as before;
for she is limited by the recipient, and because the *paśyantī* [speech] intended by others is not eternal (*acyuta*).

She could only be perceived through a limited experience characterized by the state of duality; however, at that time, there is no unity of the object to be conveyed, the conveyor, and the *paśyantī* consciousness, by which [unity] she would not fall into the status of being an object (*karmatā*). And thus, if she were to fall into the status of being an object, her self-luminosity (*svayaṃ-prakāśatā*) would be impaired; therefore, once again...

The *pradhāna* would then be nothing but its illuminator. Even though illumination is non-distinct from it, it becomes impure due to the embrace of the stage of *vivarta*, [as expressed in the phrase] "behold her who sees herself by herself. This belongs to the nature of the *paśyantī* state.
1. If what was stated—“Now, behold her as she perceives by means of her own experience through reasoning”—is intended to convey this meaning; 2.
[then it is] by those who are dependent on other conditions.
3. Of that which is to be instructed;
4. For instruction does not proceed toward what is already seen;
5. Of one who is seeing.
6. "Behold her who beholds; perceive her through your own experience"—thus, it becomes quite clear that Paśyantī functions as the object (karman).
7. But surely, since Paśyantī is itself of the nature of self-perception, how could she [be an object] in any way?

"How can it be called 'action' (karman) as before, when it does not touch even a trace of the residual impressions (saṃskāra) of action? To this he replies with the words "by the object to be conveyed" (*pratipādyena*), etc., because in that [previous state] there was dependence (*pāratantrya*), whereas here there is autonomy (*svātantrya*). Now, also by another method: "Behold her who sees by means of her own experience alone."

[The author] connects [the argument] with the words "not distinct" (*avyatirikta*) and so forth. By saying, "Behold the Self of that [world] by means of the Self," he thus supports the point that there is neither the status of being an object (*karmatā*) nor the futility of the instruction, because of the embrace of the ground of phenomenal appearance (*vivarta*).
By such statements [as these]:
"In this [system], the object to be communicated is unreal, and the communicator is unreal" (67).

The teaching of that which is unreal is examined by means of the unreal. In this philosophical system, the entire phenomenal expansion (prapañca) consisting of the object to be communicated and so forth is seen to be entirely unreal; therefore, how can there be the establishment of the "Visionary" (paśyantī), or for whom, or by what means?
By means of valid cognition.
The truthfulness of that by which it is established as valid is [itself] established. || 68 ||
If that [perception] were real, then both would be real; if it were unreal, then neither would be.

Alternatively, if the reality of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by which that [perception] is established is accepted, then the reality of both—the *paśyantī* [speech] and its means of valid cognition—would follow. If the means of valid cognition were unreal, [then neither would be].
Something would have to exist as something established.
By the utterance of the word "sādhu," who attains union with heaven and other such realms? (69)

If the state of being ignorance belongs to the Visionary [level] because of its connection with the tendency toward enjoyment, then what [use] is the variegated enjoyment for the insentient Middle [level] and those below it? (70)
But surely, even the one who is to be instructed is *paśyantī*; even the instructor is unreal and is indeed *paśyantī*; even the instruction is unreal and is indeed *paśyantī*;
and even the examiner of its true nature is unreal and is indeed *paśyantī*—so what is there for another [to do] here?

If it is asked, "What is to be said?"—the meaning is that this very point must be stated once again for the sake of further justification: "In that case, all of this has turned out to be nothing but false; enough with your senseless prattle!
Thus he speaks according to the principle that when a specific negation is made, there is an implied admission of the general.
"Perceiving [it] as something distinct" (paśyantyatirikta) refers to the investigation of *paśyantī*. "Of that means of valid cognition" (*tasya pramāṇasya*) [refers to the aforementioned].
That too is certainly undesirable.
Therefore, what is incorrect becomes correct when it bestows the fruit of the science of grammar (śabdavidyā).
In this way, for you as well, the very continuity of grammatical exposition comes to an end.

The grammarians have stated that the employment of correct words (*sādhuśabda*) results in heaven and liberation; for it is said: "A single word employed according to the scriptures becomes a cow of plenty (*kāmadhuk*) in the heavenly world. Likewise: "Those men in whom virtuous speech (*sādhvī vāk*) is predominantly established..."
Within them, there exists an abundance of the Prajāpati’s merit.
The great splendor belonging to Prajāpati is enveloped by those very subtle elements;
upon the dissolution of the body, it rushes toward its own source for the wise.
Thus, for whom would that fruit called heaven belong? If it belongs to the one who is the agent of the employment of words, then,
because the conscious power (paśyantī) perceives with the desire for that fruit, it would become impure through contact with ignorance (avidyā) due to its orientation toward the enjoyment of heaven.

In the state of *madhyamā* and *vaikharī*, activity proceeds with a primary orientation toward attaining what is desirable and avoiding what is undesirable, based on the perception of the agreeable and disagreeable. That is not so; for the determination of objects is grounded in the ultimate subject (*pāramārthika-pramātṛ*), and since that [subject], when existing in the state of duality, possesses differentiation through the intermediate stages such as *madhyamā*.

Because it is insentient due to its nature being variegated by ignorance (*avidyā*), there is no enjoyment whatsoever for one established in the state of ultimate reality; the meaning is that such [an experience] would not even be considered enjoyment. Therefore, the correctly employed word is the giver of the fruits of the science of grammar, such as enjoyment, whereas [the fruit] of *paśyantī* is, on the contrary, [liberation].

By rendering it impure, it would become ungrammatical and inauspicious; and thus, because it produces such [evil] results, even your own grammar—being as described—would be utterly ruined and fit only to be rejected. || 71 ||
What is the use of seeking after consciousness while abandoning the state of a grammarian?
(1) It is excellent when accompanied by the refinement of proficiency in grammar.
(2) By those very [words] alone, it is concealed and hidden.
3. At the moment of death;
4. through the pursuit of right knowledge.
Not only has this been stated here by you without relevance to the subject at hand.
The manifestation of consciousness has been illustrated in the investigation [of reality].

Having abandoned the status of a grammarian— which consists merely in the function of the instruction of correct words as the cause for the comprehension of meaning— one should instead pursue those things whose purpose is liberation.
That right knowledge which is to be followed through the treatises is [attained] by seeking that [knowledge]; [this is] not for the sake of an irrelevant introduction.
Now, is it not the case that the primary purpose is precisely the instruction in correct words?

He establishes [his position] with the words "not only" (*na kevalam*), etc., arguing: "Since the manifestation of consciousness was established there as a corollary (*prasaṅgāgata*) to the established system of grammar, what loss is there in this?
By this, it is implied that they possess an understanding of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) in this matter.

4. Now, as for what was said by them—"Enough of this insistence; in this way, even grammar would come to total extinction"—by such a representation, [the following is shown]: since one must speak here with correct words and not with incorrect ones, [it is said], "A Brahmin must certainly not speak like a barbarian (mleccha); for he is indeed a barbarian."
Furthermore, there is the Vedic revelation stating, "That which is a corrupt word," and likewise, "Having employed a corrupt word,

one who has maintained the sacred fires should perform the expiatory Sārasvata sacrifice. Thus, what need is there for any other purpose for the Veda, which is a treasure-house of instructions for accomplishing all human goals?
Since grammar is the primary factor because it brings about the understanding of meaning, it is an auxiliary; therefore, this is established.

Consequently, through the elegant and mature expressions resulting from devotion to grammar, scholars attain, without effort, proficiency in the diverse Vedic words, even when these are supplemented by others.

Since the Vedas expand the cognition of their own meaning through the limbs [of Vedic study], such as Nirukta and others, how could there be a subversion of their authority? Thus, having first raised the distinction of subject matter,
he accepts that very point as true by saying, "The instruction of correct words," and so forth.

5. That by which words and forms are analyzed is *vyākaraṇa*; thus its name is derived from its literal meaning (*anvartha*). Those who know or study it are *vaiyākaraṇas*. Their state (*bhāva*) is expressed by the suffix *-tva*, and that suffix of state—
The term "one who rejects other doctrines" (*dharmāntarapratikṣepaka*) is indicated by the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), which signifies the state of being a grammarian (*vaiyākaraṇatā*).
It is of no consequence that this is irrelevant to what you ought to do; moreover, it is not only in this instance.
By the term "paśyantī," what is expressed is merely a semblance of correct knowledge;

for even in the investigation of the realm of words (*śabdadhātu*), the all-pervasiveness [of the self] is obstructed by the characteristics of space, time, and so forth, as stated by the learned Bhartṛhari.
For that which is necessarily pervasive exists in all directions.
Homage to the peaceful radiance, whose form is infinite pure consciousness unconditioned by space, time, and so forth, and for whom self-experience alone is the sole means of knowledge.
Thus, by this definition, limitation—meaning being qualified—by direction, place, and time is negated.

And that is incorrect, because it [the object] is, by implication, limited by finite space and time; otherwise, if there were no qualification by direction, time, and so forth, [it would follow that it exists everywhere].

1. [The opponent argues: "A statement that is not relevant to the subject at hand is indeed beautiful because it resembles the introduction. But this is not tenable; for grammar, which is characterized as the instruction on correct words (*sādhu-śabda*), is in fact an obstacle to liberation (*mokṣa*). To explain: liberation is, in every respect, a total cessation.
Furthermore, regarding that which was stated— that speech should be spoken by the virtuous and not by the wicked—
the meaning is that there is no result whatsoever from it as to whether one is wicked or virtuous, because it creates an obstacle to the primary subject at hand.

2. For here, the all-pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*) of the venerable Bhartṛhari must be stated primarily. To explain: since he is undivided by direction, space, and time, he is "unlimited" (*aparimita*);
therefore, he is "infinite" (*ananta*), meaning devoid of boundaries (*maryādā-rahita*), that is to say, all-pervasive. Likewise, because he is devoid of limitation by time, he is infinite.

"Free from destruction" means eternal. Here, the qualifying attribute "whose form is pure consciousness" contains the reason [for this eternity]. He supports that very pervasiveness by means of the phrase beginning with "by one's own experience," through the rejection of the operations of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and so forth. [The word] "of light" is used because its nature is illumination. [The word] "to the peaceful one."
Because it transcends conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). He explains that this [reality], being of the nature of a mere appearance, is not the true form, by means of the words "space and time.
The definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is the statement of the unique essential nature (*asādhāraṇasvarūpa*).

The meaning is this: if you intend for that [absence] to establish the non-existence of that qualificand by way of being a qualifier of direction, time, and form, then it follows that this [non-existence] of the qualificand is established precisely from that which is limited; yet that is not what you accept. Or else, [if you do accept it...]
Why is it said "only from a limited [cause]"? Why is it not said "from everything"? To answer this objection, he says "otherwise," and so forth.

Pervasiveness and so forth would not exist. For that which is pervasive must necessarily exist in all directions and be delimited by all times; it is eternal (*nitya*). Pervasiveness has been indicated as a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Now, if it is held that there is an absence of delimitation by specific space and time, then that must be stated in that very way, not in general terms; and even that is not tenable, as he says:
"Its own experience is manifested by means of the present time. (73)
Thus, how can it be that they have declared this [consciousness] to be undivided by time?
For the transmigrating subject remains within whichever temporal portion he occupies; at that time, he exists precisely through that present time, or through the future and so forth.
Since its status as an object of one's own experience is perceived, how can there be no determination even by a specific time?

1. For if you intended for [the self] to be distinguished from everything, then for what purpose was its being qualified by space, time, and so forth refuted? Indeed, by this statement of yours, it follows that even those [space, time, etc. must possess some nature of their own; thus he says:
"Indeed, pervasive," and so forth.

Now, one might object: just as in the verse of Bhartṛhari the words "infinite" (ananta) express both pervasiveness and eternity, so too should it be stated here in the corroborative statement; why then was it not so stated?
"For that which is necessarily pervasive exists in all directions.
Here, with the inclusion of the doubt that "only pervasion of the directions" might be intended, he says that this is stated as an illustrative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). Thus he says:
And that which is delimited by all times is eternal.
Thus, its pervasiveness and eternity are established. It is precisely in this way, as a particular [entity].
Nor is it accepted by you that such a thing is merely delimited by specific spatial and temporal locations.
He says "thus" because it is his own experience.
For if you intended the non-limitation by time to consist precisely in being delimited by all times,
then how could this [self] be said to have "its own experience," which is the object of an experience in the present time?
And thus, it is established that this is not desired by you:
"What experience of the infinite self could there be without limitation? (74)
Where is comprehension in that which is infinite? How can there be tranquility in that which possesses radiance?
For consciousness, which is not all-pervasive, has no measurable form; indeed, no corporeal shape is observed in it. (75)

In the doctrine of differentiation (*bhedavāda*), because the six elements (*dhātu*) undergo transformation, the conjunction of space and time is inevitable; thus, their infinity would be defined as the non-termination of space and time.
Consequently, for that which has no termination in space and time, experience (*anubhūti*) cannot logically be a relation between those two.

This is the meaning. For instance, without a determination of the self’s own nature—that is, its measure—how could there be any comprehension of an infinite reality? Since its parts are endless, comprehension would have to occur in some specific portion; yet, the cognition of infinity [cannot arise] in that way.

It manifests as determining the mere substance of an object that is long in its extent, having both ends ungraspable, by means of the prior negation of those categories of objects that have been perceived; however, it is not possible for it to appear in an infinite and undivided form.
1. Indeed, how could that person of meager intellect—who, though claiming to be wise, does not know another's established doctrine with certainty and remains himself in doubt—refute another?

How can [the infinite] be grasped by one who, according to this method, has not ascertained the intention of the other? For it is said that infinity consists in being unconditioned by space and time, which is to say, the non-termination of space and time due to being remote in space and time;
and thus, an object is [defined as finite] by its proximity in space and time.

It is said that what is non-pervasive is impermanent, whereas that which is remote in space and time is pervasive and is therefore called permanent; so what loss is there [in this]? To this, he says: "Where is the experience of the infinite? (2).
Furthermore, that which was stated—"for infinite splendor"—is also not tenable; to this, he says:
3. "Those whose forms consist of pure consciousness alone"—this also shatters the portion concerning form.
4. According to the systems of the Naiyāyikas and others. 5. The ellipsis is: "if infinity is asserted by you."
6. From "yukta" up to "ityartha," he refutes [the opponent's view] by showing that infinity is indeed evident through the fact that [space and time] are not limited by place and time simultaneously.
7. By means of place and time.
He provides the justification for why [this is so]:
87) For cognition is the ascertainment of a completed form; and if [that form] were of the nature of light, [it would not be perceived].

Since there is no absence of non-appearance, how can there be tranquility? What, then, is the meaning of this expression "to the tranquil radiance"? Furthermore, what is the purpose of such a metaphorical usage? A material form (*mūrti*) is either the dimension of a non-pervasive substance or solidity; it does not consist of consciousness (*cit*). Therefore, how can they be called "consciousness-forms" (*cin-mūrtayaḥ*)? || 75 ||
In this very context, those who maintain the eternality of sound have reached a state of established consensus;
therefore, there is an identity with that very reality of sound, which is without beginning. (76)

Other grammarians indeed maintain that the essence of sound (*śabdātmā*) is eternal and distinct from *sphoṭa*, being firmly established in that very [view]. Now, even in that case, it is equal to the reality of speech (*śabdatattva*) which, in the form of *paśyantī*, is without beginning or end.
Or rather, the defects such as the absence of valid means of cognition [apply] to the nature of the *sphoṭa*. (76)
Regarding this, it is said:

"When the essence of sound is eternal, there is no distinction residing in the word itself between being spoken by a reliable authority or an unreliable one; nor can it be manifested by articulated sounds. (77)

If it is argued that [the word] is like space (*vyoman*), then there would be no distinction; for since space is always inferable, the speech of even an unreliable person would possess equal validity, because there is no difference in their eternality. Furthermore, it is not logical for an eternal entity to ever be manifested by sounds, since an eternal thing exists in a single, unchanging form.
Because of the connection with manifestation and non-manifestation. Now, just as space, though eternal and one,
is manifested by sounds—
[this applies] to those who maintain that the reality of sound is eternal.
The connection is with the word "equal" (*tulya*). He explains that very equality by saying "by the authoritative" (*āpta*).
Thus, the sense is that there would be no fixed rule, which is not desired.
Now, even if the essence of sound (*śabdatattva*) is eternal, there is still a distinction between what is spoken by the authoritative and what is spoken by the non-authoritative.

It is indeed established that even if [the word] is eternal, its manifestation is by means of sounds (*dhvani*) alone; thus, when manifested by the sounds of a reliable person (*āpta*), there is truth, and when manifested by the sounds of an unreliable person (*anāpta*), there is untruth. And so, there is no fault whatsoever. To this, he says "no."
And so forth. Just as the space within a jar and the like is not [separated] from the jar and the like, so too is sound.

In this case, there is no such equality, because in the case of space, it is always inferable through qualities such as sound, and not a manifestation known through direct perception. If you ask, "Does this same logic not apply to Śiva according to your own position? [78]
Likewise, because birth conforms to form and because [the world] has the nature of Śiva, and because it is real, there is no equality; therefore, desist from this [view]. || 79 ||

If it is asked: "In the doctrine of Śivādvaita as well, why does the same logic regarding defects such as unreality not apply to Śiva just as it does to the Word (Śabda)?"—that is not so; for when the world is produced from that which is of the nature of Śiva, it is produced in conformity with the nature of Śiva, owing to its being endowed with all powers.
At that time, it is indeed of the nature of Śiva;

therefore, the word "not" (na) in the phrase "not that" (tan na) should be construed like the eye of a crow (kākākṣivat). The meaning is that your statement "not that" is improper. For one should construe [the negation] as "it is not equal here."
But surely, one should not apply reasoning to those things that are indeed inconceivable;

such is the statement of the authoritative teacher (āpta) that must be accepted regarding this subject. What insistence can there be on [the claim] "if [they were] fallacious appearances," and so forth?
Thus, because it has been spoken by an authoritative teacher, silence alone is the refuge here; for even in the case of the inconceivable, [it is not to be subjected to logic].
For one who is engaged in mere logic (*tarka*), there could never be a final determination of the true reality (*satyārtha*). Now, if logic alone is your refuge, then why have you rejected us?
Anticipating the doubt as to what reasoning you yourselves possess in this matter, [the author] proclaims the excellence of his own view in the verse beginning with *bhavatpakṣa*.

By [the passage] beginning with "ityādi" (and so forth). The word *na kiṃ* is used for shaking the head; the meaning is: "Does anything come?"—that is, "Certainly it comes. Here, the word *iti* must be supplied. 3. In the first chapter (*āhnika*), it was stated that [the objection that] the expansion of form is censurable due to its nature is illogical.
The meaning is: "because it has been stated thus. (4) According to your view.
(5) The meaning is: "by means of your attributing refutations and so forth in this regard. Now, [the objection]:
Or rather, it should be explained as an ablative case (*pañcamī*) with the elision of the suffix *lyap*, meaning "desist from this.
The sense is: "Having entered into him, you yourselves should remain here pre-eminently and happily; that is to say, abandon your own views and take refuge in this very doctrine."

And since it is precisely of this nature that truth consists, as will be explained in detail later, let us desist from attempting to level the criticism that the non-duality of Śiva is equivalent to the position of the monism of the Word (śabdādvaitavāda).
Having stated this as a digression, he speaks while reflecting upon *paśyantī* itself:
"Now, by its very name, *paśyantī* is clearly insentient;
therefore, the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) is figuratively designated as feminine. (80)

Now, if it is maintained that [the power] is perceived merely by name through some arbitrary connection with the purpose of seeing, and if she is considered to be of the nature of the cognitive power related to Brahman by way of a feminine grammatical form,
then this is contradictory because of the lack of connection with seeing, which would result in insentience; for [insentience] resides in an insentient self.
And thus, the capacity for knowledge is untenable. || 80 ||
For those who know the words, there is the emptiness of the consciousness of all views regarding the sense organ—due to the mixing of the object known as sound—with the sense organ itself. (81)

[Objection: "Enough with this attribution of faults to you; let it be told, what do they see? [Response: For a derivative (yaugika) meaning is not possible in every case. Indeed, there are also words such as *ḍittha* and others. Therefore, by the very power of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), the designation "Paśyantī" is used here just as in the case of "kuśala" and so forth. Nor should it be said:
"What is the use of this? Nevertheless, she should be designated by the word *paśyantī*;
for even if one objects that her nature is that of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), [the author] refutes this as well by saying 'Now' (*atha*) and so forth.
This is because the meaning of the verbal root *dṛś* (to see) is connected here in its objective form."
3. By means of conventional designation. 4. Nevertheless, what object was accepted by her as she was seeing? To this he says: "In the feminine gender," etc.
5. The meaning is: since the primary sense of "seeing" (paśyantī) is impossible, it remains established as a non-etymological (ayaugika) term.
"Ah, they see a great wonder"— because seeing [it] is impossible, the state of being a conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) is resorted to there,
and in that very place lies the power of cognition (*jñānaśakti*). Now, some [interpret] "without beginning or end" here by means of the term "the principle of sound" (*śabdatattva*).

Regarding the phrase "the nature of speech" (*vāgrūpatām*), they say that by the term "supreme speech" (*parāvāk*), it is precisely the mutual fusion of these two—the word (*vāk*) and the reality of sound (*śabda-tattva*)—that constitutes the supreme reality (*paraṃ tattvam*).
And that reality of sound, which is called the object, is the form of action (*karmarūpa*) and the graspable; while the reality of speech is the grasper.

The instrument (karaṇa) is the grasper (grāhaka), and thus the ultimate reality (paramārthatattva) is precisely the non-difference between the grasped (grāhya) and the grasper; with a mocking retort to this, he says: "Sarvadarśana...

For the reality of sound, which is the supreme speech (*parā vāk*) and is without beginning or end, would fall into the state of being graspable by the hand if it were described as being within the *paśyantī* level. (82)
Since there is a cognition of that which is known as "word" (*śabda*)— which, by virtue of having the form of an object, functions as the *karman*—
and that which is well-known as the sense organ (*indriya*)— which, by virtue of being the instrument (*karaṇa*), is of the nature of speech (*vāg-rūpa*)— because of their mixture and unification,
those [authorities] have stated such things as "without beginning or end," which express the non-difference between the two.

Therefore, by that conflation, the state of ignorance regarding all philosophical systems has been attained by those grammarians who claim to understand the meaning of words. For nowhere in the Sāṃkhya or other systems is the non-difference between the sense organ and its object accepted in conventional usage. And such is the case with the word "vā" (or).

If [the Self] were described as being one with the hand because it is characterized by otherness, being without beginning or end, and because of the doctrine of non-duality, then the identity of the organ of action (the hand) with its corresponding object would also necessarily follow. || 82 ||
2. By way of being the grasper;
3. Of the *vāk-tattva* and the *śabda-tattva*; 4.
Ignorance regarding all treatises.
5. "Thus" (evam) signifies acceptance.
6. "With the hand" is an illustration; by this, it should be understood that the same applies to the other organs of action as well.

7. Now, why is it said that there is a power of knowledge in an insentient self? For in this case, a duality of essential nature is not being asserted—that the essential nature is insentient while that power itself is of the nature of knowledge. For that very power of Brahman which is of the nature of knowledge is [the same as the self].

"They see" means they are of the nature of power (*śakti*), and not some independent entity; thus, by way of this admission, he establishes his own position according to his own view, asserting that no path for the introduction of the aforementioned objections can apply to it.

8. "The venerable one’s eye of discernment has been opened; we do not know the reason why it does not blossom quickly. Thus he spoke by way of addressing him as "Bhāvat" (Your Honor), beginning with the words "tāvat" and so forth.
For action is perceived as having two parts situated in a before and an after; the reflective awareness "this is to be seen" would occur first. (83)
Just as for a maker such as a potter, there is a deliberation in the form of a desire that "the jar is the effect," so too is it established here in this case.
How could there be an expansion of that desire while she remains [in that state], as long as the subtle radiance of consciousness has not become oriented toward action? (85)
Śiva remains established as the possessor of the cosmic order within that state of aesthetic equilibrium (sāmarasya);
such is the even more subtle state of the process of phenomenal existence (bhava).

That speech, being subject to the wind-like nature of the self, does not remain stable; yet, if it were real, then let it be said that even a jar or other such objects possess the nature of Brahman. (87)

For the act of seeing, which consists of the activity of perception, possesses sequential parts; and first, there must necessarily be a deliberation such as "this is to be seen," consisting of the nature of desire, just as in the case of a potter producing a jar or similar object. This same principle applies here as well.
If this desire stands prior to the act of seeing, how can that desire itself expand— given the previously stated reasoning—
without a subtler emergence connected to the principle of consciousness (*cit-tattva*), characterized by an orientation toward the desired object of knowledge? For that [desire] too is consciousness.
The capacity for the sequential arrangement of withdrawal, orientation, will, knowledge, and action is their unification (ekībhāva).
[1] The word "not" (na) here should be understood as an acceptance, according to the maxim of shaking the head.
The meaning is that it must indeed be seen.
And if this statement applies in a general sense, then let it be postulated for a jar and other such things as well.
Of that activity;
in the investigation of the *paśyantī* [level of speech].

In that state, the venerable Śiva exists as the object of immersion, established as the foundation of order and yet devoid of sequence. Thus, even with respect to the process characterized by *paśyantī*— which pertains to the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*)— there exists another, more subtle, supreme form of existence.

Therefore, that [speech] too must be accepted as such; however, one should not maintain that speech, which is by nature moving like the wind, possesses the nature of Brahman even when it is true. If this were maintained, then because there is no difference in their being mere entities (*bhūta*), the same could be said for a jar and other such things as well. (87)
Just as all objects possess the nature of the Lord Śiva, so too does the organ of speech; yet that [nature] is not the supreme state. 88.
The activity of speech-sound (*vāk*) occurs in the throat and other parts of the mouth;
it is the instrument (*karaṇa*) for sound in the form of *nāda* and so forth, yet its essence is Śiva. (89)

Even for him, the initiation into the five principles (pañcatattvadīkṣā) has been taught in some instances; yet, in that case as well, speech is not required. Therefore, everything is of the nature of Śiva.

Although, in ultimate reality, all objects that fall within the scope of cognition— by virtue of entering into the interior of consciousness— possess the nature of the Supreme Lord characterized as consciousness, whether in that manner or otherwise; nevertheless, even so, because the organ of speech is included among all knowable objects, it lacks the quality of being unknowable, just like existence and other such attributes.
The state of the organ of speech does not become something other [than that], due to the power of *māyā*.
Regarding its being Brahman:
[one might object]—"But surely this is true; let it be said even of a jar and so forth that they are all objects."

Because it is the object of knowledge and because consciousness enters within it, its state as consisting of consciousness (cinmaya) is the supreme lordship (parameśvaratva), which is indeed complete and undivided. And although there is equality [between the individual soul and the Lord], this much is the distinction regarding speech:
that [the Lord] is not an object of perception for the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest. However, the inclusion of all objects is exactly the same in both cases.
Anticipating the objection that "Brahman-hood belongs to that very state because of its specific quality of being ungraspable by the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth," he says "Just as... and so on;
[this implies] "even though that supreme state possesses distinctions from others."
This has been indicated [above] (p.
93), because it arises from the non-apprehension of its identity with Śiva. For instance, in the case of the throat, palate, and so forth...
The activity of the wind consisting of its impact upon a portion of the mouth, which is the cause for the manifestation of sound, is called *ruta*;

that [activity] is its instrument (*karaṇa*), and this entire state is of a differentiated nature. Now, there exists the sound whose essence is mantra, which is gross in the form of audible resonance (*nāda*), as well as subtle and supreme.
That state of being the self of Supreme Śiva is what is intended and taught in the initiation manual (*dīkṣāśāstra*) during the procedure for initiation into the five principles (*pañcatattvadīkṣā*);
however, it is not the case that the world consists of speech in the form of the senses, nor is it logical that the world's supreme state is its absorption into that [speech].
Therefore, it is established that everything is indeed of the nature of Śiva. May there be auspiciousness! (90)
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Śivadṛṣṭivṛtti*, composed by the venerable master Utpaladeva. || 2 ||
(p. 94) Now, in the *Śrīśivadṛṣṭi*:
The Third Chapter:

The Doctrine of Non-duality is Established. Following the investigation of Paśyantī, the present undertaking is now directed toward those proponents of non-duality who belong to our own school. And so it has been stated by them:
We eternally worship you, O Mother, that supreme one who, being of the nature of light free from all limiting adjuncts, is designated by the name Śivā.
Thus [it is said]. To this he replies:

"Now, that which is celebrated with devotion by some as the supreme state (parāvasthā) of Power (śakti) is the God revealed through reasoning; for from that [state] comes the stage of Power (śaktidaśā). [Verse 1]
1. Strengthened by the certainty of one's own established doctrine;
2. [It refers to] those of its own kind;
3. That is to say, it does not mean refutation.

The intended meaning is this: since "power" (*śakti*) is dependent on another and because it is feminine while being a specific form of the masculine, its dependence on that [other] is already established; therefore, the designation of it as "supreme" (*parā*) is merely a matter of devotion (*bhakti*) intended to proclaim the excellence of that particular principle.

Devotion (*bhakti*) therein is an excess of love and a composition (*racanā*). By means of this composition—that is, by proclaiming its excellence through those [qualities]—the meaning is that the primacy of the possessor of power (*śaktimat*) alone is indicated.
