Now, one might object: if devotion alone is the designation for that, yet it is the possessor of power who is preeminent in excellence...
If it has already been sufficiently established [by scripture], then what is the point of employing a refutation directed at them? To this he says: "By reasoning" (*yuktyā*).

For reasoning is useful only for those with subtle vision; thus, the statement of such [reasoning] is merely a refutation, because it lacks the quality of being beneficial to everyone. This is the meaning.
And one should not think that their capacity alone is considered to be independent; thus he says "tataḥ" (from that), etc.
Because the specific characteristic [of the word] would otherwise be inexplicable, the designation of the intended object— which is accepted as being precisely a power—
as having the form of a "supreme state" (parāvasthā) is indeed figurative (bhakti); for there exists nothing beyond that which possesses the power,
since [the power], though extracted from its possessor, is nevertheless designated by virtue of a specific purpose as non-different from that possessor.

Therefore, by virtue of its dependence on that [power], it deserves to be explained immediately after it. For it is precisely by those [powers] that the state of power (*śakti-daśā*)—described as "a slight swelling" and so forth—is stated immediately after the subsequent state (*parāvasthā*).

Consequently, by those who proclaim the transcendence (*paratva*) of power, the substratum (*dharmin*), which is its own locus, is [defined] through that power which constitutes its attribute (*dharma*).

The Lord Śiva has been revealed as independent through the reasoning of real non-duality. Why, then, is there such an insistence on the feminine gender within the specific nature [of the deity], given that it is without cause? For masculinity is the common gender of both male and female, whereas the neuter...
1. The meaning is that [this] generality exists without the masculine gender.
2. Now, if power is of the nature of the autonomy of that which possesses power, then the burning power of fire ought not to be designated as something separate from the fire itself.

To explain how such a designation—whether for the purpose of indicating a logical principle (*nyāya*) or through devotion (*bhakti*)—is possible according to this reasoning, he says: "by its dependence on that. The meaning is that it [the power] possesses no independence of its own, because that would entail defects such as contradiction and inconsistency.
And this is not unintended by them, such that their statement would be relegated to the position of being refuted like that of other disputants; thus he says, "Since by them...
He establishes that specific position in detail with the words beginning, "Without cause," and so forth.
5. He asks, "What is the loss here? and replies, "For [the loss of] manhood.

6. Now, if it is argued that a fault is suspected here because the designation of the feminine gender is a specific form, then a fault likewise necessarily follows even in the masculine gender, which reveals the very nature of the possessor of power (śaktimat).

For those of coarse vision, let the neuter gender alone be accepted as faultless, so that *śakti*— meaning sovereignty (*svātantrya*)— may appropriately be designated by the neuter gender itself; therefore, he says "the neuter."

96) Since a form that is synonymous with "potency" (*śaktatā*) is not appropriately to be introduced at the occasion of designating such a Lord of the Universe, [the author] uses the expression "potency and its possessor" (*śakti-tadvat*) for the purpose of expressing non-difference.
Rebirth as a male. || 1 ||
If that designation is likewise of the nature of Śiva,
and if it is held that the Supreme Śiva is designated by means of the feminine gender, then that designation too must be expressed through the word "Śiva," according to the logic already stated.
He states their non-difference alone:
"Śiva is not devoid of Śakti, nor is Śakti separate [from him]. (2)
Śiva, being thus empowered, desires to bring about all states of existence by his will;
in the Śaiva tradition, no distinction between power and the possessor of power is ever described.

Although Śiva is not empty when devoid of power, nevertheless, how is there oneness? To this he says: "Power is not separate. For it is thus: by means of each and every variety, Śiva is capable of performing such extremely difficult deeds by mere will alone.

Even in common usage there is no difference, because the assertion of a difference between power (śakti) and its possessor (śaktimān) is untenable; in the Śaiva system, this is never described even in the case of intermediate distinctions, as it is in other systems that lack authoritative foundation. || 3 ||
Reflecting upon that very point, he says:
"Because power alone is autonomous, it is able to produce diverse entities.
This is according to the logical principle that the masculine gender denotes a universal.

2. Furthermore, a mutual distinction between these two is not logical, by which even the designation of the feminine gender would be justified; thus he establishes his own position according to his own view.
3. The term "Śaiva" is used for the purpose of stating their authoritative status, and by that, [it implies] theirs as well.

Since only their own established position has been demonstrated and not the position of other systems, for this very reason the author of the commentary stated "those belonging to our own school" (*svayūthyān*).
If its capacity were to be postulated, then there would either be an infinity of such capacities.
For if there is a distinction [between the power and its possessor], does the power produce the effect, or does the possessor of the power do so?

In that regard, if it is the power, is it capable of acting or incapable? If it were incapable, there would be the fallacy of over-extension regarding the action of what is incapable; if it were capable, then if it were to possess another power, there would be an infinite regress of the substratum of that power.

The name "Śakti" belongs to Śiva alone. Now, having established [the identity] through Śakti herself as the reality, he says "In difference" (*bhede*) in order to refute the distinction between the two.
But is this not true?

"In the Śaiva tradition, the difference between power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimān*) is never described. Nevertheless, that very sovereignty which constitutes the "power-ness" of the possessor of power is itself the expansion of power even in the attainment of the essential nature of that possessor of power; so, enough [of further elaboration].

"By means of confidence in the very nature of the Possessor of Power (śaktimat). Regarding that which was stated—"If there is such a designation, then that designation is of the nature of Śiva," and so forth—he asks therein: "Is this [designation] the Power (śakti) itself?"
3. Even from the void, the arising of all entities would occur; this is an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpatti-prasaṅga*).

4. That alone is capacity (*śaktatva*) which is the non-interruption of power within itself, because without the inherence of power (*śakti-samavāya*), the very nature of capacity cannot be established.
5. And if there is a connection with power (*śakti*), then the fruit of my desire-tree of wishes has indeed borne fruit; thus he says: "It shall be called the power of Śiva alone.
6. Now, if [it is argued that] in the case of non-difference (*abheda-pakṣa*), the designation 'power' cannot apply in any way whatsoever—
The proponent of *śakti* (the theory of power) adopts the position that these two are distinct; in order to analyze this, he says "Now," and so forth.

As for what was stated—that the capacity of the possessor of power (*śaktimat*) is an attribute (*dharma*) that is virtually identical to its own nature (*svabhāva*), by virtue of which it is designated as "possessing power"—that is not so; rather, in that case too, power is indeed distinct from the possessor of power.

He asks: "Is that [instrument] distinct from its power? Here too, the logic is as before: if that which is powerless were to act, there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga); if, on the other hand, it possesses power, then for that [power] there must be another [instrument], and for that yet another, leading to an infinite regress and the consequence of a lack of finality (anavasthā).

If it were joined with a distinct power, then that very [power] which is distinct would perform the effect; or how could that which is powerless perform it? If it were already capable, there would be an infinite regress by virtue of having to postulate yet another power.
Because it would lead to the consequence of infinity.
Furthermore:
"The possessor of power itself would be the power, because of its purpose as an instrument, just like Śiva. (5)

Because power (*śakti*) is an effect of autonomy (*svātantrya*), it could not possess the nature of Śiva anywhere. Furthermore, if power were to act by being joined with another power, it would itself be nothing other than the possessor of power (*śaktimat*). This is because, by virtue of the definition of an instrument (*karaṇa*), which is the ground for its activity, it would follow that it is an agent (*kartṛ*); the meaning is as follows: just as...
The venerable Śiva is the independent cause of Śakti, bound by his own nature and not dependent on anything else;
thus, Śiva-hood cannot exist anywhere else. Therefore, the Śaiva system is untenable for those who belong to other [Śaiva] schools.

He says "moreover" (*kiṃca*) and so forth, [arguing] that it is not only the case that the name "Śiva's power" would be established for you by the conjunction of one power with another power— by which even the fault of self-contradiction would ensue— but rather [it is impossible].

2. For agency (*kartṛtva*) is said to be the possession of power (*śaktimattva*), while instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) is the state of being power (*śaktitva*). When power is conjoined with the state of being powerful, it is quite clear that this very power [possessing the state of being powerful] is the instrument, and because of its conjunction with that [power], this [state of being powerful] is the agent; thus, even power deserves to be designated as "the possessor of power," and no other thing whatsoever does.
It may be said that "power" (śakti) is that by which something is performed; thus, it is an instrument (karaṇa).

Now, why is this being said—that when Śiva is joined with power, he alone is called "power," and furthermore, that the possessor of power (śaktimān) himself would be the power? For such is indeed the very nature of power.
That which is the capacity to produce an effect based solely on itself within its own self by virtue of its autonomy— and likewise,
that the state of being an effect is also autonomous, having that single form and not depending on anything else— this too he refutes with the words beginning "of power" (śakteḥ).
4. By the meaning characterized as the instrument (karaṇa), by means of power (śakti); that is to say, the sense is that the Lord Śiva possesses agency (kartṛtva).
5. And likewise, from where did this designation originate which was made by them?
"Power and the possessor of power are said to be the two categories of reality;
all this world is his power, while the Great Lord is the possessor of power."
Even when emitting its own power, knowledge arises within its sovereignty.

In the admission that the venerable Lord Śiva is isolated while emitting his power (*śakti*), [he] falls into the error of [denying] sovereignty because of the absence of dependence on the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), since there would be no manifestation of the object of knowledge; and that [is unacceptable]. Alternatively, in the abandonment of his own power... for indeed...

Regarding that very autonomy—knowledge of it would be exactly like this: there is no perception of the power as something separate from the possessor of the power; rather, when a single object is perceived, if some aspect of it arises, that which is similar to it and capable [of action] is thus called the "possessor of power" (śaktimān) in conventional usage.
Now, it might be argued that there is no inconsistency in the Śaiva system for those belonging to our own school, since it has been stated:

"The state of Śiva (śivatā) cannot exist anywhere else. Indeed, there is a domain for this state of Śiva; for as long as there is an immersion in the nature of power (śaktitva), to what extent can one be designated as "Śiva"? But upon the departure from that [immersion]...
Since it is isolated (*vivikta*), by whom can its designation as *śiva* be denied?

Thus, because their objects are distinct, the acquisition of their own essential nature (*svarūpa*) exists quite clearly for both. To this, he says: "If there were autonomy (*svātantrya*), knowledge would follow. This is the intended meaning: if, in this case, you [opponents] were to [assert it] on the basis of a distinction between objects...

In that case, for the sake of your argument, one might define the venerable Lord Śiva as "the supreme light containing power" by virtue of the power residing within the womb; let it be so defined, or let it not be—there is no burden on you here. Nevertheless, in the state of absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), knowledge necessarily follows.

The sense is that autonomy (*svātantrya*) is indeed a property inherent in the nature of one who is independent and possesses power; it cannot be meaningfully described without that which possesses such a nature.
2. From "in the case of acceptance" up to "there would be knowledge" is as follows:

The reading is seen in the Kapasta manuscript: "There is not even the possibility of disagreement here on your part; rather, in the case of independence (*svātantrye*), since there is no capacity (*śakti*), the consequence of the impossibility of the self-evident (*svataḥ*) establishment of knowledge regarding the nature-constituted property (*dharme*) arises, and this is not desired, for indeed—"
For you—3. Its nature as vibration (*spanda*) is, as it were, a preponderance, because it consists of slight movement.
4. It has as its essence the conventional usage of "slight movement."

The essential point here is this: there is only one such reality, which is called its own intrinsic nature (*svasvabhāva*); it is the very essence of the possessor of power (*śaktimat*) containing within it all powers (*śaktigarbha*).

When any manifestation whatsoever of cognition arises as an excess within that [reality], it is then designated as "power" (*śakti*). And by virtue of being its substratum, [the possessor of power] is identical to it.
The essence of such worldly transaction is this very union;
its core is the repose within the manifestation of the nature whose essence is movement. For this very reason, it is "capable" (*śakta*).
Together with that capacity, it is called the "possessor of capacity" (*śaktimat*); however, in reality, there is no difference between capacity and the possessor of capacity.
"It is perceived," as it is said [on page 100]: "Therefore he says..."
The coldness of snow is not separate from it, nor would the heat of fire be distinct from it.
Power (śakti) and the state of being powerful (śaktatva) are attributes (dharma) of that which possesses power; and an attribute is not different from its substratum (dharmī).
Likewise, the sensations of cold and heat in snow and fire are not perceived as separate from them. (6)
For when there is the immobilization of the mantra, that fire is no longer said to exist at that time. || 7 ||
That substance is as radiant as gold and the like; [this point] has been rendered inconclusive by those [examples].
Now, let it be granted that there is indeed non-difference between power and the possessor of power;
nevertheless, just as in the case of fire and its heat, or snow and its coldness, even though there is non-difference, it is by means of heat and cold alone [that they are perceived].

Anticipating the objection that "in common usage there is no burning by fire nor freezing by snow, and thus even though there is non-duality between these two, the doctrine of the non-duality of power (*śaktyadvayavāda*) alone is logically consistent, not the doctrine of the non-duality of Śiva (*śivādvayavāda*"), he says: "Not of the snow...
The intended meaning is this: it is indeed true [that the distinction is made] only by means of power (*śakti*).

Although it may be argued that, given the observation of conventional practice (*vyavahāra*), it is appropriate to speak only of non-duality (*advaya-vāda*), nevertheless, a property (*dharma*) cannot function within conventional discourse without a substratum (*dharmin*). For the sensations of coldness and heat can never occur—even in conventional discourse—without snow and fire respectively. Likewise...

Since such usage is observed everywhere even when there is a relation with a power (śakti), it is not logical to maintain that usage by interposing the substratum (dharmin) through that [power]; therefore, the doctrine of the non-duality of Śiva alone should be accepted as consistent with reason.

2. Although it would have been more appropriate to designate the Himalayas and fire as the examples here, it should be understood that they are employed as the subjects of the illustration (dārṣṭāntika) in order to demonstrate the superiority of those possessed of direct experience; thus he says "tathā" (so).
But surely, just as when the power of heat is suppressed by a mantra, everyone still perceives "this is fire" because fire continues to appear; likewise,
since that [object] remains established even when its power is distinct from it, how can it be said that "[it is like] one who lets go," and so forth?

Likewise, he provides a justification for how the mantra-stambhana (paralysis by mantra) could be accomplished otherwise as something distinct there, and how there can be no difference between these two, in the passage beginning with "mantra-stambhana" and so forth.
p.
101) If [it is argued that] the example [of fire] is based on the burner because of its non-separation from heat; || 8 ||
The heating power (*auṣṇya*) of fire is said to be non-different from the possessor of that power (*śaktimat*), just as the power is non-different from the possessor of the power.

This is because this "fire-ness" (*vahnitva*) does not exist; for in its absence, the heat of fire is not perceived, since at that time, although it is composed of light (*tejomaya*), it is like a substance such as gold.

Radiant. Now, if by those very elements such as gold—which consist of the great element of fire-energy (tejas) known as fire, and which are accompanied by fire—the example is given [to show] that the possessor of power is distinct from the power, there is no fault; for that fire, being hot and characterized by its burning nature, exists even in the absence of the [separate] power.
The example cited is not fire in general alone.
By the virtuous Śaivas, speech itself has been conceptualized as existing in the sequence beginning with Paśyantī;
by them, their own non-Śaiva nature has been established.
Furthermore, by those proponents of Śakti who [assert] that she,
whose nature is unconditioned light, is designated by the name Śiva—

Because it is stated thus, even those established in the Śaiva system maintain that speech itself is arranged in a sequence and conceived as the universal self through the designations *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī*; as they say:
As long as there is not even a single atom of the opening [of the eyes], so long it would not function toward the object; and that opening is considered to be an action.
And action is indeed manifold in form.
Just as in the case of one whose heat is suppressed by a mantra, the power of that fire remains distinct [from the fire];

likewise, when that power is suppressed, the fire remains in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), yet it is not known as being "the fire" [itself] through that [suppressed] power. Similarly, when the power has departed, the power is distinct; and it is not [known] through the power alone.
The meaning is that it is a designation for the very nature of that which possesses power (*śaktimat*).
Now, even though the position of the non-duality of power (*śakti-advaita*)— which is another synonym for absolute freedom (*svātantrya*)— is untenable,
other proponents of power (*śaktivādins*) again raise an objection, [claiming] that it is the Speeches beginning with Paśyantī...

Since all speech proceeds by encompassing the entire universe from every side, and because it consists of power (*śakti*), the entire universe is composed of the non-duality of speech— that is, the non-duality of power.
To the objection that this is sufficient [to establish] the non-duality of Śiva, he says "by the Śaivas," and so forth.
Having begun thus [at p. 102]:
"Apart from abiding in one's own intrinsic nature, there is no other state than that."
O Śivā, for whom there is no form of speech, subtle or otherwise, nor any proximity [to it].
Thus, his own adherence to the Ārhata (Jaina) doctrine has been stated. || 9 ||
For instance,
in the Śaiva tradition, speech is declared to be a sense organ by means of *nāda* and so forth;
through its practice, there is the attainment of results and the realization of the nature of subtle mantra.
That which is called Nāda, the supreme, has been described in the *Kālapāda* and other [texts];
and the distinction between the supreme, the non-supreme, and so forth, has been established in that very same place. || 11 ||
By this, the supreme nature of speech itself has been described here.

For in the Śaiva system, just as in the Sāṃkhya, speech possesses the status of a motor organ (*karmendriya*) only in its most inferior state; however, when consciousness is dissolved into the *nāda*, [it attains its true nature].

By such statements as these, the attainment of the fruit is said to belong to speech alone; for in the *Kālottara* and other scriptures, it is taught that [speech] has the subtle nature of mantra— that which is the supreme seed-syllable called *nāda*.

By such statements as these, the distinction between the supreme (para) and the non-supreme (apara) has been declared; therefore, how could it be improper for speech itself to possess the nature of the supreme according to this Śaiva text? The word "tu" (but/however) is used merely to fill out the meter.

1. Now, the meaning here is as follows: according to the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), it is indeed the function of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra-vṛtti*) that produces sound; this is of the nature of an instrument (*karaṇa*), and thus more remote than even the cognitive faculties (*buddhīndriya*), being of the nature of an organ of action (*karmendriya*) common to animal subjects such as animals and the like.

How can there be "otherness" (*paratva*) in that case, given that speech is accepted as being like the hands and other [organs]? Now, beginning with the words "atha" (now) and so forth, he asks this by relying on the general nature of things in their gross and subtle forms.
[This is] precisely in the Śaiva Tantra.
3. This very [point] regarding the "foot of time" has not been stated; rather, it is described by the word *pati* (lord). (p. 103) || 12 ||
It has never been stated that this applies to the word known as the "object" (*viṣaya*).

This is not so; for it was not said there that it refers to the vocal organ (*vāgindriya*) situated within the bound atoms (*baddhāṇu*), nor has it ever been demonstrated anywhere that the word known as the "object" possesses that [referential] status. Rather, [it refers to the following]:

Regarding the state of mastery over the reflected image (*pratibimba*) in meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), that which consists of the great mantra and has sound as its essence has been explained. || 12 ||
And thus Kheṭapāla spoke regarding the particular excellence of the Śabdarāśi: || 13 ||
In the commentary on the *Svāyambhuva*, the Guru [explains] with the words "Certainly" (*bāḍham*) and so forth;
likewise, in the commentary on the *Mataṅga*, it was stated by the explanatory Guru. (14)

In his commentary on the *Śrī-Svāyambhuva-śāstra*, the teacher Kheṭapāla raised the objection: "Is there ever any distinction between the words of mantras and other words? Having raised this, he replied: "Certainly; one is of the nature of Śiva, while the other is not."

By the passage beginning with "consisting of bonds" (*pāśātmaka*), he expresses the state of being distinguished through the agency of the *śabdarāśi* in its form as mantra, by virtue of its supreme nature; however, the *śabdarāśi* is not devoid of distinction merely by virtue of being sound.

For here, the meaning is that this has been said regarding that very speech which consists of the "I" (aham), whose nature is sound (śabdana), composed of the great mantra, and characterized by pure agency and vital breath (prāṇa), being uncontracted;
whereas these phonemes (varṇas) which are of the nature of māyā are merely of the nature of sound (śabda).

The objects corresponding to the jar and so forth, as well as the knowledge consisting of the non-conceptual and conceptual forms— namely, *paśyantī* and *madhyamā*— which give rise to them; and the vocal organ (*vāgindriya*), which corresponds to the hand and other instruments, which brings that [knowledge] about and produces it.
And since that [universe] is cast into the category of *māyā*, which consists of duality, how indeed could it be the supreme reality (*paratattva*)? Now, one might object:

"In whatever case it may be, its capacity to accomplish its own function is observed; what then is there to say? To this it is replied: "Even that [accomplishment] occurs through contact with the power of its own Self; thus, it is brought about by contact with the power of the Supreme."
In that regard, in the *Kālottara* and other such texts, it is stated that [speech] never [exists as such]; for this very reason, Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇa also said:
"By means of the beautiful, heart-captivating speech of the *paśyantī* [level], which is being perceived..."
Victorious is the Supreme Lord, whose greatness is manifested as bliss.
Thus it is said. And here, by the word *paśyantī*, the level of Śrī Sadāśiva, whose nature is the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), is expressed;

she is the supreme *mahāpaśyantī*, which is non-differentiated in nature and consists of the individual selves (*pratyagātman*) who are themselves the great *paśyanty*s. And by her, that majesty of bliss (*ānanda-mahiman*) [is manifested].
"That [power] is the supreme speech (parā vāk) of the Lord, which is to be made to shine forth as the essence of absolute sovereignty.
Thus it is stated in the *Mataṅga-ṭīkā* by the teacher known as Vyākhyānin.

This has been stated as a distinction. Thus it was said: [this applies] to mantras situated on the level of the subject (*pramātṛ*) and to sounds situated on the supreme level (*parabhūmi*), but never to the organ of speech (*vāgindriya*).
For the organ of speech resides only within the sphere of *māyā*, whereas sound consists of the subtle element of sound (*tanmātra*).
The supreme void, consisting of the great elements, is called the "face" of the Supreme Lord in the arrangement of the five Brahmans; and this has been demonstrated in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*.
In that regard, it is metaphorically designated as "supreme" because it is the means to that [attainment]. || 15 ||
And so it is said in the *Kiraṇa*: "In this manner, [the state] consisting of nāda, bindu, and so forth [is described].

Furthermore, because it is the means for attaining the sound of the supreme mantra (*paramamantra*), the status of being 'supreme' (*paratva*) is attributed to *paśyantī* itself through the application of metaphorical designation. And likewise in the venerable *Kiraṇasaṃhitā*:
Thus, such metaphorical objects as *nāda*, *bindu*, and so forth, have been described.
If it is argued that [the Lord] is supreme because He is the means for that [liberation], then lamps and other such things would also possess the status of being the means.
Now, what is this being said?
By those good Śaivas who maintain that speech itself exists in the sequence beginning with Paśyantī, has their own non-Śaiva nature been established?

And so forth. Because this [Paśyantī] consists of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) and serves as a means (*upāya*) for supreme consciousness (*parasaṃvit*), its "supremacy" (*paratva*) is asserted. For indeed, even when something is a means, there is the superimposition of the status of the goal (*upeyatā*);
as, for example, because the scripture is a means for the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the Supreme Lord, the scripture is said to be "nothing but the reflective awareness of consciousness."
Anticipating the objection that it might be said, "It is the same here as well," he says, "In that case, however," and so forth.
For in the *Kiraṇa* and other texts, it has been stated otherwise; in that regard:

Since it would consist merely of a means to that [end], even a lamp and the like would result in being "supreme" because they are means to knowledge; therefore, the doctrine of the supremacy of *paśyantī* among these positions within the Śaiva system is untenable. And this is so by the logic previously stated.
Even this doctrine of independent power (svatantra-śakti-vāda), though it is the subject under discussion, is untenable for them. || 16 ||
Therefore, within all aspects and in every form of practice, the nature of Śiva is to be understood as consisting in the immersion into one's own power (svaśakti). || 17 ||
Therefore, since the doctrine of power alone (śaktimātravāda) is untenable, it should be understood that in all cognitions—
whether produced by the senses or by the mind alone— the nature of the Lord Śiva, who possesses power, resides in every single form that manifests therein.
It consists of the state of essential identity with all one's own previously mentioned powers, and is accessible through instruction. || 17 ||

When the wonder "I am" arises within as the very essence of Sadāśiva— a state whose function is filled with the wonder of the infinite universe held within it— then the Paśyantī vision makes one's own self identical with the supreme consciousness consisting of that reflective awareness. At that time:
He says "otherwise" (anyathā) to address the question: "By what means could their status as the supreme [means] be denied, since they are the means to that?
2. The meaning is that the status of speech as supreme refers precisely to its ultimate purpose (*tātparya*) in the *paśyantī* state.
3. By this, the meaning is that for these [grammarians], the acceptance of the *paśyantī* as the supreme is entirely irrelevant to the present context.
4. Now, he states what is established through the untenability of all [other] views with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).

Since it has been established that this doctrine of non-dual power (*śaktyadvayavāda*) is not tenable in any way whatsoever, he states the resulting conclusion with the words "Therefore," where "form" (*ākāraḥ*) refers to the nature of the object (*padārthavapuḥ*).

Practice (*pratipatti*) is the cause for the recognition of its forms; thus it is established that this entire universe consists of these two principles alone, because everything is contained within them. Therefore, whatever is born of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvajāta*), all of that is nothing but the nature of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grahaṇa*). In that regard:

"Everywhere there is the nature of Śiva; all that is indeed composed of Śiva. The specification of a substratum (*ādhāra*), however, is with respect to those who are to be instructed. Now, one might object: 'By the principle that "that which is not manifest does not shine," this is already established; what wonder is there in this? To this he says: 'Consisting of the immersion into one's own power' (*svaśaktyāveśanātmakam*)."
The meaning is that the very principle of Śiva, which consists of the equilibrium of the five powers (*pañcaśakti*), is indeed all this collection of objects such as jars and so forth.
Just as Śiva-nature resides in the Lord who is established in Himself, so too does it reside in earth and the other elements.

Just as in the Supreme Lord, who abides solely in the state of Śiva-nature established in Himself, there is Śiva-nature characterized by the vibration of all powers, so too is that very same form present even down to the level of the earth.
Is the state of being gold desired in the lump or in the waistband? || 18 ||
Just as gold, in an ornament such as an earring and the like,
attains the state of being a figurative representation (rūpaka) there through its own inherent capacity, and not by means of an independent power.
Thus pervaded by will, and likewise by the three powers, he remains established in various states; therefore, everything has Śiva as its essence.

No, for it cannot be said that the nature of gold exists only in the bracelet (*kaṭaka*) and so forth, while the mass of gold has not yet undergone the modification of its constituent parts into those respective ornaments;
rather, in every instance, it is the gold itself that exists uniformly, endowed with the power to undergo transformation.

That which is called a "lump" (piṇḍa) is indeed gold itself that expands as a power; likewise, even a "bracelet" (kuṇḍala) expands as that very same gold as a power, though in another form. It is not that power alone, independent of gold, is the cause of its being so. For no such power is perceived apart from it.
Furthermore, there is a dispute regarding the name of the power (śakti) when it exists in the form of visible gold;

moreover, it has been stated previously that this power must also be admitted to exist when [the gold] passes into the state of a bracelet and so forth. In this way, like gold, the Supreme Lord alone possesses the aforementioned powers of will and the rest.

Because it exists through all categories of existence— characterized by their various modes such as the principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), effects, and instruments— it follows that everything is of the nature of Śiva alone,
and not of the nature of Śakti. However, this is so provided one does not resort to the distinctions of power (*śakti*) as they appear in conventional usage.
It has been stated that [the universe] consists of power (śakti).
He supports this very point by means of an illustration, beginning with the words "piṇḍe vā" and so forth.
2. When it undergoes a modification of its manifest parts; 3. [the fallacy of] infinite regress, etc. (p.
"Although the powers [appear as] the entire universe—yet in reality, it is indeed of the nature of Śiva. || 20 ||
When this has been said, a refutation of this position is set forth here:
first of all, the state of being subject to modification arises for the Śiva-principle.
In this way, insentience itself exists in the form of various modifications;
likewise, it possesses the state of having parts and a state of dependence on another. (22)

If [the soul] were to undergo transformation like milk, there would be destruction characterized by purity and impurity, higher and lower states, deficiency, and so forth; likewise, there would be the need for atonement for transgressions. || 23 ||
Where there are no hands or other limbs above, nor this [body] in the presence of the Lord, there the walking of feet and so forth is clearly prohibited. (24)
This being the case, the entire conventional discourse would be destroyed;
for if it were to proceed in such a manner, the conceptualization of causal signs would necessarily follow.

Thus, when it has been stated that everything has Śiva as its essence, opponents raise objections against this position from many angles: namely, that if the Śiva-tattva— which is composed of consciousness,
eternal, devoid of increase or decrease, and intended [as the ultimate reality]— possesses the nature of the universe, it would be subject to modification, just like clay and other such materials.

That [consciousness] has been attained—this alone is first of all a great defect. Furthermore, in its abiding in various forms as knowable objects such as earth and so forth, there is its insentience; likewise, it would consequently possess parts. This would apply even to the Lord (Īśvara), who is of the singular nature of consciousness, regarding his births and destructions.
Dependence on another and the state of being an object of enjoyment constitute a state of subordination.

If one accepts the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*), as in the case of milk and curd, there would arise the contradiction of pure and impure natures coexisting; for instance, just as pure milk [cannot become] urine.
The transformed is impure; likewise, in the state of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), there is transcendence (*paratā*) and greatness (*mahattva*).

But when the collection of effects is present, there is non-transcendence (*aparatā*) and diminution (*nyūnatva*). Furthermore, upon the destruction of the prior state, because it is non-different from that [effect], it is that very thing which is destroyed if one resorts to the theory that the effect is non-existent (*asatkāryavāda*).
Or likewise, of the earth, which is of the nature of Śiva and of the nature of the feet.
If the object [of the action] were stepping upon [the Lord] with one's feet, spitting, and so forth, there would be the occurrence of a penance (*prāyaścitta*).

In a situation where the Lord is present, such that another person’s hand or other objects like wood must not be brought over Him in that same manner, actions such as placing one's foot [upon Him] are utterly excluded because of their extreme deprecation. And thus:

If there were a contradiction regarding walking on foot and so forth, all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) would perish. Furthermore, the cause for the Lord Śiva’s abiding as the self of the universe must be investigated, because he is not an object of action (*karman*) and the like. || 25 ||
Furthermore,
here there is no contradiction with various doctrines and their respective established tenets;
for, since all things are Śiva, there is no existence of bondage and liberation.

In the absence of that [the Self], there would be the total destruction of the gods, the gurus, and the scriptures; the scripture would become useless both in its composition and in its exposition. (27)
Since all are established in liberation, to whom could there be instruction?
Dharma and adharma do not bind Śiva, nor is he the agent of those two. (28)
Consequently, the Śivadharmas, the Vedas, and so forth would be rendered purposeless; furthermore, there would be parity among the efficient, inherent, and other types of causes. (29)

In the doctrine of universal Śiva-nature (*sarvaśivatva*), there is a contradiction with all other philosophical systems as well as with one's own established tenets. This is because such [contradiction] is undesirable for them; furthermore, even for those [other systems], their Śiva-nature exists because they lack any other purpose [than this].
Moreover, even within one's own established tenets, [the existence of] *māyā*, *pradhāna*, karma, and so forth, as separate entities, [is untenable].

Because [the Lord] is described as the cause of the world; and if all entities were admitted to be Śiva, then living beings would also possess all powers and thus be eternally liberated, resulting in the absence of bondage and liberation. Consequently, there would be no distinction between what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted.
There would be a destruction of the means for attaining the goals of human life as characterized by the gods, the teachers, and the scriptures, due to the predominance of the Lokāyata view;
for while that [Lokāyata] might occasionally accept those [means] regarding perceptible objects, what [acceptance] could there be regarding the state of universal Śiva-hood?

109) For whom is there a means? Likewise, the composition, investigation, exposition, and hearing of the treatise would be useless; for all are liberated by virtue of being Śiva. For whom [is it intended]?

The teaching of the scripture [is intended] for the sake of instruction. Even for the sake of *dharma*, a scripture is inappropriate for Śiva, because, due to the absence of the *kārmamala* (the impurity of karma), neither *dharma* nor *adharma* are inherent in Him.
Nor is there any instrumentality of those two in Śiva, because the activities [of the world] have their causes in false knowledge, attachment, and so forth. And thus:

Since the Śivadharmas and other such texts, as well as the Veda, would lack the status of being means for achieving dharma (dharma-arthatva), they would be rendered purposeless. Likewise, the distinction of Śiva as the inherent cause (samavāyi-kāraṇa), the non-inherent cause (asamavāyi-kāraṇa), and the instrumental cause (nimitta-kāraṇa)—which is taught in other scriptures and is observed in the world—would not exist. || 29 ||
Furthermore, by the conceptualization of earth and so forth, Śiva would become a possessor of conceptualization;
at that time, there would be equality with the vision of those who possess experience within the reality of Śiva.

When one desire has been fulfilled through the accomplishment of its object and another desire arises again, the cause for Śiva [to act] must be stated, for the sake of which that [new desire] has emerged. (31)
There would be a contradiction with those words spoken by Śiva—which in some instances describe the unreal nature of the universe—for one who maintains that everything is real. (32)

If one holds the view that the Self remains after having conceptualized itself in the form of earth and so forth, then the venerable Lord Śiva would become a possessor of conceptual construction (*kalpanāvān*). Yet he is held to be free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*), because conceptual constructions are of the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*) due to their being devoid of any distinct objective reality. Now, the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*) is not conceptual; rather—
But that [cognition] is accompanied by experience; for experience is never non-conformable to reality (*ayathārtha*).
In such a case, what does it experience? Does it experience itself, or does it also experience another self?
Is it unexperienced, or is it experienced? And between the object of experience (*anubhāvya*) and the experiencer (*anubhāvaka*), there is indeed a distinction.

Thus, at the occasion of pointing out the aforementioned defects regarding the object of the *paśyantī* [level of speech], then, by the power of a specific intention (*viśiṣṭecchā*), that which is desired is [accomplished] through the production of the effect characterized as the world (*jagat*).

Furthermore, when there is an absence of the cause consisting of desire— which serves as the motive— what is the cause, what is the instigator, for the emergence of another desire at the time of maintenance or dissolution, or in the cognition of a cloth and so forth,
such that Śiva, being impelled by it, abandons his prior nature and a new, different nature arises? It is desire.
[Otherwise,] it would proceed as something ever-new. Furthermore, if all things were of the single nature of Śiva, they would possess ultimate reality;
and thus, that which is described in the scriptures of the Supreme Lord—namely, that the world is like an illusion or a magician’s trick—would be contradicted. 32.
To this, he replies: "In order to defend against this objection, a response is provided here.
This means that for the sake of protecting his own system from such a great objection raised by another, he [proceeds as follows].
For the purpose of protecting against or warding off an objection, when an objection has arisen here, a justification is provided either for one's own view or for this [objection] itself.
For then there would be the state of being subject to modification for the Self, whether it be gross or subtle. (33)

1. Thus it was said, "for the purpose of protecting against the objection. In that regard, as for what was stated starting with "first of all," namely that "this very thing is first of all a great fault"—in that very context, [the faults of] insentience (*jaḍatā*), having parts (*sāvayavatva*), dependence on another (*paradhīnatva*), and so forth, are included; therefore, that alone...

He says, "For when that [self]... and so forth, meaning that while that great fault is being pulverized by the principle of the *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (the established conclusion of the context), once it has lost its power, the other factors situated above it subside of their own accord. The word "that" (*tat*) is a pronoun used to indicate well-known status.

The state of not having fallen away from its primordial nature (*apracyutaprācyasvarūpatva*) within the condition of being the self of all (*viśvātmatā*) is thus intimated. The particle *hi* indicates a justification for the objection raised by another. Now, as for the alternative position: the sense is this—that in whatever cause, whether gross or subtle, there is the possibility of connection with transformation (*pariṇāma*) and so forth, [it is that which is meant by "as far as"].

In that regard, even in cases such as transformation (*pariṇāma*) where something becomes an effect, changeability (*vikāritā*) necessarily occurs; for instance, even when milk—which is gross—transforms into the form of curd, it undergoes changeability. This is likewise the case for *māyā*, *prakṛti*, and so forth, which are subtle, insentient, and composed of the three qualities (*triguṇa*).
Even upon attaining the state of an effect, it possesses that very same form; thus this is established:
as is the cause, so is the effect. It is simply the attainment of the causal form within the effect, but the cause does not follow after the effect.
Just as milk and illusion are by nature [capable of transformation], and for as long as they exist,
so too, for a yogin, a self of Śiva’s nature arises here. (34)

If the conscious self (*cidātman*) were gross, it would undergo modification in the creation of the world, just as milk becomes curd; or, even if it were subtle, it would be like *māyā* or *prakṛti*. Since the Supreme Lord, the conscious self, is neither gross nor subtle, but rather beyond those two, [he remains unmodified].
For the connection with transformations such as grossness belongs only to that which is insentient (jaḍa) in every respect, and not to that which consists of consciousness (cinmaya).
However, for that Supreme [Reality], its very abiding in whatever nature of selfhood is intended is itself its "origination," just as it is for yogins.
He says that very thing:
"By [His] will, there is the state of being all things and indeed the state of having manifold natures;
here, one should not produce the circle of entities through a modification of one's own self. (35)
1. When there is a position (pakṣa): 2. Just as subtle Māyā, being the cause, is insentient (jaḍa), its effect is likewise;
just as subtle Prakṛti, consisting of the three guṇas, [is insentient], so too is its effect.
The meaning is that it consists of the three *guṇas* and has undergone modification through its parts.

(3) Of those two, namely the effect and the modification. (4) Now, if it [the primordial matter] does not possess connection with transformation and so forth, then what is this so-called "concomitance" with it?
Regarding that which was stated—"all this has Śiva as its essence"—having raised this doubt, he says: "But of that... The intended meaning is this:
here, "Śiva-nature" does not consist in insentience and so forth, because each of those is of the nature of his mere will (*icchāmātra*).
Furthermore, the state of having Śiva as one's essence consists in the fact that their very arising is of the nature of abiding in such [a state].
The meaning is that it cannot be said, "but that very thing is exactly like that.

Furthermore, creation by will is indeed observed in cases such as dreams and mental constructs; if it is argued that objects like jars are unreal in this context because they set aside the well-known causal sequence [of clay, etc.], let it be so.

This much is granted; nevertheless, it is established that a yogi creates cities, armies, and so forth solely by the power of his will. For in that case, if it is said that the atoms instantly assembled through his will constitute the material cause (*upādāna*), then [this would be] like a well-known potter who produces a jar.

If one accepts that the collection of causes, such as the potsherds and so forth— which are appropriate to their own material cause and accompanied by auxiliary factors such as all the craftsman’s training, merit, demerit, and punishment— is indeed this very specific potter,
then it follows that this yogi is nothing other than him; for even a blade of grass would overstep established reality [if the distinction were not maintained].
The capacity to manifest the appearance of entities—whether present or absent—as perceived objects in dreams, volitions, desires, sorrows, and so forth, belongs to consciousness alone.
Because its nature is such that it follows immediately upon his will,
both are indicated here. Just as it is accepted that for yogins, the state of being all things or having multiple natures occurs through their will, so too [is it here].

This must also be understood regarding the Supreme Lord. For He does not generate the circle of existents through a sequence of transformations and modifications—such as the form of a palanquin or a funeral mound—from His own self, like a potter producing a jar from a lump of clay; rather, whatever His will is, [that it becomes].
Immediately following that, there is a persistence in the form of a desire for the desired object;
so it is also for the conscious self.
Again he said: "Just as for the yogin here there is no [need for practice] by means of various armies of bodies. (36)
In the same way, there is no differentiation for the Lord among states that are middling, superior, or inferior; rather, it is like the waves of the ocean.
1. [This applies] to both types of practitioners of the yoga of the Self. 2. Let it not be that [the world] is entered into through dreams, mental constructs, and so forth.
3. Now, let it be granted that [the Lord] possesses the capacity to perform all actions by His will, just like a yogin; nevertheless, furthermore—

Since these [bodies] clearly possess distinct characteristics during the state of persistence, what basis is there for their being established as having a single nature? To this, he says: "Just as not," and so forth.
Now, let it be granted that there is no difference between the yogin and the bodies of his army; in this regard, just as...
Since even for the Supreme Lord, the conventional usage of difference (*bhedavyavahāra*) clearly manifests, how could that [difference] among them be denied?
This is stated for the sake of making clear the perception [of this fact] to those whose vision of wisdom has been destroyed by the blindness of delusion caused by fallacious reasoning (*kutarka*).
He further reinforces this with another illustration, beginning with "Alternatively" (*athavā*) and so forth.
In that regard, water that has attained a variegated state is not called "water."
And yet, at the time of the wave, there is no destruction of that which has the nature of water.
For even when it is motionless, water remains water; though it is characterized by waves, those waves do not qualify or differentiate its state of stillness. (39)
Just as there is no division of the self for a yogin who exists through various bodies in the form of elephants, chariots, horses, and infantry, so it is with the Supreme Lord.

There is no distinction among the intermediate, superior, and inferior forms such as gods, humans, animals, and so forth, because there is a rule of oneness for that which consists solely of the consciousness of all powers. Alternatively, this illustration is extremely well-known: just as there is a difference in conventional usage despite the identity of the ocean and its waves, so it is here.

This applies to both Śiva and the universe. For in common usage, water that has attained the state of a wave is not called "water," yet its nature as water is not destroyed in its form as a wave. Thus, whether in a state of stillness or in the state of moving waves, it is indeed water, because a wave is a particular state of water; for water is characterized by its possession of those waves.

It is not merely water; let this be so, for even when characterized by waves, there is no loss to the water, as it remains in its original state. If it were that the nature of water ceased upon being characterized by waves, then water-ness would not exist even in that which is characterized by stillness; likewise, even in the form of phenomenal existence (*bhāva*), the state of Śiva remains established. (39)
For this very reason, insentience does not exist by virtue of another's will;
if insentience were perceived in the group of principles beginning with earth, [it would be so]. (40)
Such insentience is not found anywhere else; this we shall explain in detail later through thorough investigation, and it is never possessed of parts.
We shall state clearly hereafter that there is someone [who maintains] this;
for this very reason, just as in the case of a yogin, the Supreme Lord remains in such a state solely by virtue of His own will.

In the group of principles beginning with earth, there is no insentience (*jaḍatā*), because they consist of specific forms of will; however, this [world] does not have insentient *pradhāna* or the like as its material cause. Now, if it is argued that insentience in the form of being incapable of being designated as "this" (*idantā*) is perceived therein, that is not so; for just as there is no real insentience anywhere, even when something cannot be designated as "this."
We shall explain this further below through thorough investigations. Furthermore, we shall later refute the objection that if the Śiva-principle were the self of all,
it would follow that it possesses parts (*sāvayavatva*), demonstrating how nothing whatsoever could ever possess parts while abiding in its own nature as Śiva.
And since He abides as the self of the universe by His own nature, with respect to what could there be "objectivity" (bhogyatā) such that He would possess parts?
If its nature as an entity were due to its own will, how could its persistence be dependent on another? (42)
If it were said to be like milk, it would be dependent on another and insentient;
by this same method, one should examine the defects such as impurity or deficiency.
If its own nature remains unbroken, how can there be purity, deficiency, and so forth?
Just as the nature of gold persists in the gold of a bowl and the like, as well as in a crown and the like.
The gold remains exactly as it is; there is no difference whatsoever in its nature. Fire located in the house of an outcaste is not called "non-fire. (45)

If it were so, then let it be said that the injunction regarding the refinement of fire is described in the scriptures for the sake of a specific effect; therefore, that [refinement] is indeed a [transient] effect. (46)
There is no division of its own nature here, because it remains established in that way;
that [division] is merely a designation imagined for the sake of conventional usage. (47)

The existence of that which takes the form of all phenomena is not dependent on anything else, but is rather governed solely by its own will; its universal form does not depend upon the transformation of a cause, as the form of curd depends upon milk.

115) If it were said that the Universal Self is dependent on another, then He would be insentient (*jaḍa*), because dependence is logically impossible for that which is of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*). For as long as there is the form of the universe, there is only the nature of consciousness itself. By this very [reasoning]...

The defects such as the loss of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpatā*), as well as purity, impurity, increase, decrease, and so forth, must be avoided by way of [maintaining] that very nature. For one whose own form is its essential nature (*svarūpa*), when that state of being the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpatva*) remains as it is, there is an absence of defects such as impurity or deficiency; this is like the relationship between a crown and a water-drawer's bucket.

Its status as gold is due to its similarity with gold. For instance, if the fire residing in the house of a *caṇḍāla* were not fire, then this [similarity] would also be impossible. Furthermore, if fire were not inherently pure, how could it be said in the scriptures that it is joined with consecrations (*saṃskāra*) by means of mantras for the sake of accomplishing ritual effects? Therefore...

Its impurity might thus arise. But this is not so; for the effect alone is to be performed and established for the sake of conventional usage, yet there is no division within the essential nature of fire. When fire is understood as abiding in its own essential nature—its innate form—then that very nature, which is the nature of fire itself, exists everywhere; it is just like that.

The world possesses the nature of Śiva because the Lord exists in the form of those very elements, such as earth and the rest; thus, there is a distinction between the gross and the subtle, and so forth. And since there is unity everywhere, that which is imagined for the sake of worldly transaction is merely a name. || 47 ||
Even worldly convention is ignorance; there is no existence of God as such [in reality].
Or rather, He is fashioned as such by that very [convention], and thus one conforms to Him accordingly. (48)
Scripture does not serve to differentiate its essential nature, since it pertains to worldly convention.
Furthermore, the worldly convention of saṃsāra, which is called ignorance (avidyā), is not a separate ontological entity; it is none other than the Lord himself.

Now, one might object: let there be unity because it is established as being that very same thing everywhere; and let there be the mere application of a name for the sake of conventional usage. Nevertheless, even though that [object] by whose constraint the mere application of a name occurs may be something...
Although it is indeed identical to that because it appears as such, there nevertheless exists a distinction consisting merely of a name; therefore, he says "in conventional usage," and so forth.
Here, by resorting to the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) in the phrase "ignorance is not [us]," the intention is not toward negation (*niṣedha*), but rather...
The meaning is that it does not itself have the nature of avidyā, which consists of empirical transaction; thus he says, "tathātve" (if it were so).

Because it abides in suchness (*tathātva*) as the very nature of worldly conduct; and even the scripture teaches the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) pertaining to conventional practice, not for the sake of differentiating the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*),
since that very Lord has likewise fashioned the purificatory rite of fire and so forth, and thus one follows it accordingly.
Therefore, that which is imagined—consisting of His will—is this very form [of Śiva] itself; it does not bring about impurity or duality for the Śiva-principle.
Just as in a lump of gold there would be only gold-ness, even if it were not [yet fashioned into] a crown or the like. (49)
It is appropriate to say this, and that impermanence which remains [is established].

Now, let it be granted that the conventional practice of saṃsāra exists; for although it is non-different from that [reality], it is imagined as something separate for the sake of conventional usage by those who are deluded. And even though this is so...

Nevertheless, one might object: "Is the scriptural rule sufficient for that purpose? For the worldly transaction (*saṃsāravyavahāra*) has been established as real. Anticipating this, he says: "The scripture... The intended meaning is this:
as long as worldly transaction is real, so too the scripture for its sake is indeed real; however, upon its negation...
The meaning is that for him, too, there is no such restriction.

Now, one might ask: "What is this that is said, namely, 'the existence of God as suchness'? If he exists only as suchness, then there would be neither linguistic usage nor designation; and if there is linguistic usage and designation, [he cannot exist as suchness]."
He supports the alternative position—that it is designated as "suchness" (tathātva)—with the words "by this very Lord.

For this has been established by resorting to the doctrine of absolute sovereignty (svātantryavāda): just as mental impressions (saṃskāra) and so forth are imagined through sovereignty and are not ultimately real, so too is the conformity to that [imagined state].
The superiority of this [view] over the previous position is to be understood only by those of subtle intellect.
3. Therefore, it should be understood that this very form, whose essence is His will, is a single reality consisting of non-duality, wherein both aspects are equally primary.
4. Now, let it be granted that where there is the reflective awareness "I," such as when milk flows from the cow's udder; [but what of other cases?]
According to this principle, where there is non-differentiation (*abheda*) that is indeed uninterrupted, there is the state of non-duality with Śiva (*śivādvayatva*). However,

regarding the question of how it can be so in cases where there is a clear indication of "this-ness" (*idantā*) and thus the presence of transformations such as having parts (*sāvayavatva*), he says "the mass of gold" (*hemapiṇḍa*) and so forth, in order to pacify that doubt.

But if the entire sphere of existence (bhāvamaṇḍala) consists of that very nature, namely the eternity of the Śiva-principle in relation to its non-eternal effects, then how could it be non-eternal even while being composed of that?
To this he says: "That non-eternality... [and so forth].
In the case of being honored, that [transgression] is to be determined; as is the injunction regarding its transgression. || 50 ||
And for the sake of entering into the observances (*niyama*), what is the point of transgression regarding Śiva?

Furthermore, a distinction could only be spoken of in relation to the form of the world if the nature of gold were restricted solely to the lump of gold, and not to the crown and so forth. The particle *eva* (only/surely) follows immediately after "lump of gold."

This is to be understood. Furthermore, as for the objection raised regarding the perishability of the self—the *Śiva-tattva*—on account of the perishability of phenomenal entities (*bhāva*), that will be resolved through the establishment of the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*).
And as for [acts] such as stepping on the feet or spitting, which are to be avoided everywhere toward the auspicious Self (*śiva-ātman*), [these are likewise explained].

This has been stated for the purpose of accomplishing the worldly transaction of saṃsāra, which results from the entry of dharma and adharma— whose nature consists of the constraints imposed by the power of niyati (destiny) inherent in each respective [subject].
In reality, what harm does that transgression cause to the Śiva-tattva? The meaning is: none at all.
Thus, there is no emergence of a causal motive for his engaging in such activity. || 51 ||
1. When it has not yet undergone modification of its parts;
2. when it has undergone modification of its parts;
3. This is the meaning: if the effect were to exist immediately after its production, [it would have to exist] prior [to that].
If it were non-existent, then because its effect would be non-existent, the consequence would follow that the Śiva-principle is perishable;
yet, since it was previously existent, of what could there be perishability?
This very point has been stated in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*.

For the Lord, who is indeed the very self of consciousness, manifests the multitude of objects existing within himself externally by the power of his will, just as a yogi manifests a collection of things without any external material cause.
Thus [it is said].

For in the Śiva-principle (śivatattva), there is indeed an absence of both merit (dharma) and demerit (adharma); and since that [act of] transgressing and so forth leads to demerit, it should not be performed, for in such a case, the production of merit would occur.

In the absence of the worldly conventions of dharma, adharma, and saṃsāra, just as jumping does not serve his purpose through dharma, so too it does not serve him through adharma. Likewise, if such activity were to proceed [in that manner], the calculation of causal conditions would fall away.

Thus, he supports that [point] with the words "in this way. The intended meaning is as follows: for an agent of activity indeed performs an action only if he experiences some degree of superiority or the like over himself; and if he is already such [a superior being] by his own nature, for what reason would he engage in activity?
(118) If the conceptualization of forms such as Śakti arises from the loss of its own essential nature (svarūpa), then it must be explained: for what purpose does that [nature] abandon its form? 52.
To the extent that all forms possess their own inherent nature,
it is not the cause for the maintenance of the world— which is characterized merely by such a state— existing in this way without having the form of birth, transformation, and so forth.

There is no objection, because there is no prior action [to account for it]. For if the assumption of another form, such as that of Śakti and so forth, by one whose nature is peaceful (śānta) were to occur through the abandonment of the Śiva-principle, then some purpose for this must be stated here and the question asked: "For what reason does he abandon this form? However, since...
In its nature as peace, O Śiva, and also in its nature as the world, its possession of self-nature exists solely through the very form of Śiva.
That in which everything exists, established as the very nature of the three powers (śakti).
A sign is conceptualized therein; let that sign be conceptualized therein. Now, an objection is raised regarding how there could be such an appearance where there is no such reality. (54)
Where it is described that there was first a state of peaceful nature and subsequently a similar state of abiding—wherein both in the subtle and in the gross, the state of Śiva is proclaimed. (55)
In that regard, tell me: what is this "quiescence"? Does your power not possess substantiality? If it does possess substantiality, then there must be a conjunction of the three such powers. (56)

Even in the persistence and continuation [of an object], since its state is merely such a subsistence and not a modification such as birth or transformation, there is no application of a causal agent whatsoever; for if there were any increase [in its nature],
then indeed there would be an application of a causal agent.
2. Consisting of the equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) of will and the other [powers].
3. It is to be joined with speech preceded by the movement of the eyebrows.
4. In that which is not of the nature of the world, Śiva-nature consists of the equilibrium of the five powers; it is the principle of non-duality (*abheda-tattva*).
In the gross— the form of the universe— there exists, in every state, the nature of consciousness consisting of the triad of powers beginning with will (icchā).

If a cause (*nimitta*) were to be postulated for that which already exists established therein, what could possibly be postulated by way of implication? The meaning is that nothing at all should be postulated; for a cause should indeed be postulated only where there is the emergence of a certain form despite the absence of that form. Now, this objection is raised: previously...

One might argue that the cause for its novelty must be stated as being the state of quiescence (*śāntarūpatva*), the state of non-worldliness (*ajagadrūpatva*), and subsequently the state of worldliness (*jagadrūpatā*). That is not so; for where it is accepted that Śiva-nature (*śivatva*) exists even in the quiescent and that Śiva-nature alone is described even in the gross state of worldliness, there both quiescence and the form of Śiva are present.

What could it be? Tell me this: for even though your object (*vastu*) is peaceful (*śānta*), an object consists of existence (*sattā*); existence is the state of being (*bhavattā*), which is the agency of becoming (*bhavanakartṛtā*); and agency is essentially autonomy belonging to that whose nature is consciousness and which possesses powers such as will. Thus, every object is Śiva. (56)

If fire does not possess the nature of fire in the form of glowing coals—which lack the nature of action—is that state [of fire] then not an action consisting of cognition, such as a flame and so forth? (57)
If Śiva were present in this state, it could never be said that he is devoid of desire. (58)
This action does not exist in one who is devoid of desire; how then could there be action?
Or rather, it exists in one who possesses knowledge. Therefore, it should be understood that there is no state of incapacity whatsoever.
1. Even amidst the agitation of the vibration of the world-form;

2. Just as it is established that fire-ness (*vahni-tva*) is precisely the state of being [the essence] of burning and heat, such that in its absence there is no fire-ness, so too Śiva-ness is precisely the possession of the power of existence (*bhāva-śakti*), and not otherwise.
The meaning is "the state of possessing the absence of that.

3. Others [hold that] since Śiva-hood exists in the state of possessing power (*śaktimat*) and being active (*sakriyatva*), therefore another, subtle, and non-conceptual state must necessarily be sought; otherwise, indeed—
Since the supreme reality (*paratattva*) would also be subject to conceptual construction (*vikalpya*) because it is accompanied by knowledge and its object,
one should not even acknowledge the state of Śiva (*śivatva*) therein; for if that were accepted, it would fall right into the midst of conceptual construction— thus he says,
"that state" (*sāvasthā*).

120) Why is there no state of being fire in a mass of embers, which is indeed of the nature of fire, but not in that which is engaged in activities such as blazing and burning? Or rather, in that case, Śiva is indeed the fire.
Even when entered by the differentiation of those states, he is Śiva alone. This has been stated by way of the state of activity (*kriyāvasthā*).

Now, since power (*śakti*) is possible within the active, let there be Śiva-nature; however, quiescence (*śāntatā*) is inactive, devoid of both the object of knowledge and the act of knowing, and because it performs no action, it is also empty of the will characterized by the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*); therefore, [quiescence] is not [Śiva].
It cannot be said that Śiva is never thus [existent], because the act of becoming (*bhavana*) is absent at all times.

If it is admitted that Śiva remains even in the state of quiescence (*śāntāvasthā*) when gross activity is absent, then why would this act of abiding—which consists in the persistence of being—not exist? It certainly does exist.

Action is of the very nature of the agent, and the agent is indeed an independent conscious being, since independence consists in acting according to one’s own will; for in the cases of "it exists" and "it stands," there is certainly present the desire characterized by the wish to be (*bubhūṣā*) and the wish to stand (*atiṣṭhāsā*). And as long as [the agent] intends to act or to become in such a manner...

One does not even know how to remain [in that state]; for how long, then, can there be any action? Expressions such as "it becomes" (*bhavati*) and so forth are merely designations using verbal suffixes (*tiṅanta*). Therefore, it must be understood that no state whatsoever exists for anyone devoid of the power of will (*icchā*) and the other [powers]. To possess the power of will and the rest is Śiva-hood; thus, "the jar exists," "the Himalaya exists."
And just as the statement "the world exists" does not cause any addition to the state of Śiva-ness, so it has been investigated in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*. 59.
Now, multiplicity exists here in the aggregate of entities, but not in Śiva;
for that which is mutual variety is the very nature of Śiva.
Depending on the diversity of entities, its own diversity arises from them;
how everything is of the nature of Śiva shall be explained hereafter.
Now,

if it is asked: "How can this mutual diversity of entities be possible within Śiva, whose nature is solely consciousness?"— even in that case, it is Śiva himself who possesses that diverse form of the entities.
1. Regarding that which is characterized by the activity of flaming:

2. It has been stated that "Śiva-nature exists even in the quiescent, and Śiva-nature exists even in the gross; therefore, there is no calculation of causal conditions here. In order to clarify that Śiva-nature resides within the state of quiescence, he says:
"Quiescence, however, is for the purpose of taking up the signs"—this refers to the mutual variety among those things such as jars, cloths, and so forth. (p. 121)
In dependence upon that variety, diversity appears within Him—though He exists as the single form of consciousness—by virtue of those [objects].
Furthermore, everything is of the nature of Śiva because it has the essence of consciousness; this will be explained further below in accordance with logical reasoning.
If a jar capable of carrying water is not called a "jar," then let that which is merely a jar here be described as such. (62)

And if, in this world, what is not called a "pot" is one that lacks the capacity to fetch water, but rather a pot that is merely devoid of engagement in that action— then this is exactly analogous to saying that Śiva is merely himself and not of the nature of the world; for in that case, he would never at any time be Śiva.
There is no contradiction with various doctrines; this should be explained here before [the assembly].
It has been stated in the *Kālapāda* and other works that [this truth] is known even by cowherds, women, and others. 63.
Then Kheṭapāla also spoke of that unity: "Whatever power exists within the entire collection of objects, that belongs entirely to the God of gods. (64)
For the non-difference between power and the possessor of power is stated to exist everywhere.
1. [He is] indeed capable of fetching water.
2. At the beginning, he says "or it has been stated" according to his own scripture. Now, how is this so?
There is no contradiction among the various doctrines because they are conceived as having distinct and different meanings; therefore, he says, "or it has been stated.

This is the intended meaning: for the status of being scripture (*āgama*) consists in being composed by a trustworthy authority (*āpta*), and that [status] belongs first of all to the *tantra* scriptures because they were spoken directly by the venerable Lord Śiva.

Since the Vedas themselves are declared to be beginningless, they certainly exist; and since their meaning is ascertained through the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and so forth, they certainly possess the status of valid authority.
Therefore, [this applies] to the Lord alone, who is the cause of the origin of the entire universe and possesses great majesty.
Because of its connection with the distinct functions of creation, maintenance, and dissolution, it is designated as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra;
however, other [scriptures] lack authority because they were composed by those who are not authoritative.
This very threefold authority of scripture is corroborated by the passage beginning with "It has been said," and so forth.
3. The Guru says [the following] beginning with "The identity of those...
4. He states the non-contradiction of all [these views] here.
"Rudra is one," and so forth; likewise, it is stated in the Śruti that he is supreme. (65)

The Puruṣa-sūkta and other such texts declare that everything here is the eightfold form of Maheśvara, extending even to the state of being a dull-witted mortal on earth. The Vedic statement "She wept" is not a meaningless explanatory passage (arthavāda).
If existence is [required] as a constituent part of the ritual act, then non-existence cannot be established as a constituent part.
The fruit [of the ritual] is also shown from the *arthavāda* in the case of the *Rātri-kratu*s.
Furthermore, it will be explained later that there is no contradiction for us regarding this non-dual Śaivism due to various philosophical systems (*darśana*s).
Or rather, this very point has been stated within our own established doctrine (*svasiddhānta*) in the *Śrīkālottara* and other texts.
Even cowherds, women, and children constantly speak of him in such ways;

through these and other [statements], the nature of living beings as being essentially Śiva in the form of Mantra is established. The Gurus also teach the identity with Śiva. Thus, the Guru Kheṭapāla said: "Whosoever... and so forth.

Since the power of the God of gods alone has been stated to be the power of all things, and since there is no difference between power and the possessor of power, it follows that the God of gods himself is the "thing" (padārtha). This is what is being said. [He states the authority of scripture: "This is that.
1. He states the authority of scripture.
2. He states the authoritative status [of the Veda] as being uncontradicted by the learned (*śiṣṭa*).

3. Since a sentence in the form of an injunction (*vidhi*) has as its direct object that which is to be performed, let it possess authority; however, since a sentence in the form of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) lacks a direct connection to that [performance], it does not [possess authority] therein.

Anticipating the objection that "validity" (prāmāṇya) does not apply because some [Vedic passages] are devoted to injunctions (vidhi) while others are devoted to explanatory eulogies (arthavāda), and thus there is no mutual connection between them— asking how there can be a doctrine of unity (aikyavāda) everywhere— the author says:
"He wept" (sorodīt).
"And the cowherds saw him, and the water-carriers saw him"—so says the Śruti. And in the *Mahārthamañjarī*:
"Even the dull-witted know him; even the water-carriers recognize him."
To whom does that Kulanātha not clearly appear, he to whom [this] salutation is addressed?
Thus,
[the statement] "Rudra is one" indicates the oneness of Rudra; likewise, [the statement] "The Supreme Person alone is all this" [indicates the oneness of the Supreme Person].
It is stated in the Veda, and in the Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and so forth, that Maheśvara possesses eight forms (aṣṭamūrti),
wherein even the state of delusion, in the form of the earthly principle (pārthivatattva) characterized by extreme tamas, is his very own essential nature.
