Furthermore, even in the etymological derivation of Rudra’s power from the Vedic statement, "He wept" (*so 'rodīt*), their identity is declared:
"Rudra alone existed; indeed, there was no second.
Likewise:
O gods, let there be homage to that Rudra who is in the fire, who is in the waters, who is in the plants, who is in the trees— the Rudra who has entered all beings.
2. "The Person alone is all this, whatever has been and whatever is to be.
3. As it is said in the *Siddhastuti*:
You are the sun, you are the moon, you are the wind, you are the bearer of oblations; you are the waters, you are the sky, you are the earth, and you are the Self.
May they bear speech that, though seemingly limited, is in truth transformed within You.
We do not know that true reality here which you are not.

Thus, here too, the absolute identity (*ekātmya*) of the Blessed Lord Maheśvara is shown everywhere. For it is established that the entire world, existing in its state of transformation, consists of nothing but the five elements (*pañcabhūta*).
In that regard, there is a pair of states consisting of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), which are subtle.

This has been expressed by the terms *arka* (sun) and *soma* (moon), because even the dyad of "I-ness" (*ahaṃtā*) and "this-ness" (*idantā*) here finds its rest in the designations of Sadāśiva and so forth; what more, then, needs to be said of other things, wherein even the dense, composite earthly principle (*pārthiva ghanatattva*) is Śiva alone? For this very reason, at the end of that [principle], here—
This is the designation: it declares that their very self is non-difference.
That which is the nature of immediacy (*pratyagrūpa*), consisting of the non-difference of all these particular vibrations—that alone you are;
what else could there be here where your own essential nature might be denied?
"He wept; that which was his weeping (rudra) became his *rudratva*. This is the meaning:

because he, being Rudra, wept—that is, he flowed forth through the channel of power (*śakti*) and remained in the form of the universe—that constitutes the *rudratva* of this Rudra, namely, his nature of non-difference from Rudra.

(124) It is also not tenable to claim that this *arthavāda* has no real referent because its purpose lies solely in the performance of the injunction; for how could the status of being an auxiliary to the injunction belong to an *arthavāda* whose referent is unreal?

For an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is indeed that which expresses its own meaning; even in the Veda, it does not possess a false meaning. An injunction (*vidhi*) is that which impels one to act who has not yet acted; likewise, an injunction is that which directly instructs.
An explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), on the other hand, is a restatement of what has already been prompted to act; likewise.

The statement regarding "being taught through tradition" is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). Here, having raised the doubt that there is no direct instruction [in this case], it is stated that "this is an explanatory passage.
For an explanatory passage serves as a support only for a matter that has been enjoined and performed; and therefore—
Because there is no direct performance [of the act], the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) does not possess truthfulness.

(2) The meaning is: if the explanatory passage were truly a subordinate part of the injunction (*vidhi*), then how could it have as its purpose a matter that is itself untrue? For example, as in the case of the *vāyavya* [sacrifice]...
"One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white goat"—this is the injunction (*vidhi*). "Vāyu is the swiftest deity;

he approaches Vāyu with his own share; he [Vāyu] leads him to prosperity"—this is the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). In that context, the words such as "vāyavya" occurring in the injunctive sentence...
They enjoin a qualified matter independently of the words of the *arthavāda*, while the words of the *arthavāda* describe an existing fact independently of anything else:
"Vāyu is swift-moving; when satisfied with his appropriate portion, he bestows sovereignty upon one who offers that portion."

When it is said "he bestows," as in the *Rāmāyaṇa*, the *Mahābhārata*, and so forth, some [result] is understood, but nothing is to be performed; therefore, because there is no syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*), the arthavāda lacks authority— so say those who maintain that only injunctions (*vidhi*) possess authority.
On this point, the followers of Jaimini say: let there be no syntactic unity between the injunction (*vidhi*) and the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) at the level of the word;

however, syntactic unity at the level of the sentence certainly exists. For the injunctive sentence requires the excellence of the enjoined matter in order to impel a person toward action, and the explanatory passage likewise [requires it].

Since the injunction to study (*adhyayanavidhi*) culminates in the comprehension of the meaning of the fruit [of knowledge], it requires a human goal (*puruṣārtha*); therefore, the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), by means of the function of indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*), provides the excellence (*prāśastya*) required by that injunction which culminates in a human goal, and thus [functions] together with the injunctive sentence.

It attains syntactic unity with the injunction because Vāyu, by virtue of his nature as one who moves swiftly, is the deity of this animal who bestows fruit quickly; therefore, the connection between the two sentences is: "One should sacrifice this excellent Vāyavya animal. Thus, the explanatory passage (arthavāda) is a means of valid knowledge.

(125) Furthermore, in the case of the Rātri-sacrifices, since they must be performed based precisely on the authority of the explanatory passages (arthavāda), the fruit [of the action] was demonstrated by the followers of Jaimini. || 67 ||
Bondage and liberation do not differ at all, because of the universal nature of Śiva.
Why is it that everyone is not deluded by such a consciousness?
This very [consciousness] is that [reality], and it is saṃsāra; from it, bondage and liberation are established. (69)

If everything is Śiva, then because there would be neither bondage nor liberation, why does the realization "I am Śiva" not arise for everyone? To this it is replied: just as that very same [reality] is deluded, so too...
[in the case of] "the night-sacrifices," for in that instance the meaning is fulfilled by means of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) alone, and thus it is not [to be taken literally].

The status of being a subordinate part (*aṅga*) by way of dependence is indeed the status of being a subordinate part of the ritual action (*kārya*) for an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). For example, in the case of the injunction "Those who sit for these nights certainly become firmly established," where no specific qualification (*adhikāra*) is heard, the aspect of qualification is obtained from the explanatory passage itself regarding the mere injunction of the nights. For in that case:
"Those desiring stability should perform the sacrificial session (*satra*)," such is the meaning of the sentence by virtue of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).

In some cases, when there is doubt regarding the meaning of an injunctive statement (*vidhi*), its determination arises from a supplementary portion of the text consisting of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
For example, in the case of "He places the smeared pebbles," [the purpose of the smearing is determined] regarding the substance for anointing.

When there is doubt as to whether the substance is clarified butter, oil, fat, or the like, it is understood from the explanatory passage (arthavāda), "Clarified butter is indeed light," that the pebbles should be smeared with clarified butter.
2. As for what was said:
"Because all things are Śiva, there is no existence of bondage and liberation"—this objection he refutes with the words "vijñāna" and so forth. The meaning is this:
he supports the position that if all things are Śiva, there is no distinction between bondage and liberation.
When it is asked, "Why does such realization not occur for everyone? and further questioned, "If the realization 'I am Śiva' were present in everyone,

there would be no reality to bondage or liberation," the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī) supports this very position by first exposing the defects in that objection and then providing a counter-argument with only half-spoken words.
—Why should this consciousness not belong to everyone? Why are they deluded? The point is this:
that cognition of duality, such as "I am Śiva," which belongs to everyone, is itself the delusion characterized by deluded ignorance;
and thus, for the sake of removing bondage, liberation alone [is required].
And since that [state] characterized by ignorance is called saṃsāra and bondage, it is established that bondage and liberation consist of the nature of ignorance. (64)
In the case of the various Śiva-schools, however, there is truth and firmness; in other [systems], there is none.
Here, there is merely a conceptual cognition, and by that much alone, the state of bondage and liberation [is established]. (70)

But when the position is that all entities whatsoever are each of the nature of Śiva due to their connection with the powers of agency, will, and so forth, then, while that position of the manifold Śivas is true, there is a firmness regarding the distinction of objects as they exist. However, when the reality is indeed the oneness of Śiva alone, then...

In that view, there is no firmness regarding duality; rather, liberation is merely the realization of non-difference from Śiva, while bondage is the non-realization of that. Bondage and liberation possess their status as such by virtue of that mere realization alone, and not because of any actual alteration in the nature of reality.
1. But why do you attribute this unprecedented fault [to us], saying:

"Why should such consciousness not belong to everyone? Are they not all deluded?"—by which you mean that everyone is deluded regarding the reflective awareness of the unfragmented, perfectly full *ahantā* (I-ness).

He analyzes the intended meaning of the phrase "where else could there be non-delusion? by stating "vibhinna" (distinct), etc. The intended meaning here is as follows: if, in the expression "of everything," the use of the pronoun "everything" (*sarva*) is made with reference to distinct entities, then since multiplicity exists through distinction, there is indeed a difference in the objects with respect to that [multiplicity].

Thus, the established order of bondage and liberation remains intact. Now, the word "all" does not refer to distinct subjects; rather, it refers to the single, non-dual essence consisting of consciousness—the reflective awareness "I"—which belongs to everyone.

Since there is indeed an attachment to bondage through the realization of liberation via the reflective awareness of non-difference from that Śiva, our desired conclusion is established; for in reality,
according to the actual state of things, there is no such designation as "bondage" or "liberation" at all, other than by means of mere cognition.
2. Regarding the difference in ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the strengthening of the difference in objects is "the strengthening of difference" (*bhedadārḍhya*).
This refers to the other position, namely the view of identity (*ekatva*).
3. This is the meaning: [it concerns] the establishment of liberation and bondage through perception and non-perception.

As for the claim that "the non-existence of bondage and liberation [is established] because of their fixed nature," that is unproven. Furthermore, the establishment of the distinction between bondage and liberation does not undermine the intended meaning of the non-duality of Śiva;
for since bondage and liberation are merely forms of cognition, there is no possibility of them being distinct entities in reality.

(127) There is no refutation whatsoever of the notion of truth regarding that which is untrue; this statement is for the sake of establishing universal equality and for the purpose of destroying dispute. (71)

Nor is there here, as in the case of the Vedas, a sublation consisting of delusion through the perception of reality in these unreal particulars; for since all entities are established as being of the nature of Śiva,
whether they be many or one, the statement regarding their unity with the principle of Śiva [is not a sublation].

This is for the sake of establishing the equality of all things through the principle of Śiva (śivatattva), thereby preventing notions of superiority or inferiority; or else, it is for the purpose of defeating those disputants who do not acknowledge the Śiva-nature of all entities. || 71 ||

In whatever way that [reality] is, Śiva’s state is by his own will of that very nature. Let there be the nature of mere appearance for both bondage and liberation, and let there be, in reality, nothing but the non-dual nature of Śiva; nevertheless, if existence is merely a matter of appearance, then that alone—indeed, that very thing—is [bondage].

It must be accepted as authoritative. Furthermore, if everything is indeed of the nature of non-dual Śiva, then what kind of method (naya) is this that speaks of a duality of things? To dispel such a doubt, he says: "Not unreal" (nāsatya).
For in the system of the Vedas, there is a description of varying degrees of limitation; however, here [in this system], there is no multiplicity.

By such statements as "kiṃcana" (not even a little), it is declared that the notion of reality regarding unreal distinctions is nothing but delusion. The underlying meaning is this: in our system, the singular nature of Śiva must be established in every respect; and whether things possess unity or multiplicity, neither is contradicted by anyone.

3. Although, in reality, since all things are of the nature of Śiva, neither plurality nor unity entails contradiction— and thus there is no fault in describing them as such— nevertheless, the statement of the doctrine of non-duality (advayavāda) is for the purpose of declaring that within the principle of Śiva (śivatattva), there is neither superiority for anyone nor inferiority for anyone.

The meaning is that, in such a case, by speaking of multiplicity and unity, the very nature of the object (*padārtha*) would become exactly as described; thus, the doctrine of the reality of objects (*padārthavāda*) itself would be accepted.
4. Now, if the discussion of multiplicity and unity is indeed equal [in status], then...
He says: "The non-dual teaching has been established.

Thus, having first refuted the opponent's arguments, the systematic arrangement of bondage and liberation has been firmly established, and the ultimate purport of non-difference from Śiva has likewise been proven by that very means. Now, therefore—
In the ultimate sense, [the author] establishes the non-difference from Śiva even within conventional discourse by means of the passage beginning with "in such and such a way" (tathā tathā).
(128) When there is identity with That, there is no bondage; and because of the absence of that [bondage], there is no liberation. (72)

Even in the state of differentiation, Śiva exists in the form of difference by virtue of His own will, and that differentiation is of the nature of Śiva. Thus, since differentiation is of the nature of Śiva, there is no bondage; and because of its absence, there is no liberation either, as liberation depends upon [the prior existence of] bondage.

If [it is argued that] the teacher, scriptures, and so forth exist for that purpose, then since [the deity] already exists in that state, what indeed would be the purpose of the deity’s awakening through the scriptures? (73)
For what purpose has this treatise been commenced by you, and for whose awakening?

Furthermore, since Śiva alone exists in the form of differentiation (*bhedarupeṇa*), there would be no liberation; therefore, for what purpose would there be the practice of the Guru, the scriptures, and so forth? For [liberation is not possible] for the Lord who is eternally awakened.
Awakening by means of the scripture [is established] because liberation is preceded by bondage.
Furthermore, even though bondage and liberation are clearly negated here, the systematic arrangement of bondage and liberation [remains].
It should be understood that [the nature of Śiva] is indeed established, because it is described as being "thus and thus"; and this will become clear later.
(3) "Thus" means that even in its form of differentiation (*bheda*), that venerable Lord Śiva [remains so].
(4) He is called *deva* because he "shines" (*dīvyati*) or "plays" (*krīḍati*). Play is a vibration (*spanda*) that follows joy. Likewise, always...
Even though the Lord is self-luminous, the scripture proceeds for the sake of imparting knowledge not previously attained; thus, it possesses a purpose.
For others, indeed, let there be engagement with that [scripture] for the sake of knowledge, since it speaks of duality.
But for you, because that [agency] is absent, it is not logical; thus he asks, "For what purpose? (verse 7).
Nor is there any activity on your part even for the sake of manifesting that [agency], and in that case, there would be a loss of the sovereignty of the independent Lord.
(129) It has a purpose. Let other treatises be set aside; for what reason have you, who profess the doctrine of identity with Śiva, begun this treatise, and for whose enlightenment? 73.
He remains here thus by his own will, being understood as the agent of that [action]. || 74 ||
At that very moment, he becomes thus in the form of a Buddha;
he alone, intent upon that practice, shall be born [as such]. || 75 ||
Or rather, the fruit [of action] would belong to him alone upon its performance;
for in this manner, the Lord remains without purpose by His own will.
He demonstrates that very point: "Therefore, by virtue of being the author of the scriptures for us and others, and likewise by making [the soul] an object of knowledge, [He makes it] knowable."

They assume the form of disciples; likewise, at that very time, they remain in the state of being awakened; likewise, they become intent upon the practice of the scriptures; and likewise, at their own time, they exist even as the nature of fruits such as wealth and desire. || 75 ||
If that [nature] exists in it, why would there be the states of being a proponent and a respondent? (76)
Or rather, everything exists for the sake of conventional usage; conventional usage does not pertain to reality.
Know that the intrinsic nature of things pertains to reality; conventional usage never pertains to it. (77)
Since that [reality] is established as the Lord, appearing in the form of non-entities,
and since there is no difference in perception when there is unity with Him, how can there be the state of being a proponent or an opponent?
As for what was said— "for the sake of destroying the disputant"— that too exists only because of His abiding in such a manner.

Or rather, everything—including the treatises, the proponent, and the opponent—is for the sake of worldly transaction (*lokavyavahāra*). And this worldly transaction consists of the non-discriminative manifestation (*abheda-ākhyāti*) of that [reality], not something residing in the ultimate object. Furthermore, that which shines forth by its own nature is essentially of the nature of the reality that is Śiva; however, worldly transaction is never real, but rather—
It is indeed an illusion; for even that which is non-existent exists as the very self of the Lord in the form of a manifestation of non-existence.
Therefore, according to the method taught in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, even that non-existent thing shines forth [as such].
It is indeed of the nature of consciousness alone; it is merely called a non-entity because of the absence of manifestation externally. || 77 ||
Therefore it is said:
"Everything that is to be investigated should first be examined in its single form. (78)
Since every entity and non-entity is of the nature of Śiva, it must indeed be investigated in this manner hereafter.
(78) The connection with merit and demerit likewise exists because of his abiding as Śiva;
the fitness for the attainment of those fruits or their absence follows from his abiding therein. (79)
There is a connection with those two through their fruit being deficient, or through a contrary fruit, or through no fruit at all;
or else, there is a lack of connection with the fruit, or even a connection with unrighteousness (*adharma*) through its fruit being undesirable.
For that reason, the state of being appropriate or inappropriate is logical for Śiva, because of his abiding in such a manner; this is the case in every respect.
Whatever appears is of the very nature of Śiva, whose essence is consciousness. || 79 ||
The diversity of signs, inherent causes, and so forth, constitutes that variety;
there is no fault in the cause being of a single nature, for it possesses a threefold character.
Neither was a royal command issued, nor did he himself act for a specific motive.

By the word "external" (bāhya), the meaning is that while his error or unreality may apply only to the external [object], there is neither error nor unreality regarding its own essential nature (svarūpa).
2. Furthermore, as it has been stated: "Dharma and adharma are not connected to Śiva, nor is he the creator of them;
consequently, the Śaiva scriptures, the Vedas, and so forth, would lack authoritative validity."
Thus, he refutes that [objection] with the words beginning "dharma" (dharmeti) and so forth.

Here too, everything previously mentioned, such as conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) and the rest, should be followed. He explains [the term] by resorting to the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) as "in non-existence" or "in slight existence," or alternatively, as "by way of deficiency."
Regarding the term "contrary" (viparītā):
that very desire which is inherent [in the agent] is the auxiliary cause for its conjunction. || 81 ||

Or rather, that very [Śiva] possesses a threefold nature due to such designations. When Śiva alone is the cause, his diversity—consisting of the variety of being the efficient cause (*nimitta*), the inherent cause (*samavāyin*), and the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyin*)—is called a "threefold nature"; this is not a fault according to the logic already stated, because it is the King’s command.

It is taught as being equal or identical; however, even though there is a similarity in the form of a royal command, there is nevertheless a difference. Likewise, He exists as the instrumental cause (*nimitta*) both in the form of the threads and in the form of their conjunction. Alternatively, He Himself is the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), while His will is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of objects such as a jar.

The meaning is that, due to the influence of the desire of sentient beings, that very conjunction of parts is the auxiliary non-inherent cause (*sahakāry-asamavāyi-kāraṇa*). Alternatively, even though it is a single entity, there is a threefold designation according to the manner previously described, by way of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*).
All conventional usage of difference consists in the non-apprehension of non-difference. || 81 ||
No conceptual construction arises with respect to that [reality] consisting of earth and the other elements. || 82 ||
Since it is established as being just so, this would be a conceptual construction;
if that very thing is what is constructed, why not let "truth" itself be the conceptual construction? (83)
Regarding what was stated—that he is "possessed of conceptual construction" (kalpanāvān) through the conceptualization of earth and so forth:

if his agency with respect to each of those is accepted on the basis of causes such as illusion (māyā) or atoms (paramāṇu), then, because distinct entities exist, by whom could his state of being a conceptual construction be asserted? But if it is [accepted] in the absence of such [causes],...

In that case, conceptualization (kalpanā) is indeed a mere mental construction (vikalpa) because it is empty of distinct objects; and since that [conceptualization] is essentially void, the Śiva-principle itself would likewise become virtually void if it were of that same nature—this is the intended objection. He refutes this with the words beginning with "no" (na).
2. In that Śiva-tattva;
3. because it exists even as the locus for the conventional usage of its various diversities;
4. the state of being perceived in that which is not [otherwise] perceived.
5. The Śiva-principle itself is conceptualized as earth and the other elements.
6. The word "name" is an assent for the sake of pleasing others.

Nor is the nature of Śiva merely imputed to the multitude of entities perceived as earth and so forth; for, by the very state of things, the reality of Śiva is established precisely in the form of earth and the rest. Just as that which is not of such a form is determined to be of such a form:
If it were a kingdom of the mind and so forth, then that conceptualization would be something being constructed.

However, since in the actual state of reality Śiva alone is everything, earth and the other elements are Śiva himself; therefore, the meaning is that nothing is at all imagined as being "Śiva-ness. Or rather, in truth, the conceptualization occurs within that very [Śiva] himself.
That is said to be a non-entity; therefore, the designation "conceptual construction" (kalpanā) is applied to it. || 83 ||
1. Since the manifestation of the multitude of objects existing within Himself truly exists for the Lord, the reflective awareness of Will proceeds from that [manifestation].

Thus, according to the principle stated in the *Pratyabhijñā*, since everything exists even in the absence of the multitude of entities that appear as various distinct manifestations, what could there be that is not of that nature?
For what, then, could there be a manifestation as that nature—which would otherwise be a ninth manifestation, a mental construction (*kalpanā*), or something imagined? This is the intended meaning.
2. By way of the ultimate truth; 3. From the perspective of conventional usage;
4. Because it is spontaneously accomplished.

5. That which was previously of a different nature is now of that very nature. [Objection: But where else indeed does so-called "fictitiousness" exist? To this he says, "of a different nature": even in the case of a kingdom of the mind and the like, it is the power of consciousness alone to manifest those various appearances; therefore, even there, if fictitiousness were not present...
Nevertheless, in this system, the status of being imagined (*kalpitatva*) therein was accepted for the sake of supporting the arguments of the proponents.
(6) By means of absolute certainty.
(7) For if earth and so forth did not previously exist...
If that [object] had been of a different nature from its own form,

then— just like a kingdom of the mind or similar constructs— it would have appeared as having that form while being empty of reality, and thus it would have been merely imagined; however, since there is not even the possibility that it did not previously exist, it must have possessed that very form previously as well as now.
The meaning is that its being of such a nature would not be imagined [as real].
8. In that very Śiva-tattva. 9. The meaning is that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārthataḥ), there is no differentiation here.
He provides an illustration of that very point:
"Is there gold-ness in a bracelet? Is there any conceptual construction in an earring?"
In some cases, such as with the Aśoka tree or a variegated fire, conceptual construction (kalpanā) appears to shine forth. || 84 ||
I bow to those who do not understand the difference between what is established (*kḷpti*) and what is conceptualized (*kalpanā*).

The meaning is: "Is there any real gold-ness in a bracelet (*kaṭaka*), while it is merely conceptualized (*kalpita*) in an earring (*kuṇḍala*)? The conceptualization of fire in a painting, or in red *aśoka* flowers and the like, is appropriate on certain occasions.

The meaning is that Śiva is "fashioned" (*kḷpta*), i.e., accomplished and existing as such by himself in the form of earth and so forth. Furthermore, he is merely intended to be thus by himself alone through that form; for while that which is fashioned is accomplished by itself as being thus, the mental construction (*kalpanā*) [of it] occurs by itself even though it is not actually so.

Likewise, this is a mockery: that those who are not conventionally established as distinct entities, yet are treated as such in the meaning of words that consist of mere conceptualization, are worthy of praise. || 84 ||
In the Śiva-tattva accompanied by direct experience, there is no equality with the Paśyantī [level]. || 85 ||
1. Just as gold exists within a bracelet, so the universe resides within that [Self]; just as gold exists in the form of an earring, so it exists in the form of the earth and other elements.
2. This is the intended meaning: the attribution of reality to the unreal is only appropriate on certain occasions; what [else could it be]?
It must further be stated that such a possibility exists only when there is actual reality (*satya*).
[Objection: But is it not the case that just as there is a possibility of real fire in something unreal like an *aśoka* tree, so too here?
If this were so, our desired point would be established. To this, he says: "earth and so forth."

Now, one might object: even in the conceptualization of earth and so forth, let it be that [the Self] remains free of conceptual construction (*avikalpa*), because there is no manifestation of those forms [of earth etc.], since even previously it existed as having precisely that nature.
Now, that very Śiva-tattva which exists prior [to all things] must be established, by means of which even the lower [levels]...

That [state] is established for him. Now, raising the objection that "therein, what is called the reflective awareness of 'I' (ahaṃparāmarśa) is indeed a conceptual construction (vikalpa) because it consists of the nature of speech; how, then, can there be non-conceptuality therein?", he says: "In the Śiva-principle. Furthermore, as for what was raised in the prima facie argument—that at that time there is equality with the vision (paśyanti) accompanied by experience in the Śiva-principle—[he replies: "At that time..."
That too is supported by the passage beginning with "the Śiva-tattva," etc.

Here, the expression "by those who see" (*paśyantyaḥ*) is a metaphorical application of the effect to the cause; thus, the meaning is "by those who have seen [it] through the refutations of *paśyantī*."

(134) Because, like [perceiving] the fragrance of a perfumer's goods, one sees without conceptualization within the Śiva-tattva— the self consisting of consciousness, filled with the universe, and whose nature is the experience of the universe— by means of the Paśyantī [speech].

There is no parity with the previously mentioned objection; for just as a perfumer, not determining the fragrance of infinite aromatic substances by means of a limited measure, remains while gradually determining them all, so too [does one perceive] all phenomena.

Perceiving those things which are devoid of the sequence of space and time, and whose nature consists of the signified and the signifier, as being free from conceptual construction— [that is the one Śiva].
That form which was previously described through various ancient divisions, and which shines within them as an essence dense with supreme light— that is the one God, Śiva.
According to this principle—that which is permeated by the principle of the Great Universal (mahāsāmānya)—that is the Śiva-principle.
And it is stated in the Bhāṣāsūtras: "That which is the universe is within Him.
[2] Regarding the previously mentioned objection: what does He experience? Is it Himself, or...
Is the other self experienced or unexperienced? Is it sequential or non-sequential? And so forth.
Here, the mention of the "perfumer" (gāndhika) is an illustrative example.

The purpose of that [recognition] is the gradual awakening to the fragrance of those various infinite objects, and its fruit is the abandonment of conceptualization, because that [conceptualization] depends upon two entities.
(4) "Devoid of the sequence of space and time," because difference consists in the presence or absence of manifestation.

Since succession (krama) depends upon differentiation, that appearance and non-appearance [of objects] is the sovereign power (*prābhavī śakti*) of the Lord; the meaning is that if there were no such appearance, how could there be a connection with space and time?
Through an investigation into the very nature of succession, it is Maheśvara himself who causes its manifestation.
The meaning is that [the Lord] fashions the power of time. And it is said in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*:
"By means of the diversity of forms, this Lord manifests spatial succession;
and by the manifestation of the diversity of actions, He manifests temporal succession as well."
Likewise,
the succession of worldly action is possible through the power of time,
but it is not so for that which is eternal, such as the sovereignty of the Lord.
Thus,
one becomes Śiva, because these [entities] are manifested through the full sense of "I" (*ahambhāva*) as "I alone."

Just as one who possesses the notion of "I" (ahaṃparāmarśavat) may yet be free from conceptual construction (avikalpaka), so too it should be understood from the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*. For instance, when the experience of the quantity of fragrances is equal for both a perfumer and another person, the perfumer [perceives] them as being possessed of the excellence of fragrance, whereas the other person does not.
This belongs to that very void. By this, the fullness of the universe is established; this illustration applies to that extent alone. || 85 ||

For the reflective awareness of "I" within the self of Light is its inherent nature because it consists of the supreme Word (parāvāk); therefore, it is not a conceptual construction (vikalpa). For the latter is preceded by the negation of a counter-correlative (pratiyogin), and here there is no such thing as a counter-correlative. Thus it is said:

For that which is called "non-manifestation" (aprakāśa) is other than manifestation (prakāśa) only as its counter-correlative (pratiyogi); being itself unestablished, how can it possess the status of a counter-correlative? Because if it does not appear, there is an absence of its being "other than manifestation. But if it does appear, even so, what indeed is its counter-correlative? And in that case, if it does not appear [as such], [the distinction remains untenable].
Since there is no object to be excluded, how can it be conceptual?
As it is said in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*: "The reflective awareness of 'I', which, though its essence is light, has speech as its body..."
That is not conceptual construction; for it is defined as a definitive determination that entails both [aspects].
For there may indeed be an appearance of two distinct things, such as a jar and a non-jar;
however, there is no manifestation of another distinct entity apart from the Light itself.
Thus [it is said].

Now, one might ask: since the manifestation of infinite fragrances occurs simultaneously for everyone, for what purpose is the designation "of the perfumer" (gāndhika) used? To this he says: "of the perfumer," for as for others...
The meaning is that even though its radiance is infinite, its apprehension occurs simultaneously and in equal measure.

"Devoid of the fragrance of scent" [refers to] "merely that much"; this means that it is indicated by the definition provided in the passage beginning with "when he remains," which constitutes a definition through a secondary indication (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*).
Now, one might object: "Let it be so; for us, there is neither a refutation nor a non-refutation here, because you have accepted this [reality] as a 'Great Universal' (mahāsāmānya).
But as for that state of Sadāśiva and Īśvara, how does one experience it? To this, he says: "The truths," and so forth.
For one who perceives the truths as having the nature of one's own self, there is no state of equality. (86)
Furthermore, one should perceive the state of Śiva through the completion of the fruit of the ritual action;
or else, tranquility should be cultivated at the very commencement of the rite. (87)
Let it be that even this [distinction] does not lead to duality, since reality has been determined according to its true nature.
Even in the states of Sādākhya and Īśvara, there is no equality with Paśyantī;
for in those states, the objects are truly real, resting within the Self through the non-differentiation of the form "I am everything."

The cognizer perceives in this manner. However, in the state of *paśyantī*, as if in deep sleep (*suṣupti*), the various [objects] characteristic of the worldly condition remain in the form of seeds; even when one has emerged from deep sleep, the remainder is that those perceptions within *paśyantī* consist solely of ignorance (*avidyā*). Now:

The state of Śiva should be conceived as the tranquility that exists at both the commencement and the conclusion of knowledge and action; yet, if that state were devoid of the powers of will and the rest, it would be called insentient, lacking experience and being of a dull nature.
That is not so, because even if that condition were to exist, there is still no absence of all powers, by virtue of which [it could be distinguished] from the Śiva-tattva.

It might lead to differentiation; however, it has been established in the very first chapter that [the Self] is joined with the powers of will and so forth in an extremely subtle manner throughout all states. || 87 ||
Nor does there exist here in the interval that state which is purely [of one kind]. (88)
That which occurs immediately after the completion of the fruit of prior action— indeed,
because in the supreme state (*parāvasthā*) everything is one's own essential nature (*svabhāvabhūta*),
there is not even the slightest suspicion of the impossibility or possibility of experience and so forth, nor is there the appearance of "this-ness" (*idantā*).
Since everything from Sadāśiva down to the "I-not-I" (avidantā) is about to be manifested, how can there be experience therein?
Anticipating this objection—that [in that state] a similarity to Paśyantī arises—he says "satyāni" and so forth.
And let it be that in Paśyantī, the objects are indeed real, as they are non-different from the self in the form of "I."
In the expression "I" (*aham*), according to the principle that the Sādākhya [tattva] consists of knowledge and action,

it is logical that Sadāśiva experiences these two as their specific forms because he is of the nature of knowledge, and Īśvara experiences them because he is of the nature of action; however, as for the Viśeṣa [tattva],...
Because the prior state is established as being preceded by the universal due to its occurring first, [the author] says "atho" (furthermore).
Just as one desire spreads forth, another of the same kind arises again. (89)
Never does it possess an absolute state devoid of power;

nor indeed does such a state exist in the interval prior to the commencement of a second action— that state characterized by tranquility and the absence of power— because [it exists] until the attainment of the fruit of action.

Immediately thereafter, another very distinct desire indeed proceeds, having as its object the activity of supreme consciousness, but at that time there is no voidness. Furthermore, upon the attainment of the fruit of that activity, immediately after that, yet another desire of the same kind proceeds. What need is there for much? In neither case does it ever [cease].
The state of absolute isolation (kaivalya), characterized by the interval within the nature of consciousness, possesses a form devoid of power (śakti);
for indeed, where the self’s experience reaches its final limit, how could there be any desire? (90)
Furthermore, it does not follow that experience is insentient;

for where there is no cessation due to the non-attainment of self-experience, why would there be no activity of desire for the sake of the act of experiencing? Indeed, there is no lack of the desire to experience (*anububhūṣā*).

There would be experience without [an object]. Now, if it is meant that there is no experiencing of the self and thus it does not manifest, then that state would result in being insentient (*jaḍa*), and indeed it would so result. This should be construed with an interrogative intonation (*kāku*). For the experience of the self is the reflective awareness "I," and that alone constitutes its non-insentience, which provides its distinction from the insentient.
According to the principle stated in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*.

1. Thus, although there is tranquility at both the beginning and the conclusion of the commencement of knowledge and action, the emergence of the powers of will and the rest appears clearly only to those who possess such an experience in its subtle form. Now, for all [others], it is manifest—
Just as there is a connection with powers such as desire, so too, relying on logic (*nyāya*), he says "and not" (*na ca*).

In that regard, just as there is an inference of past rain through the distinction of a river's flood, so here too there is an inference of the cause from the effect; thus he says "it spreads forth" (*prasarpati*).
(138) Even though stones and such things are insentient, how is it that Śiva-nature resides in them? 91.

How there is no insentience (*jaḍatā*) therein will be investigated further on. Now, even if stones and the like possess insentience, since they are admitted to be Śiva, what fault is there in attributing insentience [to them]? This is not a fault at all. Just as there is no insentience in stones and the like, so it will be [explained] further on.
"It is investigated with excellence in its very proximity"— thus, this first previously mentioned method has been explained in detail.
Immediately after the ritual action has been completed with its fruit attained. || 92 ||
When the desire for another action arises, its cause is infinitude;
for this exists within the powers of Śiva, and they are eternally established.
It flows indeed by its own nature; that which flows is the Śiva-nature. But what is meant by "seeing without the conceptualization of 'I'";
for since everything, such as stones and the like, is merely insentient (jaḍa), there is a lack of manifestation due to that very insentience, and in the absence of manifestation...
How could such a reflective awareness as "Who am I? possibly exist without conceptualization? Not only this much;

if even that [awareness] were Śiva, then Śiva too would necessarily follow as being insentient (jaḍa). If, however, there is a difference [between them], then let stones and the like be insentient or let them be sentient—it would not entail any loss of the Śiva-nature you have accepted. Therefore...

Regarding the phrase "of the stone and so forth": here, what is to be proven is simply how Śiva-nature resides [in that], and not how Śiva-nature could reside in an insentient object. For even you admit that such things as stones are indeed insentient.
2. [This concerns] the Śiva-principle.

3. By the use of the particle *eva* here, even the possibility of insentience (*jaḍatā*) in stones and the like is excluded; therefore, it is established that insentience is far removed from Śiva-hood.
4. It should be understood that Śiva-hood is not further argued for here because it is already implied by the context.
The meaning is: "while remaining to that extent.
Alternatively, it means when the gross activity, having become fruitful, has been completed.

Immediately following that, as long as there is no finality, the possibility of desire arises for other fruitful actions; therein lies the infinitude that serves as the cause, because the powers of Śiva are infinite. And these powers of Śiva, being eternally established, flow forth by their very nature. And those powers, as they expand forth...
For this reason, Śiva is one whose nature (*prakṛti*) is that which flows forth;
he is such because his characteristic is to be so. As it has been said:
"Otherwise, however, creation would be independent, because it would possess that [independent] quality" (Svacchanda Tantra 4.5).
Thus ends the second method, explained in full detail.
Or rather, it is said:
"By whom can the will of the independent Lord be conceptualized? (94)
Alternatively, the abundance of the joy of manifestation (*vibhavāmoda*) has been stated as the causal condition (*nimittatā*).

By whom, then, could His will be conceptualized as "it may be" or "it may not be"? Sovereignty (*svātantrya*) is necessarily inherent precisely because of His status as the Lord (*īśvara*); the universe, being composed of that [sovereignty], is likewise of such a nature.
This much [is the extent].
1. The meaning is that this is the expansion of the power known as *parāparā*.
2. As it has been said by those whose intellects are intent on finding fault and who are obstructed in their search for the ultimate reality:
By the proponents of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin),
it is held that due to a specific desire, when the cause— the desire— is ceased following the accomplishment of the effect characterized as the world,
there occurs again the state of maintenance (sthiti) and dissolution (pralaya), or the cognition of a cloth and so forth.

"What is the cause for the emergence of another desire, such that when Śiva is impelled by it, his previous nature ceases and a new, unprecedented nature arises, and thus a desire manifests ever anew?"—
this [objection] they also refute with disregard, saying "of the Lord. The intended meaning is as follows:

For if the independent Lord were to be restricted by a limited will and so forth, then his very independence would perish; for one who is independent is always of an unlimited nature, characterized by a constant and ever-new arising.
And if his will were to abide as something merely prior, then, by virtue of being limited, [his independence would likewise vanish].
The meaning is that emptiness itself has arrived.
Of this—of the independent one.
But where, then?
The meaning is that, upon the cessation of the previous nature and so forth, there is the arising of another, unprecedented nature, and so on.
This much has been established. Alternatively, even in the case of absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), [the same applies].

For one whose specific nature consists in the inexhaustible relish of their own glory— the expansion of which is the manifestation of the state of being the self of all— the aforementioned [state] is always the cause for the expansion of the universal form; thus, the objection that there is no cause for the arising of a new will is refuted.
Of those statements concerning the utter emptiness of the universe, which are intended as *arthavāda* for the sake of dispassion and so forth. || 95 ||
In its intended meaning (tātparya), there is no fault; neither multiplicity of mind nor conceptual construction (kalpanā) arises.
Nor is there any contradiction with the words spoken by Śiva, such as "the universe is unreal, like a bubble," because of these [statements].

There is no fault in those who state purposes such as dispassion and selflessness, for their intent is to establish that all things have the nature of the one Śiva; nor does the fact that everything is Śiva entail the consequence of there being multiple consciousnesses.
For instance, even within a single body, there is a distinction arising from its atomic nature. (96)
1. The meaning is that there is no fault on account of the tone (*kāku*).
2. Furthermore, as for those statements by which the unreal nature of the universe is described in some places:
For one who asserts that everything is true, there would be contradiction with those things spoken by Śiva.
Thus, he supports that [point] with the word "viśva" (the universe):

because the truthfulness of the words spoken by Śiva has indeed been stated as true, yet that [truth] has been rendered distorted by those of small intellect due to lack of understanding; and that [alleged] untruthfulness—

The meaning is as follows: the unreality of parts is shown there for the purpose of generating detachment, based on the idea that "someone might become attached to a part through the pervasion of a portion," and thus the pervasion by parts is unreal. Likewise, the selflessness (*nairātmya*) of these [parts] is demonstrated in order to refute those who assert that "the very nature of a thing is its reality" in this context.

4. Here, some establish the "inverse pervasion" (*vilomavyāpti*) by asserting that whatever appears, all of that is Śiva. To explain: although the entire manifold, diverse, and distinct collection of objects—whatever it may be—is indeed Śiva alone, and thus non-dual with Śiva, nevertheless...
Because they are numerous and distinct, it follows that there would also be many distinct *śivas*; he refutes this with the words "in one" (*ekasmin*).
Regarding the phrase "because of division, down to the atom," there are two possible interpretations; [the first] involves an abundance of logical arguments (*nyāya*).

And elsewhere it is said: regarding this point, some first argue as follows—just as this external object is perceived, whether by a formless or a formed cognition, as having neither a single nor a multiple nature and thus lacking parts, so too it is untenable;
for unity and multiplicity exist through mutual exclusion, and therefore it is impossible for them to reside in a single substratum.

Therefore, the proponents of the theory of parts (avayavavādins) say: "The external object of Devadatta's cognition is a single, partless whole (avayavin); however, the parts are perceived separately—as 'hand' and 'foot'—through distinct cognitions. Thus, unity and plurality do not have multiple substrates."
141) Because the nature of Śiva is one, this fault belongs to those who maintain the doctrine of duality.
For as many atoms as there are in a single body, so many Śivas there would be—thus [it follows].

Nor is it a fault to argue that there would be a division [of Śiva] due to the division of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), leading to an infinite regress; for although there are many categories such as atoms (*paramāṇu*) and so forth, they are all of the nature of the one Śiva—so how can there be multiplicity? Indeed, Śiva does not take the form of a jar or other objects; rather, it is the jar and other objects that take the form of Śiva.
Consequently, because the nature of consciousness (cidrūpa) lacks distinctions of space, time, or intrinsic nature, there is no division.

This has been demonstrated in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*. Furthermore, for those who maintain the doctrine of the division of atoms, the essential nature of those atoms is Śiva-hood; yet that is veiled by impurity (mala).

Therefore, if for them the manifestation of Śiva-hood occurs here through the power of the aforementioned knowledge, then those Śivas would be distinct [from one another]. And since they reside within the body, if the individual souls (*aṇu*s) consist of that [Śiva-nature], why would the atoms of the body not themselves be Śiva-atoms? Thus, the doctrine of distinct atoms does not apply to the principle of consciousness (*cittattva*); therefore, this [manifestation] belongs to those very [atoms of the body].
There is a fault.
Or even from the perspective of having a single substratum, there is no fault in those [arguments] either. || 97 ||
The diversity within the consciousness of internal worms is like that between a master and his servants.

Regarding this, others say: "This is incorrect; for when Devadatta moves by means of his hand, or when his feet and other limbs move, there would be a conjunction of contradictory properties—namely, moving and not moving—in a single entity."
It might be argued that [the whole] belongs to one [part], but this is not tenable, because multiplicity is characterized by that very [plurality].
Furthermore, if it were to inhere simultaneously in each part in its entirety, there would be multiplicity;
and upon the removal of even a single part, there would be destruction [of the whole], despite its remaining in other parts.
By way of argument, if there were no destruction upon the removal of each individual part, then there would be no destruction even when all parts are removed;
therefore, those who maintain the theory of the accumulation of atoms hold that atoms alone are partless and exist in an accumulated state.
Or rather, [this occurs] through the expansion of Śiva, whose essential nature is that single consciousness. (98)
There is no equality with the Lord of the Pātañjala school and others because of the absence of distinction;
it should not be understood here as being like that, for therefore Śiva alone abides as everything. 99.

Alternatively, for those who maintain the doctrine of the differentiation of atoms, their manifold nature is not a defect; because, presided over by Śiva, whose nature is a single consciousness, these various selves are merely the unfolding of the innate *māyā* of that one alone, as is the case in the Śivādvaya system. We have also explained this at length.

This has been established in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā* itself: the non-apprehension of non-difference (*abhedākhyāti*) varies in degree according to the intensity of the experience of the *puryaṣṭaka*. This diversity exists because the consciousness of worms and other such beings consists of two aspects—consciousness that is capable and consciousness that is incapable—manifesting in the forms of master and servant. Alternatively: [3]

By that expansion of Śiva, whose single nature is consciousness, which extends to such a magnitude as to include everything down to various insects; in this view, because of the predominance of consciousness over the *puryaṣṭaka* (the subtle body), there is no difference between him and Śiva, since he himself possesses that very form. For this reason, by the power of *māyā-śakti*,...

Likewise, because unity is not manifested, there is multiplicity; however, in reality, there is non-difference. There is no equality with the *puruṣaviśeṣa* (the distinct Spirit) who is the Lord (*īśvara*) according to Patañjali, nor with that established by the Vaiśeṣikas and others, because in those systems difference is admitted, whereas here there is non-difference. In the same way, it should not be understood in the philosophy of Īśvara. Therefore:
The entire collection of existing things is established as being of the nature of Śiva; for in that state, all defects are entirely avoided. || 99 ||
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Śivadṛṣṭivṛtti* composed by the venerable master Utpaladeva. 3.
Now, one might object: if the designation of various powers arises from the predominance of consciousness (*citi*), then what of the system of Patañjali?

For they have established the definition: "Īśvara is a particular *puruṣa* untouched by afflictions, actions, their fruitions, and latent impressions. Having raised this doubt as well, he provides a justification.
"From Patañjali," etc.

[2] Now, one might object: "Granted that there is complete identity with Śiva in every respect, nevertheless, what causes this diversity of manifoldness, such that one person is endowed with many powers while another is endowed with fewer powers? To this, [it is said]:
"Thus, there is no denial of the distinction between the two.

Now, one might object: "If diversity arises from the intensity of the experience of the *puryaṣṭaka*, then since that [diversity] is dependent upon it, the *puryaṣṭaka* itself must possess autonomy; what then is the use of the autonomy of the Supreme Lord? Anticipating this doubt:
He states another alternative with the word "or" (*atha vā*).
143) Now, *atha*...
The Fourth Chapter in the *Śrīśivadṛṣṭi*. Once the refutation of the doubts regarding the defects of the [opponent's] theory to be established has been accomplished.
Now, in order to establish that all things are of the nature of Śiva (*sarvaśivatva*) by means of their own essential form (*svarūpa*), he says:
[1] "It is to be manifested," meaning it is to be made manifest. [2] "All" refers to that which is the nature of Śiva.
3. It is to be accomplished through reasoning. As it has been said:
"The Self alone, manifesting within all existents, is the pervasive Lord whose consciousness is blissful;
He is Śiva, whose flow of will is unobstructed and whose powers of vision and action are ever-expanding."
Thus, although this is in every way primarily what must be accomplished, nevertheless,
lest someone should be led astray by the dustfall of the fallacious arguments of opponents,
we shall first employ that very dust of the opponents' fallacious arguments as a means of sound reasoning (*sutaraka*).

It is struck down by the nectar of the fragrance of ethical conduct (*śīla*). For indeed, there is a disagreement among all disputants in this regard. First of all, there is opposition on every point here among those who propound a tranquil Brahman (*śāntabrahmavādins*). For that which constitutes the very nature of Brahman, its own essence, [is as follows...]
Self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) consists in reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśana*), and that has been relegated by them to the category of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Furthermore, because the flow of the power of *māyā* operates toward the manifestation of the universe, even his sovereignty (*svātantrya*) is effectively denied.
Thus, since it is contemptible due to its being composed of *māyā*, how [can it be considered self-luminous]?

In that regard, even "selfhood" is indeed accepted by them, because everything is negated by the statements "not this, not this. Since that universe is described as contemptible, how can it possess unobstructed desire therein?
And since at the time of knowledge one relies upon knowledge whose nature is a modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*), how [can it be the self]?
[The opponent asks: "How could there be the state of radiating consciousness, since activity consists solely of the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)?

Thus, for the proponents of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*), there is a total denial [of consciousness] in every respect. Furthermore, although the principle of God (*īśvaratattva*) is accepted in the systems of Patañjali and the Vaiśeṣikas, how could it be established as being the Self (*ātman*) itself, given their adherence to the doctrine of duality (*bhedavāda*)?"
In systems such as Sāṃkhya, since the *puruṣa* is devoid of activity (*niṣkriyatva*), how can there be the admission of a power of action?

For the Buddhists and others, because of the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), how can there be omnipresence (*vibhutva*) and permanence (*nityatva*)? In the doctrine of the *Śabdabrahman*, since independence is abandoned and recourse is taken to ignorance (*avidyā*), how can the state of having unobstructed will be established?

He says "parodbhāvanīyā" (to be brought forward by the opponent), meaning that since the doctrine of non-dual Śiva remains established once all other doctrines have been refuted, it must be explained in such a way that it itself comes to be the object of cognition as something already proven.
Now, it must be explained how everything has Śiva as its essence:
there exists nothing whatsoever that is powerless; even those [entities] you [mention] are indeed powerful things. (1)
If many [causes] were admitted as capable [of producing an effect], total independence would result.
Immediately after the refutation of these objections, we must now state it by way of positive affirmation how everything is established as being of the nature of Śiva; that is what is being said.

And while it is incapable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), it nevertheless exists; this much is established by its being neither manifest nor non-manifest, precisely because there is no deviation [from this state].
This is because, for this Teacher, since it is distinguished in every respect within cognition, it is treated here in this chapter in every respect.
That which is to be established is stated as "the seed-syllable of that" (*tadbījākṣara*). For it has been said: "The letter *a* is Śiva, and the letter *tha* is called Śakti.
Thus, according to the secret method (*rahasyanaya*), the state of universal Śiva-ness (*sarvaśivatva*) is primarily to be established here; and therein also—
Since that state of universal Śiva-hood must be established by means of Śakti alone, the designation of Śiva and Śakti is made here by means of the letters *a* and *tha*.
Likewise, the expression "even now" (*tathedānīm*) has also been indicated for this very same purpose; and that—
It is not analyzed here for fear of prolixity.

Now, one might object: "Since there is no other possible way, everything is established as being of the nature of Śiva simply by the refutation of the arguments of others; so what is the point of this repetition? To this, he says:
"By way of affirmation" means that although it was previously established by the very negation of everything else, it is here proven specifically by way of negation.
3. If [the universal] exists, then what is this [claim] that it is incapable of causal efficiency? For wherever...
*Sattva* means the capacity for this or that, which is to say, the performance of purposeful action (*arthakriyākāritva*). He states this very point: "Manifestation is *sattva*.

If it is capable, then that very object is indeed ultimately real and is of the nature of Śiva. For instance, the power of performing an action is agency, which is the nature of consciousness; and being of the nature of Śiva is also the nature of consciousness, because for that which is of the nature of consciousness, agency is impossible if it is devoid of will. A jar, a cloth, and so forth, possess the power of being instruments.

If that were so, then that independent form of consciousness would be nothing other than the very form of Śiva. Furthermore, many [objects] such as jars and the like are not accepted as being individually capable [of independent action]; otherwise, it would follow that all things possess such independence.
Consequently, due to this state of having distinct intentions, one might think: "Let this be new, or let it be old"—thus regarding a single thing.
Otherwise, there would follow the contradiction between the states of being new and old; yet such is not observed.
And regarding the acceptance of its capacity, [the author] asks "why? and says: "The capable.
Since the form of consciousness devoid of will is nothing at all—because it would consist merely in the acceptance of its own nature—the form of consciousness accompanied by will is the form of Śiva.
Agency.

3. Here too, the reasoning is as before: since objects such as pots and cloths possess the capacity for action, and since that which is of the nature of consciousness cannot possess agency if it is devoid of will, [it must therefore be] accompanied by will.
The meaning is that [the Self] is independent and is indeed the very form of Śiva. Here, having raised the doubt regarding their insentience (*jaḍatva*), he states the logical argument: "many," etc.
Now, all this is established through the distinction between the insentient and the sentient; for these...

Dependence on another alone appears clearly evident; for if these [entities] were of the nature of independent consciousness (*svatantracidrūpa*), they would not be dependent on anything else, since "all are independent within their own self.
In that case, the established rule as to what is dependent upon what would collapse. Therefore, he says: "And many... (bahavaśca).

And if independence is asserted by each [subject] individually with respect to a jar or other object, then because it would not be dependent on a single cognizer, a distinct and separate intention (*abhisaṃdhi*) would necessarily follow in every case;
and thus, upon the production of a jar, what new independence of its own could there possibly be? Or rather, what else?
Because there is no certainty regarding either one of two opposing views—such as whether the Purāṇa was created by a creator or not—one falls into a state of doubt.

And that is undesirable. Therefore, this is established: for that very possessor of power (śaktimat), the entire collection of objects is merely the nature of his power (śakti-svarūpa); it is not something belonging to him [as a separate entity].
By even a mere trace [of duality], non-duality alone is realized.
(6) Through continuous contemplation, it is connected with the subject. (7)
Because it contradicts direct perception. (p.
146) Now, if one [entity] possesses a superior power that is the cause for [the other] possessing an inferior power... (2)
In regard to its own effect, everything is indeed capable of being the cause;
for that which is capable, it is possible to produce [the effect]. If this were so, there would be no capacity in anything else.

Now, one [cause] possesses a superior power because it binds—that is, restricts—the power of another, and for that reason, its [the other's] power is inferior. However, with respect to its own effect, which serves as the object, every [cause] is indeed capable of binding.
For restriction applies only to that which is capable; indeed, the power to produce oil does not exist in sand.
This is possible to accomplish. Thus, if omnipotence is asserted, then other things such as pots do not possess individual capacity or independence. (3)
1. [The causes] are those that bring about cessation.
2. It is precisely by its own power. 3. Regarding this, he states the reason: "of that which is capable."
Now, why is it said that there would be the consequence of a distinction between "new" and "old" due to a difference in intention? For Śakti is indeed ancient and possesses excellence;
because this collection of objects such as the jar is produced by her, the power (śakti) of the jar and so forth belongs to her alone, precisely because it is created by her.

Because the cause is deficient, it is itself incapable; yet, due to the necessity of that [deficiency], there is no contingency of being both new and old. Furthermore, the capacity established in one instance applies to all individually;
otherwise, if there were an absence of capacity, what could serve as the basis [for manifestation]? As it has been said:
"Even that which is impelled would exist only for one who possesses what is called 'potency' (śaktatā).
This is precisely what we maintain," he says with the words "if it were so.
Thus, since jars, cloths, and other such things are of the nature of potency belonging to that which possesses potency...

Although they possess the capacity for their own respective functions, it has been established that they themselves are dependent upon Him in order to refute the objection [of their independence]. Now,
as for those who are commonly known in the world as "conscious beings" (cetana) in contrast to "insentient things" (jaḍa), they too have such a nature.
By resorting to the logic of *kaimutika-nyāya* (the principle of "how much more so"), he says "nṛpādi" (king, etc. to indicate what need there be for objects such as jars.

The meaning is this: just as when a servant serves a king or similar superior, the fruit of his own action accrues [to him] by virtue of that service because he is dependent upon them, so too it is for a living being who possesses power.

Since the state of being the fruit of one's own karma is entirely dependent on another, it is established everywhere that even when there is absolute unity, there is nonetheless a unity of the possessor of power (*śaktimat*).
For thus, dependence upon means such as kings and the like would imply that [the result] is the fruit of one's own karma;
for everyone, even though capable, is dependent [on external factors] regarding delusion and equanimity, just like God. (4)
Therefore, by means of his manifold powers which are non-different from him,
Śiva alone remains as the single capable agent, manifesting in such and such ways.
The state of being the fruit of one's own karma would depend solely upon the activities of serving kings and others.

This refers to the condition of one for whom his own objects of enjoyment are the fruits of karma. For this reason, everyone, even though personally capable, engages in action only with dependence [on others]. As it is said in the Dualistic (Dvaita) philosophy: "Even the Lord [depends on] delusion..."
He proceeds toward creation by depending upon the *māyātattva*, and toward grace (*anugraha*) by depending upon the equilibrium of karma;

yet he is neither powerless nor non-sovereign. Therefore, because his nature as Śiva is characterized by the possession of powers (*śaktimat*), and because those powers are non-different from him, he is indeed one alone, despite possessing powers whose natures are as manifold as jars and cloths.
Śiva exists in each and every manner because He consists of manifold entities such as jars, cloths, and so forth.

For the consciousness of a jar (*ghaṭacit*), which is limited to that specific form, there is a unifying synthesis (*anusandhāna*) with the consciousness of a cloth (*paṭacit*) through His sovereignty.
It would not be so; therefore, the single reality of consciousness itself possesses infinite universal forms. || 5 ||

1. Now, one might object: "In that case, does it not follow that [the Lord] consists of duality, just like the proponents of difference (bhedavādins), because according to their view, the Lord is qualified? Anticipating this objection, he says: "Therefore, for the sake of specifying that [nature],... 2. Now, if He possesses power (*śaktatva*), how can there be dependence (*sāpekṣatva*)? And if there is dependence, there can be no power at all.
Regarding the phrase "it arises," he confirms that there is dependence upon capacity by means of an illustrative example, beginning with "just as.
[He says] "equality of karma"; for such is its process: when two opposing karmas...
When two equal forces obstruct each other, there is an equilibrium of karma; from that arises the grace of the Lord (*īśvarānugraha*).

It is precisely when two karmas are oriented toward experience (*bhoga*) that they mutually obstruct one another. If there were an obstruction of the karma that bestows birth and lifespan, it would follow that the body would fall at that very moment, for [the result] is experience alone.
Because that form [of the object] causes the distraction of saṃsāra, there is favor (anugraha) in its obstruction and not in any other;
thus, how could that which is perceived as "existent" be non-existent?
For that which exists is indeed the ultimate reality (paramārtha), and from that, the ultimate reality is auspiciousness (śiva).
In all entities, the state of being the manifestation of consciousness is indeed established as the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
It has been stated that "only a potent thing is a real entity" (*vastu*), and a real entity is called "existent" (*sat*). That which is existent is not non-existent;
therefore, that alone is the ultimate reality. And because it is the ultimate reality, for that reason—
He is Śiva because he is existence (*sattva*) and because he is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Now, one might ask: how is it that he alone is Śiva by virtue of being the ultimate reality?

Why is an insentient object (*jaḍa*) not also the ultimate reality? That is not so. For how could the very existence of an insentient object be established without some form of manifestation? Indeed, existence is the state of vibrating radiance (*sphuradrūpatā*); and the state of vibrating radiance is the state of being manifest (*prakāśamānatā*).
Consequently, there is no insentience whatsoever. For manifestation is non-difference from light, and light is the ultimate reality, the form of all foundations, which cannot be denied.
And because all things, such as jars and the like, consist of the nature of light...
Due to the absence of any distinction, there is the nature of a single manifestation; for that very reason, there is the state of being the one Śiva.
This has been elaborated upon in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*.
The existence of those things conceptualized through false knowledge consists in their capacity for the manifestation of consciousness.
If it is argued that "whatever exists there [in the world] is also found here [in consciousness], so who can deny its Śiva-nature?",
then indeed the reality of these things is established by their emergence from Consciousness.
Likewise, since Śiva alone arises, how could there be duality, falsity, and so forth?

This is the underlying meaning: if the jar and other objects were of the nature of insentient matter (*jaḍa*), then, because they would not manifest, how could even their status as mere ultimate reality exist? Thus, by virtue of being of the nature of insentient matter—
Expansion. Now, "it shines forth" means that its state of being manifest is its nature of vibrating radiance;
therefore, by what could it be designated as insentient?
In that regard:
The determination "this is a jar" appears as the power of the Supreme Lord, like the Self itself, transcending name and form; it does not appear as a mere "this-ness."
Truthhood exists for the sake of conventional usage, yet it does not reside within conventional usage itself.

Just as in the case of jars and other objects, there exists for things such as silver or snakes—which are conceptualized through false cognition—a capacity for manifestation within the individualization of consciousness, namely their state of being manifest;
that alone is their existence (*sattva*) and ultimate reality (*paramārthatva*), and for this reason also, they possess that Śiva-nature. And this is indeed accepted as unavoidable.
In these [objects], reality consists in the manifestation of consciousness (*cid-abhivyakti*), since this is the expansion of Śiva in those various forms.

If both the cognition of a jar and the cognition of silver are equally real, then how is the distinction between the "correct" and the "false" established? [The answer is: that distinction exists for the sake of practical transaction (*vyavahāra*); it serves the purpose of worldly activity.
Nor does conventional truth, because it is not firmly established, constitute [ultimate] truth. 9.
And likewise, in a certain place, a royal decree may arise such that:
"But why is this said? For how can that which is perceived as 'existent' (sat) be non-existent (asat)?"
For that which exists is indeed the ultimate reality; the ultimate reality is...

And so forth; however, if [existence] were merely being-in-itself (*sanmātra*), there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For it has been determined in various places that existence consists in the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), since even in the case of silver and the like, there is not even a trace of causal efficiency. Furthermore, in the case of false cognition regarding silver and such, there is no causal efficiency whatsoever. And if...

If it were argued that even in that case [of the world], the capacity for the manifestation of consciousness (cidvyakti-śaktatā) would be heard of as being present there just as it is in a jar or similar objects, then one might ask:

"What is this method of 'correctness' and 'falsity' that is well-known in the world? This very point is established for the sake of worldly transaction (vyavahāra). Just as the existence of an insentient object is not established without the manifestation of consciousness, and in the manifestation of consciousness...
When existence— in the sense of vibrating form, that is, manifestness— is established,
there is no such thing as insentience whatsoever, because [existence] is non-different from manifestation and is the ultimate reality that serves as the foundation for all things;
likewise, the very existence of those things conceptualized through false knowledge does not occur apart from the manifestation of consciousness.

They are established; and since their manifestation as the throbbing nature of consciousness exists, and because they are non-different from that light and constitute the ultimate reality which is the foundation of all, nothing whatsoever called "falsity" can possibly apply to them.
3. Because it is not firm by way of certainty.

4. Here he states an illustration with the words "and likewise" (*tathā ca*): if reality were [established] merely by way of conventional truth (*vyavahārasatya*), then, since that is conventional truth, all transactions would be carried out entirely with counterfeit coins.

How could there be [a distinction] for those things that do not belong to conventional usage (*avyavahāraga*), given their unreality? Likewise, even if they were real at some time, how could there be reality or unreality belonging to conventional usage? The meaning is that there is no performance of a causal function (*arthakriyākāritva*) by means of something that is either conventionally real or unreal.
But the transaction was conducted with these dīnāras, which were themselves beyond the realm of commerce.

It proceeds in such a manner even in other cases, though otherwise. Just as there is indeed a transaction with counterfeit dinars by the command of a king, so too elsewhere, by mere will and according to convention, the determination of time, the beginning [of an action], and so forth occur without depending on the actual object.
Legal procedure.
If conventional reality were true, then for you, everything would be nothing but untrue.

If that [conventional reality] were truly real, there would indeed be a loss of the position you have accepted. However, if the reality of even an unreal conventional practice that has not yet taken root is admitted,
then by virtue of being of such a nature, this entire world would be real, while unreality would be the ultimate truth.

The meaning is "like conventional usage. If this world were real from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthataḥ*), then for you, this defect—consisting in a reality that is merely like conventional usage—would arise. And thus, when the doctrine of the reality of all things (*sarvasatyatāvāda*) is propounded, there would be a loss of what has been taught in the scriptures.
Furthermore, how can the attainment of Śiva be possible for him? For how indeed could unreality be spoken of? (12)
Truthfulness exists only through conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), not by virtue of an underlying causal basis.

Furthermore, regarding that very convention, the attainment of Śiva is intended as the realization of one's own nature as Śiva, meaning that Śiva-nature has arrived for him without effort. If this is so, how is it [attained] for him?
