It has been stated that even conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*) is unreal; the meaning is that, this being so, it would follow that [this very discourse] must be real. True, however, the reality of this conventional discourse exists only by virtue of its being a convention (*vyavahāratayā*), and not because of its having a foundation (*nibandhana*), that is to say, because it is firmly rooted (*prarūḍhatvāt*).
1. Here, he states an over-extension [of the argument] with the words "of conventional usage" (vyavahārasya), etc.

2. Now, if the unreality of conventional usage were established without the manifestation of consciousness (cidvyakti), then let that [usage] simply be unreal; however, since even that is not established without the manifestation of consciousness, how can there be unreality?
In this regard, raising the objection, "If there is no manifestation of consciousness (*cidvyakti*) therein, then how can it be unreal?", he says:
"Of that too" (*tasyāpi*).
The arising of conceptual construction and the like is produced only from that which already exists. || 13 ||
Since it has been determined that "this is the reality" solely for the purpose of conventional discourse, let it remain exactly so;
by whom can this state of Śiva be prevented?
Because it is bound by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and independent cognitions such as that of silver, the production of an object that is already existent is accomplished. What then?
Having spoken thus and established a convention for the sake of worldly transaction, let there be a purchase with counterfeit dinars from this day forward.

Let the year consist of the calculation of time, or let it be the beginning of the year; this is the certainty (*niścaya*). Alternatively, even if such a thing is real, it is for the sake of established worldly convention that it is determined as "time" and so forth. And let its existence remain exactly in that way as Śiva—by whom has it been prevented from arising from consciousness?

This is because of its connection with the defining characteristic of Śiva-nature. Regarding the distinction between the positions of truth and untruth concerning conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), the reason was previously stated: when that which is manifest is true, it is indeed true.
Its truth consists in its being composed of the non-recognition of its identity with Consciousness (*cid-abheda-akhyāti*). Thus, this must not be forgotten in every case.

1. Now, since by any means whatsoever there is no reality for anything even in terms of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), it follows that just as there is no arising of what already exists from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and so forth,
yet existence is nonetheless accepted because even what is non-existent is established through the power of manifestation (*prakāśa*), so too [is the case here].

Even in the case of transactions involving counterfeit dīnāras, their existence is established by the power of public perception for the sake of conventional usage such as agreements; this is just as it is here,
even without regard for the actual reality of the object.
He says "of conceptual construction, etc. (vikalpādeḥ) to show that if the conventional usage of the reckoning of time and so forth exists as imagined by this or that subject, let it be so.
Just as [it is with] conceptual construction and the like.

Since the very reality of even non-existent objects is admitted— such as in the case of independent cognition and the cognition of silver [in a shell]— and since the practical usage of even the unreal, such as the transaction involving counterfeit dīnāras and the usage regarding time and so forth, persists, how can it not be real?
The meaning is that because it consists of the non-apprehension of the non-difference from consciousness (*cid-abhedākhyāti*), it cannot be real in any way whatsoever.
152) To what [subject] is falsity attributed, and at what time would it occur?
If it is argued that "time itself would not exist," [we reply] that this is certainly not the case anywhere.
Is some production occurring at an improper time obstructed, or is the act of producing itself obstructed?
Once the effect has been produced, the activity has ceased; when it has passed away, what can be obstructed?
And when there exists a subverting means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [the cognition] arises as "this is not silver, this is not silver, it is mother-of-pearl."

If it were perceived as being established by negation, it would be false. Therefore, falsity must be produced by that subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*). For what purpose is it produced? In this regard, at what time could that silver-nature exist? The admission is that falsity consists in the fact that that very time does not exist.
That is not so; for indeed, when there is no time—that is, in the absence of time—there is no such thing as the production of anything whatsoever by that which is devoid of time.
Thus, in this way, it is by no means [possible] according to conventional truth.

This is not a determination of rightness and wrongness; rather, it establishes that all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), by virtue of being the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) itself, takes the form of rightness and wrongness—this is the full syntactical connection of the sentence beginning with "mithyātva" (wrongness). Here, the opponents say:

"This is established by the power of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) alone; therefore, let it be so. Who can prevent this state of Śiva? For indeed, [it is] the determination of the distinction between the real and the unreal, which pervades all internal and external worldly transactions—
"For this conventional usage of sublation exists as its basis"—this [position] is untenable, as he says: "falsity.
In the cognition—that is, in the knowledge of silver.

Regarding the word "thus" (*tena*): the intended meaning is this—why was it stated that because consciousness is manifested in such and such ways through both correctness and falsity, and because Śiva arises [therefrom], all this consists of the expansion of consciousness? Because falsity is itself falsely constructed by a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*).

And therefore, since truth is merely conventional truth, it does not exist as such everywhere and in every way; thus, this [position] is not established. He says, "Of what? (tatkasya). Having indicated "of what" in general terms, he analyzes it specifically with the words beginning with "therein" (tatra).
The meaning is that it is because action is impossible. Or, if the act of production were sublated, that would not be the case;
for the action has reached its completion by having produced an effect such as silver. What, then, would be the purpose of sublation regarding that which is unreal?
Because that [object] itself does not exist; and since there is now no object for sublation, what sublation could there be? || 16 ||
Furthermore, if there were sublation occurring at the time of experience, then what has been experienced could not be otherwise;
or if the sense organ itself were subject to sublation, it would be of such a nature at that very moment. (17)
By what means is that blindness produced, given its persistence over time?
Is there equality with all things, or is there sublation? If there is a relation, how can there be production? (18)
Now, if it is maintained that the sublation pertains to the experience of silver, that is not so;

for it is not logical that an experienced object should be unexperienced. Alternatively, if it is argued that the sense organ—the cause of cognitions such as [the perception of] silver or a double moon—is sublated because it is no longer a sense organ, [that too is incorrect].
1. Regarding the cognition of a mother-of-pearl shell.

2. Thus, having stated the refutation based on sublation (*bādhadūṣaṇa*) in the case of the effect, he now states the observation of the conventional usage of sublation even in the case of the cause, beginning with "Now, regarding experience," and therein, first of all:

He asks "If... by taking a middle position between cause and effect. For they understand that sublation (*bādha*) is indeed the removal of the object; yet he says "That is not so," because that [removal] is in no way possible, since the object cannot be removed as long as it appears [to consciousness]. Indeed, not...
The sense is that a subverting cognition arises in this manner: "That which appeared [to me] did not appear.
3. First of all, the sense organ itself cannot be the producer of such a cognition, as it would [otherwise] exist at all times.

The meaning is that it would entail the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of its [the cognition’s] production. Regarding this, others say: "In this case, the sense faculty is defiled by a defect. That too is incorrect. A defective cause becomes one whose power is blunted precisely in the performance of its own effect;
thus, let it simply not produce that [effect]. But what does it have to do with producing a contrary effect? No.
Even if corrupt rice seeds were to rely on the skill of producing barley sprouts, there would still be no sublation [of the rule], because of the absence of that specific cause.
That is not so; for it is not possible for a sublation (*bādhaka*) to produce blindness—that is, the non-existence—of the sense faculty.

For at the time when that cognition of silver and so forth occurs, the sense faculty is exactly as it is when jars and other objects are perceived. If it is argued that [the sublation occurs] at a different time, when the sublation arises, then...

Because it does not persist, there is sublation (*bādha*). If one accepts that sublation occurs due to its remaining for another time, then even correct cognitions existing at that time would incur what is called "sublation" by virtue of being equal to false cognitions;
and this is not tenable, because [it contradicts] that which exists in the present time.

Because cognitions of jars and the like can occur as being valid, [it might be argued that] there is a sublation of the connection between the sense organs, their objects, and so forth. That is not so; for if the connection were sublated, how could cognition be produced?
Therefore, as long as it is possible to conceive [of them], in every way there is no [sublation] regarding the perception of silver and the like.
Nothing can be negated—this is not the meaning of sublation (*bādha*).

Nor is the statement "the mother-of-pearl is not silver" a case of sublation; for it is not the case that the mother-of-pearl was apprehended as being silver, according to the cognition, nor even by way of occupying the locus of the mother-of-pearl.

1. [Objection: "The arising of a sublater at a later time" refers to the cognition of mother-of-pearl; when the cognition of mother-of-pearl occurs, the instability of the cognition of silver is the sublation. [The author] says "tatkāle" (at that time) to state that this is incorrect.
For if instability at that very moment were indeed the sublation, then for those present at that time...

The meaning is that since even correct cognitions are not stable at the time of the cognition of mother-of-pearl, there would follow the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of their being sublated as well.
[2] He states the view of the teacher Dharmakīrti with the words "śuktikā," etc., just as a pure ground...
The absence of a jar [is known] because the conventional usage of "the absence of a jar" is based upon it; therefore,
just as the cognition of the bare ground itself is the cognition of the absence of the jar,
so too is the awareness of the validity— characterized by the manifestation of the object as it truly is— contained within the cognition of the mother-of-pearl.

The meaning is this: that which appears as non-distinct from the self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) of the cognition of mother-of-pearl is precisely what is being described; the self-cognition of the invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*), which is the nature of the incorrectness residing in the cognition of silver that is contrary to the mother-of-pearl, is itself the sublation (*bādha*). To this, he states the reply: "For [it is] not silver... The underlying thought is: if...
The meaning is that this cognition would occur only if the mother-of-pearl were apprehended as silver;
in the absence of that [apprehension], there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Now, regarding the case of mother-of-pearl, silver, and so forth, in every respect...
He states the refutation by means of the conceptualization of that [object] as a support, because it does not arise dependently. This is the meaning:
the status of being an objective support (*ālambanatā*) is not tenable as being based merely on proximity;
rather, that alone is the objective support of cognition which appears within it.
The jewel-like saying that "one object appears as something else" is not new.
Thus [it is said]. (p.
155) There is nothing [that is not the Self], because everything that manifests has its own nature as its locus. In every respect...
Just as something appears, so it is; it cannot be made otherwise. This is indeed the truth, and there is nothing false in it. And this is to be understood from the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*. 18.
If there is a sublation of conventional practice, then there would be arbitrariness in that practice;
for instance, gold that is real in one place might be treated as conventional currency in a border region. (19)
Or even a transaction involving counterfeit coins and the like is observed;
or, when a transaction consists merely of the pleasure it brings to oneself. (20)
This alone is its reality: the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsamarthatva*).

Even if practical activity (*vyavahāra*) is sublated—such as the thought that "the practical activity of [treating it as] silver should not be performed"—even that does not constitute the distinction between the real and the unreal based on the occurrence of desired activity. For instance:
In certain border regions, there is a practice where genuine gold is treated as if it were iron;

furthermore, because counterfeit coins and the like are favored by the king, such a practice is observed. Alternatively, when there is merely a sense of pleasure, the transaction proceeds on that basis alone. This is precisely what [is meant].

The capacity of an object to produce delight is established by self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) in its efficacy for purposeful action (*arthakriyākāritva*); otherwise, because it would be erroneous, even the drinking and other such actions regarding the water of a dream—which is not real—would be erroneous. However, the satisfaction resulting from the cessation of thirst is established by self-awareness and does not fail to correspond with reality. That too...
And the purposeful activity that brings delight belongs to things such as a [real] peak or [illusory] water seen in a dream;
this is the summary here:
indeed, it is the very nature itself that grasps itself by means of itself.
Because an external object of apprehension, when subjected to investigation, is logically untenable.
Its own nature is eternally luminous;
through that very essence, it carries out such a worldly course here, indeed devoid of external objects.
Thus,
even that which is real may be conventional; therefore, there is no state of sublation even within conventional discourse.
Moreover, if there were a contradiction regarding the location, there would be no silver in that place.
When the time had come that the region became filled with dust, that [previous] time had already passed;
since this [new] time belongs to a different period, what contradiction can there be between two distinct times? (22)
Now, if it is argued that there is a contradiction regarding location—namely, that the silver belongs to one location while it is perceived in another—that is not so.

For at the time when that location which served as the substrate for the silver existed, that time no longer exists at the time of the subverting cognition (*bādhaka-jñāna*) of the silver-cognition; thus, the subversion is effected by the subverting cognition. It is not [a matter of spatial contradiction].

And thus, because the two—the place of the mother-of-pearl and the place of the silver—are at different times; for at the time of the mother-of-pearl and the silver, the time of the silver in the other place has already passed. Therefore, since there is no contradiction between the difference in place due to the difference in time, what sublation could there be? || 22 ||
If it is argued that one cognition is sublated by another cognition because of their mutual contradiction, this is not a case of sublation;
for they exist at different times, and thus the earlier cognition has already ceased to exist. (23)

Now, in that very same case, because of the contradiction between the cognition of silver and the cognition of mother-of-pearl, the sublation—that is, the cessation—of the cognition of silver is effected by the cognition of mother-of-pearl. That is not so.
For, now, there is no sublation whatsoever by means of either the effect or the cause.
It is established; therefore, there is indeed no contradiction. This is the intended meaning: even if that other place and time exist, what is qualified by them here, since they are not present?
Herein lies the essential point: do those two—place and time—appear as existing there?

How much more so if they are non-existent? And if you imagine that they do exist, then this silver would have appeared at that very place and time, and thus this could not be an error; for if both are non-existent, they cannot serve as an objective basis (ālambana) in the same manner as the silver.
p.

157) It is illogical for a single entity to undergo change simultaneously; however, there is no contradiction in the case of milk and curd occurring sequentially, because the previously perceived [milk] ceases by its own nature through the cessation of its perception.
Not from non-existence. || 23 ||
There is no contradiction consisting in non-coexistence prior to destruction;
rather, there exists a contradiction consisting in mutual exclusion, characterized by the nature of knowledge and ignorance. (24)

Nor is there the contradiction of non-coexistence; for knowledge, having already perished due to its momentariness, cannot be sublated by another as something contradictory—like cold being opposed to heat—as is the case with the cognitions of silver and mother-of-pearl. Nor is there the contradiction consisting in mutual exclusion.
Consisting of both knowledge and ignorance, [it pertains] to existence and non-existence... || 24 ||
If ignorance is fully understood, then it would possess self-contradiction;
for how can contradiction with its own nature be prevented? (25)
In this case, there is no contradiction consisting of sublation regarding the nature of things;
that [contradiction] is to be understood through the vision of discernment, not as an inherent nature anywhere. (26)
Likewise, because all conceptual constructions are seen to have the nature of reality, [the mantra] removes poison from the bodies of Garuḍas and others. || 27 ||

1. Simultaneous alteration is illogical; for the cognition of silver is not sublated by the cognition of mother-of-pearl, because there is no mutual contradiction between two cognitions that are established and settled within their own respective objects and their own intrinsic natures. Now, if...

If contradiction between two things consists solely in their mutual exclusion and cannot coexist simultaneously, then, because all cognitions would be mutually contradictory, the very foundation of the relationship between the sublated and the sublator could not be established; consequently, the distinction between the true and the false would utterly collapse.
2. Here, the commentary on the remaining portion of the text, starting from the introductory phrase "of existence and non-existence" (*atra bhāvābhāvayoḥ*), is missing.

Even when the ritual of consecrating a deity and so forth is performed, the fruit is not seen anywhere if it is practiced by one who lacks knowledge, despite the presence of meditation and other such means. (28)
Therefore, every existing entity is established as being joined with the manifestation of consciousness;
wherever this occurs, there lies both reality and the nature of the universe.
If there were a difference [between the object and its cognition], consciousness would not be applicable to jars and the like;
for a jar, which possesses the qualities of both the material and the immaterial, is not within the range of that [consciousness]. (30)
Being formless and not having entered into the interior of the atoms, how does it know "this is a jar" through its various distinctions for the sake of the perceiver? (31)

That which possesses attributes such as having form or being formless— such as a jar— is not capable of becoming an object of cognition while remaining distinct from that cognition whose nature is the jar. As it has been stated in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*:

As stated in [the verse] beginning with "prāgivārtho 'prakāśaḥ syāt" (1.5.2), etc., jars and other such objects would not be manifest. Furthermore, jars and the like are not formless (*amūrta*) even if they consist of atoms; for form (*mūrti*) is indeed the dimension of a substance that is not all-pervading, or else it is spatial occupancy (*deśayogyatā*).

Therefore, the meaning is that the state of those atoms being "entered" within the cognizer—who consists of consciousness and is of the nature of Śiva—is their non-difference (*abheda*). Otherwise, for what reason would that cognizer know, "This is a jar"? He could not know it at all; such is the meaning. || 31 ||

And without a single unity, there could never be the state of being an agent. For, as it is stated in the scriptures: "The determination of objects resides in consciousness; without a single subjectivity—which consists in the unification of those various distinct streams of consciousness—there would be no such thing."

It is said that this [recognition] is in no way possible without resting in a non-sequential consciousness whose nature is a single manifestation permeated by categories distinct from those [limited cognitions]. As it was stated in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*:
When entities, desiring to be established within a single cognizer through the various gateways of their respective distinct cognitions, this state of being "known" (jñāteya) becomes possible.

Since objects existing at different times and places are self-contained, their synthesis can only be accomplished by a single simultaneous appearance; otherwise, what kind of synthesis could there be?
Thus,
even in the case of things such as a rabbit's horn, there would be no grammatical connection with a case ending. (32)
In no way does the word "non-existence" (abhāva) denote anything that has non-existence as its essence.

Furthermore, this capacity of jars and other things to perform their own specific effects—which you maintain—would not be possible without their being of the nature of pure consciousness (*cidekarūpatva*). For that which is insentient (*jaḍa*) lacks intentionality (*nirabhisaṃdhi*).

This point—that [existence] is impossible due to the lack of causal efficiency (*karaṇāyogāt*)—has also been stated in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*. Therefore, whatever is existent by virtue of performing purposeful action (*arthakriyākāritva*), all that is of the nature of Śiva.
Even regarding things such as a hare’s horn, which are considered absolutely non-existent, for one who abides in that object...
In every respect, a word understood as denoting non-existence could not be connected with a case-ending (*vibhakti*),
because case-endings depend upon a grammatical factor (*kāraka*), and that which is non-existent cannot function as a *kāraka*.

Because a *kāraka* (grammatical participant) is defined by its causal efficiency (*kriyānimittatva*), therefore even in that case, when it possesses the status of a *kāraka* through connection with a case-ending, existence itself is what is called "Śiva-hood. Furthermore, as for the cognition that "the jar performs a purposeful action such as fetching water," that very [cognition] is of such a nature; it is not something separate from it.
A jar or the like is established as being of such a nature: (1) as that which is considered to be non-existent; (2) as that which is thought to be non-existent;
and (3) by way of non-existence throughout the three periods of time.
3. Therefore, the meaning here is not that there is an absolute non-existence [of the hare's horn], but rather that it is useless for conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*).
4. But surely, since the "hare's horn" is known and designated, how can there be a connection with action (*kriyā*) here?

For this injunction applies to the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) alone; since the connection with case-relations (*kāraka*) such as the object (*karman*) is not possible here, and linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is indeed dependent upon case-relations such as the object, one might ask: "How can there be a basis in action (*kriyā*)?". Anticipating this doubt, [the author states] that in linguistic usage, for those things which exist as positive entities...

He states "and in reality" (p. 160) to support that principle which is the seed of the causal factors, by means of which everything— whether in the form of existence or non-existence— is determined as being exactly the same.

In the investigation of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) itself, it has been shown that there exists that which is called the Himalaya. Even non-existence (*abhāva*), when known, is of the very nature of consciousness; and because its essence is that [consciousness], it is indeed the universal form (*viśvarūpa*).
Therefore, there is nowhere within the universe any form that is non-auspicious (*aśiva*) by nature of non-existence.
For this reason also, there is universal auspiciousness (sarvaśivatā) because of the possibility of arising from that which exists. || 33 ||
He alone remains as before, having such a nature consisting of the form of power;
that very same Blessed One manifests in the form of effects. (34)
1. For here the meaning is that the nature of the action itself is the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

2. Thus, although the Supreme Lord consists of the power of the universe, and although it is established—by means of gross observation, subtle examination, and the principle of the great universal generality—that the universe is composed of that [power], nevertheless...

Nothing whatsoever is to be added here, because there is nothing to be subtracted; thus, the purpose of that proof [is established]. Furthermore, since the goal is merely conventional usage (*vyavahāramātra*), there is both an incidental purpose—consisting in the removal of the disagreements of other disputants—and a primary purpose.
The two powers of consciousness (*cic-chakti*) and bliss (*nirvṛti-śakti*), which constitute its essential nature,
have indeed been established by way of the principle of *adhikaraṇa-siddhānta* (a conclusion established by implication) as that which projects all things. Among these,
non-dualism is first established by the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), whose nature is the unfolding and expansion of the power of consciousness.
It has been established. Now,

in order to establish that dyad by means of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), whose nature is the unfolding of the expansion of its own sovereignty, and for the purpose of manifesting the relationship between agent and object, [the author] relies upon the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*).
"First, speak on this point as well," and so forth.

Now, according to the principle that "what is non-existent cannot arise," let it be granted for now that only the existent can have the capacity for origination; however, this must be addressed: how were they situated therein prior to the state of the effect?
To the objection that this is true even in the state of the agent, he says "pure" and so forth.

But surely, let it be granted that there is the arising of only that which exists, because even in the causal state, one conceives of it as being in such a condition; however, this must be considered: that even from the existent, there is the arising of only that which is non-existent.

For instance, just as in the production of a jar, as long as [the cause] remains in its own essential nature, there is no production of the effect. In that regard, however, there is no disagreement that the effect—whether it be existent or non-existent—is not present; for the production of a jar is possible only when the essential nature of the clay and so forth has perished, and not otherwise.

In the same way, since the total destruction (*vipralopa*) of that [cause] would follow upon the production of the effect in its manifold form, the proof of the theory of non-existent effect (*asatkāryavāda*) is established even otherwise; so what is the recourse here? To this he says:
"That very [cause]," and so forth. The meaning is as follows: if there were a relationship of cause and effect, then...
The possibility of what you have stated would exist here as a relationship between agent and object;

however, the meaning is that just as he remains in his essential nature even when externalized— having internalized within himself the entire collection of scriptural compositions according to the specific meanings of those various scriptures as they are known— so too is it here.

For this reason as well, there is the state of universal Śiva-ness (*sarvaśivatā*): because the entire collection of existing things that possess origination arises as that very [Śiva] nature, even prior to its existence as an effect.

Because it is impossible for there to be contact with a contradictory non-existence. Furthermore, that very [seed] would have to be of the nature of the sprout even previously, if the sprout—which is essentially existence—exists beforehand in the form of a potentiality (*śakti*) and subsequently comes into being in the form of its effect, the sprout itself. || 34 ||
If the effect is not established as pre-existent, what is the use of producing that which already exists? Or, if its manifestation is produced here, is that manifestation itself existent? (35)

For is it performed as something non-existent or as something existent? Why is it not perceived? Is it because of the absence of manifestation, or because of infinity? If it were non-existent, there would be the possibility of its loss. (36)

If one relies on a position [of non-existence], then the entity would likewise be non-existent. Alternatively, if the effect is of the nature of existence, its production from that which already exists is untenable, because the production of what is already existent is futile;
for the intrinsic nature of the existent is not created, but rather it is merely manifested—and even that is not [the case].

This is logical, because is that [manifestation] itself existent when it is produced, or is it non-existent? If it is existent, then what is being produced by its manifestation? Why, then, is the effect not perceived? If, on the other hand, even though it exists, the effect is not perceived due to the absence of its manifestation, then [the same question applies] to the manifestation of that manifestation as well.
1. Now, having thoroughly examined the doctrine of the pre-existent effect (*satkāryavāda*) in terms of the relationship between agent and object,
and for the sake of the correct understanding of our own school,
[the author proceeds] by first stating the refutation of the dissenting views of opponents, followed by the establishment of the reasoning through the challenge of those opponents.

He establishes his own position with the words "the effect exists" (satkārya), etc. [Verse 2]. Regarding manifestation (abhivyakti): although manifestation is existent, it is considered non-existent because of the absence of actual manifestation.

Therefore, whether [the effect] exists or does not exist prior to its manifestation, its status as an effect is not evident therein; for its status as an effect resides in manifestation, and if that [manifestation] is absent,
the doctrine of the pre-existent effect (satkāryavāda) is untenable— this is the meaning.
As for what was said— that there is even the manifestation of that manifestation— it is not the case that manifestation itself is inherently real. He demonstrates this very point as being untenable.

7. Because it would entail the fallacy of fruitlessness and other defects; and if it is argued that "manifestation is produced," then even in that case, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) due to the aforementioned fallacy.

And consequently, there would be no cessation of the manifestation of the effect under discussion. Alternatively, if a non-existent manifestation is produced, then by producing something non-existent, there follows the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of abandoning the very position one has adopted.
Or, if, in order to avoid the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*), one resorts to the production of a non-existent manifestation, then [the same problem arises] as with the manifestation itself.
Even a real entity such as a sprout and so forth must be a non-existent effect; why resort to this "half-old-woman" logic? 36.
It is not so, because apart from that [place], there is honor everywhere else.
This is our position: one [reason] cannot be made equivalent to another elsewhere.
For the Vaiśeṣikas maintain that agency itself resides in Īśvara. (38)
1. Thus, manifestation brings about the state of being perceived.

2. Now, one might argue: "Let there be an infinite regress for the sake of accomplishing the effect"; to this he says, "And therefore," etc.: "Even so, there would be an infinite regress that destroys the very root."
Thus it has been said (3). But the effect is indeed existent (4).
To say that it is existent in one place and non-existent in another is a logical flaw; and that [flaw] does not mean that existence itself is not absolute—this is the meaning.
Indeed,
we are ashamed of these dialectical intellects, which are devoid of any determination of reality, which provoke mutual disputes, and whose sole essence is mere conceit.

Thus, when the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) has been established—being protected by the firm evidence of one's own experience and supported by logical reasoning—one who resorts to the fallacies of logic would never find a stable support, as they would remain perpetually wavering.

Therefore, to demonstrate through a bold assertion that the theory of the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryavāda*) is like [the theory of] manifestation (*abhivyakti*), he says: "like manifestation."
6. That manifestation. 7. If a characteristic that is unique to one thing were to be postulated for another, it would be vitiated by the fault of infinite regress (anavasthā).
8. He states the over-extension [of this argument] in that case:
"In the same way, why is it that the cognition of the Buddha does not abide in the earth and so forth? (p. 163)
Just as there is nothing other than itself that illuminates it, why should there not be something else [that illuminates] that [other]? (39)

They assert that external objects such as form and so forth are the objects of cognition, and that for them, only the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is the means of valid knowledge regarding the domain of *dharma* by necessity; therefore, there is no equality between [the Buddhist view] and this one. (40)
In this case, many [universals] would have to be postulated, nor can it be so because of their exclusion;
for the individuality of entities is established, and thus a jar is said to be "manifested. (41)
Therefore, that very self is manifest; it is not something distinct from manifestation.
What you have stated is indeed not tenable, because our position is this: apart from that manifestation, the effect is simply existent. For this is not the case in every philosophical system.

All these points must be considered equal. For instance, among the Vaiśeṣikas, God alone is the creator of the universe, and not substances such as earth and so forth. In the Buddhist system, consciousness alone is that which illuminates both itself and others, and not form and the like. Those followers of Jaimini argue that the Vedic injunction alone is the definitive authority.

Regarding the subject of Dharma, the authoritative means of knowledge is that "Dharma is a beneficial purpose characterized by Vedic injunction" (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 1.1.2), and not perception or other such means. Therefore, [this applies] to many things that share a single definition.

One should not raise the objection that because one [entity] is considered to have a different characteristic from the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), it would follow that all others are likewise identical to it. Consequently, all existing things are indeed effects; nevertheless, their manifestation (*abhivyakti*) is nonetheless unreal.

This must be established: just as there are other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) besides scriptural injunction (*codanā*) regarding dharma, and just as the earth and other substances are not the cause of the universe in the same way that the substance of God is, so too there is a logical justification here; it is not merely a matter of dogmatic assertion. Furthermore, manifestation (*abhivyakti*) is not distinct from the object itself.
1. According to the Buddhist view; 2. he says "not so" (na ca) because there is also [the fault of] reductio ad absurdum (*upapatti*) here.

It remains so because it is not perceived [as distinct]; and linguistic usage occurs precisely through non-difference. For instance, a jar is designated as "manifested" by way of its non-difference from the manifestation. Therefore, the object itself is of the nature of the manifestation. And that [object] which exists is what is produced; it is not the production of a manifestation that is separate from the object and unreal. || 41 ||
Is it that the manifestation of an already existing jar or similar object is produced by a lamp? Or [is it otherwise]? 42.
Just as the manifestation of action belongs to that which exists, so too does production belong to that which is manifested;
for there is no production of what is non-existent, since it would be equal to [the case of] another [non-existent thing]. (43)
On what basis do they proceed, given that [the object] has the nature of non-existence?

This is not at all unprecedented. For, by means of a lamp, the manifestation of an existing jar or similar object is produced; thus, it is the very entity itself that is produced. And therefore, just as there is an action known as "manifestation" regarding an existing jar or similar object—
Likewise, even in the case of manifestation (*vyakti*), which is of the nature of an existing entity, its production occurs through means such as a lamp;
or, in the case of that which is of the nature of a sprout, it occurs through seeds and the like. Thus, the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) is uniform in all instances.
For since the effect is already existent as an entity, the manifestation—which is non-different from it—is likewise existent. And this manifestation...
1 Thus, in this way—
neither through positive concomitance nor through negative concomitance—
is the manifestation of the categories established.
Thus it has been said. Now, he establishes the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of these two by means of the lamp.

But [an objection may be raised]: if it is already existent, then what is this so-called "manifestation"? If, on the other hand, manifestation means the acquisition of its own nature (*svarūpa-lābha*), then let there be only manifestation; what is the use of the doctrine that the effect pre-exists (*satkāryavāda*)? To this, he replies:
"By means of a lamp," [it is said].
Therefore, there is no distinct substratum here for the substance and its manifestation, because they possess an identical nature.
Having thus established the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) through reasoning, [the author now establishes it] by means of experience as well.
He establishes this according to his own view with the words "nor does he know," and so forth.
165) Manifestation is the nature of luminosity, belonging to the sprout and other such things which exist as being without beginning or end.

Thus, by asserting that the light of consciousness exists in various forms [of manifestation], the proponent of manifestation (*abhivyaktivādin*) has stated the theory of the pre-existent effect (*satkāryavāda*). For if an effect were produced from what is non-existent, then upon what would causal factors depend, and with reference to what would they operate and be differentiated? This is because the relationship between cause and effect [would be impossible].
1. By way of being the measure of the relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākāraka*).
Now, if the effect already exists in the cause, then what is this so-called "manifestation" (*vyakti*)? To this he says: "And manifestation... because here...

That which is the form of the great universal (mahāsāmānya), following after all the specific divisions of the categories of reality, worlds, kalās, and objects— that very thing is called Śivatva, the nature of consciousness, which is without beginning or end; in that state, there is no abiding whatsoever in the form of an effect.

Because it exists precisely in the form of the cause; however, when a form is conceptually constructed there itself through the inclusion of specific qualities—much like a lower universal—it is called the "effect.
Therefore, how and where could there be the doctrine of the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryavāda*)? He says this to show that this is a subtle method.

Regarding the phrases "of that which is without beginning or end" and "by this and by that," and so forth— it is precisely to express the actual non-difference between these two that it is stated in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*: "And this intuition (pratibhā), though colored by the succession of various objects..."
"It has been stated: 'That Great Lord is the subject whose nature is non-successive and infinite consciousness' (1.7.1).
Now, let it be granted that there is such a thing as the Śiva-principle, which is like a great universal and is without beginning or end."
Nevertheless, just as when there is clay there is a pot, and when there is the appearance of fire there is the appearance of smoke, so too,

since the relation of cause and effect is observed in the world such that "when the seed exists, the sprout is born," how can it be that consciousness alone is the cause therein, by virtue of which there is no production from the non-existent? To this, he says:

"And if" (yadi ceti). The meaning is this: if this—namely, the capacity of the former and the existence of the latter—is established even without the synthesis of consciousness (cid-anusandhāna), then...

There might be an occasion for your statement regarding the production of an effect from a non-existent thing; however, that is not possible in any way for those things which abide solely in their own nature, which possess not even a trace of knowledge regarding another object, and which are devoid of any synthetic connection.
This is possible for insentient things. For this entire path of the conventional usage of cause and effect has as its object a single continuous synthesis;
thus he states this concisely in the passage beginning with "of the causal relation," and so forth.

In the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, the engagement [of the senses] is enjoined like the form [of activity] at the commencement of cooking and so forth. Alternatively, with what end in view do they engage, and in what object does their capacity reside?

Because capacity is impossible in the absence of an object, since it has a nature that is dependent upon an object, and because at that time the object, which is the effect, is by its very nature non-existent. || 43 ||
Then, having perceived the movement within the interior of the jar as it was previously seen, [he acts]. (44)
Because it is impossible for one thing to be determined by another, there would be an extreme incongruity.
Furthermore, if the activity or capacity of the causal factors consists in their determining a sprout that has already arisen and been perceived, that is untenable.
Because seeds and the like lack consciousness, they are devoid of discernment (*akalana*). Regarding this, he states another point with the words "or else" (*athavā*);
[it refers to] that capacity (*sāmarthya*).
3. At that time, prior to manifestation.

4. Now, why is this said? Since the object does not exist at that time, in respect to what object do they possess efficacy? And if this alone is to be proven here—that [the capacity] existed previously as well—

Regarding the point that [the effect] is dependent: if it were so, then this would be established; for since even a sprout and the like exist as having already arisen previously, everything would be established by virtue of being dependent upon that. Anticipating this objection, he says "another jar," and so forth.
The intended meaning here is this: indeed, this must be stated—does the potter also...?

Is the maker of the jar of the nature of the body and so forth, or is it some conscious being distinct from that? If it is of the nature of the body and so forth—which are insentient—then this must be addressed: what is its distinction from seeds and the like, which are also insentient, since they too are categorized as inert and are incapable of cognition? Or rather...
Even though the conscious being is distinct from that [body], what follows? He says: "even where there is a conscious being," for what has occurred?
Indeed, that [body] has not become its cause such that it would depend upon it; rather, while shining forth within the consciousness of the potter, it simply emerges outwardly.

If the cause, such as a conscious potter and so forth, were to have previously perceived another jar, then what would that have to do with the other jar that is to be produced, by virtue of which [it could produce it]?
That [effect] is produced because the extreme variety of its purpose exists even though it is not [previously] established; thus there is derision:
"If [the cause were already present], the sprout would not arise, for it would lack the nature of an agent. (45)
For if there were no sentient being, there could be no collection of causal factors;
since that which is called the "object" (karman) would be non-existent, how could it have a relationship with what is unreal? (46)
Therefore, that very Blessed One, the Supreme Lord, being truly existent, manifests himself in various ways through the forms of all existing things. || 47 ||

In the case of the statement "the sprout arises from the seed and the earth," the non-existent sprout would lack causality— that is, agency— and in the case of "the potter makes a jar," what connection could there be between the other causal factors (kārakas) or the agent and an object that is non-existent? How, then, can there be a collection [of such factors]?

If [the Lord] were not the agent of these causal factors, then action would not arise from them. Therefore, the Supreme Lord, whose nature is consciousness, manifests and becomes himself in various forms through the essential natures of those states.
And since he is eternally existent, how can there be any suspicion that the effect is non-existent? || 47 ||

1. Furthermore, an effect is indeed accomplished by multiple causal factors (*kāraka*); therefore, even in the absence of one [factor], would all the others become as if non-existent? For instance, a sprout arises even in the absence of [the specific] action (*karman*), yet the cause still exists; likewise, in the case of "the potter makes a jar," [the jar arises despite the absence of other factors].

Having raised the prima facie objection (*pūrvapakṣa*)—namely, that since there is a conjunction of various factors such as the agent (*kartṛ*), instrument (*karaṇa*), object (*karman*), and locus (*adhikaraṇa*), why should these not be established even in the mere absence of an object? [the author] demonstrates that it is precisely the object (*karman*) that is conjoined with the various factors: "When the object exists, all of this is established."

With the intention that "it is not otherwise," [the author] states "the sprout" and so forth, in order to demonstrate the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the agent and the object;
for in no way whatsoever can an insentient thing possess causality, such that even a non-existent thing [could be a cause].
If the production of an effect were to occur [independently], then this would be established without effort; thus he says, "Therefore" (tasmāt).
And since it does not produce itself, by what other thing could it be produced?
If the agent and so forth were distinct [from consciousness], then they would be of the nature of that [consciousness]. || 48 ||

How could its being born be logical through [factors] distinct from itself? Furthermore, since it is itself non-existent, how could a jar or the like be born, and how could it be an agent of birth? At that time, by what capacity—nor even by another such as a potter—could it exist, being non-existent?

That which is devoid of the intrinsic nature characterized by fitness for birth would be no different from a hare’s horn; even if its producer were existent, nevertheless, that existence of the producer would not belong to the produced thing at all because it is distinct [from it], and therefore, by that [existence] as well, there is no attainment of fitness for it. For in this way, regarding that fitness for birth—
If it were to be active, its being the progenitor would be logical; if it were the progenitor, [then its activity would be possible].

Furthermore, if you say that it does not arise by itself because it is non-existent, the summary of the meaning is this: for that which is itself non-existent, such as a hare’s horn, cannot be produced by anything else.

Now, one might object: "Is this not precisely what constitutes the distinction of a cause from its effect—namely, that it produces something else? In the absence of that [production], how can it be designated as a 'cause'? Anticipating this doubt, he says "and itself," etc.
The meaning is: "This is your own position."
Furthermore, a rabbit's horn is said to be non-existent because it lacks the intrinsic nature characterized by the fitness for birth.

Consequently, its production by anything whatsoever is not logical. Thus, since everything that is non-existent remains exactly as it is, how could birth even of a non-existent thing be possible? This is the meaning.
4. The existence of the producer; the phrase "of the produced" [is understood] as being non-existent.
5. Through the existence of the producer, that produced thing attains fitness—that is, fitness for existence. 6. The existence of the producer.
It was stated that [the agent] would be joined [with the action]; he states that very justification with the words "If...
The agent and the auxiliary factors, consisting of the instruments and so forth, would be produced in nature.
But how could there be the birth of a non-existent thing from existents that are distinct [from it]? || 48 ||
Because the jar does not exist at the time of its birth, there can be no connection with the causal factors (kārakas). (49)

There is no production of that which is unconnected [to its cause]; if it is argued that it exists because the effect pre-exists [in the cause], then even though it exists, it is not perceived due to the absence of a manifesting agent (vyañjaka). (50)
Therefore, existence would have to exist as an entity by its own inherent nature;
for at the time when the birth of a produced jar begins, there is no connection between it and the potter, the lump of clay, or other such factors, because [the jar] does not yet exist.

Furthermore, there can be no production of that which lacks a relationship [to the causes], because it would follow [absurdly] that it could exist even previously or from other sources. Even in the case of a relationship that is yet to be produced (*janya*), it is precisely through dependence on those [causes] that there is a specific capacity (*sāmarthya-viśeṣa*) belonging only to the producers, by virtue of which that [effect] exists only when those [causes] are present, and not otherwise.

This doctrine of *asatkāryavāda* (the theory that the effect is non-existent [prior to its production]) belonging to someone has been refuted in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā* and other works. Now, it might be argued:

"That relation exists because the effect is of the nature of an existent thing. That too is not so, because even if this object such as a jar were existent, it would be unperceived; and due to being unperceived, [it would follow that it is non-existent].

Because relatives lack renown, there is neither the arrival of a relationship nor the state of being a manifestor (*vyañjakatva*) with respect to a jar on the part of the potter and others; for that which is in every way beyond the scope of cognition cannot be a manifestor. This applies only to an object already established (*siddha*).

But surely, it is precisely that which must be investigated: the production of the effect immediately following [the cause]. As for what existed prior to that—whether the effect exists potentially (*satkārya*) in the potter’s cognition, in the seed, or in the light of the Supreme Lord (according to your view), or whether it does not exist (according to our view)—there is no point in grasping at that, as it is irrelevant to the matter. As for that which...

Regarding that, since [the pot] is being produced at the very time its birth begins, there is a doubt as to whether it exists or does not exist; therefore, he says "at the time of birth" (janmakāle) in order to support the view that this [time] alone must be correctly discerned.
Prior to its connection with the potter and so forth, it is indeed indeterminate in other respects.

3. Now, [the author] states that only that which exists previously can be connected with all actions, beginning with the words "even in the absence of a connection with the produced" (janyāsaṃbandhe’pi).
4. By which—by the reason of prior existence.
Because it is produced by the activity of a potter and others;
just as a lamp is considered a manifestor in the case of a jar and so forth, therefore [the same applies] to the manifestor as well.

How can there be a relationship based on non-existence? For a cause would exist in the form of its effect only if there were non-distinction between the two; and that is contradicted by direct perception.
Therefore, the single existence of all things, which are not mutually contradictory, is existence itself.
The Supreme Lord exists as such by virtue of his inherent nature of abiding, not through any other cause or reason;

he is constantly associated with existence and non-existence pertaining to the cycle of transmigration, because that is his very nature. Alternatively, he is eternally connected with existence by virtue of being the causal ground of Śiva.
The doctrine that the effect pre-exists in the cause (satkāryavāda). || 50 ||
From this as well, know that the effect pre-exists: is the jar separate from the lump of clay? (51)
If [the cause] were not distinct from the effect, why would there be no production of cloth and so forth?
If they were non-distinct, it would follow that there is no material cause at all; for in that case, the cause would simply be the effect itself.
From this also, understand the validity of the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) through the fact that all things have Śiva as their essence;

for even in the case of a lump of clay and a jar, the relationship of cause and effect is established under both the doctrines of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) and its non-existence (*asatkāryavāda*).
For if the jar were distinct from the lump of clay, or likewise if it were non-existent [in the lump], [the causal relationship would not hold].
Since there is no difference in the non-existence of both a cloth and a rabbit’s horn, the former would likewise be a cause [of the latter]. But that is not the case,

because it is impossible to accept the composition of words as having a purposeful effect when the object does not exist— since such acceptance cannot be made without setting aside other possibilities— and thus clay lumps and the like would lack the very status of being material causes (*upādāna*), which is the nature of a primary cause (*prakṛti*).

The meaning is that it would not exist at all. If there were no distinction, that jar would be nothing other than the lump of clay itself, and not something new; consequently, even prior to its production, the lump would have to be the jar.
1. For there is no mutual non-difference between the potter and the jar, by which the relationship between the potter and the lump of clay could be established.

2. He states another meaning for the word "bhāvin" with the words "or else" (athavā); [it is used here] in the sense of a constant connection (*nityayoga*), as a suffix denoting possession (*matvarthīya*).
This is the reason.

Having thus established the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) by way of its being the cause, he now establishes the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect also by way of its being the effect, beginning with the words "from this also" (*ito 'pi*).

If there is a difference in name and configuration, yet no difference in the hand when it becomes a fist and so forth, then the effect exists [in the cause] as a matter of fact; for this very reason, there is non-destruction. (53)
[Objection: Even when Śiva’s form is destroyed, or even when his crown is destroyed, [he remains Śiva], just as gold remains gold.

Furthermore, since there is a difference between a lump of clay and a jar due to the difference in their names and configurations (*saṃniveśa*), there is indeed a difference [between cause and effect]; so how can the effect pre-exist in the cause (*satkāryavāda*)? [Reply: That is not so; here, the difference consists merely in name and configuration, but not in [the substance].

Just as the state of being clay is common to both [the lump and the jar]—as seen in the case of the hand, where it is equally present in the state of being a fist or an open palm—so too is the state of being existent (*sadrūpatā*) common to these two.
This has been demonstrated for the sake of establishing this point, though it is already extremely well-known; in reality, even the clay [is not different from its effects].
When one reflects upon it, that which consists of the subtle elements (tanmātras) such as sound and touch is distinct from water and the other gross elements;

this remains so as long as the state of the three gunas persists. Even while in that state, those effects which range from the Great Principle (mahat) down to earth, or even down to jars and the like, [arise].
If they were of the nature of the three *guṇas* alone, there would be a merging of the universe into oneness. However, when there is something additional to that, there arises the distinction:
"this is space consisting of the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*)," "this is earth," "this is a jar," and "this is a cloth.
Furthermore, this distinction is indeed real because it is non-different from that [reality]. Nor is it...
It is logical that what is manifesting lacks substantial reality, for by that same reasoning, it would follow that even the three *guṇas* lack it.

Furthermore, manifestation consists in being perceived, whether through direct perception or inference; in every case, there must be the nature of existence (*sadrūpatā*). And thus, the lump of clay would be something entirely different from that in which the jar comes to be.

The jar is one thing, and the clay is another; that which is common to all clay objects is the clay, while the jar is not common [to them]. And it is not possible for that which is common and that which is not common to be identical; consequently, there would be the fault of why a cloth or other such things could not be produced [from clay]. [The world] is like a mirror, possessing the reflections of the universe.

Even if one accepts the doctrine of the three qualities (*traiguṇya*), that by whose power such a connection with reflection occurs is itself the cause; yet, since even there an analysis of difference and non-difference leads to inconsistency,
the true nature is that of Śiva consisting of consciousness alone (*cinmaya*).

He states that all effects exist precisely according to the principle taught in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*: "For the effect exists as a reality. Therefore, because it exists as the very nature of Śiva, it is indestructible; for there is no destruction of Śiva, who is existent as the nature of one's own consciousness.

Regarding "destruction," it is stated thus in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*: "Even when the crown is destroyed, [the gold remains] like gold"—this is an illustration based on common worldly experience, showing that it remains as before. (53)
There is destruction in the form of a bracelet, and existence in the form of an earring and so forth.
"Even in the case of goldness, there is no loss; even regarding the configuration, let it be examined.
By means of common-world examples such as bracelets, earrings, and so forth, it is stated that there is only a difference in configuration.
"Even regarding the configuration, let the difference be examined. (54)
And by investigating that [matter], concluding precisely with the fact that Śiva is the cause, he says: "Is it declared to be pervaded by the nature of Śiva, or not pervaded? (55)

If [Śiva] were all-pervasive, He would be subject to destruction; if He were not pervasive, He would possess spatial limitation (*pradeśitā*). If His pervasiveness were limited to the crown of the head, then upon the destruction of the crown, Śiva himself would be destroyed. Alternatively, if Śiva were not pervasive, He would exist only in a specific location, excluding the regions occupied by the nature of the crown, the jar, the cloth, and so forth.

In the case of spatial location, there is the defect that it would have a divided nature and, consequently, a lack of omnipresence; thus, regarding spatial location, the fault is stated in both ways. || 55 ||
It is not so, for we do not desire the destruction of existing things. (56)

The manifestation of parts, destruction, dissolution, and total disappearance do not entail the aforementioned fault; for we do not accept destruction as the subject regarding entities—that is to say, we do not maintain that entities are perishable. Indeed, in our fundamental view...

At the time of the production of the bracelet, there is the manifestation of the gold-element alone; this is called the destruction of the previous moment of its transformation into a crown, but it is not the non-perception of all parts. Therefore, there is no fault of total destruction without residue (*niranvaya-vināśa*), nor is there a lack of continuity for the element itself, since it is merely unmanifested.
Because of its perishability. || 56 ||
Even if manifestation were perishable, [the world] would nonetheless result in being infinite. || 57 ||
In this context, destruction is merely the incapacity of the sense-faculties;
that very [incapacity] is non-manifestation, and it remains at that time in a concealed state.

Now, [the opponent might argue: "Just as for existing objects there is the arising of their mere manifestation, so too in the case of destruction, it is the destruction of that very same thing; thus, destruction is said to be the non-manifestation of the previous portion alone.
This is not correct, because is the arising of even this manifestation itself unreal or real?

Thus, the faults already stated regarding the production of an object apply here, as does the fallacy of infinite regress; likewise, the destruction of an object is not tenable, because that which exists cannot be destroyed, and the same holds for its manifestation. If it is argued that it is the manifestation itself that perishes through another manifestation, and not the existence [of the object], then the existence of that manifestation also would not perish through the manifestation of its manifestation, but rather—

Manifestation would imply infinity. Alternatively, regarding the destruction of manifestation, does it arise as non-existent or as existent? If it were non-existent, there would be a loss of the doctrine that the effect pre-exists in the cause (*satkāryavāda*) and a logical inconsistency. If it were existent, the destruction would already exist previously. Or, is manifestation produced by a cause for the sake of destruction?
Thus, as previously stated, that lack of finality constitutes infinity. In this way,

according to the principle taught in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, just as in our system the instrumentality of objects— which consists of the non-manifestation of their non-difference from Śiva— is such that they are perceivable by both types of sense organs, so too is destruction.
The absence of being perceivable by both types of faculties is non-difference from Śiva; it is the concealment by means of Śiva-nature.
That very thing has been stated as the incapacity of the senses, and likewise as that very non-manifestation; at that time, that jar or other object remains concealed as Śiva. || 58 ||
For this reason as well, there is no destruction of this jar, because it is produced again;
for it is not logical that that which has attained the state of non-existence could be produced once more. (59)
Therefore, even when a particular manifestation perishes, the Śiva-principle remains imperishable.

For this reason as well, there is no destruction of this [reality], such as a jar, because it is produced again. Indeed, for that object whose form has in every respect attained a state equal to a hare's horn, [there can be no production].

Furthermore, existence would [arise] again. But is it not the case that the previous pot was one thing entirely, which had reached the state of a hare's horn, while this other one is now being produced? This is not so; for indeed...

It was stated previously that a pot may be distinct from [another] pot; yet, through contact with other universals such as largeness, redness, and height, it remains internally situated and is made an object of the senses consisting of the non-apprehension of difference (abhedākhyāti).

Therefore, according to the sequence described, even when the non-apprehension of non-difference with respect to Śiva-tattva—which consists in the immersion of all entities (bhāvas) into Śiva-tattva—is destroyed, Śiva-tattva itself remains indestructible.
Thus, through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for origination and destruction, the universal Śiva-nature (sarvaśivatā) is established. || 59 ||
And for this reason, the state of universal Śiva-ness does not arise from any of the individual parts.
Now let this very point regarding the composite whole (*avayavin*) be investigated:
how it is established that there is both unity and non-difference among things that are distinct. (61)

Likewise, in that regard, the Lord’s power is to be fully understood as being such that there is non-difference within what is divided, and even among things that are divided, there is non-difference. (62)
Just as form resides in its constituent parts, so too does it reside in all objects;

for this reason also, there is the state of universal Śiva-ness. A whole that is distinct from its parts never appears in any visual or mental cognition. Even by those who maintain that it is distinct [from the parts]...
They maintain that cognition occurs through inherence (*samavāya*) as if there were no difference [between the parts and the whole].
This must be examined: although the parts are established as distinct within an extended appearance—since extension is absent in the partless atom alone—nevertheless, [the whole] is indeed one.

The object designated as "Devadatta" appears as a single, solid mass with its internal joints unperceived; thus, unity shines forth even within distinct parts. In that regard, just as there is this unity, so too has the power of the Lord Śiva, who consists of consciousness, been described in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, by which—
By implication, although Devadatta is non-different [as a whole], he possesses the nature of having distinct parts;
and while the parts are distinct, it is logical that there is only one "Devadatta-ness. Likewise, there is a single form residing within the distinction of the parts.
In this way, the form of Śiva resides in all objects whatsoever existing throughout the three worlds.
He clarifies that very point:
"Where are the hands and feet, and where is the head? How could there be unity [of these] when they occupy different locations? (63)
In the same way, Śiva abides as the unity of all categories of existence in the world;

it has been demonstrated in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā* itself that even the distinction between parts possesses the nature of a non-differentiated whole precisely through the nature of Śiva, which establishes the state of being Śiva within the unity of the world.
She stands firm. || 63 ||
There is no apprehension of sound and so forth by those [moments] arisen earlier, later, or simultaneously. (64)
Why is there an impulsion of the mind when it previously existed without knowledge?
O dear one, because of that very state of universal oneness, there is likewise the awakening from deep sleep.
How could the causal sign (nimitta) be consistent with the arguments concerning its prior connection or lack thereof?
Since [in reality] it is merely the waking state [of consciousness], therefore everything is of the nature of Śiva.
For this very reason, the state of universal oneness (*sarvaikatā*) is established here in this world;

because there is no cognition distinct from every object—whether sound, touch, form, or otherwise—since these are not separate from the cognitions that arise prior to, after, or simultaneously with them. To explain further:

First of all, how could cognition exist without an object? And later, even if they exist together, how can there be the relationship of grasped and grasper between two things that abide within themselves?
Furthermore, without a cognition directed toward an object, why would the mind be impelled by the self?
If it is argued that there must first be a cognition in order to grasp an external object, what is the use of impelling the mind?

Furthermore, since an external object is not known by means of the cognition of intention (*abhisandhi*), there would be no need to impel the mind for that purpose. Therefore, when the identity with Śiva, whose nature is consciousness, is established, perception remains constant at all times.

This should be understood as a mere formal process (*prakriyāmātra*) brought about by the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*), as taught in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, consisting of expressions that denote non-duality; likewise, there is the awakening of one who remains in the state of deep sleep.
How could the simultaneous utterance of sounds and so forth be possible without [their] unity? For instance, there is the cognition of high-pitched sounds and so forth.

Regarding the objection as to how [the state of deep sleep] can be established through such arguments— namely, that there must be a prior connection with it for the sake of awakening, or else there would be no connection at all— for if there were a prior connection with the cognition of sound and so forth, it would necessarily be the waking state itself,
since that is defined by such characteristics; whereas in the absence of the prior cause, which is the cognition of sound and so forth, [it remains the state of deep sleep].

How does awakening occur? This must be as follows: if there is only one primordial wisdom (*vidyā*), this would be merely a process of the non-manifestation of Śiva-nature. Furthermore, even when an obscuration is produced by ignorance consisting of intense sound and so forth, there is the cessation of the state of deep sleep (*sauṣupta*).
As for the statement "from another," it is not determinative that [the object] is established through a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). || 66 ||
Or, there exists a universal form, and that is non-different from the particular;
some entity is thus held to consist of both a different and a non-different nature. (67)

Alternatively, there exists a universal nature (*sāmānyarūpatā*) consisting of the unity of all particulars (*viśeṣa*), such as the brindled cow (*śāvaleyādi*). And that [universal] is both non-different and different from those particulars;
for, according to the systems of the Sāṃkhya, the Jains (*Ārhata*), and others, a category (*padārtha*) possesses a nature that is both different and non-different [from its constituents].

That which is thus perceived is accepted as being real; and that [reality] would not exist without the oneness of the ultimate principle—this is the connection with what is to be stated hereafter. || 67 ||
If, for a Buddhist, inference does not cease to function regarding a universal,
it is as it does with golden vessels, but not so with gold and copper.
When it is said, "Bring the gold," how could emptiness be understood? For it is never logical [to do so], because it lacks any specific contact with the object. (69)
Without the unity of reality, there could be no contradictory nature in a single entity;
how can a single thing possess both the universal and the particular? (70)

Now, if the Buddhist has no universal (sāmānya), then his desired position that inference has a universal as its object is abandoned. Furthermore, without a universal, just as when it is said "bring gold," there is no cognition [of a specific object] regarding things such as golden bracelets or earrings, so it would not be here either.
In the case of gold and copper, since it is perceived as gold alone through the non-contact with the copper, there is no relinquishment of anything in [the case of] bracelets, armlets, and so forth.

Even if the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is accepted as being a universal (*sāmānya*), why would one understand from the command "bring gold" a mere emptiness in the form of a non-preservative negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), due to the reason that it lacks contact with any particular?
Rather, [the word refers to] those things excluded from what is not gold, which produce the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) of "gold."

The phrase "it is somehow logical that the particulars themselves attain oneness" should be interpreted with an interrogative intonation (*kāku*); for it is never at all logical that even emptiness should appear [as such].
This [appearance] would not be possible without the oneness of the essence of consciousness (*cittattva*) with objects; for there can be no [oneness] of a single object alone.

Because they are mutually contradictory. This is not possible for that which is insentient and external; he clarifies this by saying "in general" (meaning as non-different) and "in particular" (meaning as different). However, because the principle of consciousness (*cittattva*) is characterized by absolute freedom (*svacchandattva*), there is no contradiction, as has been stated in the *Pratyabhijñā* itself. 70.
Without this single principle, linguistic usage does not arise; for there can be no relation between a word and its object if they were distinct entities existing in separate locations. (70)
Even though they possess contradictory forms and are perceived by different sense organs—since sound exists in the mouth and the object exists on the ground—where indeed is their meeting? (71)
The first is formless and the second is formed; how can there be a state of yoga?
Furthermore, there is oneness here, because without the nature of a single consciousness, no worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) arises;
for this [transaction] between word and meaning, characterized as the signified and the signifier, consists of a single reflective awareness (*ekaparāmarśamaya*).
As for the relation: how could that exist when there is difference of location, difference of nature such as being corporeal or incorporeal, and being perceivable by different sense organs?
He clarifies this very point of difference of location and so forth with the words "for in the mouth... Connection (*yogitā*) means relatedness (*saṃbandhitā*).
And there is a single unifying cognition even of two things that are distinct. || 71 ||
Likewise, how can there be a connection with those words for the unseen self and so forth? (72)
The connection of non-existent things, such as a hare’s horn, with a hare’s horn and the like, never occurs; likewise, there can be no linguistic usage regarding non-existent entities. (73)

If it were so by means of words, then indeed there would be the destruction of the entire cycle of existence; through unreal conventional usage, the world would become exactly like that [unreal]. (74)

How can there be a connection by means of the word "self" with the self and so forth which are not perceived, or by the word "hare's horn" with the non-existent hare's horn and so forth, or even by the word "sky-flower" with the sky-flower? There is no such fault; for it is precisely by means of a word that non-existent things [are connected].

If the applicability of words is due to their having non-existent objects, then indeed the destruction of the entire world-process (*saṃsāra*) would follow. He clarifies this: through the verbal usage of what is unreal, the world itself would become just as unreal, as would the word appearing to the world.
Likewise, how can there be a meeting with those [ancestors] for one who has just been born?
If that meeting were unreal, how could there be such things as being brought under control by mechanical devices and the like? (75)
Therefore, because of the identity of reality, all of that is also appropriate through a word that is non-different from the mantra, even though it appears distinct. (76)

How is it that [the word] does not denote Devadatta as it does Yajñadatta? If you say it is because of being conventionally assigned (saṃketita) here, then what has convention accomplished in this case? (77)

If it were conjunction, it would not be possible for sound to reach distant objects, whether corporeal or incorporeal; nor could it apply to the pair of the uttered and the destroyed, since the uttered has perished.

If it consists of the forms of the signifier and the signified, from where does this restriction arise—that one has the nature of being the signifier while the other has the nature of being the signified? (79)
