If they exist in the form of the signified and the signifier, there is a connection between the signified and the signifier;
furthermore, the oneness of the world exists because it is not apprehended by direct perception. (80)

Because conventional discourse is connected with specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) in every respect, and because it is not possible [otherwise] in the world, valid cognition pertains to conventional discourse. (81)
What kind of activity is there that resembles the cognition of infants, the mute, and so forth?
Since [the mind] is associated with conceptual construction, how could there be a perception of things as they truly are? (82)
Therefore, the object of knowledge must be a single entity; how could there be a perception of it as divided?
Likewise, inference would not be possible if there were no concomitance (anvaya) between smoke and fire anywhere.
Even when two previously unperceived things have been grasped at that time, if the relationship between them has not been grasped, fire is not cognized [as being present]. (84)
If the universal were without distinction, how could there be valid cognition due to that lack of distinction?
Furthermore, if the particular were also something previously non-existent, how could there be any synthesis [of the two]? (85)
If it is argued that there is no meeting with the thing-in-itself due to its similarity, nor can there be inferential status here based on smoke alone. (86)
If it be argued that [the universal] is perceived because of its connection with that [particular], we reply: in a relation there is no residing in two [loci];
nor is there perception of it through the apprehension of only one of the two, because a relation resides in both. (87)

If fire and its connection [to smoke] were to be inferred by means of the observation of smoke, then the fault of mutual dependence (itaretarāśraya) would result here, which is difficult to avoid. (88)
As long as there is no reckoning of the fire, so long there is no reckoning of yoga; or, as long as there is no reckoning of yoga, it is incapable of the reckoning of the fire. (89)
(180) Furthermore, based on the words of a reliable authority, one's conviction regarding the truth of a matter here may be unsteady;
for a speaker who is not an iron-like [firm] person never speaks the truth. (90)
Even that [object] might appear otherwise due to the non-destruction of attachment and aversion;
thus, even the unreality of one's father and others is not certain in that case or elsewhere. (91)
Therefore, it is not logical that there can be even the apprehension of those [entities] when things are distinct;
this is also established by reflecting upon their momentary destruction.

Indeed, through the conceptual alternatives of being capable or incapable—as illustrated by the examples of a lamp’s flame and so forth—stability is not established for you; yet it is established even by direct perception.
Stability and momentariness are established through the investigation of the means of valid cognition;
how could that which is of a non-contradictory nature be contradictory? (94)
As long as there is no establishment of all entities as being identical, how can there be for another the attainment of the realization of momentary destruction? (95)
Furthermore, this nature of being Śiva in all things is established;
likewise, the comprehension of meaning from either a sentence or a word is not otherwise possible.
Or, because sounds are momentary, they cannot manifest [the sphoṭa];
furthermore, even in the view that the sphoṭa is manifested by them, how could there be a sequence in that case as well? (97)

Since the reality of the *sphoṭa* is partless, how could there not be a perception, for the Grammarians, of objects that consist of the nature of the *sphoṭa* and have the form of manifestations? (98)
Therefore, even in such a matter, there would be logical consistency here through unity;
likewise, by the power of the self's will, activity does not arise in the collection of the senses.
If it is argued that his mind is not impelled because of a deficiency in the physical impeller (the body),
then such a [deficiency] would apply everywhere, for such a logic holds true in all cases of unity. (100)
Furthermore, neither the perception of distinct entities nor cognition itself would be possible through conjunction, if it were to occur by means of seeing and so forth. (101)
It is not so; for what effort would there be on the part of a cognizer merely from the conjunction of the sense-faculty and the object?
When a conjunction has occurred in one [person], how could another possess the status of a cognizer? (102)
Now, the knowledge of memory is described because it is non-different in time from the mind;
it follows the present action, being both commenced and yet incomplete. (103)

This is merely a process, since there is a nature of prior and posterior in action; for indeed, there is a sequence among the factors of action (kārakas) with respect to their own respective objects. 104.
Where two words, preceding and following, possess identity in time, it is there that [the object] is led by the mind; does that [object] possess the nature of a real entity? (105)
If it is argued that it is not form because it possesses a corporeal nature, then how can it be a quality?
For how could the form of the possessor of the quality be led elsewhere by those afflicted with thirst? || 106 ||
Furthermore, that cognition cannot belong to the mind, because it is an instrument and is insentient; if that is so, what role does the self have in this matter? (107)
If it is argued that [cognition] is produced through its connection with knowledge, why is it not postulated that it occurs in the external object?
Furthermore, by means of the mind, the quality of being a cognition would then accrue to the mind itself. (108)
"In this way a jar of such a kind exists here"—thus the self is awakened;
in this manner, the description would be similar to that of what was previously seen. (109)
If consciousness is merely this much by virtue of the description of the mind,
then how can there be an immersion into the formless through the penetration of one's own innate power? (110)
Or rather, when an object has already been perceived by that [sense organ], what is the use of [further] action by its own self?
For conjunction is the union of two things with non-distinct locations, arising from their own essential natures. (111)
Now, it is said that the object known by the mind has that same location [as the sense organ];
but if so, whose state of being a yogin is described? Or rather, [is it] from the perspective of its own essential nature? (112)
How can there be a refinement of that which is formless?
If it is argued that this very nature [of the refinement] exists within the self, whereby an adherence occurs, [we reply: 113.

What kind of mixture could there be between consciousness, which is formless, and this [object]? If it is argued that the object itself becomes the cognizable (prameya) through its distinctness from consciousness, [that too is untenable]. 114.

If it is argued that [the object] is known by the mind through the sense-organ, and that [the sense-organ] in turn through its own cause, then this is clearly a case of a blind tradition (*andhapāramparya*). (115)
What is the use of self-impulsion here, whether [the object] is known or unknown externally?
For if it is known, since its nature is that of cognition, for what reason would there be impulsion? (116)
When that [other world] is unknown, by whom is the mind impelled with the thought "go there"?
This is logically possible only through the identity of the two—the object impelled and the agent who impels. (117)
Therefore, it should be known that the Śaiva reality is established as a complete unity;
likewise, through the application of recollection, how could such a thing be recollected? (118)

Whether that which was seen possesses the state of being seen, or whether it is indeed cognition itself—it is established as possible only when the identity between the seen and the memory is maintained. (119)
p.
183) Likewise, that determination "this is that very same [object]" arises from recognition;
how can this be logical in the case of two cognitions occurring at different times? (120)
Whether there is identity or non-identity between two things, how can there be identity between two distinct entities?
If there is non-identity, the cognition "this is that very same thing" would not occur in the case of a pot and a staff. (121)
Therefore, identity is clearly established here in this transmigratory existence;
this very same principle applies to conjunction when it exists as a real entity.
Furthermore, in this regard, they are either mutually identical in form or otherwise;
therefore, there is a union of all entities precisely through their oneness.
And let this same principle apply to the bearers of the palanquin;
therefore, through the thorough knowledge of another's mind, the identity of the object of cognition [with that mind] is established. (124)
In this world, the unity of caravans, armies, forests, and so forth, exists clearly.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, characterized by the raising of objections regarding logical inconsistency, in the *Śrīśivadṛṣṭi*. 4.
Now begins the fifth chapter in the Śrīśivadṛṣṭi.
Now, if there were no commonality among all things without a single reality, then how could this unity exist when there is such differentiation? (1)
That too exists here at all times; it is described here for that purpose, just as there is equality and a single nature within all phenomena. (2)
Therefore, let it be heard that there is never any distinctness [between them];
since all things possess consciousness, by what could a distinction be stated? (3)
Even amidst distinctions, there is pervasion by that [Reality], and even amidst non-differences, unity is established;
all possessors of will are indeed pervasive and omnipresent. (4)
Likewise, all are formless; all consist of knowledge and action;
likewise, all are sources of power, and all are characterized by will and self-awareness.
All possess self-limitation and are eternally established;
all possess expansion and bliss, and are united with liberation.
If there were a diminution of desire and so forth in all things such as jars and the like,
then fire would not exist elsewhere— in another body, in a snake, or in a small lamp.
Whether due to firmness in one of little splendor or through equality with Śiva everywhere,
[this power] becomes all-pervasive in every object of will and the like.
If it is argued that there is a distinction [of Śiva] due to suffering and so forth, even in that case there is no lack of auspiciousness (aśivatā),
because even in suffering there is expansion, since one maintains fortitude for the sake of alleviating that suffering.
Bondage is seen in them, as is persistence even in insects and the like;
yet where there is union with liberation (nirvṛti), there alone Śiva-nature is manifest. || 10 ||
If it were ever appropriate to say this of those possessing consciousness, it would certainly not be fitting for material things such as the earth or a jar. (11)
In this way, consciousness does not exist in a jar; for through knowledge, one desires to act upon its own object, whereas an insentient thing lacks such cognitive awareness. (12)
How can a person, as an agent, produce knowledge that is luminous within an insentient object?
Nor is consciousness, which is non-insentient by nature, manifested by that which is insentient. (13)
How could one who is not insentient remain [inactive] due to the power of volition and desire when external success is achieved?
For agency in actions such as standing and so forth does not belong to the insentient. (14)
If agency is merely figurative, then the action itself must also be unreal. Or, if it is argued that [the self] is the "instigator," for that which is already active is what instigates. (15)
Knowing itself to be the agent, the jar performs its own action;
when its own agency is unknown, the jar does not proceed to act.

If there were no activity due to the ignorance that "this [action] is mine" or "that [result] is mine," then the worldly convention of "the bank wishes to fall" would not be established for a cow. (17)
If you claim that consciousness is known to exist in a jar and the like, how can that be?
Since there is an absence of movement, opening of the eyes, and so forth, what will you do when it is in a state of swoon? (18)
To whom, indeed, would that [consciousness] be manifested in the absence of the unfolding of the vital breaths and so forth?
However, under the doctrine of universal consciousness, the Cārvāka cannot be established here. (19)
If consciousness were present in each individual atom, it would follow that jars and other objects consist of multiple conscious entities; thus, the very discourse of atoms would be untenable. (20)
Or likewise, due to the manifestation of the Śiva-principle, or otherwise, consciousness exists in each individual [element] in an unmanifest form. (21)
Furthermore, they too possess consciousness; through the yoga of knowledge, knowledge arises within themselves by their own power regarding the Self.
For if knowledge were not produced within them concerning the Self, [they would not be conscious]. (22)
If their apprehension were to occur through Devadatta in some other way, what could Devadatta do here? [For] if the eye itself were to impel [the cognition] toward the jar. (23)
The individual soul (golaka) does not go [to another body] here, because it is non-different from power (śakti);
or rather, if there is cognition, it occurs right there, in the state of the experience of the possessor of power (śaktimat).
Because the self is all-pervasive, its presence in the body would be redundant;
or else, because it is insentient, it would require a capacity, and by that capacity, the body would become the jar.

Previously, when [the capacity] for bringing about Śakti was being examined, it was considered whether the eye was capable or not; yet, if that capacity of the eye were also to be postulated, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress. (26)
If the capacity for action were prior to the power itself, then the power would possess the status of being already potent.
Furthermore, there is no external object for the mind, nor does it have any outward extension whatsoever.
What could power do here in the pot? It would have to enter after grasping it;
yet, it is not logical that it should grasp its base, belly, and so forth. (28)
p.
187) Likewise, because it is a quality of the aspect (*ākāra*), movement is not distinct from the substance;
nor is there a cognition of that capacity by which it might make [the object] known. (29)
If there were power within [the object], even though it is perceived internally, a connection with the mind is not possible because the mind does not enter [into the object]. || 30 ||
Since you possess mastery over the senses, why do you maintain this body in vain?
If what was presented to me by the eye is now offered to the Self by the mind, then [the purpose is fulfilled]. (31)
When that [Self] is directly perceived within oneself, the word of the authoritative teacher becomes clear;
even those conceptual constructions residing in the latent impressions then come toward the mind.

If it were argued that [the self] is perceptible because it moves along with the rays of the eye, like the rays of the sun, then the reflection of objects would not be tenable for the self either. (33)
Because reflections are unreal, and because these [reflections] are formless and beyond the range of perception,
therefore a jar remains established while cognizing its own self.

If the process [of creation] occurs through that very eye due to its identity with Him, how then is it established? Likewise, is the process [established] from the emanation of Śiva, or from the Self? || 35 ||

If, by the vision of another such as a blind person, this jar does not manifest here, then is there likewise a manifestation of its Śiva-nature? Or is there a corresponding will of the jar itself? (36)
By this very same reasoning, one who possesses desire does not perform his own action if he is without desire; for this reason alone, there is liberation.
If liberation were non-existent, the manifest powers of knowledge and action would not function;
since they arise from karma, their sovereignty is thus established. (38)
(188) Through the reflective awareness of pure action, the state of acting according to one's own will is honored;
for all things, in their form as objects, possess significance through their commonality.
Furthermore, they are designated as "pervasive" because they pervade their own effects;
however, if they are not themselves perceptible, they are certainly not grasped by the eye. (40)
Because of the connection with external parts and the separation from those within,
the cognition "the cloth is grasped as a whole" would never be valid.
Omniscience [is not established] because of non-entry [into objects], due to the presence of obstructions and so forth;
nor can it be inferred in other things by virtue of having different constituent parts. (42)
And previously, no connection [of those parts] with other parts has been grasped;
therefore, they are never grasped by perception through anything else. (43)
Let this consciousness, which consists of that knowledge, be reflected upon as residing in that very place;
moreover, there is never any apprehension of others through inference.
What universal (sāmānya) is apprehended there by means of smoke that is not apprehended at all?
Since it is unapprehendable at that time, for you, the particular (viśeṣa) remains at a great distance.
In this case, the location has not been grasped according to the appearance of the column of smoke;
nor is any certainty perceived here regarding whether it is in a low or short place. (46)
In this case as well, the conceptualization that "it exists somewhere" is merely a conceptual construction, because there is no certainty that "wherever there is smoke, there is fire. (47)
There, the smoke situated in the sky does not contain even a single spark of fire;
yet the entire region pervaded by that smoke would become composed of fire. (48)
Or else, by means of the parts at its base, those [rays] too would attain upwardness in an instant;
yet the base would never be connected with them for the eye. (49)

At the time of perception, however, there can be no connection with the upper parts [of the fire], because the fire is situated at a great distance; thus, those parts that are in contact with the fire remain unperceived. (50)
Nor is fire the producer [of smoke], for it is observed only in relation to wood;
therefore, where there is a blazing fire but no wood, there is no smokiness.
If you argue that knowledge—"fire is here"—is produced by smoke because of its proximity to fire, why is there not also proximity to the hearth and other such things? (52)
Since it has been seen elsewhere, where is its perception [of fire]? From that perception, there is the perception of fire.
In this case, of what would there be the status of being the subject (dharmin), such as a mountain or the like? 53.
Since its totality is not apprehended, how can there be the status of being the subject (dharmin) when it is unperceived?
If it were perceived, then, like all pots, fire would be seen in every part of it. (54)
If it is argued that inference for oneself is not like this [involving words], then [the object] would not be established by means of words;
for one cannot point out "this is fire here" or "this is smoke" without having seen it.

How could that cognition be produced by being designated as "this"? For if it were an instrument, there would be a requirement for an agent; if it were an agent, there would be a requirement for that [instrument]. (56)
In that case, since fire is required [as a cause], its status as a producer is established;
for whatever cognition arises having a certain object, it is like the perception of that very object. (57)
Furthermore, the cognition of fire from smoke is not established as an invariable rule;
for fire produced from dry grass or birch-bark may blaze within a house that has the shape of a cave. (58)
Having produced a great smoke, you were struck by water at that very moment;
therefore, there is only reliance on smoke for you, and no attainment of fire. (59)
Therefore, when that [self] is being designated, fire should not reveal its own nature,
having perceived itself by means of itself as remaining in a state of humility.

By this very same method, the distinction between the qualifier and the qualified among the properties and so forth within the subject and other members of the opponent's inference is undoubtedly established through the [analysis of] the nature of the subvertible and so forth. (61)
Otherwise, an objection to inference is formulated by others through such examples as "of states, places, and times," and so forth. (62)
Wherever and whenever there is activity, there is a meeting;
for in that very place, due to the connection with the state of being an agent, there arises a further relationship. (63)
Furthermore, there is no deviation whatsoever in the nature of stable entities;
could the sun ever become something other than illuminating at any time or in any place? (64)
Meanings are understood through words everywhere; how, then, can there be certainty?
If the cognition of meaning arises from the *sphoṭa*, which is manifested by those [sounds], where is the final determination? (65)
Since that [person] is also visible in every respect, by whom can certainty be obtained?
If there were no activity such as eating and so forth, worldly transaction would be abolished. (66)
Since inference does not exist, the thesis and other members of the syllogism are of no use; for it cannot be constructed by others, such as cowherds with water-clocks, because it is impossible.
Smoke cannot enter a vessel that is devoid of fire;
therefore, this is merely a description devised for the purpose of making another person blind.
p.

191) As for the claim made by some that [the reason] is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatva*) because it refers to a universal (*sāmānya*), that is not a valid objection here;
for [the reason] is qualified by direction, location, and so forth, due to its application to this specific instance. (69)
Even when perception occurs, there would not be a grasping of all particularities;
for even in a perception preceded by particulars, there remains a non-particularity [of the universal] which is established through inference. (70)
Therefore, inference is not [invalidated] by the criticisms and such that have been voiced;
thus, by the principle previously stated, the self-apprehension of entities remains established. (71)
Nor can it be apprehended through the word of a reliable person, whether in its general or specific form;
for in its general form, it would incur the same refutation as that stated regarding inference, and in its specific form [it is unestablished]. (72)
Otherwise, it would follow that [the Veda] is a matter of direct perception; yet even if it were authoritative, there would still be no certainty.
Furthermore, independence is not appropriate for a word, since it exists as a constructed composition. (73)
In that case as well, there would be a dependence on a manifestor; for there is indeed a state of being dependent on another.
Nor can it be established by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) and so forth, because such [a manifestor] is not applicable to that [eternal word]. (74)

Furthermore, if intuition (*pratibhā*) is described as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it does not stand to reason, because its nature is like a "crow-and-palm" coincidence (*kākatālīya*), such as [the accidental] crossing of a horse and so forth. (75)
Even for one born on that very day, that latent impression (vāsanā) belongs to another birth;
it is either the dharma of that particular species or the nature of such knowledge.
Because the state of Śiva is all-pervasive and because he is omniscient, it follows that therefore this should be understood: everyone [realizes] their own self by means of the Self. (77)
Knowing that he remains far away—whether in heaven and the like, or in hell—and likewise knowing the established state created by Śiva through the processes of perception and so forth. (78)
(192) Because of the arising of right view through the destruction of the delusion that there is no other world,
and because of the emergence of movement from the one who holds the true vision of the soldiers of Yama; || 79 ||

If it is argued that consciousness does not arise everywhere because of the trembling of the earth or the movement of Śeṣa and others, then what other consciousness could there be for wind and so forth, given their coming and going? (80)
Because the deity is present everywhere as one's own self, it is described as being present even in insentient objects;
thus, by means of a boat or other such things, lamps and the like are seen to serve as meditative aids.

If it were well-established there in that manner because of its being established there, then the duality of the two would exist simultaneously; since this is not the case, that [duality] is unobservable.
If it is asked, "Why again is there spatial location [for that]?", [the answer is:
because all material entities, from the subtlest of the subtle onwards, exist in that manner [as having spatial extension]. (83)
If it is argued that these [atoms] are to be known only through their parts as long as they remain unperceived, then why is there no perception of atoms simply because of their corporeality? (84)

If it is argued that because of its subtlety it is invisible, untouchable, and formless, then that which is composed of those [atoms] which are themselves invisible must likewise be so; for such is the nature of a composite. (85)
Is their visibility due to aggregation? Does that cause a loss of their nature as form, or a blending of their own essences? If it is not so, then they must be immaterial.
Those which are situated at the rear therein are each formless;
for the perception of entities cannot occur otherwise than through their formlessness. (87)
It is said that for those who hold that the nature of cognition is the object itself, the apprehension of that [object] occurs because of the apprehension of that [cognition];
however, if it were not of the same nature as that, there would be no apprehension of one through the apprehension of another. (88)
p.
193) Thus, by the internalization of the powers of the senses, the common state of materiality is pervaded; for formlessness follows immediately after that.
How can there be a configuration of forms in the sky, which is eternally blue?
Phenomena exist by the will of the Self; that formlessness remains ever-present.
Whether in the world of illusion (māyīya), or in the material realm (prākṛta), or otherwise, its state of having form is precluded by its connection with formless causes. || 91 ||
Whether through connection with ignorance (avidyā), or by virtue of its nature as power (śakti), so too it applies to knowledge when it has an external form or even the form of sound. || 92 ||
For this alone is logical: that [the object] is external to the jar and so forth, because it is seen by yogins even when it has emerged from behind a wall or similar obstruction. (93)

If it is argued that the destruction of the effect [the word] occurs due to the intervention of the first syllable and so forth, then according to the method of those who know the nature of things, that very process is merely a conventional construction (prakriyā). 94.
Upon the destruction of an effect, its subsequent effects are destroyed by that [destruction];
thus, hundreds of thousands of moments arise in succession through the successive destructions of each preceding one. (95)
Likewise, regarding their production, there would be an infinite succession of moments due to the power of God’s will;
yet a single moment is not such [an infinite succession], for that would contradict God’s will.
The object of definition cannot consist of many moments because it would possess duration;
nor can it be momentary, for that [doctrine of] momentary destruction will be refuted here later on. (97)
When [Śiva] exists in some place as a dense form through his own power, so too does he abide in the state of formlessness; thus, the equality of all things is manifest. (98)
Because of his omniscience, even at that time— when he was not yet trained— an infant born on that very day swallowed milk and other substances without remainder. (99)
And because of the taking of morsels by one staying in the mother's womb, and because of the swimming of untrained living beings through the waters of a river; || 100 ||
If omniscience were [innate], would not all embodied beings be omniscient?
For indeed, everyone would be omniscient by virtue of the power of mental volition. (101)
Through a mind characterized by volition, that respective knowledge is undoubtedly attained;
and the reality of such volitions has been established previously. (102)
Or because of the suitability for grasping all entities, or due to their sequential existence;
or by means such as direct perception, or even by way of being without means. (103)

Alternatively, due to the force of various conventional designations, or because the state of omniscience is attributed [to them], all are established as omniscient by virtue of being the self-nature of all. || 104 ||
All entities exist everywhere, knowing their own self;
the pot knows through my self, or I know through the self of the pot. (105)
I know [him] as Sadāśiva, or he knows me as myself;
Yajñadatta [knows him] as Śiva, and Śiva [knows him] as Yajñadatta.
The jar knows through its own nature as Sadāśiva, and he [Sadāśiva] knows it through its own nature as a jar;
all entities are of the nature of all things, by virtue of being the essential form of everything. (107)
Everything exists here as everything, through various states of being and forms;
the nature of my own form resides in the pot, and the nature of the pot resides in me. (108)
Śiva himself remains knowing his own self through various states;
he is the manifestation of consciousness, divided into manifold distinctions, and infinite. (109)
Thus, when all things are established in universal equality, everything is thereby described as being omnipresent and having the nature of Śiva. (110)
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Equanimity," in the *Śivadṛṣṭi* composed by the venerable master Somānanda. 5.
(p. 196) Now, in the *Śrīśivadṛṣṭi*:
The Sixth Daily Lesson:
Now, there is no difference between power and the possessor of power, as in the case of substance and action;
action is established as distinct from the substance, yet it is not non-existent. (1)
Thus, in this manner, the manifold variety of the world resides within the Śaiva system as belonging to the omnipotent Possessor of Power; it does not exist, however, in other philosophical systems.
Just as the various doctrines have been conceived, such as the theories of Brahmā and others, up to the various theories of a self—let all of that be thoroughly investigated. (3)
Regarding that which is called the manifold Brahman by certain Vedāntins:
by what cause could there be such manifoldness in the one Brahman? (4)
In that manner, those [parts] are always distinct by their own nature;
they remain distinct indeed, and there is no unity prior to their state as a lump of clay.

The duality of jars and other objects does not exist because the jar and so forth persist eternally; rather, the postulation of a causal condition must be assumed, for ignorance arises from that [duality]. (6)
If entities were to exist as having attained that [nature], then for us there would be the truth of all things;
yet if there is no connection with ignorance and so forth, this is not something distinct from that.
p.
197) Other scholars of the Vedānta maintain that the Self alone attains the state of the universe because it is its material cause; yet others hold it to be of the nature of an illusion. || 8 ||

Others, however, maintain that the universe does not possess the nature of reality; likewise, there are proponents of the self (ātmavādins), as well as others who assert the existence of the elements, the individual soul, and the supreme self, and yet others who deny these.
Those who maintain the doctrine that the self is like a spark of fire declare that Brahman is that realization in which the expansion of the notion "not this" no longer proceeds.
And others, by way of being reflections, or those whom Brahmā himself assumes as his own self at the beginning of creation; from that, the establishment of difference [arises]. (11)
Thus say those who maintain that the Self is established in this way for the sake of sport;
thus spoke those who [previously] lacked awakening, whereas later Brahman becomes awakened.
If, however, there were distinctness in each body, then there would likewise be a difference consisting of worldly existence;
or else, for those for whom the analogy of the sun and its rays upon the surface of water is established. (13)
Whether it is ignorance that knows, or ignorance itself that binds the self, or whether it is that very [self]—for those Vedāntins who hold such a doctrine, [it is as follows]: 14.
Ignorance alone must be postulated as that which is connected to Brahman in all cases;
thus, the unreality of all entities is necessarily established. (15)
Furthermore, others who are experts in the Pañcarātra declare with certainty:
"Brahman exists, known by the name Vāsudeva; he alone is the Lord of the universe. (16)
Both knowledge and ignorance are established as his two means of accomplishment;
through ignorance he creates the world, and through knowledge he liberates the bound souls.
Nor is there any coloring of this [Self] by those two, because it is awakened and sovereign;
likewise, for others as well, the state of being the self of the world occurs through their own very knowledge. (18)

And ignorance does not subvert this [knowledge], because it is that very ignorance which is the means for its attainment, as stated by the Blessed One through such insights into reality as "by vigor," and so forth. (19)
For this very reason, the state of possessing the universal form (viśvarūpatva) is demonstrated in the Gītās;
the logical justification for neither of these two positions is tenable.
If ignorance were a real entity, it would be identical with knowledge;
or if it were not a real entity, that which is unreal cannot be the means for establishing what is real. (21)
Likewise, its connection with that which is of an inferior nature is contradicted;
likewise, there is the postulation of another cause for the origination of the world. (22)
If ignorance (*avidyā*) and the rest are the efficient cause (*nimitta*), then [the system] reaches equality with the Vedānta.
In the second alternative, what could its nature be here, given that it would possess such qualities as insentience (*jaḍatva*)? (23)
If one establishes a connection with knowledge, then the conception of another Lord [is unnecessary];
for the Ārhata-s, however, Jina is the God, and the souls exist individually. (24)
"Your power is not present in every body; rather, those who are awakened are identical with that [power].
Thus they say, yet even for them there is the conceptualization of a connection with ignorance.
Through the destruction of one's own ignorance, one certainly becomes an Arhat and a god;
for those for whom the god is formless and merely empty, what [meaning] is said? (26)
Even for those Sāṃkhyas who maintain the doctrine of the soul's independence, and for those who do not accept a Lord (Anīśvara),
there exists a stain called non-discrimination (aviveka) which constitutes both bondage and liberation.
(199) How can there be a distinctness of the Lord from all selves?
For the Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas, however, bondage and liberation exist as separate states. (28)
For those who maintain that the nature of the Self is always that of God by virtue of being Prakṛti, and that it is Brahman devoid of consciousness, that very state is nothing but insentience. (29)
For they say that all this [is known] through the compendium of Nārada;
yet, is this not rather the dullness of those for whom Time is the sole cause?
For those who maintain that there are six elements, there would be a lack of pervasion regarding the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth;
if, in that case, one takes the side of *cit* (consciousness), it would follow that [consciousness] is constantly perceived.
But for those who propound heaven and liberation, bondage and release are established; those Buddhists who are proponents of external objects rely upon duality. (32)
For the proponents of consciousness (Vijñānavādins), knowledge itself is real while external objects are unreal; for how could that which is unreal possibly arise from what is real? (33)
If it is asked how this can be so for those possessed by desire, its truth has already been stated; however, if [knowledge] were a causal instrument, it would entail a dependence upon an agent. (34)
If [the self] were the agent and [the intellect] mere cognition, there would be a requirement for an instrument;
if it possessed both forms, the contradiction of transition [between states] would ensue. (35)
If there were no succession [of moments], our doctrine would be established as a single, ultimate reality;
nor, on the other hand, is a nihilistic position tenable if things are subject to momentary destruction. (36)

"I know him, and he knows me"—such [reciprocal cognition] involving an agent and an instrument is not possible within a single moment of consciousness; for if there were two such [entities], there would be a destruction of the moment. (37)

The times of the division [of the body] and the grasping of time are distinct; since [the agent] has perished, whose fruit would it be? For from whence could there be a sequence between action and its fruit? (38)
If "possessing distinction" were the definition [of consciousness], there would be no such illustrative example;
for the cognition of the apprehended object and the apprehending subject appears as if it possessed distinction. (39)

And if the appearance of external objects belongs to the pure [consciousness] through ignorance in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), then no impure latent impression could ever exist within that which is pure. (40)

Prior to the operation of the eyes and other senses, there arises first a perception of the jar such as that which belongs to one who has not yet been born—that is, a desire of such a kind [as is innate]. (41)
When desire arises prior to knowledge, the conception of a knower becomes manifest;
for there is no objectless jar perceived, since the purity of the knower [is required] for apprehension. (42)
At the time of its arising, does it first know itself or the external object?
Given the diversity of appearances, how could there be simultaneous apprehension? (43)
Or, if there is a gradual determination [of the object], it must persist for another moment;
having seen that persistence, when there is complete determination, a twofold nature of the moment is then asserted. (44)
When consciousness arises, it is not considered that the object is established;
nor is there a lack of reality in the class of objects, nor is there a disregard for the apprehension of non-entities. (45)
Whether manifest or unmanifest, knowledge shines forth for him; because it is of the nature of pure awareness, it is indestructible, for reality is never perishable.
Furthermore, in the case of the light of a lamp, there is neither permanence nor agency;
rather, the lamp and such things possess the status of an instrument (karaṇatva) in the act of seeing that [light]. (47)

If it were said that the Self is luminous, immovable, and eternal, yet [requires] another to be known, then there would be an infinite regress due to the necessity of an instrument for knowledge. (48)
The lamp is the eye [of perception] because it reveals the results of successive stages; thus, it does not contradict that [thesis].
How could there be perishability in an entity without another cause? (49)
Now, since its nature is perishable, how can there be the arising of that form?
Furthermore, how can both arising and perishability exist as two such intrinsic natures? (50)
Furthermore, it is not logical for that [cause] to produce its own effect while in a state of perishing.
If it were to perish after having produced the effect, then it would have to persist for another moment. (51)
Or, if it performs its causal function, why does it not have a perishable nature? If it were produced by other causes, it would be dependent upon those other causes. (52)
It is logical that an entity produces another entity, not because it persists for a moment;
for a pot is not produced from [another] pot, even with the dependence on inherence and other such factors. (53)
Either the state of being the inherent cause belongs to that which has perished, or to a jar that has not perished;
[yet] that which has perished cannot be its agent, while that which has not perished possesses its own essential nature. (54)
Whatever exists is momentary; thus existence itself is within the range of the senses.
If it is argued that the sense organ is mistaken due to similarity, [we reply] that it is not so, provided it was previously unimpaired during the initial apprehension. (55)
For even in the case of the example, where there is similarity perceived by direct perception, the momentary nature is grasped;
yet in the series of lamp-flames, it is the flickering that is perceived, not their destruction.
Nor do the alternatives of succession or simultaneity apply to auxiliary causes,
because their power is already established when they are present, and thus many of them remain in that state simultaneously.

The non-difference of entities possessing diverse powers is like that of gold [in its various ornaments]. Their distinctness and novelty arise from the emergence of the activity of external manifestation. (58)
If being a real entity consists in the capacity for causal efficiency, then since that capacity is absent in things such as mother-of-pearl [mistaken for silver], they would lack reality;
yet, because it has already been stated [that they do possess some form of reality], they are indeed real entities.
Does the pot perish by acting upon itself, or does it perish while not acting upon itself? In either case, it remains exactly as it was.

Or what does it do then? While acting, does it not produce an entity that is either non-different or different from that jar and so forth? For if it were non-different, it would be of such a nature [as the jar]. (61)
If [the destruction] were something other [than the jar], what would happen to the jar here when another thing arises?
Whether [the destruction occurs] through itself or through another, the same [logical difficulties] apply here as well. (62)
Or perhaps these conceptual constructions perish; even so, this much alone remains. Even in that state, does one who performs some action perish in such a manner? (63)
Furthermore, conceptual constructions arise again, yet they do not function toward non-existence;
for you, it is the jar itself that is the instrument, while the causal complex is the producer. (64)
If there is perception of a non-entity that is void, how can it have a cause?
For if it were so, then even a jar, being equally void, would produce many things. (65)
It would not cause the destruction of the jar while remaining related to it, because when the jar arises from the lump of clay, that [destruction] is produced by that very [lump]. (66)
Wherever there is dependence upon another cause regarding form, it is established accordingly;
for instance, the dependence on a mallet or similar instruments in the case of a jar's perishable nature. (67)
Or rather, what is there to be destroyed such that the lump of clay would not be the producer of the jar?
If it were not destroyed, nothing at all would exist, and the jar itself would simply not be born. (68)
For when causes perish, the destruction occurs through the nature of those causes;
if it were thus that the lump of clay itself would perish, then it would indeed perish. (69)
Is that lump of clay called a "pot" after having performed some action, or not?
If it were not performed, there would be no making of the jar; if it were performed, its nature as a pot would be established. (70)
How can there be a determination of the cause for the production of a jar, given that activity [of the cause] would not occur otherwise unless its prior state had perished? (71)
In the case of contradiction, you have no example whatsoever of a staff and a jar;
for you do not accept that darkness can be destroyed by light. (72)
Since destruction is not something produced, there can be no obstruction to it for you;
nor is obstruction possible for that which is permanent, nor is it appropriate for that which is momentary. (73)
Non-existence is properly understood as being produced by such things as a skull;
for that which is real requires a cause, just as in the production of a jar or similar objects. (74)
Even regarding the nature of things as perishable or imperishable, conceptual constructions do not operate here; for those things perishable through the presence of causes do not exist at all.
Because it possesses intrinsic nature, reality remains as one; for it abides in that state, whether through difference or non-difference, it does not possess a manifold form. (76)

In that case, for you, there would be no status as inference due to the absence of a universal; yet that [inference] will exist through exclusion (apoha), and how is even that [exclusion] established? (77)
(204) Is the denotability of the word "bring the jar" achieved through the negation [of the word itself], or do you understand the jar through the exclusion (apoha) of non-jars and the like? 78.
Either emptiness is rendered meaningless within emptiness in the domain of words, or else objects such as jars and the like would simultaneously attain infinity in the world. (79)
Once the connection with the expressed meaning has ceased, there is only aversion toward the injunction;
for is "impossibility" not a general property, or is it not indeed non-specific? (80)
If even that were of the nature of a non-entity, nothing at all would have been stated.
This much alone constitutes the connection with the denotable object: that it consists of an internal radiance. (81)
Furthermore, apprehension is to be understood as having another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) as its object;
for is there not the manifestation of fire, though it is beyond the senses, through smoke by virtue of their relationship? (82)
The connection with the sense organ is imperceptible; when one is at a distance, it is inferred by means of its capacity.
Therefore, neither the absence of cognition nor the [object's] emptiness is logically tenable. || 83 ||
Since that which is empty lacks the nature of awakening, who here is awakened by what?
For there is neither awakening nor sublation of an empty thing by means of emptiness.

If emptiness exists, then a means of valid cognition is appropriate; for it is only through conventional reality that conventional reality is to be negated, since there is no connection [between them]. (85)
If that [exclusion] were empty, it would belong to that [object]; therefore, the Buddhist position is illogical.
Exclusion (apoha) is applicable elsewhere, because there is no connection between words and their referents. (86)
Because everything would possess the nature of all things, this [creation] is not tenable here;
as for what has been cited by the Buddhists, beginning with "If it were like a hide," and so forth—[87]
(205) Since all cognition exists everywhere, all of that [denied by others] has been refuted;
furthermore, even those conceptual constructions (vikalpa) asserted by the Cārvākas do not constitute a sublation.
Because it is the essence in all things, because it is non-inert everywhere, because it is the intrinsic nature of all entities, and because even non-existence is itself an existence. (89)

Because of the application of terms such as "pot" and "mat" to their respective objects, and because non-existence consists in the form of the potsherds and so forth, its status as a real entity is established. (90)
If even non-existence were a real entity, there would be no destruction of anything;
furthermore, if non-existence were produced, its attainment would not be possible.
In all entities such as earrings and the like, the nature of gold remains entirely unimpaired due to its pervasive presence;
likewise, the all-pervading Śiva-nature remains entirely unimpaired.

Since it is established that [your view] is superior to all other forms of knowledge, what will you say regarding your own doctrine, wherein diversity is proclaimed as both bondage and liberation? (93)

The impurity of the selves has been declared as their state of differentiation with respect to all objective entities; this was truly said for the sake of one who desires to ascend [to higher levels], in order to facilitate the practice of that sequence. 94.
For otherwise, if it were of a single uniform nature, doubt would arise;
moreover, without [the need for] awakening, that initial state would be effortless. (95)
Being stainless here due to the absence of bondage, liberation, and so forth, what could he do?
Nor would he require any further conviction, for it is established instantaneously by this single statement alone.
For that purpose it was said by the Lord, not with the intention of explaining the views of others:
"And how could there be a co-location of many atoms in a single place? (97)
p. 206) If, on account of being formless, there were substantiality even in that which is formless,
then in the case of substantiality, there would indeed be a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), because it conforms to various modes of existence.
That space which is pervaded by one [atom] would likewise be pervaded by others;
since they are mutually pervasive, there would be a relationship of the pervaded and the pervader between them. (99)
If another [entity] exists there, it would not be pervaded by what precedes or follows;
how then could space, cognition, mind, and so forth, abide in a single location? (100)
This fault belongs to you alone; it does not exist in us in that way, because [the self] is established as being all-pervasive within the bodies of all beings. (101)
Who can obstruct consciousness, which resides within the bodies of all?
If it is argued that [consciousness] is obstructed by actions due to their correspondence [with results], then consciousness itself cannot be obstructed by actions. (102)

Even when there is no causal connection to past actions (*akarmahetuka*), for a yogin, there is no state of being a corpse in another's body, because that body remains as the manifestation of another self. (103)
In that regard, if action were the cause, then even through yoga there would be a transition here;
at that time, a single awakening would be overwhelmed by hundreds of awakenings. (104)
If that [the individual soul] were sublated, there would be no pervasion by another, nor would there be identity with it due to non-pervasion;
furthermore, because of the multiplicity of Śivas even in liberation, there would be a plurality of leaders.
Even though he possesses supreme sovereignty, his state regarding liberation remains subject to degrees of excellence;
and even when there are many leaders, the status of being a leader is not impaired.
Likewise, because of the diversity in the fivefold activity, there would be non-action;
that stage which is unlike any other is the supreme, ultimate stage. (107)
Furthermore, why is that which is entirely similar called "conformable"?
Because, through omniscience, it conforms to the single activity of all [beings]. (108)
Because cyclic existence is not to be protected, and because of the removal of the impurities such as hatred;
or else, because of being satisfied by the supreme bliss of the manifestation of one's own self-nature. || 109 ||
Because the fivefold activity is centered upon Him, its manifestation does not occur even in liberated souls; however, that [activity] resides eternally in Śiva, who is beginningless.
If [you argue that] persistence [of the world] is due to some excess or passion, then that is a flaw;
for why would the beginningless Śiva-principle not possess its own inherent fragrance? (111)
If they possess agency even in that state, why is it not of such a nature? Or else, it is like the king who performs his royal duties with ease. (112)
Just as his own nature does not diminish, so it is likewise in the case of the supreme cause;
if that is so, then why is any distinction not prevented even in liberation? (113)
Just as it is for others, so too is it for this [self]; therefore, such faults arise due to its manifold nature. (114)
Therefore, since the state of being the one Śiva is established here, neither bondage nor liberation—nor likewise purity or impurity—is possible for that which is one. (115)
Two forms are logical; however, the simultaneous occurrence of birth and so forth would not be possible if there were a perception of anything other than Śiva who possesses such a nature. (116)
A logical flaw would follow [if you held otherwise], but such a thing never occurs here.
How could there be bondage and so forth in oneness, as you maintain for the dualists regarding the letters *ka* and the rest? || 117 ||
Just as there is a variety of different limbs belonging to a single self,
such as simultaneous binding and pain, so too is there the state of possessing various bodies. (118)
Even though there exists a diversity of forms, there is no distinction in their state of absolute isolation (kaivalya).
Therein, even a single entity may possess diverse forms, while many may possess a single form. (119)
All are established as Śivas by way of their omniscience and other attributes;
likewise, all are all-pervasive, and all are self-consciousness itself. (120)
Even in this state, no difference in name exists;
by whom has its uniformity been destroyed, even though it persists as a universal? (121)

There is no distinction in their state of being *śiva*, just as there is none among individual cows such as the brindled one (*śāvaleyādi*), despite the differences in the arrangement of form and other qualities among those individuals. (122)
There is no such distinctive feature among cows and other [animals] as there is here;
since those who are liberated are devoid of distinctions, by whom could their unity therein be prevented? (123)

Alternatively, because all effects [are produced] simultaneously, because [the Lord] is accepted as being free from envy, and because the perfection of the universe [is achieved] by that much, there is no lack of variety in his omniscience. 124.
Whether in the Śaiva system that posits a plurality of self-natures, or in the Śaiva system that maintains non-duality,
the fact that everything possesses the nature of all things and is the self of all is unimpeded.
Because it is endowed with infinite power and because it is undiminished within its own powers, the state of Śiva resides everywhere; this is especially so for the proponents of Śaivism. (126)
Therefore, through oneness, the state of Śiva, which is the range of all things, is to be known.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Non-excess of the Vision of Equality."
Now begins the seventh chapter in the Śrīśivadṛṣṭi.
Now, while the Śiva-tattva stands as the all-pervading direction, it is being discussed here;
for whether that [tattva] is known or unknown, the state of Śiva remains unimpeded. || 1 ||
Whether fire is known or unknown, does it not produce light? Is gold not gold when unknown; would it then become a stone? (2)
This is true; nevertheless, in this world, gold, as soon as it is recognized, is employed for enjoyment through its value and so forth, and for the purpose of giving. (3)
An unrecognised wish-fulfilling gem would clearly still be a wish-fulfilling gem;
nevertheless, who can prevent it from being recognized for the sake of accomplishing one's purposes and enjoying its fruits? (4)
For once gold is known, cultivation (bhāvanā) proceeds as the means [of realization], having been cognized a single time through valid cognition, scripture, or the words of the Guru. (5)
Once the state of Śiva, which resides in all things, is known through firm realization,
there is no further need for any instrument nor even for contemplation anywhere.
Even when [the tree] is known, because of the firmness of the tree, the ground, and so forth, there is no operation of the senses and such;
the cognition does not proceed toward the surface of the earth, nor is there any objective entity, nor any instrument.
Therefore, whether Śiva is unknown or known, you are indeed Śiva;
for all this [world] has fallen away from being anything other than that through the practice of such contemplation.
Although this state of affairs is thus established and understood by men, nevertheless, for the sake of the work of painting, the method must be explained with diligence. (9)
Just as fire, though recognized as being like a wish-fulfilling gem or gold—which are the causes for the clarity of that knowledge—still performs functions such as illumination; || 10 ||
Nevertheless, when applied with reason, it shines forth even more intensely within the house by means of even a single lamp,
and not so by a mass of fire.
Therefore, the means must be explained for the successful accomplishment of the visible effect;
that [means] is the first emergence of desire, which is the orientation toward action upon one's own self. (12)
Containing within itself all variegated effects in the form of a pod, it is the emergence of the arising of desire, which is devoid of liberation through the delight of its own nature. || 13 ||
The variegated manifestation (citi) of the Supreme One, which possesses the form of the other, is said to be the power of the Supreme Lord; it exists like substance and action.
Action does not exist apart from substance, nor is it non-existent;
for indeed, no effect whatsoever arises without that action.
Nor does anything proceed from substance alone;
therefore, it should be understood here in this way as being of the nature of power (śakti), possessing a differentiation of forms.
The first arising of will is the state of being the locus of the unity of all existence;
it possesses the form of pure constituent parts consisting of the nature of empowered consciousness.
(211) Delighting in the singular flavor of its own bliss, possessing a body for the sake of its own effects,
one who is thus situated either through meditation or through awakening partakes in that very nature. (18)
Its vibration is the movement of will, its precedence is the union with bliss;
it possesses the splendor of the power of both the earth and the lord of the earth, being supreme due to its absorption in the full consciousness.
He attains such pervasiveness, wherein the performance of worldly pleasures subsides; he is of the nature of tranquil bliss, pure, and has fully embraced the functions of vision and action.
Śiva has attained his arising from the abundance of consciousness that is quiescent in the midst of the void;
even for him, [his power] is unstable and non-different [from him], like the flash of lightning.
It exists as an orientation toward the knowledge of future distinctions and their functions,
possessing the intention to create through its own nature and to bestow grace upon that [creation].
The Śaiva power, which bestows the goals of Śaivism, shines forth established [within];
therefore, that very power itself consists of the primordial creative impulse (*prākkalana*) toward external effects. (23)
With her will subdued, consisting of knowledge, and possessing a body spread through vibration,
she arises as a unified manifestation whose body is fashioned from the arts of Vidyā and Mantra.
This state of Sādāśiva, which consists of the conceit of authority, is fully perceivable in the ether like the spreading of sparks of fire. (25)
Through its union with that [impurity], it becomes defiled; yet from that very source arises the sovereignty over all.
It bestows the exertion of that lamp of power, which is like a ray of light.
Then, through her gross limbs composed of mantra, she who is intent upon all ritual actions becomes,
in the form of the Lord, the embodiment of her own entire range of functions.

The power of that [Self] as well has attained universality, like a lump of clay becoming a jar; for as long as one crosses over the dense earth of ignorance, māyā, and so forth, [so long does this power expand]. (28)
In that same way, the Lord, through the power of his inherent nature, [manifests] jars and other objects;
and through the infusion of his own power, the riches of Śiva arrive.
When the supreme self consists of the power of action (kriyā-śakti), there is in some cases the nature of Piṇḍa-Śiva;
in other cases, through knowledge within the internalized state, there arises the nature of Pada-Śiva.
In the mere will, there is the state of Śiva as form within the wave;
in that which transcends it, there is the state of Śiva who transcends all objective existents within the mere agent.

Through the firm placement of the fingers, through firm and steady gazing, through the movement of the internal state as it revolves, and through leaping so that the vision remains unimpaired; || 32 ||
Through the attainment of the illusion of a mass of atoms [in the presence], even insentient things acquire consciousness;
because of the projection of universal consciousness and its resulting uniformity, such a desire arises everywhere.

But at the time of arising through dependence, this omnipresent Lord, because of his universal nature, grants the experience of creation; yet due to the firm establishment [of consciousness], there is a dissolution into formless knowledge and consciousness.
Through absorption in the application of the yoga of knowledge, the arrival of action occurs;
by means of will, grace, and splendor, there arises that agency which is the state of the Great Lord.
If consciousness were inherent in the body or its states, it would follow that consciousness possesses autonomy;
or, if there were a connection between contentment and bliss, these two would possess autonomy due to their firmness. (36)

Through attachment to suffering and through attachment to other things, there is a state of blissful cessation regarding the collection of limbs of this inert body, by means of a thought appropriate for firmness in intoxication. (37)
Through the firm rooting of the nature of all insentient objects within oneself, there arises the fullness of that realization;
for, by means of the great awakening, one's own body becomes permeated with self-identification [with the Divine]. (38)
Likewise, because it functions similarly in another body, there is a distinction of the intellect;
this is like the manifestation of the "existent effect" (satkārya) and so forth, which is beyond cultivation and has its roots eradicated.
Through the power of being intent upon the weight of each respective state, there arises the measure of the manifestation of each;
this is the great emergence from the existence of the radiant, supreme, throbbing spark of light.

The presence of the deities, their emanations, and their manifestations; clarity of meaning, face-to-face engagement, the transition to another body, and the great qualities of the scriptures. || 41 ||
There is a transition into other bodies and even a relinquishing of others, due to the movement of consciousness within the range of the sequence of the inward-turned mouth, eyes, and so forth. (42)
Through contact, there is the awakening of that [power]; the same state exists elsewhere as well.
There is firmness regarding the deity within one's own body, and the capacity to subdue the serpents and other [obstacles]. (43)
Likewise, the very contemplation of all forms is itself [the deity], through the union with the proximity of the gross [form] situated externally within one's own internal creation. || 44 ||
The greatness of the Self is to be known, as well as the infinity of creation from it;
through the non-deluded casting of one's vision upon gross existence, one attains oneness with That.
Having attained oneness with the universe, it is conceived as pervading everywhere; wherever it may be, it remains dissolved in repose within the fourfold power (śakticatuṣṭaya).
When the mind is bound from the cycle of transmigration by the medicine of the contemplation of Śiva, the entire universe is perceived as having a single essential nature.

Just as wood, walls, and other such things, when infused with mercury, attain the state of being gold, so too, through the penetration of the power of each respective *tattva*, all things become of a single form. (48)
Through stability, he fashions his own self from the states of both non-existence and existence;
within his own body, a firm power has attained mastery over the eyes and other senses.
In the same way, O Lord, by means of His own power, Śiva abides as the reality within all entities through His constant union with them, even though He appears otherwise elsewhere. || 50 ||
May auspiciousness, which is the virtuous cow of plenty that milks all desires, spread among men.
Thus, when the meaning is established, the meaning of a word is its "word-meaning-ness" (padārthatva). 51.
Because the status of being an object is equal [in both cases], the arising and ceasing of the mind occurs repeatedly;
for in all instances, one remains established in the form of reality through the absence of the mind. (52)
In essence, the expansion of the state of experience should prevail everywhere;
for the stable form of everything indeed consists of that very Self in all its aspects. 53.
In every form, the beautiful and ever-shining arrangement of the Great Form is established everywhere in unity; this firm growth is to be produced, unassailed by passion and the like. (54)
It is held that all excellence indeed originates from truth;
at its root lies the penetration of power, while in its middle stage, these two are equal.

Having understood that the penetration of the root must be accomplished, there arises a corresponding emergence through the attachment to the intellect, vision, and conviction regarding the reality of all formless things. (56)
The manifestation of disappearance arises correctly, as does the departure through devotion; this is the understanding of the great ones whose minds are free from the sense of "mine-ness. (57)
Consciousness, unimpeded, spreads in all directions when the minds of the virtuous have properly attained attachment to the sense of "mine. (58)
This entire infinite world originates from mental construction;
when one has fully realized that "all this is mine," one's existence becomes composed of that alone.
In the same way, their creation of objective existence proceeds from conceit, arising from the sense of "mine" and attachment toward each group of deities. (60)
Those divine [powers] spread forth effortlessly in every direction;
spreading forth in their entirety, they are indeed indistinguishable and absolute.

Desires pertaining to all objects of experience arise solely through the power of constant play; yet, due to the influence of entering into specific attachments and notions of "mine," they become great.
The arising of immeasurable existences through the manifestation of subtle forms occurs when the Śiva-tattva has become threefold: [as] Svaccha, Kāla, and Kalākala.
He is entirely attached to all things, yet he possesses the manifestation of various forms;
in his power, there is unbroken power, and in him there is constant wisdom and vigor.
The supreme Manu, possessing complete agency, rules over Sarasvatī;
through the absorption of the sense of "mine" regarding the objects of knowledge, he creates a new world. (65)
Through *kalana* (the act of fashioning), there arises the density of consciousness; through *vedana* (feeling), the pervasion of all consciousness;
through *sneha* (affection), the fulfillment of all desires; and from *kāla* (time), the occurrence of all seasons.
In the state of *niyama*, there is the restraint of all [faculties]; in the *pralayākala* state, there is isolation (*kaivalya*).
Indeed, for one’s own self, the objects are unobstructed, possessing unconditioned sovereignty. (67)
(216) Through the conceit of [attaining] all aspects, by one who is firmly attached with the thought "this is mine," an infinite attainment of all aspects indeed arises. 68.
This physical [transformation] is not declared by this scripture to occur through a bodily form;
rather, it is recorded in such statements as, "by water, there shall be the nature of water," and so forth. (69)
Through the pervasive contemplation of the bodies of women and others as being filled with affection, the entire world comes under one's control; how much more so a single body?
Contemplating within oneself a beautiful form with the thought "I am all," one should not think "I alone am supreme"; such would not be the method of attraction.
If one meditates upon the loathsome body of anyone while regarding me as being in all [beings],
then that person becomes hateful to me alone, and consequently, I become hated by him.
If [the mantra] is pervasive, one should contemplate one's own body wandering through the bodies of the enemies;
when they have fled mounted upon camels, the entire universe becomes eradicated. || 73 ||
"Something has pervaded my enemy's body; I shall withdraw my own.
I shall become inert"—with such a thought, death is established. (74)

When the pervasiveness [of the practice] is firmly established, by contemplating at night either the single moon or the Self arisen and streaming forth, who would not experience the nourishment of someone? (75)
Contemplating the nature of consciousness as being pervasive throughout all selves, or as residing in a single, indestructible mass, he shall become undecaying and immortal. (76)
As one meditates upon the youthful Self as a cloud above oneself from which dark nectar flows, that old age completely dissolves away.

(217) That which is called meditation (*dhyāna*) here is that by which everything is perceived in all its aspects; it is that virtuous reflection (*cintā*), possessing the eye of meditative cultivation, which sees all things. (78)
By whichever sense organ an object is perceived, in each and every case that true Śiva-nature is characterized; its meditation is likewise described. (79)
In whatever cognition the thought "I am Śiva" becomes established in the mind, that very contemplation in such a state is also declared to be meditation (dhyāna). (80)
That state in which constant renunciation is present— whether one is walking, standing, running, or even eating— is the yoga of the supreme yogi.

Whether Śiva-nature is cultivated or not cultivated, for me there is only the state of Śiva; through the firmness of always regarding [all beings] as equal to my father, mother, and so forth, I possess the state of a yogin.
Nevertheless, there is a resemblance to a treasure-chest, gold, and so forth; the reality of yoga is the manifestation of all states of being through my will, [expressed as] "I am Śiva."
Therefore, may the yoga that perceives "Śiva is everything" always abide within my mind through the continuous expansion of the stream of His powers. (84)
Recitation indeed exists even in the state of non-restraint; this recitation, arising through various forms, is always present in all things and directed toward all objects. (85)
Through practice, I am that which is here called the supreme recitation (japa);
generating volitional intentions, I abide as the sounds within the mouth.
Indeed, that is to be known as *japa*; for it is threefold, beginning with *satya*.
"There is no bondage for me, nor is there liberation for me; those two exist merely as impurities. (87)
By means of this practice, bathing is considered to be purification;
whether in suffering or in happiness, in all forms of practice. (88)
The joy of the mind that thinks "I am Śiva" is considered the supreme bath in water;
for the intellect is pure, and this world consists of that [intellect], and I am likewise of such a nature.
Thus, the ritual bath for purification has been described as the cleansing of the water of conviction;
all states of being, having the form of Śiva, are contained within the fire of Śiva. (90)
Thus I am Śiva, well-satisfied; this is the supreme Homa as it has been declared.
Whatever is not mine in this form, that is mine in another form.
Therefore, I am free from desire through this satisfaction; such is another kind of oblation.
I derive no pleasure from worship, nor do I feel any distress from non-worship. (92)
Worship is that which is always performed by worshippers without distinction;
and my worship here, in this very form, is that which exists within the self of Sadāśiva. (93)

Whether one thinks, "I am always being worshipped" in the presence of the Linga and other icons, or "the worship is performed," or "the worshipper, the act of worship, and the object of worship—all this exists as Śiva. (94)
What is the point of worshipping others with this physical body or with satisfaction?
My worship consists in sacrificing everything that is enjoyable in every possible form. (95)
Wherever I eat, I am attached to enjoyment through perception;
yet I am Śiva, absorbed in spiritual practice, and I am Śiva, even as the sacrificer.
By this very state of reality, Śiva alone is the supreme sacrifice; by whatever means, wherever, and by whomever he is worshipped here in this world. (97)
I perform this sacrifice; it is the supreme sacrifice because it is Śiva. I go to Śiva, I go as Śiva, by means of Śiva, accomplishing Śiva. (98)
"Though divided, I am indeed undivided; such is my activity as Śiva.
Śiva is the enjoyer, Śiva is the object of enjoyment, and among all things, Śiva is the means. (99)
Having enjoyed [the object], the state of Śiva arises; thus remains the nature of the enjoyer.
Śiva is the agent, Śiva is the action, and I am Śiva, consisting of the instrument. (100)
For the virtuous, Śiva alone is the state of the fruit and the operation;
what need is there for the cultivation (bhāvanā) and the instrument (karaṇa) for Śiva, who is eternally manifest? (101)
In whatever manner we are established, such is the conduct of one who is awakened;
whether it be that which is seen, that which is touched, that which is smelled, or that which is tasted. (102)

Whatever is to be heard is [perceived] as the manifestation of Śiva; it is always resorted to as Śiva-ness, whether in that which is to be understood, that which is to be grasped, that which is to be expressed, or even in pleasure and so forth. (103)
When Śiva-nature is established, one who is firmly intent upon it becomes the all-pervading Śiva;
for through the union with fortitude, that which is to be contemplated, that which is to be identified with, and that which is to be realized, [become one]. (104)
Established in pleasure, pain, and delusion, I am the supreme Śiva.
All this that has been set forth is entirely of the nature of Śiva. 105.
"Śiva is not the giver by his own intellect, nor is Śiva the enjoyer; this is known from the scriptures.
Thus has it been told in its entirety: that the entire universe arises in the form of Śiva by the command of the feet of the Great Lord, who is experienced like a dream.
By the power of realizing which, the Self—being entirely composed of auspiciousness—attains perfect expansion through every mode of being in its entirety. (106)
(220) Formerly, the secret teachings of Śiva and others resided within the cavities of the mouths of the great-souled sages; it was precisely through them that the act of grace was performed. 107.
When the Kali age had set in, when they had departed for the realm of difficult access, and when the teaching, headed by the village of Kalāpi, had been completely severed; 108.
Wandering on Mount Kailāsa, the Lord, having descended to the surface of the earth in the form of the Śrīkaṇṭha manifestation, urged [him] forward for the sake of bestowing grace.
"O Blessed One, act in such a way that the sage named Durvāsas, who is a perpetual celibate (ūrdhvaretas), does not cut off the secret [tradition] contrary to the scriptures."
Then that Blessed One, having received the command from the God of gods, exerted himself and created a mind-born son named Tryambakāditya.
He transmitted the secrets to him in their entirety;
he, for his part, then went properly to the cave named Tryambaka.
There he mentally created a son marked with that name;
having attained perfection, that son likewise leapt up into the sky.
Likewise, he was successful through the birth of a son; thus fourteen were born, until the fifteenth son, who was an expert in all the scriptures.
Once, while he was seated engaged in worldly affairs, he looked out;
then, indeed, a certain Brahmin woman [appeared] before him, who was outward-looking.
Having seen that maiden, who was endowed with auspicious marks and suitable for himself, she—charming with beauty, youth, and grace—passed from his sight. (116)
Having properly approached his wife, who practiced the same dharma, he himself entreated her father and diligently brought that Brāhmaṇī back. (117)
Born from a Brāhmaṇa marriage, he was of such a nature;
wandering about, he eventually arrived in Kaśmīra over the course of time.
He was Saṅgamāditya by name, and his son was Varṣāditya;
his son, moreover, was the venerable one known as Aruṇāditya.
From him was born one of such a nature named Ānanda;
from him I was likewise produced, being such as I am, known by the name Somānanda. (120)
I have composed this treatise titled *Śivadṛṣṭi*.
Thus, among these [works], the one called *Tryambaka* is known as *Ambā* in the local dialect.
Established through disciples, grand-disciples, and others, this Maṭhikā has flourished extensively.
Thus, this treatise has been composed by me in brief. (122)
Even when this [method] is employed, teachers are requested regarding its comprehension.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Designation of Completion."
This *Śivadṛṣṭi* is completed.
It is the work of the venerable master Somānanda, the most eminent teacher among the great Māheśvara masters.
